01 · Executive summary · the strategic proposition

Turn mandatory concentration-risk reporting into a competitive capital-allocation advantage.

The Bermuda Monetary Authority requires us to identify, group, measure and report our concentrations: to counterparties, in our investments, in our reinsurance recoverables and collateral, and in the risks we insure. We have a budget to do that. The proposal is to spend it on one governed enterprise risk-intelligence layer that produces the regulatory return as its first output, and then extends the same entities, relationships and exposures into daily underwriting, investment, retrocession, collateral, cyber, catastrophe and portfolio decisions.

Who this is written for. This blueprint is written for [Company], a Bermuda-registered general-business reinsurer, [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E] (the long-term classes apply if the entity writes life and annuity business) supervised by the BMA under the Insurance Act 1978 and the applicable Insurance (Prudential Standards) Solvency Requirement Rules; where the company is the designated insurer of a BMA-supervised insurance group, the group rules also apply. Every schedule, capital charge and filing date cited below is the one applicable to that class and must be re-checked if the class or group status changes.

The data-center map we already built is the working prototype of one module of that layer, the mega-project accumulation view. The picture is now bigger: the same discipline applied to every concentration the company carries.

The money spent satisfying the BMA is not throwaway compliance cost. It becomes the foundation of the portfolio-intelligence system that decides where the next dollar of capital goes.

Headline ranges are illustrative orders of magnitude drawn from the lever analysis in the profit section, not forecasts. Gate G1 replaces them with the company's own measured figures before any optional spend is released.

Decision requested

Approve a two-track programme on the existing compliance budget. Track A produces the 2026 year-end concentration schedules in parallel with the existing process, files the first quarterly return from the platform by 31 May 2027 and the 2027 year-end from it (Gate G1), and is never delayed by Track B. Track B, released gate by gate, extends the same data into capital, pricing, retrocession, collateral and investment decisions.

Four options were considered, from minimum compliance to everything at once; they are compared, with illustrative cost bands and what is left standing under each, in the case on one page. The recommendation is Track A now, Track B gated.

How to read this page

Pick a reading path and the sections written for you stay bright; everything else stays available but recedes. Hover any dotted term for its definition, or open the glossary. Every worked example uses illustrative numbers and says so; nothing here is company data. Every regulatory statement carries a source or a "verify" marker.

What is new in versions 3 to 5

Version 2 argued by architecture. Version 3 adds the profit case with levers, KPIs and a gated budget; rewrites the BMA section around the entity's class and the capital-charge mechanics; adds end-to-end worked examples for counterparty, collateral, affiliated reinsurance, asset look-through and hexagon accumulation; describes the data-center map that already exists; adds the operating model, the questions executives ask, and a glossary. Version 4's additions (cedent intelligence, the true-net retro waterfall, credit quality, evidence and data-rights objects) were folded in, and version 5 records two decisions: no PSOLD licence, and SEMI World Fab Forecast as an option at Gate G4. Corrections and decisions are listed in what changed.

The case on one page

The executive summary, the resolution and the options considered, why now, the assumptions register, what is deliberately out of scope, the plan against the filing calendar, and what changes for each role.

BoardCEOCFO

2.1 Executive summary: the case on one page

The Bermuda Monetary Authority requires us to file, every year and every quarter, who we are most exposed to once related companies are counted as one. We have budget to do that. This paper asks the Board to spend that budget on one governed concentration layer instead of four spreadsheets, because the same data is the input to every capital charge in the BMA formula, every retrocession and collateral decision, every investment limit and every large line we quote.

Fund Track A (mandatory, ring-fenced to the filing calendar) now; pre-approve Track B in three tranches released only on measured evidence at the gate before each (G1 releases Phase 2, G2 Phase 3, G3 Phase 4). See the resolution.
Track A: $4 to 8M over the period to the first year-end filed from the platform. Track B: $5 to 11M of optional build across three gated phases plus about $1.5 to 2.5M a year of additional vendor-data and platform run cost on top of Track A's $1 to 2M (about $3.5M a year in total with every phase live, in the illustration), each tranche cancellable at its gate (budget table).
Two certain levers (reporting cost, capital release from correctly measured charges) worth about $4.4M a year on a $2,000M capital base and paid for by the mandatory track. Six optional levers (retro and collateral cost, pricing on marginal capital, investment yield inside measured limits, quoting speed, loss avoidance, rating-agency confidence) worth about $23M a year at mid-range in the Atlantic Re illustration if all deliver, before netting the overlaps between them; the optional build pays back inside its second year at mid-range and does not pay back if only the measurement levers deliver, which is why it is gated (economics).
The data center map: 6,285 registry sites, 28,161 power plants, 212 cited power-dependency edges, a hexagon accumulation grid and a read-only Databricks deployment design. It is the prototype of the asset side of one module; it holds none of our treaty, facultative or cedent data yet (what exists).
Year-end 2026 lock is 31 December 2026, thirteen weeks from this paper's date; Track A runs the 2026 year-end schedules in parallel with the existing process, files the first quarterly return from the platform by 31 May 2027 and reaches G1 at the 2027 year-end (dated plan). If the Board wants the 2026 year-end itself filed from the platform, that is a separate decision with a stated risk.
Three tests: at 24 months, the 2027 year-end concentration, recoverables and collateral schedules filed from the platform with zero auditor or BMA data follow-ups, and a Finance-reconciled capital-charge delta from correct grouping and linked collateral; then, as each optional phase reports at its gate, the tenth of the first ten decisions taken on the platform and reproducible from its evidence.
The winning ambition eats the mandatory deadline; entity resolution is wrong; underwriters do not adopt; a vendor licence blocks the portal; a key person leaves. Each has a control, an owner and an early-warning signal in the risk register.
One executive sponsor (CFO or CRO), one product owner from Portfolio Management, one data steward, a monthly Concentration Committee chaired by the CRO. Ten to thirteen FTE during build, seven to nine in run, of which roughly four to five are new hires and the rest redeployed time (team).
Key takeaway: the Board is not asked to believe the profit ranges. It is asked to fund the measurement the regulator requires anyway, built so that the measurement can be used, and then to decide tranche by tranche on numbers Finance has reconciled.

How to read the numbers in this document. Every worked example is illustrative and runs on one invented reference company, Atlantic Re: $2,000M of available statutory capital, a $1,400M BSCR and $5,500M of invested assets, so dollar figures and percentages of capital are comparable between examples. The counterparties are invented too: the ACME Financial Group and Reinsurer XYZ carry the bank-in-four-ledgers and letter-of-credit story wherever it appears; Northbridge and Retro Re B are a second family used to show the same mechanics on a larger balance; Kestrel, Lakeshore, Beacon, Falcon and the Orion campus each name one thing only. Limits quoted in the examples are those in the limit framework. Gate G1 replaces every illustrative figure with the company's own.

2.3 Why now: three clocks are running at once

The case for one concentration layer has been true for a decade. Three things make September 2026 the moment to act, and each is a reason the Board would regret waiting.

1. The regulator is tightening the same screws, year after year

  • 2024: the Group Solvency Requirement Rules were amended (operative 31 March 2024) and the BMA published its papers on collateralised reinsurance, liquidity risk and private credit, written for the long-term sector but signalling the supervisory direction for any Bermuda balance sheet that holds private assets (see BMA minimum and lever 4).
  • 2025 year-end: every return and attachment moves to the SubmIT portal; the BSCR model carries a data-validation score the supervisor sees on every submission; a Bermuda corporate income tax schedule appears for the first time; the Class C, D and E Amendment Rules 2025 add public asset and liability disclosure from 1 January 2026 (see calendar).
  • 7 January 2026: the Insurance Amendment (No. 2) Act 2025 widens group supervision, so the question "which entities are in the group whose concentrations we report" can change by regulatory designation, not only by acquisition (see the glossary entry).

Each change raises the cost of the spreadsheet approach and lowers the cost of the platform approach, because the platform stores facts and the schedules are views on them. A regime that changes every December favours the design that absorbs change as a versioned factor table.

2. The AI build-out is creating a class of risk our models do not see

Hyperscale campuses worth billions of dollars are being built faster than any previous generation of industrial asset, most of them under construction (so the exposure is delay in start-up, not only property damage), and clustered on a small number of substations and grid nodes. The prototype's own ledger shows 1,050 MW of live interconnection-queue positions on one 345 kV node in western New York across two campuses 35 km apart that any county-level aggregation would call diversified (see the Kintigh example); the repository records 111 registry sites tagged AI, and the ERCOT figure it uses as a stand-in shows 9,042 MW of approved large load against 3,883 MW operating. The four largest cloud providers have guided to combined capital expenditure in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year (verify the current figure from their latest quarterly filings before this goes in a Board pack). Facultative submissions on these campuses arrive now, in the size and speed that Scenario J describes; the question "what else of ours is downstream of the same power" is being answered today by silence.

3. The property-catastrophe cycle has turned

Property-catastrophe reinsurance pricing peaked at the 2023 renewals and has been softening since the 1 January 2025 renewals, with broker renewal reports recording risk-adjusted rate reductions at the January and mid-year renewals of 2025 and 2026 (verify the direction and size against the latest Guy Carpenter, Aon or Gallagher Re renewal report before quoting a percentage). In a hard market a reinsurer earns its margin from rate; in a softening one it earns it from selection, from the capital each deal really consumes, and from the cost of the protection and collateral it buys. Levers 2, 3 and 4 in the profit section are worth more, not less, as rate falls; lever 1 is worth more when released capital can be redeployed at a hurdle the market still pays. The window in which a mid-size reinsurer can build this before the market forces it is the next two renewal cycles.

Key takeaway: the compliance budget arrives at the moment when the regulator's data demands, the market's margin squeeze and a new accumulation class all point at the same missing capability. Building it as spreadsheets answers the first clock and ignores the other two.

2.5 Deliberately out of scope

The programme is narrow on purpose. The items below are adjacent, sometimes tempting, and excluded. Each has a reason and, where relevant, the later paper that would bring it in.

  • Replacing any system of record. Treasury, investment accounting, the ceded-reinsurance system, the underwriting and contract systems and the claims system stay as they are. The platform ingests and governs their feeds; it never becomes the place a balance is booked (see sources of truth).
  • Building or replacing catastrophe, cyber or capital models. Verisk and CyberCube outputs are consumed and versioned; the internal capital model is called, not rebuilt. An application to the BMA for internal-model approval is a separate decision with its own governance.
  • Pricing models for individual lines. The workbench supplies marginal capital and a hurdle; the technical price of a treaty or facultative risk still comes from the actuarial pricing tools each desk uses.
  • Financial reporting. IFRS 17, US GAAP and statutory financial statements are untouched; the platform reconciles to them and feeds the CSR schedules, nothing more.
  • The cedent and broker portal (Phase 5). Deferred until General Counsel has signed the licence position for every data source and the data-use register for cedent files (see licensing).
  • Licensing PSOLD or Rapid Valuator. Verisk's ISO size-of-loss curves and ground-up loss-cost tool are not bought: the delivery route is unclear, the curves are out of sample for hyperscale campuses and fabs, and the per-risk book is priced from cedent transparency, engineering MFL, our own claims and the map (see what we do instead). Revisit trigger: if per-risk XoL on ordinary commercial property becomes a material line and cedents will not provide transparent severity work, the decision is re-opened at a gate.
  • Climate-scenario and other disclosure programmes. The same accumulation grid and event-footprint pattern could serve climate stress testing later; it is not in this budget and is not promised.
  • A general-purpose data warehouse or 'single customer view'. The canonical model has six objects; requests to add domains that are not concentration risk are refused by the product owner and escalated to the sponsor.
  • Any investment in data centers themselves. The map is a tool for insuring and reinsuring these assets; it is not a thesis about owning or financing them.
  • Long-term (life) business, unless assumption 1 in the register is false, in which case the long-term section applies and the scope is re-papered.
Key takeaway: every one of these exclusions protects the filing date. A request to add one of them is a Track B change and goes to the sponsor with its effect on Track A stated.

2.6 The plan against the calendar: which year-end we are aiming at

This paper is dated 27 September 2026. The 2026 year-end lock (groupings, ratings, collateral balances, EBS valuations as at 31 December) is thirteen weeks away, and the 2026 Capital and Solvency Return is due by 30 April 2027. That is too short to build, reconcile, audit and sign a new production process with a straight face, and too long to leave the platform untested. The mandatory track therefore runs on a three-step calendar:

DateMilestoneWhat is filed, and from whereGate or evidence
October to December 2026Phase 0: entity graph loaded from treasury, custodian, ceded-re and collateral extracts; top-50 counterparties resolved with evidence; limit register loaded; imagery and viewer decisions for the map recordedNothing yetBoard adopts the risk appetite (Phase 0 deliverable); the BMA supervisor is told, in a method conversation not a numbers conversation, that the 2026 schedules will be produced in parallel on a new platform
31 December 2026Year-end lock taken twice: the existing process and the platform snapshot, same date, same source filesn/aMapping version and source loads recorded for the parallel run
January to April 2027Parallel run: Schedules XXI, XVIII, XIXA and V(c) produced by the platform beside the existing process; every difference reconciled and explained; capital-charge before-and-after documented2026 CSR filed on 30 April 2027 from whichever figures Finance signs; the platform's schedules and the reconciliation go in the working papersG0 (new): the parallel run reconciles to the general ledger with every difference explained; entity-resolution error rate measured on a Finance sample
31 May 2027First quarterly return (ten largest unaffiliated exposures, intra-group transactions) produced from the platform, if the company files at entity levelQuarterly return, from the platformFirst live filing; auditor and BMA follow-ups counted from here
31 December 2027 lock; 30 April 2028 filing2027 year-end schedules filed from the platform2027 CSR, from the platformG1 as defined in the budget table: filed from the platform, reconciled, signed by Finance, capital-charge delta documented

The faster option, and its risk. If the Board wants the 2026 year-end itself filed from the platform, Phase 0 and 1 compress into thirteen weeks plus the four-month filing window with no parallel run. The risk is a restatement or a BMA query on a number nobody has reproduced twice. This paper does not recommend it; it records the option so that the Board chooses the slower path knowingly.

The optional gates keep their relative spacing: G2 six to nine months after G1 (late 2028 or early 2029), G3 after one full renewal season with the workbench live (the 1 June 2029 renewal at the earliest, otherwise 1 January 2030), G4 three to six months after G3, when the first large property facultative submission is matched to a canonical campus. The roadmap table and the budget table are dated to this calendar; no other calendar appears in this document.

03

One foundation, two levels of ambition

The regulatory minimum answers what we must disclose and govern; the winning system answers where the next dollar of capital earns the best risk-adjusted return.

BoardCEO

The minimum system answers: "What concentrations must we disclose, govern and hold capital against?" The winning system answers: "Where can the next dollar of capital earn the best risk-adjusted return?" Both run on the same data. The difference is who uses it, how often, and whether capital is a once-a-year calculation or a resource we manage deal by deal.

This section is written for a general-business reinsurer (BMA Class 4, 3B or 3A). A long-term reinsurer (Class C, D or E) files under the long-term instructions handbook instead, with different risk modules and schedules, but the two levels of ambition and the capital yardsticks below are the same; where the class changes the answer we write "[Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E]" and the BMA section gives the detail.

3.1 The two levels, dimension by dimension

Dimension
Regulatory minimum
Winning reinsurer
Counterparty
Top exposures, grouped to the legal parent where the schedule requires it; the ten largest asset counterparties carry an explicit capital charge
A live corporate-family graph (subsidiary, parent, global ultimate parent) plus economic interdependencies the legal tree does not show: the same bank as custodian, letter-of-credit (LOC) issuer and bond issuer, seen as one exposure
Investments
Asset values, ratings, counterparty concentration as the schedules ask for them
Issuer, parent, sector, geography, fund and look-through risk (what a fund actually holds), so a limit breach is visible before the trade, not after quarter-end
Reinsurance
Recoverables, affiliated reinsurers, collateral and the reporting fields, populated once a year and reconciled to the ledger
Gross assumed exposure → net of retrocession (what we retain) → retro recoverable (a debt each retrocessionaire owes us) → collateral and set-off (how much of that debt is secured) → residual credit exposure by counterparty group → net retained loss plus credit-risk capital
Insurance
Required natural-catastrophe and geographic reporting, aggregated to the schedule's zones
Nat cat, cyber, mega projects and cross-treaty / facultative dependencies on one grid, so two "diversified" risks that share a substation or a cloud region are counted once
Capital
BSCR computed by Finance at year-end from the schedules, and the ECR ratio restated each quarter, after the book is written
BSCR, rating-agency capital and the internal model runnable per deal, so TCL headroom is a managed resource: every quote shows the capital it consumes and the return on it
Frequency
The reporting cycle: the annual capital and solvency return, plus a quarterly financial return that for [Class 4 / 3B, or D / E] already lists the ten largest unaffiliated counterparty exposures, any linked exposures above 10% of statutory capital and surplus, and the ECR ratio
Per graph: counterparty and asset data daily; insurance positions on bind, using stored event-loss tables; full model re-run quarterly and on model version change; regulatory snapshots locked at quarter-end
User
Finance, risk and regulatory reporting
Executives, Portfolio Management, underwriting, treasury, investments and ceded reinsurance, each with their own view of the same graph
Outcome
A correct, on-time filing and an ECR ratio comfortably above the 120% Target Capital Level
Price, resize, restructure, diversify, hedge, retrocede or deliberately add risk, measured in ECR dollars: the capital each choice frees or consumes

Plain-English yardsticks used in the grid. BSCR = the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, the BMA's risk-based capital formula: factors applied to our assets, liabilities and exposures, summed with a diversification (covariance) adjustment, plus operational risk and any BMA add-on. ECR = the Enhanced Capital Requirement, the capital we must actually hold: the higher of the BSCR (or an approved internal model) and the MSM, the Minimum Solvency Margin, a statutory floor. TCL = the Target Capital Level, 120% of ECR: not a capital requirement in itself, but falling below it triggers extra reporting, enhanced monitoring and a remediation plan. ECR ratio = available statutory economic capital and surplus (the economic balance sheet measure of our capital) divided by ECR; 120% is the TCL line. [BMA-GB] [BMA-LT]

3.2 Concentration is a capital charge, not just a schedule

Why the regulatory minimum is already about money. Every dollar we concentrate in one bank, one issuer or one retrocessionaire carries an explicit extra capital charge in the Bermuda formula. Managing those concentrations actively is not compliance hygiene; it lowers the capital we must hold, which raises return on equity on the same book. Three places the general-business BSCR does this, as the instructions handbook sets out [BMA-GB]:
  • Asset concentration (D6). A concentration-risk charge applies to all exposures to our ten largest asset counterparties, on top of the ordinary market and credit charges. The tenth-largest name is a capital decision, not an accounting footnote.
  • Reinsurance credit risk (D9). The charge on our retro recoverables is reduced by a diversification adjustment of up to 40%, computed as 40% × (1 − largest net reinsurance exposure ÷ total net reinsurance exposure). One retro partner holding half our recoverables gives us half the credit; spreading the panel earns the rest.
  • Catastrophe module (D10). A 10% credit-risk charge applies to the ceded part of the catastrophe PML (probable maximum loss; in the BMA formula it is the average of the worst 1% of modelled annual outcomes, the 99% TVaR) that is not covered by collateral or other funded arrangements (collateral counts at 98% of its value). Unsecured cat recoveries cost capital; collateralised ones cost less.
The BMA section walks the factors and a ledger-to-schedule example; the counterparty section shows the collateral arithmetic; the eight profit levers are sized in the profit section. The long-term handbook has its own modules: for [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E] verify the applicable charges against the current instructions handbook.
Worked example: the reinsurance row, read left to right (illustrative)

We take risk from cedents (assumed), pass part of it on to retrocessionaires (retro), and are left holding the rest (net). The part we pass on becomes a promise from someone else to pay, so we must track who owes it, whether it is secured, and what happens if they fail. That promise is itself a concentration. All figures illustrative.

StepAmountWhat it means
Gross assumed loss (1-in-100 hurricane)$500mWhat our cedents' treaties would send us
Net of retrocession$300mWhat we keep after our retro programme responds
Retro recoverable$200mOwed to us by four retrocessionaires: A $100m, B $60m, C $25m, D $15m
Collateral and set-off$130mTrust and letter of credit balances plus premium we still owe them
Residual credit exposure by group$70m, of which A $50mUnsecured; A is also our largest bond issuer, see wrong-way risk in the counterparty section
Net retained loss plus credit-risk capital$300m + about $7m of capitalIn the catastrophe module the credit charge is 10% of the ceded PML not covered by collateral, with collateral counted at 98%: 10% × ($200m − $130m × 0.98) ≈ $7.3m. Once the loss becomes a balance-sheet recoverable, the rating-based reinsurance credit charge (D9) applies to the same $70m instead. Both are the numbers the ECR and our pricing need

The regulatory minimum reports the $200m and the collateral. The winning reinsurer prices the $70m, notices that A carries 71% of it, and either buys collateral, moves the next placement to B and C, or accepts the concentration on purpose with the capital cost written down.

3.3 What "daily" honestly means

Bank balances change daily; hurricane models do not. The right promise is that every new deal is reflected the day it is bound, using loss tables we computed in advance, and that the full model is refreshed on a fixed calendar. Promising a daily full re-run of every catastrophe model sets the CRO up to fail.

Counterparty and asset graphs

Daily. Positions, ratings, cash, collateral balances and corporate-family changes refresh overnight; a material event (a downgrade, a merger announcement) is applied intra-day.

Insurance graph

On bind and on endorsement. Each contract's stored event-loss table is added to the accumulation the day it is signed; no model is re-run for one deal.

Full model re-run

Quarterly, and whenever a vendor model version changes, so that a change in the answer can be traced to a change in the model rather than in the book.

Regulatory snapshot

Locked at quarter-end: data version, model version and ledger version recorded together, so the filed number can be reproduced a year later.

Key takeaway: the minimum and the winning system are the same graph at two cadences and two audiences. The minimum files a correct return and holds an ECR ratio above 120%; the winning reinsurer treats concentration charges, TCL headroom and the unsecured part of every retro recoverable as capital it can free or spend, deal by deal.
04

How the compliance budget becomes profit

Eight profit levers, each with a mechanism, a KPI and an owner, and a gated budget that protects the compliance deliverable while the same data starts paying for itself.

BoardCEOCFO

4.1 The thesis in one paragraph

The BMA is paying for the plumbing. The return comes from the taps we can open once it exists.

The compliance budget buys one thing the company does not have today: a single, governed answer to "who are we exposed to, through what, and how much, once related entities are counted as one". The BMA needs that answer for its schedules. The same answer is also the input to every capital charge in the Bermuda formula, to every retrocession and collateral decision Treasury makes, to every investment limit the CIO manages, and to every large line an underwriter is asked to sign. Today each of those decisions is taken on a partial, hand-assembled view, so we hold capital against risks we cannot prove we do not have, pay for collateral the regulator does not count, and quote large deals slowly. Every lever below does one of two things: it lowers the capital the formula demands for the same risk (releasing capital), or it raises the return on the capital we already hold. The mandatory work is never delayed for the optional work; the optional work is released only when the mandatory work has produced measured evidence.

The capital frame, in plain English. BSCR (Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement) is the BMA's risk-based capital formula: it charges capital for each risk we carry and gives some credit for diversification. ECR (Enhanced Capital Requirement) is the capital we must hold: the higher of the BSCR (or an approved internal model) and the statutory minimum margin. TCL (Target Capital Level) is 120% of ECR; it is not a hard requirement, but falling below it triggers extra reporting, enhanced monitoring and a remediation plan. The ECR ratio is available capital divided by ECR, and its headroom above 120% is the resource this whole document is about managing. [BMA-GB] (2024 Capital and Solvency Return Instruction Handbook for Class 4, 3B and 3A insurers, section A1.2, verified; check the current year's handbook for our class before quoting).

Rating-agency capital is a second referee. S&P's 2023 insurer capital criteria and AM Best's BCAR each run their own formula, with their own credit for collateral and diversification, and for many Bermuda reinsurers the rating agency, not the BMA, is the binding constraint on a given deal. [SP-RBC] [AMB-BCAR] (the linked paper is AM Best's Understanding BCAR for US Property/Casualty Insurers, May 2020 edition: recoverables are charged by reinsurer rating and collection pattern; trusts and letters of credit offset at most 90% of the recoverable factor; funds held offset 100% up to the recoverable. AM Best re-issues this document; substitute the current global or Bermuda-applicable BCAR criteria and check the figures before circulation.)

4.2 Where the money comes from: eight profit levers

Each lever names the mechanism, the data it needs, the KPI that proves it, the owner and an order of magnitude. Every range in this table is illustrative. It is the size of prize a mid-size reinsurer should test for, not a forecast; Gate G1 in the budget table replaces the ranges with measured numbers before any optional spend is released.

Lever and ownerMechanism (plain English)Data the lever needsKPI that proves itIllustrative range
1. Capital release from correctly measured charges
CFO CRO		The BSCR charges what we can prove. Collateral we cannot link to the reinsurer balance it secures is charged as if it did not exist; a fund we cannot look through is charged as "Equity Securities, Other Investments", the top of the ladder; five bank accounts we cannot resolve to two groups are either over-grouped (inflated concentration charge) or under-grouped (a compliance failure). The credit charge on reinsurance balances is applied to the balance net of qualifying collateral (collateral less a 2% haircut, never more than the net exposure) and then reduced by a diversification adjustment of up to 40%, which shrinks as our largest single reinsurer's share of the total grows. [BMA-GB] (C25.2 g to i, D9.9 c to d, B6.7 to B6.9, Instructions Affecting Concentration Risk a to d). The cash charge carries the same 40% diversification logic, driven by the largest single bank balance as a share of total cash (Instructions Affecting Fixed Income Investment Risk d to e), so resolving bank groups correctly moves that charge as well.Entity-resolved counterparties with control and economic interdependence links; collateral instruments linked to the obligation they secure; fund holdings with underlying positions; geocoded exposures with retrocession attachedBSCR (and BCAR / S&P capital) delta attributable to data corrections, reconciled by Finance; % of recoverables with linked qualifying collateral; % of fund assets under full look-through; ECR ratio and TCL headroom trend100 to 400 bps (basis points; 100 bps = 1%) of BSCR; credit-on-recoverables and look-through usually the largest parts

Treasurer Ceded Re		Retrocession is the reinsurance a reinsurer buys. A letter of credit is a bank's promise to pay if a reinsurer does not, and we pay an annual fee for it; funds withheld means the premium is kept as security instead of being paid over. Regulatory credit for collateral is capped at the net exposure, so any over-collateralisation is pure cost. Once every instrument is linked to the obligation it secures and to its issuer's group, Treasury can see collateral that earns no credit, LOC banks that are also our bond issuers, and which retro layer removes the most capital per dollar of ceded premium.LOC register (issuer, beneficiary, face, fee, expiry, obligation supported); trust statements; retro contracts with layer and attachment (the loss level at which a retro layer starts to pay); capital-model output per layerCollateral fee per $ of recognised collateral; $ of over-collateralisation; capital relief per $ of ceded premium by treaty; LOC-issuer concentration vs appetite5 to 15% of annual collateral cost; 2 to 5% of retro spend re-allocated, or the same relief for less premium
3. Pricing and capacity on marginal capital
CUO Portfolio Mgmt		Marginal capital is how much extra capital the whole portfolio needs if we add one deal: small when the deal diversifies us, large when it stacks on an existing peak. RORAC is the deal's expected profit divided by that marginal capital; the hurdle rate is the RORAC below which the deal destroys value. Capacity envelopes replace flat limits: an underwriter sees how much line is supportable at what price given what is already on the campus, the H3 hexagon and the cedent (the insurer that buys reinsurance from us).Treaty and fac positions with limits, attachment, premium; modelled loss by location and H3 cell; a capital model runnable per marginal deal; retro attachmentShare of premium written above hurdle RORAC; dispersion of marginal capital across the book (falling means better use of diversification); capacity utilisation by zone vs appetite1 to 3 points of combined ratio on the re-shaped segment, or 50 to 150 bps of portfolio return on equity over a renewal cycle

CIO		Issuer, group, sector and look-through limits measured on resolved entities stop two errors: phantom breaches that force sales, and hidden breaches that later force sales. Under the BMA's look-through ladder, missing data is itself charged, so yield is being paid for capital that better data would release. The BMA's 2024 papers on collateralised reinsurance, liquidity risk and private credit were written for the long-term (life and annuity) sector, but they show where supervision is heading for any Bermuda balance sheet that holds private credit: bottom-up stress testing, high-quality liquid collateral and documented liquidity evidence. Whether and when they bind a general-business reinsurer should be confirmed with the BMA relationship manager; either way, the higher-yielding private assets the CIO wants are only defensible inside a measured framework. Levers 7 and 1 arrive first because they are measurement, not behaviour change. Levers 2 and 4 are Treasury and CIO decisions that can be taken the quarter the data is trusted. Levers 3, 5 and 6 need the workbench and a full renewal cycle. Lever 8 accrues.

Against the spend

Assume the compliance budget (mandatory track) is $6M over 18 months and the optional increment is $9M of build over two years plus $3.5M per year of run cost (vendor data, platform consumption, support). These are placeholders to be confirmed by procurement.

  • If every lever delivers at mid-range: $27.4M per year at full run-rate, of which $4.4M (levers 1 and 7) belongs to the mandatory track; the $23.0M attributable to the optional increment is set against $3.5M of run cost and $9M of build. Even allowing for the ramp in the timing diagram (levers 3, 5 and 6 arrive in months 12 to 24), the optional build pays back inside its second year.
  • Sensitivity: if only levers 1 and 7 deliver (the two measurement levers), the annual value is $4.4M. That is comparable to a mandatory-only run cost of roughly $1 to 2M per year (a placeholder inside the $3.5M above, to be confirmed by procurement) but does not justify the optional increment, which is exactly why the optional tranches wait for Gate G1 evidence.
  • Sensitivity: capital release at the bottom of its range (100 bps, $14M released) halves lever 1 to $1.7M; the case then rests on levers 2, 3 and 4, all of which are decisions rather than measurements. The board should treat the case as unproven until Gates G1 and G2 have reported.
  • Sensitivity: cost of capital. At a 10% hurdle instead of 12%, lever 1 is worth $2.8M; at 15%, $4.2M. The lever is proportional to what released capital can earn, so it matters more in a hard market.

Levers 2 to 6 overlap in places (a better-priced deal and a cheaper retro layer can be the same capital), so a real plan should net them; the illustration deliberately does not, and the board should ask for the netted version at G2.

Decision this example supports: fund Track A now on the compliance budget. Commit to Phase 2 at G1 only if Finance's measured lever 1 delta is at least the bottom of the illustrative range (100 bps of BSCR, $14M released on Atlantic Re's numbers) and the collateral earning no regulatory credit is material; otherwise hold at the mandatory platform, which the measurement levers alone pay for.

The rule. No optional spend proceeds until the mandatory return is defensible: filed from the platform, reconciled to the general ledger, signed by Finance, with the capital-charge before-and-after documented. Optional tranches are released only on measured evidence at the prior gate, and each gate is a real decision with three outcomes: continue, pause, re-scope. A gate that is never allowed to say "pause" is not a gate.

4.5 KPI scorecard at 6, 12 and 24 months

Three families of KPI. Compliance KPIs prove the mandatory track. Decision KPIs prove the outputs are being used. Financial KPIs prove the levers. Targets are illustrative and should be reset at G1 with the company's baseline. Months are counted from the start of Phase 0 (October 2026) for every Track A KPI, and for a KPI that an optional phase delivers from the gate that releases that phase (Phase 2 from G1, Phase 3 from G2, Phase 4 from G3), so no optional column runs ahead of the dated plan.

4.6 What the board should ask at each gate

Before approval
Which BMA class are we, and which handbook, schedules and filing dates apply? Which capital measure binds on our biggest deals: BSCR, S&P, BCAR or the internal model? What is our ECR ratio today and how much of the headroom is trapped by data we cannot prove? Who is the single accountable sponsor?
G1: is the mandatory return defensible?
Were the year-end schedules filed from the platform and reconciled to the general ledger? What did the concentration and credit charges do, in dollars, when related entities were grouped correctly and collateral was linked? How much collateral earns no regulatory credit and what does it cost us per year? How many overrides carry evidence, an approver and effective dates? What is the entity-resolution error rate on a sample Finance checked by hand?
G2: is the balance sheet measured?
What share of fund assets is under full look-through, and what is each remaining rung of the ladder costing in capital? Has the CIO taken a limit decision on the platform, and did the limit register produce any phantom breaches? Show the netted value of levers 1 to 4 on our numbers, not the illustrative ones.
G3: are underwriters using it?
In the renewal just completed, what share of large deals were quoted with a marginal-capital and RORAC figure? What share of premium was written above hurdle? Did turnaround, hit ratio or signed line move against the baseline? Which desks refused to use the workbench and why?
G4: does the map earn its keep?
How many large property fac submissions were matched to a canonical campus automatically? How many campuses carry treaty plus fac overlap above appetite, and what was decided on each? Has counsel answered the licence question before anything is shown outside the company?
Every gate
Is the mandatory track still on the filing calendar? What is the run cost now, and which of it stops if we pause here? Who left the team since the last gate?

4.7 How this fails

A candid list. Each of these has sunk a comparable programme somewhere. The controls are the ones a board can actually check.

  • Data quality at source. Ceded-reinsurance, treasury and investment systems carry names, not identities; if the feeds are not fixed at source the graph resolves garbage faster. Control: data owners named per domain, a quality score per feed reported at every gate, and no filed number without a passing score.
  • Entity resolution accuracy. A false merge creates a phantom concentration (trapped capital, or a regulatory finding if it hides under-grouping elsewhere); a false split creates a compliance failure. Control: every grouping and override carries evidence, approver and effective dates; Finance samples the top groups by hand before filing; the error rate is a G1 KPI.
  • Adoption by underwriters. A capacity workbench nobody opens produces no lever 3, 5 or 6. Control: capacity envelopes embedded in the underwriting authority framework, not offered beside it; a pilot desk chosen with the CUO; G3 measures use, not availability.
  • Vendor licence limits. D&B redistribution terms, Regrid per-record billing, CyberCube scope and the ODbL share-alike question on OSM-derived map geometry each constrain what can be shown to whom. Control: a licence register maintained from Phase 0; counsel's answer required before Phase 5; caching rules enforced in the pipeline.
  • Over-building. The "winning" ambition eats the mandatory deadline: three graphs built in parallel and none filed. Control: Track A ring-fenced and dated to the filing calendar; Track B cannot borrow Track A people; the gate can say pause.
  • Model risk in marginal-capital numbers. A RORAC computed from an unvalidated capital run misprices real deals. Control: model validation and version lineage (see #governance) before any RORAC reaches an underwriter; marginal capital labelled as such and never confused with allocated capital.
  • Key-person dependency. One engineer holds the entity graph in their head. Control: a named data steward and deputy; the override workflow documented; the question asked at every gate.
  • Ranges mistaken for forecasts. The illustrative numbers in this section are quoted back as commitments. Control: this document says "illustrative" on every one, and G1 replaces them with measured figures before anyone is held to them.
Key takeaway: the compliance budget is spent either way. Spent on spreadsheets, it produces a filing and nothing else. Spent on one governed concentration layer, it produces the same filing, a measured capital-charge delta, and the evidence the board needs to decide whether to fund the levers that make the company a more profitable reinsurer. The board is not being asked to believe the ranges; it is being asked to fund the measurement and then decide.

After tax. Bermuda's corporate income tax applies at 15% from 1 January 2025 to in-scope groups (confirm scope with Tax; the 2025 CSR carries a CIT schedule, see calendar). If the company is in scope, the mid-range annual value of $27.4M is about $23.3M after tax, and the return on capital moves from 18.2% to about 19.4% rather than 19.6%; the build and run costs are deductible on the same basis, so the payback period is essentially unchanged. The ranking of levers does not move. Gate G2's netted value estimate should be presented after tax.

05

Target architecture at a glance

One reinsurer-owned knowledge graph and concentration engine, fed by internal systems of record and licensed external data, serving the regulator and daily decisions from the same facts.

DataCRO

The centre of the proposal is not a single vendor product. It is a reinsurer-owned knowledge graph and concentration engine that connects data from many systems and external sources. Three graphs feed one engine; the engine feeds stress, capital and limits; those feed Portfolio Management and, from there, underwriting and capital actions.

5.1 The three graphs, in one sentence each

  • Counterparty graph: who we are exposed to, resolved to the global ultimate parent (the top of the ownership chain) and joined by economic interdependence, so that "ACME Bank" as custodian in the treasury system, as letter-of-credit (LOC) issuer in the ceded-reinsurance system and as bond issuer in the investment system is one node with one limit. Example (illustrative): treasury, investments, ceded reinsurance and receivables each show a different ACME legal entity, none large on its own; the graph shows ACME Group at $155m direct ($70m of cash at two entities, $65m of bonds held through three funds, a $20m receivable) plus $120m of letters of credit ACME has issued to secure our recoverables, $275m in all, which is what the ten-largest test and our limit are measured against (worked in the counterparty section).
  • Asset graph: what we own and what we insure, from securities and funds through collateral to physical places (parcels, buildings, mega projects), so that a security can be looked through to its issuer and a risk can be placed on a map. Example: a $2bn data-center campus appears once, with its substation, its water utility and its operator's parent, whether it arrived through a facultative bond, a property treaty or a corporate bond (illustrative; the issuer look-through side is worked in the asset-concentration examples and the substation and water-utility links already exist in the data-center map, its subsection).
  • Insurance graph: the cedents, treaties, facultative certificates, claims and their shared dependencies, so that accumulation is computed across contracts rather than per contract. Example: three treaties from three cedents each write "a data center in Loudoun County"; the graph puts them in the same H3 cell (a hexagon on a global grid) behind the same substation and counts them as one clash (illustrative; the hexagon accumulation method is worked in the insurance-accumulation section).

5.2 One branch of the asset graph already exists

The mega-project branch of the asset graph is not a proposal. It is the data-center map prototype in this repository (dcmap), built on MapLibre (an open-source map renderer) with a self-hosted PMTiles basemap (a single-file tile archive, no tile server) and h3-js (Uber's JavaScript library for the H3 hexagonal grid) for aggregation [MAPLIBRE] [PMTILES] [H3-JS]. It holds 6,262 distinct sites with a corrected-coordinate ledger, and a power-dependency ledger of 212 edges: 170 of them link sites to 127 named substations and each cites the NYISO interconnection-queue entry or PJM TEAC filing it came from; the other 42 link sites to co-located power plants and cite a press report or a utility-commission docket. The map draws those dependencies as lines. That ledger is the working implementation of the "supplies power" relationship the enterprise graph needs. One edge from the prototype: a 525.5 MW Crusoe AI campus in Texas is net-metered behind the 265.5 MW Goodnight 1 wind farm under PUCT dockets 58881 and 59220, with full-campus curtailment within 30 minutes in an ERCOT emergency; that is a power dependency no treaty schedule would show. The data-center-map subsection of the insurance section gives the full inventory with measured numbers, the licensing constraints, and the Databricks path already designed.

The enterprise step is a join, not a rebuild: attach cedent, treaty and facultative data to the sites that already exist, so that each hexagon on the map carries our aggregate limit, our net retention and our retro recoverable as well as the megawatts. Two constraints from the prototype shape that step. First, scale: MapLibre fails silently at roughly 189,000 vertices in one in-browser data source, and the prototype already hit it with 19,367 building footprints, so cedent location files with hundreds of thousands of risks must be served zoom-banded, H3 hexagons at country and world zoom, viewport-clipped dots at metro zoom, exactly as the Databricks design specifies. The hexagon view is therefore the executive view by necessity, not decoration. Second, data rights: most of the registry is under the ODbL share-alike licence and several layers are licensed for internal use only, so any cedent or broker portal must be able to withhold layers; the operating-model section carries the data-rights register and the counsel decision that gates external access.

Design principle: every regulatory data record should become a reusable node, edge or fact in the enterprise graph. Do not create a dead-end BMA spreadsheet architecture. The test for each schedule field is: which node or edge does it come from, and which other decision reuses that node or edge?

Owned, not bought

Vendors supply data (ratings, corporate hierarchies, cat models, parcels) and tools (the lakehouse, the map). The graph, its identifiers and the limit framework are ours; they are what the BMA audits and what the underwriter prices from.

One identifier per thing

Each counterparty carries its LEI (Legal Entity Identifier, the global company ID used in financial reporting) or D-U-N-S number, each site a stable site id, each contract its policy number, so that a schedule row and an underwriting screen point at the same record.

Versioned by construction

Data, model and ledger versions are stamped on every output. A regulatory snapshot is a set of version numbers, and a decision made on Tuesday can be reproduced with Tuesday's graph.

Key takeaway: three graphs, one engine, one set of identifiers. The mega-project branch is already running as the data-center map; the enterprise programme joins cedent, treaty and facultative data to it and extends the same pattern to counterparties and investments, with the same versioning and the same licence discipline.
06

What the BMA minimum is trying to accomplish

Which return and schedules apply depends on the entity's class; the standard formula charges concentration and counterparty default, which is exactly where compliance data meets capital.

CFOCRO

The BMA is not asking for a spreadsheet of big names. It is asking four precise questions about who could hurt us, and it charges capital on the answers. Get the questions right and the same data becomes the first honest measurement of where our capital is being spent.

Read this first: which return, which schedules, which capital factors and which filing dates apply all depend on the company's BMA registration class. This blueprint assumes a general-business reinsurer (Class 4, 3B or 3A). If the company, or any entity in the group, is a long-term (life or annuity) insurer (Class C, D or E), the long-term rulebook applies to that entity and the items marked below must be re-checked. Confirm the class against the table below (#bma-class) before anything else. CFO CRO

6.1 The class decides the rulebook

Bermuda regulates property-casualty reinsurers and life reinsurers under different Prudential Standard Rules, with different balance-sheet forms, different schedule sets and different capital factors. The schedule numbers overlap between the two rulebooks (both have a "Schedule XXI"), which is why citing the wrong handbook is easy to do and expensive to discover in April.

6.2 Four places, four different questions

It is tempting to assume that one schedule (Schedule XXI) collects every concentration. It does not. The general-business return asks for concentration information in four places, and each has a different scope, a different valuation basis and a different capital consequence. [BMA-GB]

WhereThe question in plain EnglishWhat goes inWhat does NOT go inCapital consequence

The Cat Return (Schedule X, handbook C19) is a fifth concentration view for natural catastrophe: it is covered in #insurance, and its own credit charge on ceded catastrophe recoveries is noted below.

6.3 What the BMA is trying to see, and why

Large counterparties

A reinsurer fails in one of two ways: a loss event bigger than its capital, or a debtor that does not pay. The ten-largest lists exist to show the second route. The regulator wants the name, the amount, the rating and the type, so it can judge whether one failure could breach the ECR, the Enhanced Capital Requirement, which is the minimum capital the BMA requires the company to hold.

Related and connected parties, grouped

Ten $50M exposures to ten subsidiaries of one bank is one $500M exposure. The BMA requires related or connected entities to be treated as one counterparty under two tests, described in the next block. The point is to stop a concentration hiding behind legal-entity names.

Intra-group exposure

Reinsurance ceded to an affiliate does not move risk out of the group; it moves it around. The BMA asks for every intra-group reinsurance and retrocession arrangement, gross and net, so it can see whether the entity it supervises is really protected or merely re-labelled. See #affiliated.

Recoverables by rating and collateral

A recoverable is a promise from another reinsurer to pay part of our claims. Its value depends on the promisor's rating and on whether it is secured. Schedule XVIII forces both to be stated per reinsurer, which is what makes the credit charge computable.

Investment concentration

Bonds, equities and funds are where a reinsurer's capital actually sits. Schedule XXI, valued on the Economic Balance Sheet and looked through to underlying holdings, shows whether that capital is spread or stacked on a few issuers. See #assets.

Catastrophe accumulation

The Cat Return shows the net probable maximum loss after retrocession, the reliance on vendor models, and the liquidity needed to pay a catastrophe quickly. It is the regulator's window on whether our biggest event is smaller than our capital. See #insurance.

The grouping rule, in the regulator's words

For Schedule XXI, and for the concentration charge, a single counterparty includes all related or connected counterparties captured by either of two tests: a control relationship (one entity directly or indirectly controls the other; the general-business Schedule XXI instruction C31.2b(a) reads "majority shareholding in or significant influence", while the concentration-charge instruction reads "majority shareholding or effective management", so a 20% to 50% associate can be caught even where Basel would not group it) and economic interdependence (if one entity ran into funding or repayment trouble, the others would be likely to as well). The general-business handbook states both tests in C31.2 and, with the word "either", in C31.2b, and repeats them in the concentration-risk instructions (D6); the same wording appears in the long-term handbook and the Group Rules. [BMA-GB]

Executives should know where the wording comes from. It is borrowed almost word for word from the Basel Committee's large-exposures standard for banks (LEX10.10), which is why a bank-grade corporate-family graph, not a name-matching macro, is the right tool. One difference matters: the Basel text tells a bank when it must investigate interdependence (LEX10.18: exposures above 5% of Tier 1 capital, a bank's core equity); the BMA text has no numeric trigger. We should set our own investigation trigger, for example any single counterparty above 5% of statutory capital and surplus, inside the 7.5% amber limit in the limit framework. [BIS-LEX]

Worked example: two tests, one family (illustrative)

Control. ACME Bank NA, ACME Funding LLC and ACME Asset Management LLC are all majority-owned by ACME Financial Group. Our cash at the bank, our bonds issued by the funding arm and the ACME paper inside an ACME-managed fund are one counterparty on Schedule XXI.

Economic interdependence. Coastal Funding Trust is not owned by ACME, but its only source of repayment is a liquidity line guaranteed by ACME Bank. If ACME Bank cannot fund, Coastal cannot repay. Coastal joins the ACME counterparty even though no ownership link exists.

What the regulator wants to avoid. ACME appearing four times in the top forty and never once in the top ten.

Decision: record ACME and Coastal as one counterparty on Schedule XXI, attach the ownership records and the guarantee as the grouping evidence, and have the CRO approve the economic-interdependence link before groupings are locked at 31 December. CRO

6.4 Where the capital actually moves

The profit thesis of this document rests on a simple fact: the BMA standard formula charges capital on the same counterparty and collateral data it asks us to file. Two charges are driven directly by that data. Factors below are those in the Class 4 and 3B Rules as amended in 2024 and the Group Rules; long-term insurers use the Class C, D and E Rules, whose factors should be confirmed from that rulebook. [BMA-C4-24] [BMA-GR]

1. Concentration charge (Schedule XXI, handbook D6, Rules Table 5A)

Every dollar of exposure to the ten largest grouped counterparties attracts an extra charge, in addition to the ordinary market and credit charges, at a factor set by asset class and BSCR rating (a scale from 0, the strongest, to 8, unrated or weakest). Selected factors: cash 0% (rating 0) rising to 9% (rating 8); corporate and sovereign bonds 0.4% (rating 1, AAA), 0.8% (AA), 1.5% (A), 3.0% (BBB), 8% (BB), up to 35%; letters of credit recorded as our own asset on Form 1EBS line 14(d) 20% (not letters of credit held as collateral against recoverables, which never enter Schedule XXI); listed equity in developed markets 35%; other equities 45%; strategic holdings 20%; infrastructure 25%; advances to affiliates 5%; real estate 10% to 20%; collateral loans 5%. Look-through applies. A wrongly grouped family understates the charge (a regulatory finding) or overstates it (trapped capital).

2. Reinsurance credit charge (Schedule XVIII, handbook D9, Rules Table 8)

Reinsurance balances (receivable plus recoverable, the greater of current and projected) are charged on net qualifying exposure: gross balance, less payables with a contractual right of set-off, less qualifying collateral. Factors by BSCR rating: 0% (rating 0), 0.7% (1, AAA), 1.5% (2, AA), 3.5% (3, A), 7.0% (4, BBB), 12% (5), 20% (6), 17% (7, as printed in the Rules), 35% (8, including unrated reinsurers that fail the PCR test below; unrated reinsurers that meet it are rated 4). The total is then reduced by a diversification credit equal to 40% multiplied by (1 minus the largest single reinsurer's share of total net reinsurance exposure). Spreading retrocession across more reinsurers is worth up to 40% of the charge.

How collateral reduces the charge (handbook C25.2, verified)

  • Qualifying collateral is the collateral placed in our favour less a 2% reduction for the market risk of the collateral assets, and can never exceed the net exposure (balance less set-off payables). Over-collateralising one reinsurer does not help another.
  • The BSCR rating applied is the higher of the reinsurer's rating and the letter-of-credit issuer's rating; where the LOC covers only part of the exposure, the exposure is split into the covered and uncovered parts and each takes its own rating.
  • A domestic (Bermuda) affiliate reinsurer is rated 0 regardless of its credit rating, so an internal cession carries no entity-level credit charge. That is precisely why the group view must look through it (#affiliated).
  • An unrated reinsurer that meets its prescribed capital requirement in a jurisdiction applying the IAIS core principles is rated 4; otherwise 8. A single consolidated residual line is rated 8.
  • Funds withheld where specific assets are allocated to us and we bear their market risk are not credit exposure at all: they are reported on Schedule IIA and charged as investments we hold, looked through.
  • In the catastrophe module, ceded catastrophe recoveries that are not funded carry a separate credit charge; both the Class 4/3B handbook (D10.5, CRPML) and the Group Rules (paragraph 37) apply 10% to gross PML less net PML less funded arrangements, with the same 2% collateral reduction. [BMA-GR]
Worked example: one letter of credit, one line of the ECR (illustrative, simplified)

Reinsurer XYZ, rated BBB (BSCR rating 4), owes us $180M of recoverables. We owe XYZ $10M with a contractual right of set-off. Net exposure is $170M.

Without collateral: $170M at 7.0% = $11.9M of required capital before the diversification credit.

With a $120M letter of credit from ACME Bank, rated A (BSCR rating 3): qualifying collateral is $120M less 2% = $117.6M (below the $170M cap, so all of it counts). Net qualifying exposure falls to $170M minus $117.6M = $52.4M. The $50M not covered by the LOC stays at XYZ's 7.0% ($3.5M); the $2.4M haircut remainder of the covered portion takes the higher of the two ratings, ACME's 3.5% ($0.08M). Charge: about $3.6M. Capital released: about $8.3M on one reinsurer, before the diversification credit moves as well.

The wrinkle that matters: an ACME downgrade does not by itself remove the collateral. The 2% haircut and the cap at net exposure in handbook C25.2(g) do not depend on the issuer's rating, so under the BSCR a downgrade only moves the covered $2.4M remainder to XYZ's 7.0% (about $0.08M more). The $8.3M comes back if the downgrade breaches the letter-of-credit eligibility clause in the retro wording (or a U.S. cedent's credit-for-reinsurance rules) and ACME's LOC is cancelled before a replacement is posted: the exposure is then uncollateralised again at $11.9M. The same bank may also be our largest cash counterparty on Schedule XXI. Choosing which reinsurer, which bank and how much collateral is a capital decision. Decision: keep the ACME LOC, add a downgrade-replacement trigger to the retro wording so XYZ must substitute collateral if ACME falls below A-, and set one combined limit on ACME across cash, bonds and LOCs (the 25% collateral-provider limit and the 7.5% amber line in the limit framework) so a single downgrade cannot hit three schedules on the same day. Ceded Re Treasury

The interaction between the collateral deduction (C25.2 g to h) and the rating split (C25.2 i) as implemented in the BSCR model should be confirmed in the 2025 model before these figures are used for a real filing.

The yardsticks, in one line. The return computes the ECR, the higher of the BSCR (or an approved internal model) and the MSM (Minimum Solvency Margin, the legal floor); the TCL (Target Capital Level) is 120% of the ECR, and although "not a capital requirement per se", holding less triggers extra reporting, enhanced monitoring and a remediation plan (handbook A1.1 to A1.2, D1.13 to D1.14). Every capital effect in this document is measured in ECR dollars and ECR-ratio points. [BMA-GB]

6.5 Compliance calendar

A naive flow runs every source into one grouping step and one package. The flow below has two regulatory lanes that share one entity graph, plus the catastrophe lane described in #insurance. 6.7 What is the minimum data needed?

The table lists each data domain with the column that is usually missing from a compliance plan: which BMA schedule it feeds. Two capital denominators are in play and must not be blurred: the 10% materiality test in Schedule V(c) and the quarterly return is against statutory capital and surplus (at group level, 5% of available capital and surplus for a single intra-group transaction and 10% for a linked series); Schedule XXI and the concentration charge are on EBS asset values, reported unconsolidated for the entity and consolidated for the group.

6.8 From ledgers to the regulatory concentration table

Worked example: Atlantic Re and the ACME family (illustrative; all figures invented, $ millions)

Atlantic Re, the reference company used throughout this document, has statutory capital and surplus of $2,000M, so the Schedule V(c) materiality line is $200M. Five ledgers hold five things that involve the ACME family and one reinsurer that uses an ACME bank; the cash, bonds, LOC and recoverable are the ones Scenario A and collateral concentration use, and the fund look-through and the Coastal notes are what the minimum did not show.

1. Collect the raw records
Treasury: $70M cash at "ACME BK NA". Custodian: $65M bonds, issuer "ACME Funding". Fund administrator: $250M in a credit fund, of which look-through shows $25M of ACME paper. Collateral system: $120M LOC issued by "ACME Bank London" in our favour, securing Reinsurer XYZ. Ceded system: $180M recoverable from Reinsurer XYZ (BBB), $10M payable to XYZ with contractual set-off.
2. Resolve to legal entities
Three spellings of ACME Bank become one legal entity identifier. ACME Funding and ACME Asset Management resolve to their own entities. Reinsurer XYZ resolves to its Bermuda legal entity, not the group name.
3. Apply the grouping tests
Control: ACME Bank NA, ACME Bank London, ACME Funding LLC and ACME Asset Management share a majority parent, ACME Financial Group: one counterparty. Economic interdependence: Coastal Funding Trust (we hold $15M of its notes) repays only from an ACME-guaranteed line: joins the ACME counterparty. Reinsurer XYZ is unrelated to ACME: separate counterparty.
4. Build Schedule XXI (assets only, EBS values)
ACME counterparty = $70M cash + $65M bonds + $25M look-through + $15M Coastal notes = $175M, in four lines by asset type and rating. The $120M LOC is not our asset and is excluded here. XYZ's recoverable is excluded here. Rank against the other nine largest asset families.
5. Build Schedule XVIII (reinsurers)
Reinsurer XYZ: balance $180M, set-off payables $10M, collateral $120M, qualifying collateral $117.6M, net qualifying exposure $52.4M, rating split between BBB (uncovered) and ACME's A (covered). Rank against the other nine largest reinsurers.
6. Build Schedule V(c) (everything, unaffiliated)
ACME: $175M of assets plus $120M of LOC dependency = $295M across five records (cash, bonds, look-through fund holding, notes, letter of credit), above the $200M line. Reinsurer XYZ: $180M recoverable, below the 10% line on its own but listed because it ranks in the ten largest. Both listed with name, value, location and transaction type; both repeat in the quarterly return.
7. Rank against capital and charge it
ACME is 14.8% of statutory capital and surplus on the V(c) basis and 8.8% on the Schedule XXI basis. Concentration charge on Schedule XXI, assuming ACME ranks in our ten largest and every ACME instrument including the Coastal notes is A-rated (BSCR rating 3): cash $70M at 0.3% ($0.21M) plus bonds and notes $105M at 1.5% ($1.58M) = about $1.8M (Table 5A factors). Credit charge on XYZ: about $3.6M with the LOC, $11.9M without (see above). Both figures flow to the ECR.
8. Reconcile and evidence
Schedule XXI totals tie to Form 1EBS asset lines; Schedule XVIII ties to lines 11(e), 12(c), 17(c); Schedule V(c) names match both. Every amount drills to the ledger record, the entity mapping, the grouping evidence and the approver.

What the minimum did not tell us, and the winning system does: that ACME is simultaneously our largest cash bank, a top-ten issuer and the bank behind $120M of our reinsurance security, so an ACME downgrade would hit Schedule XXI, Schedule XVIII and our liquidity on the same day. That is wrong-way risk, and it is the subject of collateral concentration and the scenarios.

Decision for the board: ACME sits above the 10% line on Schedule V(c) and above the 7.5% amber line in the limit framework, so management records one of three answers before the return is filed: cap cash held at ACME, move part of the XYZ security from the ACME LOC into a trust, or accept the exposure with a written rationale the Risk Committee has approved. Board Treasury

6.9 What auditors and the BMA will ask

  • Class and rulebook. Which class is the entity, which Rules and which year-end handbook edition did you use, and can you show the version of the BSCR model you filed on?
  • Completeness. How do you know the ten largest are the ten largest? Show the full ranked list, not just the top ten, and the cut-off logic.
  • Grouping evidence. For each grouped counterparty, what is the evidence of control (ownership records, source and date) or economic interdependence (guarantee, funding dependency), and who approved the grouping?
  • Look-through. Which funds, CLOs (pooled corporate-loan vehicles) and ABS (asset-backed securities) were looked through, at what date, from which administrator files, and what was left un-looked-through and why?
  • Valuation basis. Are Schedule XXI amounts on the EBS basis and unconsolidated, and do they reconcile to Form 1EBS line by line?
  • Set-off and collateral. For every payable netted on Schedule XVIII, show the contractual right of set-off. For every collateral amount, show the instrument, the obligation it secures, the 2% reduction and the cap at net exposure.
  • Ratings. Which agency rating was used for each reinsurer and each LOC issuer, as at what date, and is it a financial-strength rating as the handbook requires?
  • Affiliates. Which reinsurers were rated 0 as domestic affiliates; which unrated reinsurers were rated 4 versus 8, and on what evidence of their home-regime capital?
  • Intra-group. Is every intra-group reinsurance and retrocession arrangement listed, with gross and net limits by rating, premium flows and the internal share, and does the quarterly list agree with the annual one?
  • Consistency across schedules. Do the names on Schedule V(c) agree with Schedule XXI and XVIII, and does the 10% test use statutory capital and surplus rather than an EBS figure?
  • Materiality above 10%. For any exposure or linked series above 10% of statutory capital and surplus, what did management and the board decide to do about it?
  • Lineage and retention. Can each filed number be traced to its source records, mapping, model version and approver, and are workings retained and producible on request (the handbook expects work papers to be kept available for examination)?
  • Attestation. Do the two directors and the CRO or CFO who sign the CSR declaration, and the CEO who signs the published FCR, have a view of the evidence behind the concentration figures before they sign?
Key takeaway: the minimum is four schedules, two capital charges and a calendar. Building it as four spreadsheets satisfies April; building it as one counterparty graph with legal-entity identity, grouping evidence, collateral direction and look-through produces the same schedules and, as a by-product, the first accurate measurement of how much ECR each bank, issuer and reinsurer costs us. That measurement is the starting point for every profit lever in #profit: it is the same data, filed once and then used every day.

6.10 If the group also writes long-term business: what changes, and what matters more

This blueprint is written for a general-business (property and casualty) reinsurer. If any entity in the BMA-supervised group is a Class C, D or E long-term insurer, three things change and one thing becomes more important. Everything below should be confirmed against the current Long-Term Instructions Handbook and the Class C, D and E Rules by the Head of Regulatory Reporting before it is relied on.

What changes

  • The rulebook, the balance sheet and the schedules. The long-term entity files on Form 4EBS under the Class C, D and E Solvency Requirement Rules, using the Long-Term handbook. Both handbooks have a Schedule XXI, but the section numbers, the cash schedule numbering (XIX at C16 and XIXA at C27 in the long-term handbook) and the factor tables differ, so the Gold tables that produce the schedules carry a class attribute and a rulebook version, and never assume the general-business layout.
  • The 2024 enhancements. The BMA's changes to the long-term regime (operative 31 March 2024, verify) reworked the scenario-based approach for asset-intensive business, added lapse and liquidity requirements and the LLSBA template, and were followed by the 2024 papers on collateralised reinsurance, liquidity risk and private credit. For a long-term entity those papers are not indicative, as they are for a Class 4 reinsurer in lever 4; they are the supervisory expectation.
  • Prior approvals and disclosures. New or modified block reinsurance transactions need prior BMA approval (see the glossary); the Class C, D and E Amendment Rules 2025 add an asset and liability statement and public disclosure from the 2025 year-end (see calendar). Both need the affiliated-reinsurance register and the asset graph to be current, not annual.

What matters more

A life reinsurer's risk is on the asset side. Its BSCR is dominated by market and credit charges rather than the catastrophe module, its largest exposures are issuers, fund managers and sponsors rather than cedents, and its growth since 2020 has come from affiliated and third-party cessions of US annuity and life reserves, often on a funds-withheld or modified-coinsurance basis (the cedent keeps the assets and we take the investment and insurance risk on them). Three consequences for this programme:

  • The counterparty and asset graphs are the whole game. Schedule XXI look-through, issuer and sponsor grouping, and the private-credit ladder in Scenario I are first-order capital numbers for a long-term entity, not second-order. Assets managed by an affiliate of the group, or by an affiliate of the cedent, raise the economic-interdependence question at the manager level as well as the issuer level, and the override workflow must be able to record that.
  • Affiliated reinsurance is the supervisor's first question. The group view in worked example 5 (who really carries the risk, what is locked in trust, whether capital can move) is what the BMA and the US cedent's regulator both ask of a Bermuda life reinsurer. US state regulators have added their own test: the NAIC's asset adequacy testing guideline for ceded reinsurance (AG 55, effective for year-end 2025 filings, verify) requires the US cedent to demonstrate that reserves ceded to us remain adequate on the assets actually backing them, which means our asset data will be examined through the cedent as well as through the BMA.
  • Insurance accumulation matters less; liquidity matters more. The H3 grid and the mega-project module are a general-business tool. The long-term entity needs the encumbrance and liquidity view (which assets are in which trust for which cedent, what a surrender or collateral top-up calls for, by currency and by month) that the limit table already sketches for posted collateral.
Programme elementGeneral-business reinsurer (this paper)Long-term entity in the group
Mandatory schedules from the platformXXI, XVIII, XIXA, V(c), quarterly return, Cat ReturnXXI, XVIII, XIX and XIXA, V(c) on the long-term handbook numbering; LLSBA template; asset and liability disclosure
Largest capital leverReinsurance credit charge and collateral linkage; catastrophe recoveries credit chargeLook-through and concentration charge on the investment book; affiliated-cession structure
Track B priorityAsset look-through and limits (Phase 2), then the capacity workbench (Phase 3), then mega-project and cyber accumulation (Phase 4)Asset look-through and limits first (Phase 2), liquidity and encumbrance view second; workbench and map optional
