Key takeaway: if there is a long-term entity in the group, the same graph is built once and serves both rulebooks, but the order of the optional tranches changes: the asset side comes first and the map comes last. The Board should know which rulebook each entity is on before it approves the sequence.
07

Counterparty concentration: from sorting a spreadsheet to understanding the real group

A counterparty concentration exists only once every exposure across treasury, investments, ceded reinsurance, collateral and receivables resolves to the same economic group.

CROTreasuryCeded Re

A reinsurer does not truly have "counterparty concentration" until every exposure across treasury, investments, ceded reinsurance, collateral, brokers and receivables resolves to the same economic group, and until the system can say, for each dollar, whether it is money someone owes us or a safety net someone has promised us. Those are different things, and the BMA counts them in different places.

Plain English first. A counterparty is anyone whose failure would cost us money: the bank that holds our cash, the company whose bonds we own, the retrocessionaire (a reinsurer that reinsures us) that owes us a recoverable (money due to us after a loss), the bank that issued a letter of credit (a bank's promise to pay if a reinsurer does not) and the broker holding our premium in transit. Concentration risk is the danger that several of those are, underneath the different names, the same group.

Worked example: the ACME group appears in four systems (illustrative)

What finance may see

Bank account : ACME Bank NA $70M Bond issuer : ACME Funding LLC $65M Receivable : ACME Securities $20M LOC issuer : ACME Bank London $120M

Four names, four systems, no total.

What the enterprise graph should see

ACME FINANCIAL GROUP (global ultimate) ├─ ACME Bank NA cash $70M ├─ ACME Funding LLC bonds $65M ├─ ACME Securities receivable $20M └─ ACME Bank London LOC $120M Direct credit exposure $155M (cash + bonds + receivable) Protection dependency $120M (LOCs securing recoverables from Reinsurer XYZ)

Two rows, never one "$275M gross linked amount".

Try it: one group, four ledgers, two numbersillustrative calculator · $ millions · not company data
Direct credit exposure (cash, bonds, receivables)
Protection dependency (LOCs securing other people's debts to us)
Everything that touches the group (the Schedule V(c) view)
Largest single ledger line
Status of the direct exposure

A bank guarantee is not a deposit: the LOC is not money we have lent the group, it is our safety net for someone else's debt, so it is shown as a dependency rather than added to the direct exposure. The point of the entity graph is the gap between "largest single line" and "direct exposure": a silo reports the first, the group view reports the second, and the regulator, the rating agency and a stressed treasurer care about the second and the dependency together.

A bank guarantee is not a deposit. If ACME fails we do not lose the $120M letter of credit; we lose our safety net for someone else's debt (Reinsurer XYZ's $180M recoverable, see collateral concentration). The LOC only costs us money if both Reinsurer XYZ and ACME fail. Adding it to the deposits overstates what ACME owes us and, worse, hides the real consequence of an ACME downgrade: under Schedule XVIII the collateralised part of a recoverable is rated at the better of the reinsurer's credit rating and the LOC issuer's credit rating (on the BMA's 1-to-8 BSCR rating scale, where 1 is AAA and 8 is below CCC- or unrated, that is the lower number), so a downgrade of ACME can strip the benefit of the LOC and raise the BSCR credit charge (the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, the BMA's risk-based capital formula) without a single dollar changing hands. The right question about ACME is therefore not "how big is the number" but "how many of our safety nets depend on this one bank, and what happens the day it is downgraded".

What each BMA schedule sees in this example. CFO The same four items land in three different places, and a CFO who files $275M on Schedule XXI would over-report:

WhereWhat it countsACME amountWhy

Related entities are grouped by control or economic interdependence. [BMA-GB]
Schedule XVIII (ceded reinsurance)Reinsurance balances and the collateral held against them$120M appears as collateral on Reinsurer XYZ's lineThe LOC lifts the rating of the covered portion to ACME Bank's rating; the exposure is split if the LOC covers only part.

Section numbers are from the BMA 2024 year-end General Business handbook (C31.2c, C25.2(i), C16.2b(c) and C16.2.b.4); the 2025 year-end edition, published 18 December 2025, governs the current filing, so re-check the numbering there before filing. The long-term handbook has parallel sections (C15 for ceded reinsurance). [BMA-LT]

The counterparty universe is wider than banks and reinsurers

The biggest names a reinsurer depends on are often not banks at all. The broker holding our premium in transit is a top-three concentration for most reinsurers, and a collateralised retrocessionaire's only promise is the cash sitting in a trust. Each type has its own measure of exposure, and the graph must carry all of them.

7.1 How the group entity graph is actually built

Three external sources do the heavy lifting, in this order: a free backbone, a paid extension and an optional challenger. Worked examples of resolving one bank across four ledgers follow in the worked examples.

Free backbone: GLEIF LEI Level 2. Plain English: the LEI (Legal Entity Identifier) is a 20-character public ID for a legal entity. GLEIF, the not-for-profit that runs it, also publishes who each entity's parent is, for free, wherever the parent has an LEI too. Entities report their direct accounting consolidating parent and their ultimate accounting consolidating parent; the whole data pool is searchable free of charge without registering, as a bulk file or an API. Nearly every regulated reinsurer, bank and listed issuer, and most funds, carry an LEI, so this seeds the graph at no cost and is a free cross-check on anything we buy. [GLEIF]

Paid extension: Dun & Bradstreet Corporate Linkage. D&B returns the corporate family tree for any D-U-N-S number (D&B's own nine-digit business identifier). Plain English: a Parent owns more than 50% of another company; the Domestic Ultimate is the highest parent in the same country; the Global Ultimate is the highest parent anywhere in the world. The "Enhanced" family-tree product returns the ultimate parent and every related entity, which is what a connected-counterparty group needs. D&B also sells Minority Linkage (ownership below 50%), the right feed for the BMA's economic-interdependence test. Note: D&B Direct 2.0 is the legacy API and D&B Direct+ is the current platform (its documentation sits behind a customer login); contract for the Direct+ equivalents. Buy D&B for private cedents, brokers and the long tail where parents have no LEI. [DNB-LINKAGE]

Optional challenger: S&P Business Entity Cross Reference Service (BECRS). If we already license S&P, BECRS maps D-U-N-S, LEI, CUSIP (the US security identifier), CIK (the SEC filer number) and rating-agency identifiers to one S&P entity ID with majority-ownership ultimate parents. It is the natural cross-check on D&B and the bridge from securities to issuers on the asset side. [SP-BECRS]

1. Ingest every counterparty name from every internal source.
Banks, bond issuers, cedents, brokers, reinsurers, LOC banks, trustees and custodians, ILS vehicles, derivative counterparties, asset managers, premium debtors, affiliates.
2. Normalise identity.
Legal name, aliases, address, LEI, D-U-N-S, NAIC company code, S&P entity ID, internal counterparty ID, tax ID where permitted. One golden record per legal entity.
3. Seed the hierarchy with GLEIF Level 2 FREE.
Direct and ultimate accounting parents for every entity that has an LEI.
4. Extend with D&B; challenge with S&P BECRS INTEGRATE.
Fill gaps where the parent lacks an LEI; log every disagreement between sources for a data steward to resolve.
5. Create effective-dated parent/child edges.
Ownership changes over time. Do not overwrite history; a 2024 return must still reproduce the 2024 tree.
6. Add economic-interdependence overrides.
The BMA groups counterparties by control or by economic interdependence: if one would be unable to fund or repay, the other likely would too (handbook C31.2). Ownership data never shows that; a person must assert it. Store reason, evidence, approver and effective dates.
7. Keep the legal roles separate.
Obligor (who legally owes us), guarantor (who signed a guarantee, if anyone) and rating-bearing entity (whose rating the regulator lets us use) are three different fields, not one.
8. Aggregate to the chosen reporting group.
Legal entity → domestic ultimate → global ultimate (control group) → connected group (control plus economic interdependence). Each schedule picks the level it needs.

Why rolling up is necessary but not sufficient. Rolling everything up to the parent tells us how much trouble one family's failure would cause; it does not tell us who is legally on the hook. A parent does not guarantee a subsidiary unless it signs a guarantee, ratings attach to specific legal entities, and the right of set-off (netting what we owe against what we are owed) exists only between the two entities named in a contract. So the graph must support two views at once:

Control group (aggregation_group)

Everything under one global ultimate. Answers "what does the failure of the ACME family cost us?" Used for Schedule XXI grouping, appetite limits and contagion stress.

Connected group (connected_group)

Control group plus economic-interdependence overrides: a supplier that lives off one customer, a fund whose only investor is one bank. Also the BMA's definition. Used for Schedule XXI and V(c) when the override is approved.

Recovery analysis, by contrast, works at the obligor level: if ACME Securities defaults on the $20M receivable, ACME Bank NA is not liable unless a guarantee says so, and the recoverable from Reinsurer XYZ is still owed by Reinsurer XYZ even if ACME's LOC lapses.

7.2 Collateral concentration: how it is actually done

Collateral must be modelled as a relationship, not mechanically subtracted from the underlying exposure. A letter of credit reduces the credit exposure to one reinsurer while introducing a dependency on the issuing bank. And collateral runs in two directions: protection we receive from our retrocessionaires, and, for a Bermuda reinsurer far more often, assets we post for our cedents. This section covers both; six end-to-end worked examples follow in the worked examples.

Diagram: Reinsurer XYZ owes us $180M; ACME Bank's $120M letter of credit secures part of it. One obligor, one guarantor bank, one safety net, and a dashed wrong-way link between the two (amounts illustrative).

Regulatory / reporting view (Schedule XVIII)

Report, per reinsurer, the gross balance (receivable + funds held not already in Schedule IIA + recoverable), the payables we can legally set off, the collateral placed in our favour, and the qualifying collateral: collateral less a 2% haircut, never more than the net exposure. The credit charge is then applied at the better of the reinsurer's and the LOC bank's credit ratings (the handbook says "whichever is higher", meaning the stronger credit rating, which is the lower number on the BMA's 1-to-8 BSCR rating scale, 1 = AAA, 8 = below CCC- or unrated), split pro rata if the LOC covers only part of the balance. A domestic (Bermuda) affiliate is rated 0 whatever its credit rating; an unrated reinsurer is rated 4 if it is regulated in a jurisdiction that applies the IAIS Insurance Core Principles (the global supervisory standard, "ICPs"), imposes both a minimum and a prescribed capital requirement and fully meets the prescribed one; otherwise it is rated 8. Funds withheld with specific assets earmarked for us are treated as investments we hold (market risk, looked through on Schedule IIA), not as credit exposure. The charge is based on the greater of current and projected future balances (D9.2). The regulator's 2% haircut is fixed, and the same 2% applies to collateral held against catastrophe recoverables in the cat-risk module. [BMA-GB]

Economic risk view

Our internal haircuts for timing, jurisdiction and wrong-way risk (the obligor and its collateral provider failing in the same event) sit alongside the regulatory number, never inside it. Run separate stresses: reinsurer default alone; LOC bank impairment alone; joint reinsurer + LOC-bank stress; collateral haircut and timing stress; downgrade of the LOC issuer below the eligible rating.

Try it: how much protection survives a wrong-way stress?illustrative calculator · $ millions · simplified, not the BSCR formula
Collateral recognised against the recoverable
Net credit exposure, reporting view
Net credit exposure, joint stress (bank impaired, trust haircut)
Expected credit loss, reporting view
Expected credit loss, joint stress
Status

Defaults are the Reinsurer XYZ balance worked in the BMA section with the $20M trust from the step-by-step above added and no set-off, so the reporting-view exposure here is not that example's $52.4M. Recognised collateral is capped at the recoverable. The stress removes part of the LOC and haircuts the trust, then applies the same default assumption. The reporting view and the stressed view are both correct; they answer different questions.

Why the two views must be kept apart. CFO CRO The regulator lets us reduce what a retrocessionaire owes us by what we owe them only if the contract says we can net the two, and lets us count collateral only up to the debt it secures, after a small haircut. Over-collateralisation on one contract does not offset under-collateralisation on another, because collateral is obligation-specific. If our system nets and offsets more freely than the rules do, the regulatory number and the management number will disagree, and both will be distrusted.

Step-by-step collateral concentration calculation
1. Start with the obligation.
Example: $180M recoverable from Reinsurer XYZ, less $10M we owe XYZ under a contract with a right of set-off: net exposure $170M.
2. Attach collateral instruments to that obligation.
Example: the $120M LOC from ACME Bank that the BMA section works, plus a $20M trust added here to show a second instrument (which is why the net qualifying exposure in step 4 is $32.8M rather than that example's $52.4M). Each instrument carries an obligation_id; collateral with no obligation is "orphan" and earns nothing.
3. Resolve every collateral issuer, trustee and custodian to its ultimate group.
ACME Bank London → ACME Financial Group, the same family that holds our cash and bonds.
4. Calculate regulatory protection by instrument and eligibility rules.
Qualifying collateral = ($120M + $20M) × 98% = $137.2M, which is below the $170M net exposure so no cap applies; net qualifying exposure $32.8M. Split the $170M into the $120M portion rated at the better of XYZ's and ACME's credit ratings and the $50M portion rated at XYZ's alone.
5. Surface the two findings that are worth money.
(a) Over-collateralisation: collateral above net exposure earns zero regulatory credit, so we (or the party posting it) are paying LOC fees for protection the BMA does not count. (b) Orphan collateral: LOCs the ceded-reinsurance system cannot tie to a recoverable are charged as if they did not exist. Both feed lever 2 in #profit.
6. Apply internal economic haircuts separately.
Timing (how long to draw), jurisdiction (can we enforce), and wrong-way risk. Never overwrite the regulatory figure.
7. Aggregate collateral-provider concentration.
"How much of our credit protection depends on ACME Bank?" and "how much of ACME do we already hold as cash and bonds?"
8. Run the downgrade and wrong-way stress.
If ACME is downgraded below the eligible rating: which recoverables become uncollateralised, what is the added BSCR credit charge, and which trust or LOC replacement do we need within the notice period? Could XYZ and ACME be impaired in the same systemic event?
9. Expose the answer in the app.
Gross recoverable, set-off, recognised collateral, internally stressed collateral, net credit exposure, collateral-provider concentration and a collateral-efficiency ratio (recognised ÷ total, with the annual fee on the unrecognised part).

All amounts illustrative.

Funds withheld, trusts and letters of credit move risk to different parties

Funds withheld means the cedent keeps our premium as security instead of paying it to us. That protects the cedent but means a large cedent that goes bust owes us a lot: the credit risk points at the cedent, not the other way round. Trusts and letters of credit are the reverse: our assets sit with a bank for the cedent's benefit. Each structure moves risk to a different party, so each must be recorded as its own kind of relationship with a stated risk-bearer.

InstrumentWho holds the assetsWho bears asset riskCredit risk points atBMA treatment when we are the reinsurer
Funds withheldThe cedentCedent, unless specific assets are earmarked for usThe cedentSchedule IIA (looked through) if we bear the asset risk; Schedule XVIII like a recoverable if not
Single-beneficiary trust (e.g. New York Regulation 114, the trust rule US cedents commonly require)A trustee bank, for one cedentUs (the grantor)Trustee (operational), cedent (release)Encumbered asset on our balance sheet; look-through market risk
Multi-beneficiary trustA trustee bank, for all US cedentsUsTrustee; trusteed-surplus top-upsAs above; larger and stickier
Letter of creditNothing moves; a bank promisesNeither, until drawnThe cedent relies on the bank; we owe the bank fees and covenantsOff balance sheet for us; the facility bank is a concentration
GuaranteeNothing moves; a parent or third party promisesNeitherThe guarantorOnly the rating-bearing entity's rating counts

Collateral we post

Treasurer CFO Because we are outside the US, American cedents only get regulatory credit for our reinsurance if we lock up assets for them in a trust or a bank letter of credit, or if we qualify for reduced collateral as a Reciprocal Jurisdiction reinsurer (Bermuda has been on the NAIC's Reciprocal Jurisdiction list since 1 January 2020; the reinsurer must meet capital, solvency-ratio and reporting conditions to use it). Those locked assets cannot be used elsewhere, cost fees and yield, and concentrate us on a handful of trustee and LOC banks. Managing collateral structure is as much a source of return as managing investments. [NAIC-1] [NYDFS-1]

The posted-collateral register the layer must hold:

  1. Inventory. Every single-beneficiary trust (cedent, trustee, balance, eligible-asset rules, funding ratio: assets in trust divided by the amount the contract requires), the multi-beneficiary trust (and its trusteed surplus, the cushion above liabilities that the NAIC model regulation requires; verify the amount against the cedent state's adopted version), every LOC facility (bank, facility size, drawn amount, fee in basis points, covenants, expiry) and every funds-withheld balance by cedent.
  2. Encumbered vs free assets. Encumbered assets are assets pledged to someone else. The register must show, by asset class and by bank, what is locked, what is free, and how much liquidity that removes from the investment portfolio and from a cat-loss payment plan.
  3. Collateral cost as a pricing input. LOC fees, the yield drag of trust-eligible assets versus our target portfolio, and over-collateralisation above what the cedent's rules require. This cost belongs in the treaty pricing model, not only in the treasury budget; see lever 2 in #profit.
  4. Reciprocal Jurisdiction status by cedent state. The US Covered Agreements (the US-EU and US-UK treaties that remove reinsurance collateral) cover EU and UK reinsurers only; Bermuda is not a party but has had the same relief since 1 January 2020 through the NAIC's Reciprocal Jurisdiction list, provided the reinsurer keeps capital and surplus of at least $250M, a solvency ratio at or above the level the NAIC set for Bermuda, and files the required certifications and consents. The register must show which cedents already accept us with reduced collateral, which states have not adopted the model, and what we must maintain to keep the relief. Losing the status is a collateral call on the whole US book.
  5. Top-up triggers. Which cedents can demand more collateral and when: after a cat event, after a rating downgrade, when reserves increase, or when the funding ratio falls below the contract threshold. The wrong-way case is obvious: the same hurricane that raises the reserve also raises the top-up.
Executive note. For a general-business [Class 4 / 3B / 3A] reinsurer the posted-collateral question is mostly about US property-casualty cedents, Reg 114 trusts and LOC facilities. For a long-term (Class C / D / E) reinsurer it is dominated by funds-withheld and modified coinsurance blocks (the cedent keeps the assets and reserves on its own balance sheet and passes us the investment result), where the asset risk we bear on the cedent's balance sheet needs prior BMA approval when affiliates are involved (see affiliated reinsurance). Same register, different weights.

7.3 Affiliated reinsurance: what does that actually mean?

Plain English: affiliated reinsurance occurs when one insurance or reinsurance legal entity transfers risk to another entity within the same corporate group. It can improve the capital or risk profile of an individual legal entity, but it does not remove risk from the group as a whole.

Approval vs disclosure. For a general-business [Class 4 / 3B / 3A] reinsurer, intra-group reinsurance is a disclosure obligation (Schedule V(c) and every quarterly return), not, on the face of the Insurance Act's material-change list, a transaction that itself needs BMA sign-off: s.30JA(1) catches transfers of a line of business "other than by way of reinsurance". That is an inference from the list rather than a BMA statement, so counsel should confirm it treaty by treaty, and a new affiliate cession large enough to be an "expansion into a material new line of business" for the receiving entity is itself a listed material change. [BMA-MCN] For a long-term (Class C / D / E) reinsurer the bar is higher: any asset backing policyholder liabilities with credit or equity exposure to an affiliate, related or connected party needs prior BMA approval, and new or amended block reinsurance deals need prior approval. [BMA-LT] [WALKERS] Group oversight tightened on 7 January 2026 (Insurance Amendment (No. 2) Act 2025): the designated insurer of a BMA-supervised group must still notify the BMA within 30 days when any group member, in Bermuda or elsewhere, makes a listed material change, and must now give the BMA 30 days' prior notice, with a no-objection window, before any Bermuda-domiciled group member amalgamates with, acquires or merges with another firm; confirm scope with counsel. The affiliated-reinsurance graph should therefore carry an "approval / notification status" attribute on every intra-group edge.

Diagram (amounts illustrative): US Insurance Co cedes a $500M layer to Atlantic Re; Atlantic Re buys $200M external retrocession, so $300M stays inside the group boundary. Only the retrocession moves risk outside the group; the Reg 114 trust or LOC that Atlantic Re must post back to US Insurance Co is not drawn, and it is why the group also ends up with locked-up assets.

When does the US entity actually get to count it? "At the US entity level the $500M may be transferred" is true only under two conditions. First, the US cedent gets statutory credit for a cession to its Bermuda affiliate only if the affiliate is a certified or reciprocal-jurisdiction reinsurer, or posts qualifying security (trust or LOC) in the cedent's state. [NAIC-1] Second, the treaty must pass the accounting risk-transfer tests (SSAP 62R for US statutory, ASC 944 / former FAS 113 for US GAAP): the reinsurer must have a reasonable chance of a significant loss, or the deal is booked as a deposit and gives no credit at all. Moving risk from our US company to our Bermuda company therefore helps the US company's ratios only if the US regulator recognises the transfer, and that usually requires us to ring-fence assets for the US company's benefit. The group ends up holding the same risk plus a locked-up pile of assets. Group-level views must show both the risk and the trapped capital.

Capital is not fungible across the group without regulatory approval. Surplus in Atlantic Re cannot simply be dividended to US Insurance Co after a loss; each regulator protects its own policyholders first. An intra-group cession that looks capital-efficient on paper can leave the group with the right amount of capital in the wrong entity.

Two views of the same treaty. The same internal treaty looks different depending on where you stand. To Atlantic Re, the entity that received the BMA budget, the US affiliate is its largest client and possibly its largest debtor: premium receivable, funds withheld, share of PML (probable maximum loss, the loss from a defined severe event), share of reserves and limit against risk appetite. Its single-cedent concentration and the tail it assumes from that one affiliate may dominate Atlantic Re's cat and reserve charges. To the group, it is an internal transfer that changes nothing until outside reinsurance or capital is added. Our reports must show both, and the regulator asks for both: the entity's Schedule V(c) and the group's Schedule V(c). [BMA-GR]

Legal-entity view (Atlantic Re)

Affiliate as cedent: premium written, receivable ageing, funds withheld and who bears its asset risk, share of 1-in-100 and 1-in-250 PML, share of reserves, limit versus appetite. On our own BSCR a domestic affiliate we cede to is rated 0, so internal cessions carry no reinsurance credit charge at entity level.

Group view

Does risk leave the group? External retrocession, collateral we posted to our own subsidiary, trapped capital by entity, and the intra-group cession that eliminates on consolidation. Material intra-group transactions: 5% of group available capital and surplus for one transaction, 10% for a linked series, or qualitatively high-risk.

What the affiliated-reinsurance dashboard should show
QuestionRequired view
Who ceded to whom?Legal-entity flow graph with approval / notification status on each edge
How much limit moved?Gross and net exposure limits by treaty; for the BMA, outstanding reserves at the reporting date
How much premium moved?Gross and net premium written in the period by entity pair
Did group risk actually leave the group?External retrocession, collateral and capital layer
Is the cession collateralised and does the collateral qualify in the cedent's state?Trust or LOC in favour of the US cedent, eligible assets, funding ratio, reciprocal-jurisdiction status
Does the transaction transfer risk under accounting rules?SSAP 62R / ASC 944 risk-transfer test result and date; deposit accounting flag
Is one affiliate carrying too much?Entity view: affiliate as cedent versus capital and appetite. Group view: trapped capital by entity
Is the transaction material to the BMA?Exposure versus 5% (single) / 10% (linked series) of group available capital and surplus; greater than 10% of entity statutory capital and surplus
What must be filed each quarter?Intra-group transactions and all intra-group reinsurance and retrocession that arose since the last return; quarterly returns fall due on the last day of May, August and November (2025 year-end filing requirements, item 6); an insurer inside a group for which the BMA is group supervisor reports these items through the group's quarterly return instead
What are the BMA fields?Counterparties and location; exposure limits gross and net by counterparty rating (outstanding reserves); premium flows gross and net; the proportion of our reinsurance that is internal (affiliate reinsurance ÷ total, where we are the cedent); more than 25 transactions with one pair may be aggregated
How is the affiliate rated for capital?A domestic (Bermuda) affiliate reinsurer is assigned BSCR rating 0 in Schedule XVIII regardless of its credit rating, so internal cessions carry no reinsurance credit charge at entity level, which is exactly why the group view must look through
What happens after a catastrophe?Event loss flow through internal and external reinsurance, collateral top-ups triggered, and which entity ends up short of capital

BMA fields and materiality thresholds: GB handbook C16.2b and C16.2.b.1 to C16.2.b.2, Group Rules definition of "material intra-group transaction" and Schedule V(c). [BMA-GB] [BMA-GR]

Key takeaway: Build one entity graph (GLEIF for free, D&B for the gaps, S&P as challenger) that keeps obligor, guarantor and rating-bearing entity as separate roles; record every collateral instrument as a relationship tied to one obligation, in both directions, with the regulator's 2% haircut and net-exposure cap kept apart from our own haircuts; and show every intra-group treaty from both the entity's and the group's seat. Do that and the Schedule XXI, XVIII and V(c) numbers fall out of the same tables that tell Treasury which LOC fees are wasted and which bank we are quietly betting the company on.

7.4 Worked examples: counterparty, collateral and affiliated reinsurance, end to end

Six situations, each with illustrative numbers and a clear "what the decision-maker does differently" ending. They extend the ACME case in the counterparty section and the Reinsurer XYZ collateral case in collateral concentration; they do not repeat them.

CFO CRO Treasurer Ceded Re CIO Board

Common base for every example (illustrative). Atlantic Re, the reference company used throughout this document, is a Class 4 general-business reinsurer (the BMA's largest property and casualty licence class) with statutory capital and surplus of $2,000M (the capital base the BMA's 10% counterparty test is measured against) and a BSCR of $1,400M (the capital it must hold). Limits quoted below are those in the limit framework: single counterparty amber at 7.5% of capital, red at 10%; collateral provider 25% of recognised collateral; affiliate cedent 35% of gross written premium. Every dollar figure below is invented to make the mechanics visible. The percentages and rules are quoted from the BMA 2024 General Business handbook [BMA-GB] and the capital factor tables in the Group Solvency Requirement Amendment Rules 2024 [BMA-GR24]; the Insurance (Prudential Standards) (Class 4 and Class 3B Solvency Requirement) Amendment Rules 2024 carry identical Table 8 credit factors and Table 5A concentration factors (checked against the rules text); re-check the current year-end handbook and rules before any filing.

The chain these examples walk through

For a reinsurer, "ceded" and "retro" are the same transaction: retrocession is the reinsurance a reinsurer buys, and a cedent is the insurer that buys reinsurance from us. The chain runs from gross to net in six steps:

GROSS ASSUMED LOSS what cedents can claim from us │ ↓ NET OF RETROCESSION what we keep after our own protection │ ↓ RETRO RECOVERABLE a debt each retrocessionaire now owes us │ ↓ SET-OFF AND COLLATERAL how much of that debt is legally netted or secured │ ↓ RESIDUAL CREDIT EXPOSURE by legal obligor, then by connected group │ ↓ NET RETAINED LOSS + CREDIT-RISK CAPITAL (Schedule XVIII, D9) + CONCENTRATION CAPITAL (Schedule XXI, D6)

Two rules from the handbook shape everything below. First, the BMA counts a payable against a reinsurer's balance only where "there is a contractual right of set-off" (C25.2 e). Second, qualifying collateral is the collateral placed in our favour "less a 2% reduction" and "shall not exceed the net exposure" (C25.2 g), and the balance takes the BSCR rating of the reinsurer "or the rating of the letters of credit issuer, if any, whichever is higher" (C25.2 i(i)). The handbook says "higher" without saying higher credit quality or higher BSCR number; the reading used throughout this section, and the one the industry applies, is the better credit quality. [BMA-GB]

Worked example 1: one bank, four systems, one global ultimate (illustrative)

Treasurer CRO CFO A second family, alongside ACME, to show the mechanics on a bank that also writes our derivatives. Finance sees four unrelated names. The entity graph resolves them through their LEI (the 20-character Legal Entity Identifier every regulated counterparty carries) and D-U-N-S number (Dun and Bradstreet's company key) to one global ultimate, Northbridge Financial Holdings plc, under the BMA's control test (C31.2 a).

ViewWhat countsAmount% of $2,000M capital base
Direct credit exposure (we lose money if Northbridge fails)Cash + bonds + unsecured derivative value$148M7.4%
Protection dependency (our safety net for someone else's debt)LOC securing $150M of Retro Re B's balance$150M7.5%, contingent

Capital effect (illustrative, Table 5A factors). As separate names, neither the deposits nor the bonds made the top ten, so they attracted no concentration charge. Grouped, the family is the second-largest asset counterparty and the charge on it is 0.2% on $85M of rating-2 cash plus 1.5% on $60M of rating-3 bonds, about $1.1M of ECR on top of the ordinary market and credit charges. That is small; the same factor table charges 35% on listed equity and 20% on letters of credit held as an asset, so the number grows fast if the family also appears in the equity book. [BMA-GR24] The derivative exposure is charged in the credit-risk module, not through Schedule XXI: the D9.4 credit formula carries a separate C_CROTC term for counterparty default risk on over-the-counter derivatives, and the $3M net-of-CSA figure is what that term and the Schedule V(c) list see.

What the decision-makers do differently.

  • Treasurer Desk sub-limit, inside the 7.5% amber line: no bank family above 5% of capital in direct exposure. At 7.4% Northbridge is a whisker below the 7.5% amber line; moves $50M of deposits to a second family and direct exposure falls to 4.9%.
  • Ceded Re Limit: no bank family provides more than 25% of collateral we receive. Asks Retro Re B at 1 January to split the $150M LOC across two issuing banks.
  • CRO Adds "protection dependency" as its own limit line, separate from direct exposure, and puts the Northbridge family on a downgrade watch list (example 3 shows why).
  • CFO Files Schedule V(c) with the grouped $298M rather than four names below the 10% line, and carries the $145M of cash and bonds as one grouped line on Schedule XXI, consistent with Form 1EBS as C31.2a requires.
Worked example 2: an economic-interdependence override, with the approval record (illustrative)

CRO Ceded Re Cascade Re is an A- rated retrocessionaire that owes us $90M net. Its audited accounts show 80% of its gross premium comes from one client, Lakeshore Insurance Group. Lakeshore is also our cedent (premium receivable $35M) and a bond issuer we hold ($25M). No ownership link exists: the D&B tree and the LEI parent records show none. The BMA's second grouping test still applies, economic interdependence: "if one of the counterparties were to experience financial problems, in particular funding or repayment difficulties, the other(s) as a result, would also be likely to encounter funding or repayment difficulties" (C31.2 b). The wording is borrowed almost verbatim from the Basel large-exposures standard for banks, which also sets a trigger for investigating such links wherever exposure to one counterparty exceeds 5% of Tier 1 capital (LEX10.18); the BMA text has no numeric trigger, so we set our own. [BIS-LEX-1]

The override record. An override is a governed fact, not an analyst's opinion in a spreadsheet. These are the fields the approval record carries (they extend CounterpartyRelationship in the data model):

FieldValue in this caseWhy it is there
override_idOVR-2026-014Citable in the filing working papers
from_entity_id / to_entity_idCascade Re Ltd → Lakeshore Insurance Group Inc (global ultimate)Direction of dependence
relationship_typeECONOMIC_DEPENDENCYDistinct from PARENT / SUBSIDIARY so it can be switched off per report
regulatory_basisBMA GB handbook C31.2(b)The test being applied
dependency_measure80% of Cascade Re gross written premium, FY2025 audited accounts; 62% of its receivablesThe evidence in numbers
trigger_ruleSingle-source share of revenue at or above 50%, or of assets at or above 25%Our stated threshold, since the BMA gives none
evidence_refsCascade Re annual report p.41; Lakeshore annual filing; broker security reportRetained for the five-year retention period
applies_toSchedule XXI grouping: yes. Schedule V(c): yes. Schedule XVIII: no (reported per reinsurer, C25.2). Internal limits: yesOne override, several consumers
proposed_by, approver_1, approver_2Credit analyst; CRO; Head of Ceded ReinsuranceFour-eyes approval
effective_from / effective_to2026-02-15 / openHistory is never overwritten
review_date2027-02-15, or on a rating action or Lakeshore resultsOverrides decay
confidence, statusMedium (public accounts, one year); APPROVEDFilters and audit

Effect. Before the override the largest connected group we could see was $90M (4.5% of capital). After it, the "Lakeshore connected group" is $90M + $35M + $25M = $150M, 7.5%, exactly at the amber line in the limit framework and above the CIO's 6% desk sub-limit inside it. Note what does not change: the Schedule XVIII credit charge, because that schedule is per reinsurer and its diversification adjustment uses "the largest net reinsurance exposure, on an individual reinsurer basis" (D9.9 d). The override changes Schedule V(c), the Schedule XXI grouping of the bonds and our appetite, not the credit factor. Only the $25M of bonds is a Schedule XXI asset: the $90M retro balance sits on Schedule XVIII and the $35M premium receivable on Form 1EBS line 10 and in the credit module, so the $150M is a Schedule V(c) and internal-limit number, not a Schedule XXI number.

What the decision-makers do differently. CRO treats the 7.5% as an amber breach with an owner plan due within ten days, not a debate. Ceded Re caps Cascade Re's line at renewal and requires an LOC from a bank outside the Lakeshore group. CIO buys no more Lakeshore paper until the group is back under 6%. CFO reports the $150M as one linked series on Schedule V(c) (C16.2b c: "series of linked unaffiliated counterparty exposures"), groups the $25M of Lakeshore bonds with any other Lakeshore-family assets on Schedule XXI (the only one of the three balances that is a Schedule XXI asset type under C31.2c), and keeps OVR-2026-014 in the working papers.

Worked example 3: a collateral calculation, then a joint reinsurer-default and LOC-bank stress (illustrative)

Ceded Re CRO Treasurer Collateral concentration worked the ACME and Reinsurer XYZ case; this example adds set-off, a trust and a joint stress on a larger balance. Retro Re B is A- rated (BSCR rating 3). Its balances with us, in the order the handbook lists them (C25.2 c to h). IBNR below is the reserve for losses that have happened but have not yet been reported to us:

(c) Gross balance reinsurance balances receivable (billed) $ 60.0M recoverable on unpaid losses, incl. IBNR $190.0M total $250.0M (e) Payables to Retro Re B WITH contractual right of set-off $ 30.0M (a further $10M payable has no set-off clause: ignored) Net exposure = 250.0 - 30.0 $220.0M (f) Collateral placed in our favour LOC, Northbridge Bank (Europe) SE, AA, rating 2 $150.0M trust, US Treasuries, trustee Custodian Bank C $ 40.0M total $190.0M (g) Qualifying collateral = 190.0 x 0.98 = 186.2, capped at 220.0 $186.2M (h) Net qualifying exposure = 220.0 - 186.2 $ 33.8M

Rating and charge. The part covered by the LOC takes the higher of Retro Re B (rating 3) and Northbridge (rating 2), so it is reported at rating 2; the rest stays at rating 3 (C25.2 i(ii)). The credit factor for rating 3 is 3.5%, so, splitting the balance as C25.2 i(ii) requires, the $3.0M residual on the LOC-covered $150M is charged at rating 2 (1.5%) and the $30.8M residual on the uncovered $70M (after the $39.2M qualifying trust) at rating 3 (3.5%): about $1.1M before the diversification adjustment. Because a qualifying LOC already removes 98% of the balance it covers, the rating uplift only ever matters on the 2% residual. Unsecured, the same balance would cost 3.5% of $220M, about $7.7M. The collateral therefore releases roughly $6.6M of ECR. If these were catastrophe recoveries inside the cat module, the uncollateralised part would instead carry the flat 10% credit charge, again with a 2% collateral haircut (D10.5). [BMA-GB]

Internal economic view. We keep our own haircuts beside the regulator's fixed 2%: the LOC at 100% (AA issuer, evergreen, meaning it renews automatically unless the bank gives notice, here 60 days) and the trust at 95% (valuation and timing), so economic protection is $188M and net economic exposure $32M.

Collateral-provider concentration. Across all retrocessionaires we hold $410M of collateral. Northbridge issues $150M of it (37%); Custodian Bank C is trustee for $95M across three trusts (23%). That is the number no single treaty file shows.

StressProtection assumedExposure after protectionExpected loss (LGD 60%: we recover 40 cents on the dollar after a default)
Base: Retro Re B defaults, collateral good$188M$32M$19M
Northbridge impaired alone (Retro Re B pays)LOC honoured 50%: $113M$107M uncovered, no loss yet$0M, but 5.4% of capital now unsecured
Joint: Retro Re B defaults and Northbridge impaired$113M$107M$64M
Regulatory: Northbridge downgraded to BBB+ (rating 4)Collateral still qualifies at 98%$33.8M unchangedRating uplift lost: covered part reverts to rating 3

The last row matters for what a downgrade actually does. Under the BMA text the collateral keeps qualifying (the handbook text cited here sets no rating floor for the LOC issuer; verify against the current instructions handbook). The cliff is elsewhere: for a US cedent taking statutory credit, an LOC must be issued by a qualified US financial institution and stays acceptable after the issuer loses that status only "until their expiration, extension, renewal, modification or amendment" (NAIC Model 786, Section 11 A(3)); the model also requires an evergreen clause with at least 30 days' notice of non-renewal (Section 13 D). [NAIC-1] So the real question is: which LOCs renew in the next 90 days, and who replaces the issuer?

What the decision-makers do differently. Ceded Re applies the 25% collateral-provider limit from the limit framework, so Northbridge at 37% is a breach; replaces $50M of the Northbridge LOC with a second issuer at renewal, which takes Northbridge to $100M of $410M (24%), and writes a replacement trigger into the treaty (new issuer within 30 days if the bank falls below A-). Treasurer tracks every LOC expiry and notice period in the collateral register, with an internal 90-day warning, not the 30-day legal minimum. CRO sets a joint-stress limit: expected loss under reinsurer-default-plus-bank-impairment at or below 2% of capital per collateral family.

The posting side is where most of the money is.

Direction 1: security we receive. A $100M balance owed to us by a retrocessionaire rated A- (rating 3, factor 3.5%).

Putting a price on the choice. For Cedent Z, the trust costs about $1.2M a year plus trapped over-funding; the LOC about $2.1M plus a bank concentration; funds withheld costs a $10.5M capital charge (about $1.05M a year at a 10% cost of capital, illustrative) plus a $300M credit exposure to the cedent, in exchange for keeping the interest spread. None of these numbers appears in a treaty file; all of them appear once collateral is a first-class relationship with a direction, a beneficiary, a custodian and a cost.

What the decision-makers do differently. Treasurer chooses the structure per cedent on total cost: fee, yield drag, capital charge and the value of liquidity, and tracks encumbered versus free assets daily. CFO makes Reciprocal Jurisdiction relief a standing objective with the capital and solvency-ratio covenants it implies. Ceded Re prefers trusts or funds withheld from weaker retrocessionaires and accepts LOCs only from banks outside the collateral-provider limit. CRO caps encumbered assets as a share of liquid assets so that a cat event cannot find the cash already locked up.

Worked example 5: an affiliated chain where the group view and the legal-entity view disagree (illustrative)

CFO CRO Board A different treaty from the one drawn in the affiliated-reinsurance dashboard and Scenario D, on the same group structure. US Insurance Co cedes a 60% quota share of its $1,000M US casualty reserves to its Bermuda affiliate, Atlantic Re ($600M). Atlantic Re funds a Reg 114 trust of $630M (105%) for the US company, cedes $150M of those reserves to an external retrocessionaire rated A+ under an aggregate cover, and cedes a further $80M to Group Re II, a Bermuda-domiciled affiliate. On Atlantic Re's own Schedule XVIII that last balance is rated 0 "regardless of its credit rating" because Group Re II is a domestic affiliate (C25.2 i(iii)), so it carries no credit charge at entity level, which is exactly why the group view must look through it.

MeasureUS Insurance Co (legal entity)Atlantic Re (legal entity)Group (consolidated)

Ceded to an affiliate$600M to Atlantic Re$80M to Group Re IIEliminated
Ceded to third parties$0$150M$150M
Net retained reserves$400M$370M$850M
Recoverable from an affiliate$600M, secured by a $630M trust$80M, BSCR rating 0None
Assets locked up for an affiliate$0$630M in trust (11.5% of $5,500M invested assets, illustrative)$630M trapped

Three readings of one treaty. To the US regulator, $600M of risk left the company. To Atlantic Re, one affiliate is its largest client, 55% of its premium and the reason 11.5% of its assets are locked in a trust. To the group, $850M of the risk is still inside and $630M of assets cannot be used for anything else. The "risk transferred" of the first reading and the "risk retained" of the third are both true.

The questions the CFO must be able to answer to the BMA. They come from Schedule V(c) of the CSR (the Capital and Solvency Return, C16.2b) and from the group return; whether the quarterly return asks for the same detail should be verified against the current instructions handbook. The first four are the C16.2b disclosures that the affiliated-reinsurance dashboard already frames; the last five are the ones a treaty file cannot answer:

  1. Which counterparties, in which locations, and what is the purpose, term and cost of the arrangement?
  2. Aggregated exposure limits, gross and net, by counterparty rating: the BMA reads this as outstanding reserves at the reporting date ($600M gross, $400M net for the US entity).
  3. Aggregated premium flows, gross and net, between the entity pair for the period.
  4. What proportion of the reinsurance Atlantic Re buys, and of the business it assumes, is internal?
  5. Is the transaction material? At entity level the BMA treats an intra-group exposure above 10% of statutory capital and surplus as material (C16.2.b.1); at group level the Group Rules treat a single intra-group transaction above 5% of available capital and surplus, or a linked series above 10%, as material [BMA-GR]. Here $600M against $2,000M is 30%: material on every test by a wide margin.
  6. Does the collateral qualify in the cedent's state, and by how much is the trust over-funded?
  7. Does the contract transfer risk under the cedent's accounting rules (SSAP 62R / FAS 113 in the US), or is it financing?
  8. What is the top-up obligation on the trust after a reserve strengthening, and where does the cash come from?
  9. Can Atlantic Re move capital to the US entity in a stress, and what approval does that need?

What the decision-makers do differently. CFO refunds the trust at 102% rather than 105%, releasing $18M, and shows the group net of $850M beside the entity net of $370M in every board pack. Board applies the affiliate limit in the limit framework, no single affiliate cedent above 35% of gross written premium, and records US Insurance Co at 55% as a breach with a dated plan to bring the internal share down at the next treaty renewal. CRO tags every intra-group edge with its approval or notification status and its materiality test result, so the quarterly return is produced rather than assembled.

Worked example 6: wrong-way risk, one hurricane and one sovereign (illustrative)

CRO CIO Ceded Re Wrong-way risk is the situation where the party protecting us is most likely to fail exactly when we most need the protection. Two cases.

Case A: the same hurricane. Retro Re F is a collateralised retrocession vehicle (an ILS fund, whose investors post the full limit in cash up front) with a $100M limit fully backed by a trust. Retro Re H is a traditional A-rated retrocessionaire whose balance is secured by a $60M LOC from Bank G, a regional bank headquartered in Florida with 70% of its loan book in the state. After a 1-in-100 Florida hurricane:

LineBefore the eventAfter the eventComment
Recoverable from Retro Re F$0$100MFully collateralised, but the trust may be held back for loss development and there is no reinstatement: the protection is gone for the second storm
Recoverable from Retro Re H$20M$180MNow the largest reinsurance exposure on Schedule XVIII
LOC from Bank G securing Retro Re H$60M, sound$60M, issuer under deposit flight and loan losses from the same stormStress: honoured at 50%
Unsecured exposure to Retro Re H$0$120M on paper; $150M in the stress7.5% of capital, from one event, in the one week we also need cash for claims

Case B: the same sovereign. Retro Re S is domiciled in Country S; its $120M balance is secured by a $90M LOC from Bank S, whose liquid assets are mostly Country S government bonds; our investment book holds $80M of the same sovereign; two of our cedents are Country S insurers. A sovereign downgrade lowers Retro Re S's rating, Bank S's rating and the value of our bonds on the same day. The regulatory rating of the covered part of the balance follows the higher of the two ratings (C25.2 i(i)), which now both fall together, so the uplift evaporates; the concentration schedule sees the bonds; nothing in either schedule sees that the three are one risk unless the graph carries a sovereign tag on the obligor, the LOC issuer and the collateral assets.

What the decision-makers do differently. CRO adds a wrong-way attribute to every collateral relationship: correlation to peak peril zones and to a sovereign, scored and limited. Ceded Re requires LOC issuers for catastrophe recoverables to be domiciled outside the peak zone they secure, and requires ILS trust assets to be Treasuries or government money-market funds with release and top-up terms stated. CIO includes contingent LOC dependency in the Country S limit, so the $80M of bonds and the $90M LOC count as one sovereign exposure.

Common mistakes these examples are designed to prevent.

  • Netting without a legal right of set-off. The $10M payable in example 3 reduces nothing. The BMA deducts a payable only where "there is a contractual right of set-off" (C25.2 e); an internal system that nets everything overstates the regulatory position and understates the capital.
  • Counting collateral twice. One trust pledged to two obligations, or an LOC recognised against a recoverable on Schedule XVIII and again as an asset on Schedule XXI. Collateral secures one obligation; the data model must carry the obligation it secures, and the 98% qualifying amount is capped at that obligation's net exposure.
  • Overwriting ownership history. A parent sells a subsidiary in March; if the edge is overwritten, the year-end return cannot reproduce the March grouping. Edges are effective-dated and never deleted.
  • Ignoring LOC expiry and notice. For LOCs we post to US cedents the legal minimum is 30 days' notice of non-renewal (Model 786, Section 13 D); for LOCs we receive from retrocessionaires the notice period is only what our treaty and the instrument say, so it must be captured per LOC; a facility that lapses in the week after a catastrophe leaves the recoverable unsecured when the credit charge and the cash need are both at their peak.
  • Mixing legal and economic groups. Rolling everything to the global ultimate tells us how much trouble one family's failure causes; it does not tell us who is legally on the hook. The obligor, the guarantor, the rating-bearing entity and the aggregation group are separate roles on every exposure.

Key takeaway: every one of these six decisions is a capital decision with a named owner, and none of them can be taken from a treaty file, a bank statement or a bond ledger on its own. The enterprise graph exists so that the same bank family appears once as direct exposure ($148M), once as protection dependency ($150M), once as a collateral-provider concentration (37% of collateral received) and once as a wrong-way exposure, and so that the person accountable sees all four before the event rather than after it.

7.5 Credit quality must sit beside the concentration amount

$250M owed to a strong, stable counterparty is not the same risk as $250M owed to one that is deteriorating (illustrative). The worked examples above size every exposure and net it against collateral; this subsection adds the second column the Board will ask for, the credit quality of the group behind the number, and the early-warning flags that move before a limit is breached.

Plain English first. A Financial Strength Rating (FSR) is a rating agency's opinion of an insurer's ability to pay its policy and contract obligations, on AM Best's scale from A++ (superior) down to D (poor). An issuer credit rating is an agency's opinion of a specific legal entity's ability to pay its financial obligations generally, which is the rating that attaches to a bank, a bond issuer or a reinsurer's holding company. A rating outlook (positive, stable or negative) says which way the agency expects the rating to move over an intermediate period (about 36 months at AM Best), and under review (a "watch") says a rating action may come soon, typically within six months, because something has just happened. The size of a recoverable tells us what we could lose; these four things tell us how likely it is, and how fast that likelihood is changing.

What the amount alone hides

Two retrocessionaires each owe Atlantic Re $150M. Both sit at the 7.5% amber line of the limit framework (#op-appetite). One is rated A with a stable outlook and has been for a decade; the other is rated A- with a negative outlook, was placed under review last quarter, and its owner has just announced a sale. The exposure report shows two identical rows.

What the enriched record shows

The same two rows carry the rating, the outlook, the date of the last rating change, an internal credit grade that can move faster than the agency, the approved limit and its utilisation, and a trend flag. The second row is amber on three of them before anything is breached, and the Concentration Committee sees it a quarter before the downgrade, not a quarter after.

The counterparty-group record, enriched

The group record in the counterparty graph (#groupgraph) already carries the resolved global ultimate, the gross exposure, the collateral and the stressed net. It gains the credit block below. The FSR belongs to insurers and reinsurers only; for banks, issuers and brokers the issuer credit rating is the relevant opinion, and the rating is always stored against the rating_entity the regulator lets us use, never against the group as a whole.

CounterpartyGroupCredit # one row per connected group x valuation date - group_id # the global ultimate or connected group - rating_entity_id # the legal entity whose rating we may use - gross_exposure # from CounterpartyExposure, summed by group - collateral_and_guarantees # qualifying collateral after the 2% haircut - stressed_net_exposure # after internal haircuts and wrong-way stress - pct_statutory_capital_and_surplus # against the $2,000M base - am_best_fsr # A++ .. D; insurers and reinsurers only - issuer_credit_ratings[] # agency, scale, value; AM Best, S&P, others - rating_outlook # POSITIVE / STABLE / NEGATIVE - watch_status # UNDER_REVIEW_NEG / UNDER_REVIEW_POS / # UNDER_REVIEW_DEV / NONE - rating_change_date # last action, any agency - bscr_rating # 1..8 from the handbook table, keyed on the # issuer-scale rating (a+ to a-), not the FSR letter - bscr_mapping_version # which year's handbook produced the mapping - internal_credit_grade # our own 1..10, may lead the agencies - approved_limit # from the limit register - utilisation_pct # stressed_net_exposure / approved_limit - trend_90d # RISING / FLAT / FALLING on stressed net - early_warning_flags[] # OUTLOOK_NEG, WATCH, CDS_WIDENING, # UTILISATION_GT_80, LOC_ELIGIBILITY_AT_RISK, # SAME_GROUP_ALSO_LOC_ISSUER - source_feed # AMB_RI / SP / INTERNAL / MANUAL - valuation_date

Source for the insurance and reinsurance names. AM Best describes itself as the only global credit rating agency focused solely on insurance, and its reinsurance information service is where the Financial Strength and issuer credit opinions on reinsurers, with their outlooks and recent rating actions, are published [AMB-RI]. AM Best's own guide defines the FSR as an independent opinion of an insurer's financial strength and ability to meet its ongoing insurance policy and contract obligations, on a scale from A++ to D [AMB-FSR]; its companion "Guide to Best's Credit Ratings" (October 2023 edition, read 2026-09-28) sets outlooks over an intermediate period of about 36 months and Under Review with positive, negative or developing implications, typically resolved within six months, and it is the issuer-scale rating (a- rather than A-) that the BMA table reads. Verify the current edition with the vendor before these designations are hard-coded as enumerations. The rating feed itself is a licensed dataset with display and redistribution terms (see #op-licensing); the register row for it should say whether a rating may appear in a document sent to a cedent. Bank and issuer ratings come from the S&P and other agency feeds already in the vendor list (#vendors). INTEGRATE

Why the rating is a capital number, not a comfort number

The BMA's credit charge on reinsurance balances (#bma) is a factor applied to the net qualifying exposure by BSCR rating: 0.7% at rating 1 (AAA), 1.5% at rating 2 (AA), 3.5% at rating 3 (A), 7.0% at rating 4 (BBB), and steeper below [BMA-GB]. A one-notch move from BSCR rating 3 to 4 (issuer scale a- to bbb+, FSR A- to B++) therefore doubles the charge on that reinsurer without a dollar changing hands, and the diversification credit (40% multiplied by one minus the largest reinsurer's share) moves with it. The rating on the record is what tells Finance which day that happens.

Worked example: two retrocessionaires, same amount, different credit (illustrative)

Decision. Ceded Re opens the downgrade clause in the Retro Re D contract now: a collateral top-up trigger on any move below A- and a substitution right, so that when the notch comes the charge does not. This is the same question Scenario A asks of the LOC bank ("if ACME is downgraded below the eligible rating, which recoverables become uncollateralised and what is the added BSCR credit charge", #scenarios), applied to the reinsurer instead of the bank. Both need the same three fields: the rating, the eligibility threshold in the contract, and the notice period. Ceded Re CRO Treasurer

Two ratings for one group. The FSR of the operating reinsurer and the issuer credit rating of its parent can differ by several notches, and the LOC bank behind it has a third. The record keys each rating to the legal entity it belongs to, and the Schedule XVIII calculation uses the better of the reinsurer's and the LOC issuer's, exactly as #collateral sets out. A group-level "average rating" is never stored.

Derivatives, repo, securities lending, FX and liquidity

Counterparty concentration does not stop at bonds and recoverables. The hedges, the financing trades and the cash we have promised to post can create exposures to the same groups that are invisible in a long-only view of the investment portfolio, and they can turn a credit event into a liquidity event on the same afternoon. Plain English for the three that executives meet least often: a repo (repurchase agreement) is a secured loan dressed as a sale, we hand over bonds for cash and buy them back later, so the risk is to the counterparty and to whoever issued the bonds; securities lending is lending our bonds to a borrower against a pool of collateral, so the risk is to the borrower and to that pool; and variation margin is the cash that moves daily between us and a derivative counterparty as prices change, which is a liquidity demand as much as a credit exposure. The same entity graph ingests all of them, each as an edge to a counterparty and, where one exists, an edge to a collateral instrument:

PositionCounterparty edgeCollateral edgeConcentration it creates
Derivative receivable or payable (swaps, options, FX forwards under an ISDA)Counterparty group, net of set-off inside the master agreementCSA collateral (the credit support annex that sets margin terms): what we hold and what we have posted, by issuerBank group: unsecured mark-to-market plus the posted collateral we would have to recover from an insolvent bank
Repo and reverse repoCounterparty group (the cash or bond taker)Collateral issuer of the bonds exchanged, with haircutTwo-sided: the bank, and the issuer of the collateral, which may already be a top-ten bond holding
Securities lendingBorrower group; the lending agent if it indemnifiesCollateral pool by issuer, currency and liquidity bucketBorrower group; reinvested cash collateral adds a second issuer concentration
FX forwards and hedgesBank or clearing counterpartyCSA or clearing-house marginBank group, and currency concentration: the share of hedges that depend on one bank in one currency
Margin and variation collateral, received and postedCustodian holding it; counterparty it belongs toIssuer of the collateral securities; liquidity bucket (same-day, one-week, one-month)Custodian group; issuer group; a liquidity demand that rises in the same stress as the hedge
Committed liquidity facilitiesBank or facility provider (the lender)None received; may be secured on our assetsProtection dependency on a bank group, alongside the LOC banks in #collateral
Maturity ladder (cash and near-cash by date, against expected outflows)Every counterparty above, by the date its cash flow falls dueEvery collateral instrument, by release or expiry dateThe liquidity stress horizon: the week in which collateral calls, LOC replacement and claims payments coincide

The last row is the one that ties the table together. A maturity ladder lines up what we can turn into cash on each future date against what we may be asked to pay, including the top-up triggers in the collateral register and the variation margin a market move would call. The BMA's 2024 liquidity paper is addressed to the long-term sector, but the ladder it expects, with stressed outflows against liquid assets by horizon, is the same tool a general-business reinsurer needs the week after a hurricane [BMA-LIQ]. The liquidity dimension in #assets gives each investment position its bucket; this table gives the same bucket to the collateral and the margin.

The rule: keep two exposure numbers, and never derive one from the other. For every position above the record stores the gross legal exposure (what we would claim in the counterparty's insolvency, before any netting the contract may or may not allow) and the netted, collateralised economic exposure (after the set-off the master agreement grants and after the collateral we actually hold, at its stressed value). The two are kept because the views that consume them differ: the regulatory return nets only where there is a contractual right of set-off and counts collateral only up to the net exposure after the 2% haircut (#collateral), while the internal stress applies our own haircuts, a wrong-way scenario in which the collateral issuer and the counterparty fall together, and a liquidity horizon. A system that stores only one of them forces someone to reconstruct the other in a spreadsheet, and the two numbers then disagree at exactly the moment the Board is comparing them. The limit framework in #op-appetite should name, for each limit, which of the two it is measured on.
Worked example: the same $12M, three ways (illustrative)

Worked example 1 above resolved NB Markets Ltd's FX forwards to the Northbridge group: $12M mark-to-market in our favour, $9M of collateral held under the CSA. The record carries $12M as gross legal exposure (a bank insolvency would leave us claiming $12M and holding $9M of its collateral to sell), $3M as the collateralised economic exposure, and, in the wrong-way stress, $5M: the $9M of collateral is Northbridge-group commercial paper, which the internal haircut writes down to $7M on the day Northbridge itself is the problem. The credit block on the group record flags SAME_GROUP_ALSO_LOC_ISSUER because Northbridge Bank (Europe) SE also stands behind $150M of Retro Re B's collateral. One bank, four systems, and a fifth line, the collateral it posts to us, that only the graph can see. Treasurer CIO

Key takeaway: put the credit quality of the group next to the amount it owes us, keyed to the legal entity whose rating the regulator accepts, with the outlook, the watch status, the date of the last change and our own grade, so the Concentration Committee sees deterioration a quarter before the BSCR credit factor doubles; and bring derivatives, repo, securities lending, FX, margin and committed facilities into the same graph as two numbers each, gross legal and netted economic, because the return and the stress test net differently and both must be reproducible.
08

Asset concentration: the balance-sheet side we still need to add

Issuer, look-through and structural concentrations on the balance sheet, measured against limits and capital with the same worked-example discipline as the insurance side.

CIOCRO

Concentration does not stop at the liability side. The same bank that issues our letters of credit (a bank's promise to pay us if a reinsurer does not, which the reinsurer pays a fee for) may be the largest bond issuer in our portfolio, the same sponsor (the private-equity or asset-management firm that raises and runs a fund) behind a private-credit fund may be the parent of a cedent, and the same fund whose contents we cannot list is being charged by the BSCR (the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, the BMA's risk-based capital formula) as if it were an unlisted equity holding, the top of the BMA's charge ladder. This section describes the balance-sheet half of the concentration picture, why the BMA's look-through rules turn data quality directly into required capital, and what the asset graph must contain. Worked examples with numbers follow at the end of this section (#ai-worked-examples); the capital arithmetic for all four charges is in #bma-capital, and the profit case for the investment book is lever 4 in #profit-levers.

8.1 Three views of asset concentration, and who owns each

The CIO manages the investment portfolio against limits; the CRO sets those limits and answers for the capital they consume; the CFO files the numbers and carries the charge. All three need the same three views, measured on the same resolved entities that the counterparty graph in the counterparty section (#counterparty) already holds.

Issuer concentration

Bond, equity, loan, deposit, derivative and letter-of-credit exposure to one issuer (the legal entity that owes us the money) and, above it, to one global ultimate (the highest parent anywhere in the world). Plain English: an issuer hierarchy tells us that a bond issued by a finance subsidiary in Delaware is really exposure to its parent in Tokyo, so the limit is tested against the parent. MUST

Look-through concentration (regulatory and economic)

Look-through means measuring a fund, CLO (collateralised loan obligation, a bundle of corporate loans sold in slices), ABS (asset-backed security) or private vehicle by the assets inside it, not by the wrapper's name. The BMA requires Schedule XXI (the concentration-risk schedule in the annual capital and solvency return, listing the ten largest counterparties) counterparties to be measured on the underlying assets inside funds, CLOs, ABS and fund-of-one structures (a fund with a single investor, us, so its contents are ours to report), and asks for look-through in the ten-largest-unaffiliated list where available [BMA-GB]. The winning system extends this to sponsor, manager and collateral-type views. MUST

Structural concentration

Sector, country, currency, rating, manager, sponsor, collateral type, maturity and liquidity buckets. These are the limits in the investment guidelines; the engine measures them on look-through positions rather than on wrappers, so a "diversified" fund line does not hide a sector bet. INTEGRATE

The first two views are regulatory: they feed the Schedule XXI concentration table and the concentration-risk capital charge. The third is mostly economic, but the BMA's 2024 papers (below) now expect the liquidity and private-credit slices of it to be evidenced, not asserted.

8.2 Look-through is a capital price list, not optional detail

The BMA charges a fund by what we can prove about its contents. Full look-through is the default; where it is not achievable the handbook sets a ladder of partial options, and every fund, CLO or private vehicle whose underlying positions we cannot load is charged at the top of the ladder, as an equity holding of type "Other" [BMA-GB] (sections B6.2 and B6.9). The asset graph's job is to move assets down the ladder.

RungWhat we must be able to proveHow the BMA charges itHandbookWhat it means for the CIO
1. Full look-throughEvery underlying position as of the valuation date, valued on EBS rules (the Economic Balance Sheet, the BMA's market-consistent valuation basis)Each underlying asset in its own risk module: bonds in fixed-income risk, equities in equity risk, and each counterparty in concentration riskB6.2(a), B6.3, B6.5, B6.6The fund costs what its contents cost. Yield is earned against the true charge.
2. Partial: target allocationA target asset allocation granular enough for the calculation, and evidence the fund is managed strictly to itCapital on the target allocation instead of the actual holdingsB6.7Acceptable for mandates with tight guidelines; needs the manager's attestation on file.
3. Partial: investment limitsThe fund's allocation limits, where no target allocation existsThe fund is assumed to invest to the maximum allowed in the highest-charge asset class first, then downwards until its limits are used upB6.8Deliberately punitive: the rules assume the worst mix the mandate allows.
4. No look-throughNothingThe whole investment is treated as an equity holding of type "Other" for capital purposesB6.2(d), B6.9An investment-grade bond fund we cannot see into is charged in the "other equities" bucket, the one the handbook uses for unlisted equities, hedge funds, commodities and other alternatives (C4.3m). Verify the "Other equities" factor in the current BSCR model; it is not printed in the handbook text.
Rung 1 Full look-through $300M fund -> $240M bonds + $60M equities, each charged as itself Rung 2 Target allocation $300M fund -> charged as 80/20 per the mandate, if strictly managed Rung 3 Investment limits $300M fund -> charged as the WORST mix the limits allow Rung 4 No look-through $300M fund -> $300M of "Other" equity (data quality decides the rung; the rung decides the charge)

Diagram: the BMA look-through ladder in handbook section B6, applied to one illustrative $300M fund. The capital difference between rung 1 and rung 4 is $300M multiplied by the gap between the "Other equities" factor and the blended factor of the underlying positions; both factors must be taken from the current BSCR model.

Four details make the ladder wider than it first looks:

  • It reaches beyond funds. The scope covers collective investment vehicles, segregated-account assets and liabilities, deposit assets and liabilities, other sundry assets and liabilities, and derivatives (B6.4), and it applies to fund-of-funds by iteration (B6.10). Funds held by ceding reinsurers and funds held under retrocession with identifiable assets are also reported on a look-through basis in Schedule IIC (the return's schedule of funds held by ceding reinsurers) (C5.4a), which is the same funds withheld data (premium the cedent keeps as collateral instead of paying it to us) that #collateral needs.
  • It reaches into three charges at once. Look-through applies to the shock-based market risks (equity, interest rate, currency), to fixed-income risk for bond funds, and to concentration risk (B6.1, B6.5). A fund stuck on rung 4 is mis-charged three times.
  • Schedule XXI is measured through it. A counterparty exposure "shall be reported on the valuation of individually underlying assets", that is, on look-through, for all amounts on the balance sheet, and the ten largest counterparties must include related or connected parties under the control and economic-interdependence tests that the counterparty section (#counterparty) describes (Instructions Affecting Concentration Risk, (b) and (c); C4.3i). A separate list, the ten largest unaffiliated counterparty exposures in the Schedule of Risk Management (Schedule V, not Schedule XXI), must include cash, investments including hedge funds, receivables, recoverables and letters of credit, on a look-through basis "if the information is available"; an insurer with no investing activity still lists its cash, bank by bank (C16.2.b.3, C16.2.b.4). That list is the one place the return puts asset and reinsurance counterparties side by side, which is why the asset graph and the counterparty graph must share one set of ultimates.
  • Hedge funds have a named fallback. Where the exact underlying holdings of a hedge fund (a lightly constrained fund whose positions change without notice) are not known, the BMA advises allocating the balance proportionately to the fund's approved investment guidelines and disclosing the method in an attachment (C3.iii). That is rung 2 or 3 in practice, and it needs the guidelines loaded as data, not as a PDF.

Long-term (Class C / D / E) reinsurers file Schedule XXI under the Long-Term handbook with the same look-through requirement for hedge funds and diversified fund-of-one structures (C18.ii) [BMA-LT]; the ladder itself is the same section B6 in both handbooks, so the design below does not change with class.

Why this is money and not compliance. "Where data is available" was the wrong phrase in v2. Under the ladder, unavailability is itself charged. Every fund on rung 4 is yield we are paying full-price capital for; every bond-heavy fund moved to rung 1 releases most of that capital for the same holdings. The CIO and CRO should treat the rung distribution as a managed number with an owner, exactly like duration or credit quality.

The KPI the board should see each quarter is the share of fund-type assets at each rung. The tiles below are illustrative targets for a mid-size reinsurer, not our current position; the first job of Phase 1 is to measure the real distribution.

85%+
Rung 1: full look-through (illustrative target; measure the baseline in Phase 1)
< 10%
Rung 2: target allocation, with manager attestation on file (illustrative)
< 5%
Rung 3: investment limits (illustrative)
0%
Rung 4: no look-through, charged as "Other" equity (illustrative target)
1. Inventory the wrappers
Every fund, CLO, ABS, fund-of-one, segregated account and deposit line from the investment book of record, tagged with its current rung and the reason.
2. Load the contents
Manager holdings files, trustee reports and CLO collateral tapes, mapped to the same security master as our direct holdings. This is data plumbing, not analytics.
3. Resolve the contents
Each underlying security to its issuer and global ultimate, so fund contents join the issuer view and the Schedule XXI grouping (next subsection).
4. Evidence the rung
For rung 2 and 3 funds, store the mandate, the target allocation or limits and the attestation, versioned, so the filed rung is reproducible at audit (see #op-model-governance).
5. Report and move
Rung distribution and the capital at stake per fund on the CIO's dashboard; a fund that cannot be moved down the ladder is a candidate for replacement, priced with the charge included.

8.3 Issuer hierarchy: who we are really lending to

Issuer concentration limits fail quietly when they are tested against legal names. A Delaware finance subsidiary, a Dutch holding company and a Tokyo parent can be three lines on three desks and one credit. The counterparty graph in #counterparty resolves cedents, reinsurers and banks to a global ultimate; the asset side needs the same resolution for every security we hold, and it comes from a different kind of feed.
