Diagram: the security-to-ultimate-parent chain the issuer view needs. The LEI (Legal Entity Identifier, a public 20-character code for one legal entity) is the join key that lets a bond issuer and a reinsurance counterparty be recognised as the same company.

Two vendor facts matter for the buy decision in the buy / integrate / build section (#vendors). Bloomberg's Legal Entity Data covers over four million public, private and government entities, cross-referenced to the LEI [BBG-1], and its Corporate Structure product is described in Bloomberg's own marketing (which we could read only in search results, so confirm the scope in the licence) as adding the immediate and ultimate parent, the obligor (the entity legally liable for the debt) and the LEI for over six million entities; ICE's Business Entity Service supplies issue-to-issuer-to-immediate-parent-to-ultimate-parent linkages [ICE-1]. One of these is probably already licensed by the investment team. D&B's family-tree linkage [DNB-LINKAGE] resolves companies, not securities; it is the right tool for cedents, brokers and sponsors and the wrong tool for a CUSIP. The asset graph therefore has two entry points and one set of ultimates. INTEGRATE the security hierarchy; BUILD the merge to the counterparty graph's global ultimate, because that join is specific to our own counterparties and none of the feeds reviewed here delivers it ready-made.

Worked example: one credit, three desks, four holdings (illustrative)

The fixed-income desk holds $60M of senior notes issued by Kestrel Finance LLC (Delaware). The fund desk holds a $500M unit of the Global IG Bond Fund, of which 6% is Kestrel-entity paper: $30M on look-through. Structured credit holds a $40M tranche of CLO 2024-1, managed by Kestrel Asset Management, with $6M of loans in the pool to Kestrel-sponsored companies. Treasury holds $25M of operating cash at Kestrel Bank NA, which also issues a $30M letter of credit in our favour. Ceded reinsurance carries $50M of recoverables (money a reinsurer owes us for losses we have paid or reserved) from Kestrel Re. Legal-name limits see a bond fund, a CLO and three unrelated Kestrel names, the largest at $60M. The issuer hierarchy resolves the asset-side legs to Kestrel Group (Tokyo): $60M + $30M + $6M + $25M = $121M, which is what Schedule XXI's control test surfaces; on Atlantic Re's invested assets of $5,500M and statutory capital and surplus (the capital the regulator counts, roughly assets minus liabilities on the statutory basis) of $2,000M (illustrative) that is 6.1% of capital. The counterparty graph in #counterparty adds the legs Schedule XXI does not carry: the $50M recoverable (a Schedule XVIII item) takes the enterprise exposure to $171M, 8.6% of capital, with a further $30M of contingent reliance on the same group through the LOC. Example 1 at the end of this section (#ai-worked-examples) works the asset-side capital consequence of the $121M in detail; the recoverable and collateral legs are worked in the counterparty section.

8.4 The BMA's 2024 papers: the live constraint on yield

In August and September 2024 the BMA published three papers that describe what it now expects to see behind the higher-yielding parts of a reinsurer's balance sheet: collateral structures (6 September 2024; asset-intensive reinsurance, funds withheld and modified coinsurance (modco: a treaty where the cedent keeps the assets backing the ceded reserves), with approval granted more readily where collateral is high quality and the structure is robust), liquidity risk (30 August 2024; a liquidity management framework, regulatory and internal stress testing, board-approved programmes, and a 105% liquidity coverage ratio, which the BMA's report states long-term insurers must meet: liquid assets worth at least 105% of the outflows in a severe stress), and private credit (5 September 2024; direct loans, CLOs and private placements, with "regular bottom-up stress testing and scenario analysis" and thorough CISSA coverage, the insurer's own Commercial Insurer's Solvency Self-Assessment). All three rest on the prudent person principle (the rule that an insurer must invest as a careful owner would, only in assets it understands, can value and can monitor) [BMA-2024-PAPERS]; the liquidity report itself is public [BMA-LIQ].

Plain English: the private-credit and structured yield the CIO wants is available only inside a measured framework. The BMA is not saying "hold less"; it is saying "show us the contents, the liquidity under stress and the concentration, from the bottom up". All three papers, and the 105% liquidity coverage ratio in particular, are written about the long-term (life and annuity) market, and a general-business reinsurer [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E] should treat them as the direction of supervisory expectation and verify which requirements bind its class against the current instructions; a Class C / D / E reinsurer should treat all three papers as directly applicable, since they are addressed to asset-intensive long-term business.

None of this is extra work if the asset graph is built as described: the evidence the BMA asks for is a by-product of the data the ladder already requires. The alternative, producing it by hand for each on-site review, is the cost the compliance budget was meant to remove.

8.5 What "asset concentration" should look like in the winning system

The v2 list of twelve dimensions stands. What was missing was the question each one answers, the plain-English reason a non-investor should care, and the columns that turn a list into a decision. All measures are computed on look-through positions resolved to global ultimate; a dimension measured on wrappers and legal names is a dimension that will be wrong on the day it matters.

The top concentration dimensions and the question each answers
#DimensionQuestion it answersPlain-English example
1Global ultimate issuerHow much of our capital rides on one corporate family?Kestrel Group across bonds, loans, deposits, LOCs and recoverables (example above)
2Legal issuerWhich entity actually owes us, and under which law?Kestrel Finance (Delaware) is the obligor even though the credit is Tokyo's
3Industry / sectorAre we long one economy?Regional banks, data-center REITs (listed property companies) and utilities can all be one AI-capex bet
4Country / regionWhere does a sovereign, currency or legal shock land?Corporate bonds whose parents are Japanese are Japanese risk whatever the issuing entity
5Rating / NAIC designationHow much sits one notch above a cliff?The NAIC designation is the US regulator's 1-to-6 quality grade; a BBB- cliff is a forced-sale risk under both NAIC and BSCR factors
6Asset class and look-through rungWhat is charged as what, and why?A bond fund on rung 4 is charged as "Other" equity
7Private-credit sponsorWhich one manager's underwriting are we trusting?Three direct-lending funds from one sponsor share one origination team and one style
8Fund / managerWhich operational relationship could fail?Manager default, key-person and valuation risk concentrate by manager, not by fund
9Mortgage / real-estate geographyDoes our asset side share a peril with our liability side?Commercial mortgages in Florida sit under the same wind we reinsure (the hexagon accumulation view in the insurance-risk section, #ins-chain, can host them)
10Structured-finance collateralWhat is inside the CLO and ABS tranches?Two CLOs from different arrangers can hold the same leveraged loans
11CurrencyWhat moves if the dollar moves?Unhedged EUR assets against USD liabilities is a market charge and a mismatch
12Liquidity / maturity bucketWhat can we sell in 30 days without a loss, and what can we not?The 2024 liquidity paper's stress asks exactly this; private credit is in the "cannot" bucket

For each dimension the dashboard carries the same seven columns, so that every view reads the same way and a limit breach on any of them routes to the same owner:

Dimension row (one per value, e.g. one per global ultimate) Exposure $ look-through, EBS valuation, resolved to global ultimate % of total assets % of statutory capital & surplus Internal limit from the limit register (#op-appetite), with utilisation BSCR charge attributable including the look-through rung and the concentration charge Stress loss bottom-up scenario per the 2024 private-credit expectations Trend quarter on quarter, with the date of the last data refresh Top contributing positions the securities, funds and accounts that make up the row

Diagram: the dashboard columns. "BSCR charge attributable" is the column v2 lacked; it is what turns a concentration view into a capital decision.

Worked example: a dimension row the CIO acts on (illustrative)

Dimension 7, private-credit sponsor. Row: Falcon Capital, the sponsor that Scenario I in the scenarios section found. Exposure $120M across three funds and a direct co-investment loan, all on rung 1 once Fund Gamma's holdings file arrived (the committee made it a condition). 2.2% of invested assets ($5,500M) and 6.0% of statutory capital ($2,000M) against the sponsor limit of 5% of capital ($100M) that Scenario I set: 120% utilised, breached. Stress loss under the bottom-up private-credit scenario $14M. Trend: up from 4.2% of capital two quarters ago as new commitments funded. Top contributors: Fund Alpha ($38M), Fund Beta ($31M), Fund Gamma ($26M), the direct co-investment loan ($25M). Decision: the CIO pauses the fourth fund commitment, the CRO records the breach and the remediation, and the CISSA narrative for the year quotes this row. Without look-through the row would have shown three fund names on rung 4, a larger capital charge, and no sponsor at all.

8.6 Sources of truth: our books, then the market

The authoritative current position for our own company comes from internal investment accounting and custody: the investment book of record (Clearwater Analytics is the usual candidate for an insurer, with multi-basis GAAP, statutory and IFRS accounting and NAIC and Solvency II reporting [CWAN-1]) and the custodian's holdings files. Security-level risk decomposition by factor, sector and issuer comes from an existing risk platform such as Aladdin Risk [ALDN-1]; we do not rebuild it. The issuer hierarchy comes from Bloomberg or ICE as above. The buy / integrate / build section (#vendors) lists these as three separate rows for that reason: book of record, risk analytics and entity hierarchy are three different purchases.

S&P Global's SNL Insurance Regulatory Data carries the statutory filings of 8,800+ U.S. P&C and life entities (NAIC) and EU insurers (EIOPA / Solvency II): investments from Schedule B, BA and D parts 1 to 5, enriched with issuer type and duration; reinsurance relationships from Schedule F/S; and loss and reserve history from Schedule P [SP-SNL]. Plain English: it tells us what every U.S.-filing cedent and reinsurer owns, whom they reinsure with, and how their reserves have developed. It is for benchmarking counterparties and cedents, and for the wrong-way risk question in #counterparty (the risk that a counterparty fails in the same scenario that makes us need it) (does our cedent hold the same assets we do?), not for our own books.

Important: S&P / SNL should never replace our books and records. The filed Schedule XXI and the concentration charge are computed from the investment book of record and custody, on EBS valuation, and reconciled to Form 1EBS (the economic balance sheet form in the return, whose asset lines the concentration charge is computed from); SNL is a second opinion about other people's balance sheets. OPTIONAL for Phase 1, PHASE 2 for cedent and counterparty benchmarking.
Key takeaway: on the asset side, data quality is a capital factor. The BMA's look-through ladder charges what we cannot prove at the top rate, Schedule XXI is measured through the same look-through and the same control and interdependence tests as the liability side, and the 2024 papers make bottom-up evidence the price of private-credit yield. Build one asset graph on resolved issuers and fund contents, report the rung distribution as a managed KPI, and the compliance filing, the capital release and the CIO's yield strategy become the same piece of work.

8.7 Worked examples: from the balance sheet to the accumulation grid

Six situations, each worked with numbers, that show what the enterprise engine measures on the balance sheet and in the underwriting book, why the headline number is usually wrong, and what decision each one leads to. Every figure below is illustrative unless it carries a citation. The company is Atlantic Re, the reference company used throughout: capital $2,000M (the default in the counterparty calculator) and invested assets $5,500M, so the percentages are comparable across examples and with the scenarios; the 6%-of-capital single-group sub-limit in Example 1 is the CIO's desk sub-limit inside the 7.5% amber line (the same 6% that counterparty Example 2 applies) in the limit framework, tighter than the calculator's 10% default.

How to read this section. The asset examples (1 and 2) belong to the CIO and CRO. The accumulation examples (3 to 6) belong to the CUO, Portfolio Mgmt and CRO. The CFO should read the capital consequence in each. The regulatory mechanics cited are from the BMA 2024 Year-end General Business Capital and Solvency Return instructions (the 2025 edition, published 18 December 2025, supersedes it and must be re-checked before filing); where a value could not be verified in the documents we checked, the example says "verify".

Example 1. Issuer look-through: one group hiding in four holdings

The look-through section explains Look-through and the BMA's four-rung ladder of partial look-through. This example shows what it does to one number. Plain English: if we own $500M of a bond fund and 6% of that fund is one company's paper, we own $30M of that company, whatever the fund is called, and the BMA measures the concentration charge on that $30M, valued on the EBS (economic balance sheet, the BMA's market-value basis) [BMA-GB] (Instructions Affecting Concentration Risk, b) and d)).

Worked example: Kestrel Group across the investment book (illustrative, $ millions)

Kestrel Group is a diversified financial and industrial group with a finance subsidiary, a bank and an asset-management arm. Each holding below was booked by a different desk under a different name. The Global ultimate vs domestic ultimate distinction matters here: the global ultimate (the highest parent anywhere in the world) is Kestrel Group for all four.

The BSCR consequence. The concentration-risk charge is a separate capital charge, on top of the ordinary market and credit charges, that applies to all exposures to the ten largest asset counterparties. The handbook is explicit that a counterparty exposure is measured on the look-through basis, that a counterparty includes all related or connected counterparties (control, or economic interdependence), and that amounts are on an EBS valuation and unconsolidated basis [BMA-GB] (D6.1 to D6.3, "Instructions Affecting Concentration Risk" a) to d); Schedule XXI, C31.1 to C31.2g). The charge is the sum, over asset classes and BSCR rating buckets, of a BMA factor times the asset value. Kestrel at $60M is outside our top ten; Kestrel at $115M to $121M (depending on whether the CLO collateral is grouped) is inside it, and once inside every dollar enters the charge. The factors are published in Table 5A of the Class 4 and 3B Solvency Requirement Rules as amended in 2024 (the handbook itself only points to the asset values in Schedule XXIA column H): for example 0.4% on AAA bonds, 0.8% on AA, 1.5% on A, 3.0% on BBB, 0.1% to 0.3% on cash at a rated bank, 1.8% to 3.5% on A to BBB asset-backed tranches, and 35% on listed equity. For Kestrel as an A-rated group the blended factor is about 1.3%, so the $121M attracts roughly $1.6M of additional required capital for as long as we hold it (a standing requirement reported in every quarterly and annual return, not a recurring cost); a BBB group would attract about twice that, and an equity stake 35%. Verify the factors against the Rules current for the entity's class before filing.

Why the $40M CLO tranche is shown separately. Owning a tranche managed by Kestrel is not lending to Kestrel. If Kestrel fails, the loans in the pool do not disappear, but the manager may be replaced and the tranche repriced. That is an operational dependency for us and a judgement call under the BMA's economic-interdependence test (the CLO keeps paying if Kestrel fails, so we would not group it, but we record why), so it sits in its own row, the same logic that the counterparty section applies to letters of credit.

Decision. CIO proposes: stop new Kestrel purchases immediately; let the 2031 notes run off or sell $21M to return to $100M, inside the $120M sub-limit with headroom; ask the bond-fund manager for a monthly look-through file so the number is not a quarterly surprise. CRO records the breach, the plan and the expiry date.

Key takeaway: the number that is filed and charged is the grouped, looked-through number. If the investment book cannot produce it daily, we will discover it on the day the return is prepared, which is the most expensive day to find it.

Example 2. Structural concentration: a sector limit, a breach, four ways out

Structural concentration is exposure to a characteristic rather than a name: one sector, one country, one rating band, one sponsor, one currency. It rarely fails as a single default; it fails as a correlated repricing. For a reinsurer it has a special twist, wrong-way risk: the same shock that hits the assets can hit the liabilities. A technology-sector credit sell-off and a wave of data center construction claims are not independent.

The enterprise engine shows that the same sector already carries $190M of allocated insurance capital, so the true question is whether the company wants more of one economic bet, on both sides of the balance sheet, in exchange for the loan's spread. That is a CEO-level question, and the engine turns it into one page.

How to read an EP curve (for the accumulation examples that follow)

Every accumulation number below comes from a catastrophe model's loss distribution. Four terms carry the whole story.

AAL, average annual loss

The long-run yearly average of modelled loss. It is the pure premium: what we would pay out per year, on average, over thousands of simulated years. It says nothing about how bad one year can be.

EP curve, exceedance probability

For each loss size X, the probability of losing more than X in a year. The return period is one divided by that probability: a 1-in-100 loss has a 1% chance every year. It is not a calendar; over 30 years the chance of at least one 1-in-100 year is about 26%.

OEP vs AEP

OEP counts the single largest event in a year; AEP counts all events in the year added together. Occurrence retro layers, reinstatements and per-event treaty limits respond to OEP. Aggregate covers, capital and the BMA charge respond to AEP. AEP is always at least OEP.

PML and TVaR (tail value at risk)

A PML is one point on one of those curves: always say which curve, which return period, gross or net. TVaR 99% is the average of the worst 1% of years, which is the BMA's yardstick: net, annual aggregate, including reinstatement premiums, for the year following the relevant year [BMA-GB] (Instructions linked to C19, Schedule X, items a) and b); D10.3 to D10.5).

Worked example: one Florida wind EP curve, gross of retro (illustrative, $ millions)

1-in-502%380430Retro attachment decisions

Two "1-in-100" numbers on the same book differ by 40% here, and by more in multi-storm seasons. Every chart in the app carries the curve, the return period and the basis in its label; a number without those three words is not allowed on a slide.

Example 3. Accumulation on the H3 grid: five cells and one facultative offer

An H3 cell is one hexagon in a global grid that comes in 16 sizes, called resolutions. The engine converts each insured location to a cell and aggregates by cell, so that the campus, the metro and the region are the same data rolled up three ways. Three resolutions do most of the work [H3-RES].

ResolutionAverage cell areaAverage edge lengthWhat it representsQuestion it answersWho uses it
r5about 253 km²about 9.9 kmA metro or a countyHow much of the Florida or Bay Area book sits in one storm or fault footprint?CRO, Board heat-map
r7about 5.2 km²about 1.4 kmA campus, an industrial park, a substation's immediate service areaDo our treaty and facultative positions overlap on the same campus, and does the retro treat it as one risk?Portfolio Mgmt, underwriters
r9about 0.1 km²about 200 mOne building or one hallWhich building is the largest single-fire-division exposure, for terrorism and per-risk retro?Underwriters, engineering

The cell numbers are after contract terms: each contract's event-loss table (the model's list of simulated events with the loss each one causes to that contract) is run through attachment, limit, share and reinstatements first, then allocated to cells. Summing ground-up modelled loss by cell gives the cedent's loss, not ours; that financial-structure layer is what the insurance section calls the contract engine. Three capital numbers must be kept apart: allocated capital (the cell's share of today's total capital under a coherent rule such as contribution to 99% TVaR; additive, right for maps), stand-alone capital (what a deal would need on its own), and marginal capital (how much total capital rises if the deal is added now; not additive, right for pricing and line decisions). The map carries allocated capital; marginal capital is computed on demand against the live book.

Example 4. A peak zone: Florida wind, gross, ceded, net, and the capacity envelope

Retrocession is the reinsurance a reinsurer buys. For a reinsurer, "ceded" and "retro" describe the same transaction: what we pass on to our retrocessionaires. A reinstatement premium is the extra premium we owe to restore a retro layer after a loss has used it; it falls due exactly when we are paying claims, which is why the BMA includes it in the net PML. It is charged pro rata to the limit restored: a full 350 recovery costs the whole 21 layer premium, a 300 recovery costs 18. A capacity envelope is the amount of additional exposure, expressed in the risk-appetite measure, that Portfolio Management (the function that owns the shape of the book rather than any one deal) hands to the underwriters for a renewal season, with the price it must earn.

Example 5. Geographic diversification that hides one substation

Three risks 15 to 40 km apart sit in three different r7 cells and three different r5 cells, all green. They share one 345 kV substation with a single transformer bank whose replacement lead time is measured in years. This is the accumulation that Mega Project Asset Intelligence exists to find, and it must be measured in the right unit. Loss of off-premises power does not damage the buildings; it triggers contingent business interruption (CBI, cover for lost income caused by damage at a supplier, here the utility) under a sublimited extension with a waiting period (most wordings also require physical damage at the utility's plant and many exclude overhead transmission lines), and for a project under construction it triggers delay in start-up (DSU, cover for the lost income caused by late completion). Full TIV only accumulates if the dependency is also a common physical cause, such as a shared flood plain or wildfire corridor.

Worked example: two data centers and a fab on the Bluff Creek substation (illustrative, $ millions)

Scenario J in the scenarios is the facultative offer that lands on this yard as its fourth tenant; the Kintigh rows in the data center map section are a real cluster of the same shape from the prototype's ledger.

Total 160 from one event, before retro. Whether our retro sees it as one occurrence depends on the retro wording's definition of an event, which the contract engine holds as data. This is also a clash: one event reaching two treaties and one facultative certificate that were priced as if unrelated.

How it is discovered. Not from coordinates. The dependency graph stores a SUPPLIED_BY relationship from each canonical mega-project asset to its substation, from the utility's interconnection filings (the prototype's 212 edges each cite a PJM or NYISO filing) and, once licensed, the S&P 451 and Verisk data center references, and the query is a few lines.

MATCH (a:Asset)-[:SUPPLIED_BY]->(s:Substation) WHERE s.transformer_banks = 1 WITH s, collect(a) AS assets WHERE size(assets) > 1 RETURN s.name, [x IN assets | x.name] AS assets, reduce(t = 0, x IN assets | t + x.cbi_sublimit_our_share + x.dsu_our_share) AS dependency_accumulation ORDER BY dependency_accumulation DESC

Decision. Portfolio Mgmt adds Bluff Creek to the named-dependency list with a 200 limit; the fab's DSU share is not increased at renewal; the underwriter of DC-2 asks the cedent whether the campus has a second feed under construction, which is worth a credit if true. CRO notes that the AI campuses being written today are mostly under construction, so the DSU column, not the TIV column, is where the big number is.

Example 6. Cyber single point of failure: hundreds of insureds, one identity provider

A SPoF (single point of failure) in cyber is a technology that many insureds depend on at once: a cloud region, a software vendor, a payment processor, or an identity provider (the service that signs employees and customers into everything else; if it stops, so do they). Cyber reinsurance is mostly written as quota share (we take a fixed percentage of every policy) and aggregate excess of loss (we pay when the cedent's total losses from an event or a year exceed a threshold), so the accumulation is measured on ceded aggregates and event definitions, not per-risk lines. Two things make the number bigger than the cyber book suggests: silent cyber (cyber-caused loss under property, marine or casualty treaties that never mention cyber), and the fact that the Bermuda standard formula has no cyber catastrophe charge (cyber premium and reserves still take the ordinary premium and reserve risk charges, but there is no cyber scenario alongside the terrorism one), so the accumulation figure has to be our own estimate in the CISSA (the Commercial Insurer's Solvency Self-Assessment, Schedule IX, where we tell the regulator how much capital we think we need and why) [BMA-GB] (C18, C20.2; man-made perils listed are terrorism, credit and surety, marine and aviation).

What the six examples have in common. In each one the headline number, the one a single system produces, is smaller than the real one: 60 versus 121, 7.1% versus a two-sided bet, 22 versus 31, a 1-in-100 that reads 191 on one curve and 448 on the one the appetite is set on, three green cells versus 160 from one transformer, a cyber book versus 92 across cyber, property and investments. The engine's job is to produce the second number every day and to attach the decision and the owner to it. Insurance-risk accumulation: where our existing architecture is already strongest

Catastrophe accumulation, mega-project dependency risk, cyber single points of failure, and the data-center map that already exists as the prototype of the mega-project module.

CUOPortfolio MgmtCRO

An accumulation is simply how much of our money sits inside one shape on the map, or behind one event. This is the side of concentration risk where the company already has real tooling: a licensed catastrophe model, a working mega-project registry with a hexagon grid (the Mega Project subsection #mega and the data-center map subsection #dcmap), and a clear view of which cyber vendors to compare (#cyber). What is missing is the join between the assets we can see and the treaty and facultative lines we actually hold, and a consistent vocabulary for the numbers the map shows.

Verisk Touchstone supports zonal, event and other geospatial accumulation analyses: accumulating exposure inside Lloyd's realistic-disaster-scenario zones, custom zones, historical-event and scenario footprints. Every integration in this blueprint should therefore target Synergy Studio's APIs, with Touchstone as the bridge, and the migration is the natural moment to benchmark against Moody's RMS before renewing (see the buy table in #vendors). Diagram: the engine has three layers; the middle one (contract terms) is where a ground-up loss becomes our loss, and it is the layer most accumulation tools skip.

9.1 The five numbers every chart must name

Two "1-in-100" numbers can differ by a third depending on whether they count the worst single storm or the whole hurricane season. Every chart, table and hexagon in this system states which curve, which return period and which basis (gross or net of retrocession, the reinsurance we buy on our own book) it shows. The definitions below are the house standard.

AAL: average annual loss

The long-run yearly average loss from the model, in other words the pure premium before expenses and profit. If the model says a treaty loses $0 in most years, $30M in one year in ten and $200M in one year in a hundred, its AAL is roughly $5M a year.

EP curve: exceedance probability

The probability of losing more than X in a year, for every X. A "1-in-250" loss is the point on the curve with a 0.4% annual probability of being exceeded. It is a curve, not a number, so a single figure must always say where on the curve it was read.

OEP versus AEP

OEP (occurrence) is built from the single largest event in each year and drives per-occurrence treaties, per-occurrence retro layers and reinstatements. AEP (aggregate) sums all events in the year and drives capital and aggregate covers. AEP is always at least as large as OEP.

PML: probable maximum loss

The loss at a chosen point on one of those curves. "PML" on its own is meaningless: write "OEP 1-in-100 net" or "AEP 1-in-250 gross". Older engineering usage (the largest loss a single fire could plausibly cause) is a different concept and is labelled MFL or "engineering PML" here.

TVaR 99%: the BMA yardstick

The average of the worst 1% of years. The BMA's catastrophe charge uses the net PML at the 99.0% TVaR level on an annual-aggregate basis, after retrocession, including reinstatement premiums, for the year following the relevant year, and the modelled losses must include demand surge, storm surge, fire following earthquake, secondary uncertainty and second and subsequent events. [BMA-GB]

Return period and basis

Return period is 1 divided by the annual exceedance probability (1-in-250 = 0.4%). Basis is gross (before our retro) or net (after it). The regulator's number is net, aggregate, TVaR 99%; the underwriter's number for a per-occurrence line is usually gross OEP at the treaty's attachment. Both are right; they answer different questions.

Worked example: one season, two "1-in-100" numbers (illustrative)

Suppose a modelled year contains three storms that cost our property-cat book $60M, $40M and $30M gross. The occurrence loss for that year is $60M (the worst single storm); the aggregate loss is $130M. If years like this one sit at the 1-in-100 point, the OEP 1-in-100 is $60M and the AEP 1-in-100 is $130M. A per-occurrence retro layer of $50M excess of $25M pays $35M on the first storm, $15M on the second and $5M on the third, and each recovery costs a reinstatement premium; the BMA's net TVaR figure is computed after those recoveries and with those premiums added back. A dashboard that shows "$60M PML" beside "$130M PML" without labels will be read as a data error by the board and as a disclosure error by the auditor.

For a long-term reinsurer [Class C / D / E] there is no catastrophe module at all in the long-term BSCR; its tail shocks sit in the mortality, longevity, morbidity and stop-loss modules, but the same discipline applies: name the shock, the confidence level and the basis on every number.

9.2 From a hexagon to a portfolio number: the financial-structure layer

A $1bn ground-up loss in one hexagon might cost us $10M or $100M depending on where our treaty attaches, how much of the annual aggregate is already used up, and whether the cedent's own facultative cover pays first. The map shows where the exposure is; a contract engine turns it into what we would actually pay. Summing modelled loss by hexagon without applying contract terms produces the cedent's ground-up loss, not ours, and any capital or pricing number built on it is wrong in a way that always flatters the peak zones.

1. Place and event.
Each insured location sits in an H3 cell (a hexagon of a chosen size; defined in the H3 paragraph of #mega). Each modelled event has a footprint and an event code, so the same hurricane is recognised across every contract it touches.
2. Per-contract event loss table after terms.
For every treaty and fac position: ground-up loss to the cedent, less inuring covers and cedent retention, through attachment, limit, share, reinstatements, aggregate deductible, hours clause and occurrence definition. The output is an ELT or YLT (event or year loss table) per contract, on our paper.
3. Programme, entity, group.
Contracts roll up to the programme (the cedent's whole placement), then to our legal entity (the BMA return), then to the group (the group return and rating-agency view), with outward retro applied at the level where it attaches.
4. Curves and capital.
Only now are AAL, OEP, AEP and TVaR 99% computed, and only now is capital allocated back to cells, contracts and cedents.

Not every cedent gives us locations. The engine must carry three data-granularity tiers and show each honestly on the map:

TierWhat the cedent suppliesTypical businessHow the engine treats itHow the map shows it
Location-levelAddress or GPS, TIV, occupancy, construction, sometimes the insured nameFacultative, large-account treaties, mega-projectsModelled per location; joined to the mega-project registry by site_idPoints, and exact hexagon fills
Zone-levelAggregates by CRESTA zone (industry-standard accumulation zones), county, postcode bandMost property treatiesDisaggregated to cells with a stated method; the disaggregation is a model assumption and is versionedHexagon fills marked "disaggregated" with a hatch or badge
Cedent-model-outputOnly the cedent's own model results (their AAL and EP curve)Smaller cedents, some retroConverted to our view of risk with an adjustment factor per peril and region; never placed on a hexagonA cedent-level badge on the portfolio view, not on the map
Worked example: the same $1bn loss, two answers (illustrative)

A modelled event causes $1,000M of ground-up loss to a cedent's schedule inside one resolution-6 hexagon. The cedent has $150M of facultative cover on its largest building that inures to the treaty, and retains $300M. We write 25% of a $100M excess of $300M layer. After the fac pays, $850M remains; the layer attaches at $300M and is exhausted, so our share is $25M plus one reinstatement premium. Now suppose we also hold a $75M fac line on that largest building, written by a different underwriting team. The building's loss exceeds its facultative cover, so that cover pays in full and our $75M line (part of the $150M that inured to the treaty) pays $75M. Our loss from one hexagon is $100M, not $25M, and the extra $75M was invisible in the treaty accumulation because fac and treaty were never joined on the campus. That join is the single most valuable thing #mega delivers.

9.3 Three capital numbers, one map

The capital cost of a new data-center line depends on how many data centers we already have in that grid cell and that retro layer. So the number on the map is the deal's share of today's capital; the number the underwriter needs is what tomorrow's capital would be with the deal added. Both are useful; they must not be confused, and putting "marginal capital" on a hexagon is the usual way they get confused.

NumberPlain EnglishAdditive?Where it livesUsed for
Stand-alone capitalWhat the deal would need if it were our only riskNo (ignores diversification)Pricing tool, as a ceilingSanity check; treaty wording limits
Allocated capitalThe deal's share of total capital under a chosen rule, here the Euler contribution to 99% TVaR: the average loss the position contributes in the worst 1% of yearsYes: cells, contracts and cedents sum to the totalThe hexagon column allocated_capital; reports; RORAC historyReporting, heat maps, where the book earns its return
Marginal capitalHow much total required capital rises if we add this deal now, given everything already on the bookNo: depends on what is already there and on the order deals arriveComputed on demand in the Capacity Workbench against the live portfolioLine-size decisions, the RORAC price (expected profit divided by marginal capital), capacity envelopes
Worked example: one line, three numbers (illustrative)

A $50M fac line on a hyperscale campus needs $50M of capital stand-alone (on its own it could be a total loss). Under Euler allocation it carries $12M of the portfolio's capital, because in most of the book's bad years it does not lose. If the campus sits in a hexagon where we already hold $400M of treaty exposure, adding the line raises total required capital by $45M (marginal), because it loses in exactly the years the book already loses; in an empty hexagon the same line adds $20M. Expected margin $4M: RORAC is $4M divided by $20M, 20%, in the empty cell and $4M divided by $45M, 9%, in the peak cell, against a 12% hurdle. The map shows $12M; the underwriter must see $45M or $20M. The profit mechanics of this lever (lever 3) and the capital model it runs against are in #profit; the calculator after the H3 walkthrough below lets you move the line and watch the marginal number climb as the cell fills.

Which capital? The binding constraint for a Bermuda reinsurer is usually the BSCR (the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, the standard-formula capital number), then the ECR (the enhanced capital requirement the BMA enforces) and the TCL (the target capital level, 120% of the ECR, above which the BMA expects us to stay), then the rating-agency capital model, then internal economic capital. The engine must be able to run the marginal calculation against whichever binds, and #profit and #bma say which one binds today.

9.4 Non-natural accumulation: clash, contingent BI, casualty and man-made catastrophe

The scariest losses for a reinsurer are not one big building but one event that hits twenty of our contracts at once: a hurricane that triggers property, marine, energy and auto treaties, or a court ruling that hits every casualty cedent. Our engine must recognise the same event across contracts, not just the same place on a map.

Clash and the "one event" definition

Clash is one event producing losses under several of our contracts, cedents or classes. It is the reason treaty and fac overlap matters and the reason every loss carries an event code. Each contract's hours clause (how many hours of a storm count as one occurrence) and its occurrence definition decide how many "events" one hurricane is; the engine stores those terms and applies them per contract, then reconciles the event code across the book. Clash retro is bought on that basis and its attachment is where the accumulation report must stop being per-class. The per-risk mirror image is the retro programme's maximum any one risk (the most our retrocession will treat as a single risk: a building, a fire division or a campus within a stated distance); if our fac share plus our treaty shares on one campus exceed it, the excess is unprotected retained exposure, the second check the campus identifier makes possible (Scenario B in #scenarios, and the retro any-one-risk line in the calculator below).

Contingent BI and DSU

Contingent business interruption pays an insured for lost income when a supplier, customer or utility it depends on is damaged, not the insured's own property. Delay in start-up (DSU, also ALoP) is the construction-phase equivalent: the project opens late. Both are sublimited, carry waiting periods (often 24 to 72 hours for utility service) and often exclude overhead transmission lines. The mega-project dependency story in #mega produces loss through these extensions, which is why the accumulation is measured in sublimits and indemnity periods, not in full campus values.

Casualty accumulation

One defendant, product, chemical or court decision can hit every casualty treaty at once (asbestos, opioids, PFAS-type mass torts). The engine groups casualty exposure by industry, named insured group and product family, and the reserve concentration that results (one cedent, one class, one accident year) is what the BMA's reserve-risk charge and Schedule XI triangles are built on. #assets and #bma cover the balance-sheet side.

The BMA man-made module and terrorism

The standard formula's man-made catastrophe submodule covers terrorism, credit and surety, marine and aviation; the terrorism scenario is a concentration calculation: the sum insured for the largest building concentration, after deduction of amounts recoverable from outward reinsurance. The mega-project registry with footprints is exactly the tool that finds the largest single building concentration in the book. Cyber is not in this module (see #cyber). In the 2024 year-end handbook for Class 4, 3B and 3A insurers this is Schedule XA (section C20, with the scenarios described from D10.6 onward); confirm the reference against the handbook for the filing year before it is cited in a return. [BMA-GB]

Worked example: largest building concentration for the terrorism scenario (illustrative)

The registry's footprint layer joins three treaty schedules and one fac line to a single 120,000 square metre hall on a Northern Virginia campus: cedent A treaty $40M, cedent B treaty $25M, cedent C treaty $15M, our fac line $75M, total $155M gross on one building. Outward per-risk retro recovers $60M above a $95M retention, so the net figure the terrorism scenario uses is $95M. Without the campus identifier the four positions sit in four spreadsheets under three insured names (landlord, tenant and contractor) and the filed figure would be the largest of them, $75M: an understatement the BMA would treat as a data-quality finding. The charge itself is calibrated to a one-year 99% TVaR and its mechanics are in handbook section C20 and D10.6 to D10.8; #bma covers where the resulting capital moves.

The prototype already runs one non-modelled event pattern end to end: a USGS earthquake feed, ShakeMap footprints for events within 200 km of a registry site, and an exposure panel that lists shaken sites worst-first by intensity (#dcmap). That is the template for every peril: event footprint times asset registry, and a Verisk footprint would plug into the same panel.

9.5 Mega Project Asset Intelligence: already prototyped, now to be governed and joined to our book

This layer is not a future build. It is built. The data-center map in the repository is a governed registry of 6,285 live sites worldwide with campus boundaries, building footprints, 28,161 power plants, 214 semiconductor fabs, a substation dependency ledger of 212 edges citing their grid filings, a hexagon accumulation grid and a read-only Databricks deployment design. The full inventory with measured counts, file paths and licences is in #dcmap; this section says what the layer is for, what is true about the vendors around it, and where it stops.

What the prototype proves. Asset identity (one row per place, every source row cited), campus geometry, power and water dependency as data rather than inference, growth trajectory for AI sites, and on-site generation. HAVE  What it does not yet do. Join to treaty and fac lines, carry TIV or modelled loss, or compute allocated or marginal capital per campus. BUILD  The map becomes a profit lever the day a fac submission is matched to a campus and the existing treaty lines on that campus are shown beside it (Scenario B in #scenarios; lever 5 and lever 6 in #profit).

Whose interest is insured, and what a shared dependency really accumulates

A "$500M data center" fac risk must say whose interest is insured. The colocation landlord's shell and plant, the hyperscale tenant's IT equipment, and the contractor's builder's-risk policy with DSU during construction are three different insureds, three sets of values and three periods; the registry already sees this in its own data, where county deeds name the title-holder and OpenStreetMap names the tenant (STACK Infrastructure on the deed, Amazon Web Services in the building, 12 rows). The mega-project asset therefore carries an insured interest field (owner or landlord, tenant, contractor, lender) on every exposure joined to it, and this is the seam to the counterparty graph in #counterparty: the entity holding title is not the entity running the compute.

If a shared substation fails, the buildings are not damaged; the tenants lose revenue, and most policies pay only a limited amount for that after a waiting period. The shared-power problem is real but measured in sublimits, not in the full value of the campuses. During construction the bigger exposure is delay: a burnt transformer with a two-to-three-year lead time can stall a multi-billion-dollar project. The engine therefore reports two numbers for every dependency cluster.

Worked example: two campuses and a fab on one 345 kV yard (illustrative values on a real pattern)
AssetInsured interestTIV joined to itPhysical-damage accumulationDependency accumulation
Campus A, operatingLandlord shell $900M; tenant IT $1,100M$2,000MCounts only if the dependency is itself a common physical cause (flood plain, wildfire corridor, shared battery-storage fire)Utility service interruption sublimit $25M, 48-hour waiting period, overhead lines excluded
Campus B, under constructionContractor builder's risk $1,500M with DSU$1,500MAs aboveDSU: $12M per month for a 24-month indemnity period, capped at $150M; a transformer outage is the credible trigger
Fab, operatingOwner-operator $4,000M$4,000MAs aboveCBI sublimit $20M, 72-hour waiting period
Cluster$7,500M$7,500M only under a common physical cause$195M

The pattern is not hypothetical: the prototype's ledger shows 1,050 MW of live interconnection-queue positions from two campuses 35 km apart hanging off one substation in western New York, each row linked to its NYISO filing (worked example in #dcmap). What the join to our book adds is the two right-hand columns, and the question "which of our treaties and fac lines sit on those campuses" that neither column can answer today. The same pattern is worked with different illustrative values as Example 5 in #ai and as Scenario C in #scenarios; the three agree on the method (physical damage only under a common cause, dependency measured on sublimits and DSU) and differ only in the numbers chosen.

Parcels: Regrid, and what the prototype already does with it

Traditional exposure files carry address, GPS, TIV (total insured value: the sum of building, contents and business-interruption values at a location) and a broad occupancy, usually without the insured business name. Regrid resolves a GPS point or address to a standardised parcel (the legal lot of land), its owner, matched addresses, zoning and building footprint; the API has a point-lookup endpoint that takes latitude and longitude and covers 160M+ parcels (all U.S. counties, plus Canada and parts of Europe). Regrid bills by parcel records returned, not by call: "returned means billed", empty responses are free, and a point search with a radius returns and bills every parcel inside the circle. Self-serve plans include 2,000 records a month with $0.10 (Standard) or $0.15 (Premium) per additional record; above 10,000 records a month Regrid moves you to an enterprise licence. Calls are limited to about 200 per minute and 10 concurrent. [REGRID-API] [REGRID-BILL] [REGRID-PLANS]

The prototype already caches every resolved parcel per site with a placement-aware invalidation rule (a cached parcel counts only while the current dot is inside it; an empty answer is re-asked once the dot moves more than 50 m, because an empty answer costs nothing and hides every parcel the county has added since) and a paid-run guard that refuses a billed run without explicit confirmation (file references and cache counts are in #dcmap). Regrid is one of six parcel sources beside Precisely, IGN France, HM Land Registry, Registers of Scotland and Japan's Ministry of Justice, plus 179 free county and state layers that cover most U.S. sites. The enterprise build keeps both rules, moves the cache into a Unity Catalog table (the Databricks governance layer, #databricks), uses a zero or minimal radius, and de-duplicates cedent locations before calling. Precisely's bulk-licensed Parcel Boundaries and Buildings is the challenger if procurement prefers a one-off nationwide load over per-record billing. [RG-5] HAVE

Data-center reference feeds: two vendors, one canonical campus

S&P Global Market Intelligence's Datacenter & Energy Intelligence joins the 451 Research Datacenter KnowledgeBase (facility-level data-center records) with Capital IQ Pro power-plant and transmission data. Its published proximity method finds power projects within a set radius (S&P's example uses 25 miles) of planned data centers and flags transmission constraints, interconnection queues and grid connectivity, which is exactly the shared-dependency signal this layer needs. The prototype already computes a "generation within 25 km" column from open sources, so S&P 451 is an optional paid overlay to be tested against what the open sources give. [SP-451] [SP-3] OPTIONAL

Verisk now sells a U.S. Data Center Exposure Database (launched 3 September 2026): building-level geocodes, footprints and physical and operational attributes for more than 2,500 U.S. facilities, usable inside Touchstone and Synergy Studio. We should license it as a second reference feed, not as a replacement for Mega Project Asset Intelligence: it is U.S.-only, data-center-only, and one vendor's view. Our layer's job is to reconcile Verisk, S&P 451 and open sources into one canonical campus, add semiconductor fabs, power plants and shared dependencies, cover the more than 130 countries the registry already spans (139 when the architecture document measured it on 2026-09-23; the current registry file carries 158 country codes), and keep our own verified coordinates when vendors disagree. [VER-DCDB] PHASE 2

The map stack, corrected

The prototype renders on MapLibre GL JS (open-source, GPU-accelerated vector maps) with PMTiles basemaps (a single file of map tiles served straight from object storage by HTTP range requests, no tile server and no per-tile bill) and h3-js for the hexagon grid. That is the default stack for the Mega Risk Map. Esri ArcGIS Location Platform is an optional upgrade for premium basemaps, imagery, feature services and enterprise permissions: 2 million free basemap tiles a month, then $0.15 per 1,000, plus 1,000 free basemap sessions then $4 per 1,000. The often-quoted "2 million" figure is a basemap-tile allowance, not an API-call cap, and it is irrelevant when tiles are self-hosted. Esri's actual roles today are as a public-records protocol (ArcGIS REST point queries against the 179 county parcel and permit services) and as one option for licensed satellite imagery on a shared deployment, a Phase 0 decision. [ESRI-PRICE] [MAPLIBRE] [PMTILES] HAVE

Geocoding (turning an address into coordinates) is priced by results returned: 20,000 free per month then $0.50 per 1,000 if the result is not stored, but $4 per 1,000 with no free tier if we keep the result, and this architecture keeps every result. Budget the Esri geocoder as a paid, stored service or geocode once through an alternative and store our own coordinates. [ESRI-GEOCODE]

One measured engineering limit shapes the enterprise map: MapLibre's rendering worker fails silently at roughly 189,000 vertices in one browser-side layer, and a cedent location file of a few hundred thousand risks would hit it immediately. The answer already designed (#dcmap and #databricks) is zoom-banded: H3 hexagons at resolutions 3 to 6 when zoomed out, viewport-clipped and capped dots when zoomed in, and server-side filtering, search and framing. The hexagon grid is therefore the executive view by necessity, not a nice-to-have.

H3: the accumulation grid

H3 lays a grid of hexagons over the world at 16 sizes ("resolutions"); resolution 9 cells are roughly a city block, resolution 6 roughly a town, so the same insured location rolls up cleanly from campus to metro to region, independent of county, ZIP or CRESTA (the insurance industry's standard accumulation zones) boundaries, and every neighbour of a hexagon is the same distance away, which squares cannot offer. Use the H3 v4 API (h3-js 4.5, July 2026): the function is latLngToCell; older examples using geoToH3 are the v3 name. The prototype bins every site with h3.latLngToCell, offers resolutions 2 to 7 by hand or chooses one automatically so a cell is never narrower than 16 px on screen, and the 2D map and the 3D globe bin into identical cells; the Databricks design already writes the same grid server-side as a GROUP BY h3_longlatash3(...) into pre-aggregated serving tables and flags the H3 Java 3.7.0 versus h3-js 4.5 parity test. This is built for the registry's own measures (count, MW, project value, floor area, year built); the enterprise step adds the insurance measures to the same cells. [H3-AGG] [H3-JS] [DBX-5] HAVE ADD INSURANCE MEASURES

How H3 accumulation works on the Mega Risk Map (seven steps and the column list, about one minute)
Convert every insured location to an H3 cell. HAVE
latLngToCell(latitude, longitude, resolution) with h3-js v4 in the browser, or h3_longlatash3 in Databricks SQL; both must agree, and the parity test proves it.
Choose multiple resolutions. HAVE
Fine resolution for campus and building clusters; coarser for metro, regional and portfolio views. Resolution is chosen by on-screen cell width so a cell is never a smear and never a continent.

H3 is the accumulation index; parcels supply geometry; the registry supplies canonical campus and dependency relationships.

Data-use governance: resolving a cedent's anonymised location to a named owner

Cedents give us their exposure data to price their treaty, not necessarily so we can identify their clients and compare them with a competitor's book. Most wordings allow portfolio accumulation; fewer allow re-identification; EU and UK cedents add data-protection law. Before the map makes it easy, the operating model in #operating keeps a data-use register: for each cedent and broker feed, the permitted purposes (pricing this treaty; portfolio accumulation; cross-cedent analytics), retention, and whether re-identification of insureds is allowed. The default is accumulation-only use, with named-owner resolution held behind an access control and logged. The parallel licence constraint on the registry's own data (ODbL share-alike on OpenStreetMap-derived geometry: internal use is safe; a public or paid release merging it with licensed parcels needs a decision and counsel) is set out in #dcmap and #operating.

9.6 Cyber accumulation

Cyber losses do not respect the line of business they were written in. A cloud-region outage can trigger cyber policies, property business-interruption extensions and technology E&O at the same time. The Bermuda standard formula has no cyber charge, so we must show the regulator our own estimate, and the same campus we map for fire is the one whose outage we should model for cyber.

Affirmative cyber

Policies and treaties that explicitly cover cyber events. Cyber reinsurance is overwhelmingly quota share (we take a fixed percentage of every policy and of every loss) and aggregate excess of loss (we pay once the cedent's total cyber losses in a year exceed an attachment, up to a limit). Accumulation is therefore measured on ceded aggregates and on event definitions (waiting periods before an outage counts, hours clauses that decide how many "events" a multi-day incident is), not on per-risk lines. Per-risk cyber facultative exists but is a small part of the book and is not where the systemic accumulation sits.

Silent cyber

Non-affirmative cyber: property, marine, energy, casualty and specialty treaties that never mention cyber but would respond to a cyber-caused fire, explosion, spill or liability. This is the accumulation regulators worry about most because it is not priced, not limited and not in any cyber model by default. The engine tags every treaty with its cyber position (affirmative, excluded, silent) and includes the silent share in every systemic scenario.

War and state-backed exclusions

Whether a systemic event is covered at all depends on attribution. The Lloyd's market has required standalone cyber policies written or renewed since 31 March 2023 to carry a state-backed cyber-attack exclusion (the LMA model clauses LMA5564 to LMA5567, revised in January 2023, or a legally reviewed equivalent); many non-Lloyd's cedents use the same wordings, many do not, and the wording on each treaty and each underlying policy decides how much of a state-attributed event reaches us. The engine stores the exclusion wording and the attribution assumption on every scenario. [LLOYDS-1]

CISSA, because the formula is silent

The BMA man-made catastrophe submodule covers terrorism, credit and surety, marine and aviation; cyber is not in it. Cyber accumulation must therefore be quantified in the CISSA (the Commercial Insurer's Solvency Self-Assessment, Schedule IX: the insurer's own view of the capital it needs, which the BMA reviews alongside the formula). The systemic scenarios below, their probabilities and the silent-cyber share are the CISSA evidence; #bma covers the filing. [BMA-GB]

Cyber concentration is not primarily geographic. It concentrates through shared cloud providers, software, identity infrastructure, payment providers and other single points of failure. CyberCube Portfolio Manager is the cyber portfolio model (it quantifies attritional and catastrophe cyber loss and shows how a retro structure changes volatility, capital and retained loss), and CyberCube SPoF Intelligence is a data add-on that maps each insured's digital supply chain (cloud, software, identity, payment providers) so that single points of failure shared across cedents can be found and stressed. The challengers are Verisk Cyber Risk Navigator (worth comparing while the Verisk relationship is renegotiated for Synergy Studio), Guidewire Cyence and Kovrr, each a credible second opinion on portfolio accumulation; the buy decision and cost sit in #vendors and #profit. [CYB-PM] [CYB-RE] [CYB-SPOF] [CYB-4] [CYB-5] [CYB-6] BUY IF MATERIAL

The link that only we can make. A hyperscale campus is simultaneously a property risk and a cloud-region dependency. The canonical mega-project asset in #mega is the same node that CyberCube's SPoF data calls a cloud region or hosting provider, so one asset record carries the property TIV, the CBI sublimits and the cyber dependent-BI exposure of every cedent whose insureds run on it. When the campus is the subject of a fac quote, the underwriter sees the cyber aggregate that already depends on it; when a cloud outage scenario runs, it lists the property and DSU positions on the same campus. No vendor offers that join because no vendor holds both books.

SHARED CLOUD REGION = MEGA-PROJECT CAMPUS (#mega) │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┬──────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Cedent A Cedent B Cedent C Cedent D cyber QS cyber agg XoL property BI tech E&O (affirmative) (affirmative) (silent / ext.) (affirmative) └─────────────┴──────┬──────┴──────────────┘ ▼ ONE EVENT CODE · waiting period · hours clause · war exclusion ▼ Cyber accumulation loss → CISSA scenario → portfolio capital

Diagram: one outage, four contract types, one event code; the campus at the top is the same record as in #mega.

Worked example: a 36-hour cloud-region outage (illustrative)

An outage at a hyperscale region hosted on a campus in our registry lasts 36 hours and is attributed to a criminal group, not a state. Cedent A cedes 40% of a cyber book on quota share: its insureds' dependent-BI claims after 12-hour waiting periods total $50M, so we pay $20M. Cedent B has a cyber aggregate excess-of-loss with a $75M attachment and $100M limit, and had used $30M of aggregate already this year; the outage adds $60M, so the aggregate reaches $90M and the layer pays $15M. Cedent C's property treaty is silent on cyber; its insureds' utility-and-service-interruption extensions respond after 24-hour waiting periods for $8M to our share. Cedent D's technology E&O treaty picks up $12M of claims against a software vendor that ran on the region. Total $55M from one event across four treaties in three classes, of which $8M was never priced as cyber. The same event with a state attribution and Lloyd's-style exclusions on cedents A and B would pay $20M; without exclusions on the property and E&O treaties, the silent share is unchanged. The CISSA scenario records both numbers and the attribution assumption.

For a long-term reinsurer [Class C / D / E] cyber is an operational-risk and third-party dependency question rather than an underwriting accumulation; the same SPoF data serves the outsourcing register, and the CISSA is the same place to show it.

Key takeaway: the insurance side is where we are furthest ahead and where the numbers are most easily misread. Name every curve, return period and basis; put a contract engine between the hexagon and the portfolio; show allocated capital on the map and compute marginal capital on demand; recognise one event across contracts, not one place; and join the mega-project registry we already have to the treaty and fac book, because that join is the profit lever and the terrorism, CBI and cyber scenarios all run through the same campus record.

9.7 The data-center map: what already exists, and where it fits

The data-center map (dcmap) is the working prototype of Mega Project Asset Intelligence (#mega) and the proof that this team can build the enterprise layer: a governed registry, a dependency graph, a hexagon accumulation grid and a Databricks deployment design, all in the repository today. It is one module of the architecture in #architecture, not the architecture: it knows where the assets are and what they depend on, and it knows nothing yet about our treaty book, our facultative lines or our cedents (the insurers who buy reinsurance from us).

How it plugs into the enterprise graph

The canonical data model in #data-model has six objects. The prototype already produces three of them for the mega-project domain, and produces none of the insurance-side objects. That is the exact seam between "built" and "to build".

Asset EXISTS

Site, campus boundary, building footprint, power plant, substation, fab, water utility, transmission corridor, each with a stable id (site-…, sub-…) and its source rows. This is the Asset object, keyed and citable.

Relationship EXISTS

"Supplies power" (212 edges, each citing a filing), "belongs to campus" (footprint to site), "served by water utility", "generation within 25 km". Stored as rows, not inferred at query time, which is what #data-model asks for.

Scenario EXISTS, one peril

Event footprint × asset registry, built for earthquakes with USGS ShakeMap: a footprint arrives, the shaken sites list themselves worst-first. A Verisk or in-house footprint for any peril would plug into the same panel.

Exposure MISSING

No cedent location file has been ingested, so no TIV, no limit, no occupancy from our book is attached to any site. The underwriting export ships estimated_tiv_m = 0.0 and says why: "inventing one here would launder a guess into a pricing input".

Contract MISSING

No treaty or facultative position is joined. Scenario B in #scenarios (a $500M fac risk on a campus already in two treaties) cannot be run until this join exists.

Entity PARTIAL

Operators are an inference (73% resolved in Virginia), and county records name the title-holder while OpenStreetMap names the tenant: STACK Infrastructure on the deed, Amazon Web Services in the building, 12 rows. Both are kept. The link to the counterparty group graph in #groupgraph is not made.

Worked example: one 345 kV yard, two campuses, five queue positions (from the prototype's dependency ledger, not illustrative)

The ledger records five NYISO interconnection-queue entries whose named point of interconnection is the Kintigh 345 kV yard in Niagara County, New York (four entries) or the Kintigh/Niagara - New Rochester 345 kV circuit that runs through it (WNY STAMP, queue 0580, which taps that line at its own on-site 345/115 kV station; the ledger note records that no second substation was found) (OpenStreetMap name "Somerset Substation", operator NYSEG). Two resolve to registry sites, both vouched on 2026-09-07 against the review notes:

LoadQueueMW requestedFeedBackup powerRegistry site

WNY STAMP0580300primaryyesWNY STAMP Data Center

Two campuses about 35 km apart, in different counties (Somerset in Niagara County and the Town of Alabama in Genesee County), would look diversified on any postcode or county aggregation. The ledger shows 1,050 MW of live queue positions on one 345 kV node: 750 MW named to the Kintigh yard itself and 300 MW (STAMP) tapped from the circuit that runs through it. The ledger also carries this yard under two ids (sub-kintigh and sub-somerset, the same OpenStreetMap way at the same coordinates), which is why queue 0359 shows a primary and a secondary feed that are physically one substation. That is Scenario C in #scenarios with real rows behind it, and each row links to the NYISO filing it came from [NYISO].

Caveats the ledger itself carries. "Backup power: yes" means different things on the two campuses: the Lake Mariner rows are vouched as lithium-ion UPS with no diesel generators on site and no established ride-through duration, while the STAMP row is vouched as 12 emergency diesel generators from the SEQR application of record. For a dependency view, minutes of battery and days of diesel are not the same "yes", and the ledger's backup_hours is unset for Lake Mariner. Queue MW is requested, not delivered: as recorded in the repository README, ERCOT's public reports showed 3,883 MW operating against 9,042 MW approved, a 43% realisation rate, and the repository uses that as the stand-in for every market (verify against ERCOT's current large-load report before it is quoted to the Board) (README.md, "Utility deliverable capacity"). Whether the substation has the headroom is structurally unobtainable from public data: PJM classifies nodal load as confidential and ERCOT publishes by load zone only. What the join to our book would add is the insurance question this section cannot yet answer: which of our treaties and fac lines sit on those two campuses.

Decision. CUO Until deliverable 3 is live, the Kintigh yard, not the county, is the accumulation unit for both campuses: any facultative submission on Lake Mariner or WNY STAMP is referred with the other campus's known positions attached, and the referral note records 1,050 MW of queue positions on one substation node. Portfolio Mgmt Deliverable 3 is tested against this yard first, because the rows already exist.

Licensing: the constraint that shapes the enterprise design

Version 2 priced vendors but never addressed the terms on which each dataset may be used or redistributed. The licence register is the binding constraint on "turn the registry into cross-cedent intelligence" and on any cedent or broker portal, and the enterprise design has to be built around it rather than discover it later.

Licence classSourcesWhat it obliges us to doDesign consequence
Share-alike (ODbL 1.0)OpenStreetMap, Overture, IM3 atlas, Protomaps basemap: most of the registryInternal use is safe (ODbL 4.5(c): use of a derivative database within an organisation is not use "to the public", so the share-alike duty in section 4.4 is not triggered), with one catch for an insurance group: ODbL's definitions (section 1.0) say "Publicly" means anyone other than the licensee and entities it controls by more than 50% ownership, so a deployment that reaches the parent or sister companies is public use under the licence unless the licensing entity is the group parent. When use is public, the harder rule is 4.4 (the derivative database must itself be offered under ODbL, which cannot coexist with Regrid's and Precisely's "do not redistribute"), not only the 4.6 duty to offer a copy; 4.5(b) means a map image or report served to a cedent is a Produced Work and does not by itself create a derivative database, though the 4.3 notice still applies. A public or paid release of a database that merges OSM geometry with licensed parcels could oblige us to offer the whole derivative database (ODbL 4.6). Recorded as open, needs counsel [ODBL].Keep ODbL-derived layers separable from licensed and proprietary ones in the schema from day one, so a shareable database can be offered without the paid rows in it.
Licensed, do not redistributeRegrid [DCM-11], PreciselyHeld for internal use; billed per record returned; never republished as a bulk layer.Row filters and column masks in Unity Catalog (Databricks' governance layer, where a table's access rules live) on the parcel attributes; a grant that matches the licence; tokens never in the browser.
Display onlyEsri World ImageryTiles fetched by the browser, never stored; credit line required; not licensed for a shared deployment without a subscription.Imagery provider decided before anyone outside the build team opens the app.
Attribution is a conditionEpoch AI (CC BY 4.0) [EPOCH], Global Energy Monitor, PeeringDB, HM Land Registry, Registers of Scotland, IGN, Japan MOJExact credit wording on every surface that shows the data.Credit strings live in one constant and travel with the data into Unity Catalog table comments.
Open questionFCC Broadband Data Collection aggregatesThe Fabric Location ID is CostQuest IP; aggregation to H3 does not obviously launder it.No fibre layer is built until this is resolved.
RefusedSEMI World Fab Forecast (per-seat; refused by the prototype on price, and now an optional purchase decided at Gate G4), CSET/ETO (non-commercial), Wikipedia (share-alike, used only as a name worklist), HIFLD via Esri, Google Maps places and imagery (bulk extraction; the Map Tiles API with a key, cited above as an imagery option, is a separate product under its own terms), DataCenterMapRecorded so the decision is not re-litigated by someone who has forgotten it.The refusals list is part of the register, and the enterprise register inherits the practice.
1. Licensing becomes enforceable, not documented
On a laptop "do not redistribute" is a note. In Unity Catalog it is a row filter, a column mask and a grant on dcmap.curated.parcels_regrid and parcels_precisely.
2. Queries run as the viewer
Databricks Apps forwards the signed-in user's token (X-Forwarded-Access-Token) once user-authorization scopes for SQL warehouses, Unity Catalog tables and Genie are added to the app and each viewer consents on first use (with no scopes added the token carries only identity-read scopes, which cannot touch data); Genie and SQL then run on-behalf-of that person, so the filters apply per viewer instead of to the app's service principal [DBX-AUTH].
3. The ledger stops being anonymous
X-Forwarded-Email is written into an edited_by column beside the existing "how I know" note.
4. No dashboards with embedded credentials on licensed columns
A dashboard published with embedded credentials runs as the publisher for every viewer and silently defeats the row filters. Publish without them, or build on a view that excludes licensed columns.
5. Decide two things before map step 0 ships to anyone else
The imagery licence, and who will see the app. Moving to a shared workspace "is a change in licensing posture you should make deliberately". Regrid and Precisely redistribution has no step assigned in the repository; this blueprint assigns it to map step 1.

Any cedent or broker portal (Phase 5 in #roadmap) must be designed so the ODbL-derived and licensed layers can be withheld while the insurance-side answer is still served. The governance section (#governance) should carry the licence classes above as a "data rights" subsection, and the open-questions table below as what the Board should know is unmeasured.

The Databricks path, already designed

The repository contains a written target architecture and a migration plan with estimates (docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md). For executives, the design reduces to six decisions.

Two numberings, do not confuse them. The roadmap in #roadmap numbers the enterprise programme Phase 0 to Phase 5 (Phase 0 is the BMA counterparty prototype; Phase 3 is the capacity workbench; Phase 4 is mega-project and cyber accumulation, where this map joins the book). The map's own migration plan also counts from 0. In this section the map's steps are written map step 0 to map step 4; every unqualified "Phase n" refers to the enterprise roadmap. Map step 0 (read-only on Databricks Apps) is built; enterprise Phase 0 is not.
DecisionWhat it means in plain termsWhyStatus
Unity Catalog Delta tables are the registryEvery file the pipeline writes today becomes a governed table (dcmap.raw, dcmap.curated, dcmap.serving). The concentration tables this blueprint adds (cedent exposure, treaty and fac positions, counterparty) become new schemas beside them.Genie (Databricks' natural-language question tool: an executive types a question, it writes and runs the SQL) can only read tables, and licensing can only be enforced on tables.Designed; map step 2, about 4 to 6 weeks
Lakebase (Databricks' managed Postgres database) is the ledgerHand corrections, dropped points, simulated events and saved views go into a transactional database [DCM-9], insert-only with a superseded_by column.A Delta append per keystroke is the wrong shape; a web form wants constraints and single-digit-millisecond reads (the design's assumption; Databricks publishes no latency figure for Lakebase). The correction history is the point.Designed; map step 1, about 2 weeks
Genie answers questions, not camera moves"Take me to London" is matched deterministically in about a millisecond; "which operators have the most MW in Virginia" goes to Genie, which returns SQL, rows and a row count, and any answer carrying coordinates becomes a map action.A four-second camera move feels broken; a number with no SQL behind it would be the one dishonest surface in the app.Designed; map step 3b, about 2 to 3 weeks after map step 2
