The browser holds a bounded number of features regardless of dataset size.See the scale limit below. Needs any compute other than a classic SQL warehouse on Databricks Runtime 17.0+ (the design picks serverless because an app that idles overnight should not hold a cluster), plus a parity test between the server's H3 (Java 3.7.0) and the client's (h3-js 4.5); the design itself expects the test to pass, because the 64-bit cell index is unchanged between H3 v3 and v4 and only the function names differ, so the test guards an assumption rather than closing a known gap [DBX-5].Designed; map step 4, when the data demands it
Four storage tiers, not oneUC Volume for the 1.6 GB tile archive and imagery; Delta for the registry; Lakebase for the ledger; app memory for the derived payloads (403 MB, rebuilt in 427 ms).Each tier does the one thing it is good at; "do not turn a working in-memory model into a query per request out of architectural tidiness".Volume tier built (map step 0)
Map step 0 first, aloneThe app runs unmodified behind workspace SSO, read-only, off a volume. Three of the eleven open questions (replica behaviour, cold-start time over the Files API, outbound egress for tiles) are measured by this deployment and by nothing else.The design document's own words: "Phases 0 and 1 are the migration. Phases 2 to 4 are the platform." (map steps 0 to 4 in this section's naming)Built 2026-09-23, verified locally 2026-09-26, not yet deployed to a workspace
The scale limit that shapes the enterprise map. In this app's configuration MapLibre's rendering worker fails silently once a single GeoJSON source reaches roughly 189,000 vertices: no error, isSourceLoaded() stays false, the layer simply never appears. This is a measured symptom, not a documented MapLibre limit; MapLibre's own large-data guidance is to lower the source's maxZoom and tolerance, and the threshold will move with those options, the MapLibre version and the machine. The repository hit it twice (a 3.6 MB coastline, deliberately left out; 19,367 footprints at 308,000 vertices, now served per viewport from /api/footprints). A single cedent location schedule can carry hundreds of thousands of risks, so the enterprise map will hit this on the first file. The zoom-banded design (hexagons above zoom 10, viewport-clipped dots below, pre-baked tiles for stable context layers) is the only version that scales, and it is why the H3 grid is the executive view rather than a nice-to-have. The design document estimates that server-side filtering, search and framing are "perhaps two-thirds of the work, and all of it in app.js".
The eleven open questions the repository carries, for the Board
  1. Does Databricks Apps ever run more than one replica of an app? (Map step 1 makes the ledger authoritative regardless.)
  2. Cold-start time reading about 60 files from a Volume: 427 ms locally, unmeasured over the Files API. Measure at map step 0.
  3. Outbound internet from an app, for the Google tile proxy. Test at map step 0.
  4. Basemap and imagery licensing on a shared deployment. Decide before map step 0 ships to anyone else.
  5. Regrid and Precisely redistribution: row filters, on-behalf-of tokens and a matching grant. This blueprint assigns it to map step 1.
  6. GEOGRAPHY is public preview; prefer GEOMETRY at campus scale.
  7. H3 version parity between SQL and h3-js: the 100-site test.
  8. H3 on Runtime 17.0+ runs on any compute except classic SQL warehouses; the design picks serverless.
  9. Cost: today the app costs one laptop. Model it before map step 2.
  10. Dashboards published with embedded credentials defeat the row filters.
  11. Is ten million dots real? It decides whether map step 4 is optional.

Source: docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md section 12; databricksapps/README.html "The three measurements".

The next three deliverables

Each turns one gap in the "where the prototype stops" table into the production Mega Project module, and each has a test a reviewer can run without trusting the builder. They also shrink Phase 4 of #roadmap: version 2 wrote the mega-project build as a 6 to 9 month phase centred on Esri ArcGIS and S&P 451; the asset side exists, so Phase 4 reduces to these three joins and, once G3 releases it, can start as soon as one cedent schedule is available (the cedent-exposure join itself begins in Phase 2).

1. Registry onto the lakehouse, with identity MUST Data

Deploy map step 0 to a workspace, then map step 1: Lakebase ledger, on-behalf-of tokens, pens re-enabled. Imagery and viewer decisions recorded first.

Acceptance test. (a) The app is reachable only through workspace SSO. (b) An edit saved in the app appears as a ledger row carrying the editor's email and survives an app restart. (c) A second test account without the Regrid grant opens a Virginia site page and sees no Regrid or Precisely attributes; the first account does. (d) The 100-site H3 parity test passes: SQL and h3-js return identical cell ids. (e) The three map-step-0 measurements (cold start, egress, replicas) are written down with numbers.

2. Cedent exposure join BUILD Portfolio Mgmt Data

Ingest one cedent location schedule into exposure.cedent_locations, match each location to a registry site_id by point-in-campus-polygon, then by distance, then by address, and record the basis on every match. TIV comes from the schedule; the registry never fills it in.

Acceptance test. (a) A match report by tier: inside campus boundary, within 250 m, address match, unmatched, with counts. (b) Every matched row shows its basis and a reviewer can open the source row from the site page. (c) TIV and location count appear as two new measures in the same H3 cells that today show MW and count. (d) No row in the registry has been given a valuation; the export still writes 0.0 where the schedule gave none.

3. Treaty and fac overlay, and the hot-cell report BUILD CUO Portfolio Mgmt

Load treaty and facultative positions keyed to cedent and location, join them through the exposure table to site_id, and add gross line, net line and allocated capital (a coherent, additive allocation such as Euler contribution to 99% TVaR) as H3 measures beside TIV. Marginal capital, the rise in total capital if a deal is added now, is computed on demand against the live portfolio and never stored per cell, because it is not additive.

Acceptance test. (a) For one named campus the site page lists every treaty and fac line touching it and the substation it shares, with the filing behind the edge. (b) A top-20 hot-cell list by gross line, each cell traceable to its source positions. (c) Scenario B in #scenarios is answered for one real campus with our numbers, and the answer is reproducible from tables a second person can query. (d) A person without the treaty grant sees the asset layer and none of the positions.

Worked example: what the join adds to one hexagon (illustrative)

Take an H3 resolution-6 cell over northern Virginia, about 36 km² [H3-RES]. Today the cell carries columns the registry can fill; the join adds columns only our book can fill. Marked by whether each exists on 2026-09-27.

cell resolution n_sites n_ai mw_current capex_usd_m ft2 <- exist today (registry measures) 86 2a1072 7ffffff 6 41 6 1,180 9,400 18,300,000 gross_tiv net_tiv treaty_line fac_line aal aep_1in250_net allocated_capital top_cedent <- do not exist; deliverables 2 and 3 2,900 1,450 610 140 21 380 95 (cedent A)

Illustrative figures in US$ millions except counts and MW; the cell id is a placeholder. Even the left block is a floor: mw_current sums only the sites with an Epoch figure (67 registry-wide), so a cell's MW is what has been looked up, not what is drawn. The point is the boundary: the left block is measured public data, the right block is our confidential book, and both sit on the same key so a hot cell can be opened down to a treaty and up to a substation.

Decision (illustrative). Portfolio Mgmt With net TIV of 1,450 against allocated capital of 95 and a 1-in-250 net annual aggregate loss of 380, the cell is set to "capped": existing lines renew, new facultative lines above 25 need the CUO's sign-off, and the cell is reviewed when the next cedent schedule lands. Without the right-hand block that decision cannot be taken at all, which is what deliverables 2 and 3 buy.

Key takeaway: the map proves the pattern (governed registry, cited relationships, event-times-asset scenarios, honest gaps) and the Databricks path is designed and partly built. What the compliance budget buys is not the map: it is the three joins that make the map answer insurance questions, delivered on the lakehouse with the licences enforced. Everything in this section that is not one of those three joins already exists.

9.8 Non-catastrophe property severity: what we do instead of licensing PSOLD

The catastrophe model answers one question: what happens when a single event hits many of our locations at once. It says nothing about the far more common loss, one fire in one building. That second question has its own science, its own vendor products, and its own failure mode for the assets this document is about. It belongs in the architecture, but not in the same box as the catastrophe model, and the executive sponsor has decided that it will not be answered by buying Verisk's curves.

PSOLD (Verisk's ISO Property Size-of-Loss Database) is a set of severity curves: for a commercial property of a given type and insured value, how likely is a loss to be small, medium or a total loss. Verisk's Touchstone 8.0 help (2022) described it as a separately licensed database used to distribute non-catastrophe primary expected losses into excess layers, built from 20 years of U.S. claims reported to ISO with each loss linked to its exposure by amount of insurance, state, occupancy, coverage and peril; the curves can be scaled for construction and protection, and the software can produce frequency and severity measures in each layer for comparison with actual experience [PSOLD-1] [VER-5a]. That is the tool a cedent, and many reinsurers, use to price a per-risk XoL layer (a contract that pays the part of any one risk's loss above an attachment point, up to a limit) when no catastrophe is involved.

Decision recorded in version 5: Atlantic Re will not license Verisk ISO PSOLD, and not ISO Rapid Valuator either. Four reasons, each on the record so the question is not re-argued from a brochure.
  • The delivery route is unclear. The Touchstone page we could read is the 8.0 help (updated 31 January 2022). Verisk's database reference for Touchstone 2021 (9.0) states that non-catastrophe peril detailed loss analysis is no longer available in Touchstone and no longer a separately licensable analysis type, and that the AIRPSOLD prepared database was withdrawn with it [PSOLD-3]; Touchstone itself is being succeeded by Synergy Studio (the mega-project subsection). PSOLD is still sold through ISO, alongside ISO Rapid Valuator, but the Verisk product page returned only its title to our automated fetch, so the product-level description above rests on the 2022 help text and Verisk's 2021 excess-and-reinsurance product overview [IRV-1]. A licence whose platform we cannot name is not one to sign.
  • The curves are out of sample for our largest exposures. PSOLD is calibrated on ordinary U.S. commercial property claims by occupancy and insured-value band; a hyperscale campus or a semiconductor fab sits above the bands and outside the occupancy families (the red callout below).
  • Our per-risk book is priced from other evidence. Cedent transparency (the package below), the engineer's maximum foreseeable loss, our own claims, the map's identification of the campus, and the combined treaty and facultative view. None of these is bought from Verisk, and the worked example below reaches a better price with them than the curve reaches on its own.
  • The licence would be cost without a decision it changes. Cedents already run PSOLD and brokers already show its output; a second run of the same curves on our side adds a number, not a challenge.
Revisit trigger, in one sentence: if per-risk XoL on ordinary commercial property becomes a material line and cedents will not provide transparent severity work, the decision is re-opened at a gate. Until then both products carry NOT BUYING in the buy, integrate, build table.

Two sciences, two questions

Catastrophe modelling (Verisk, Moody's RMS)

Question: what happens when one event, a hurricane, earthquake, flood or wildfire, hits many insured locations at once? Outputs: AAL, the EP curve, PML, event footprints, correlated loss across the whole book. Unit of analysis: the event. Where it lives: the accumulation engine in the financial-structure layer.

Non-catastrophe severity (the cedent's PSOLD output, our claims, engineering)

Question: how do individual property losses distribute by size, and how much non-catastrophe loss will penetrate a per-risk layer? Outputs: a severity view by occupancy and insured value, expected excess claim count, limited severity, expected layer loss. Unit of analysis: the single risk. Where it lives: the pricing view for per-risk treaties and facultative property, next to engineering, fed by what the cedent supplies and what we already hold, not by a licensed curve.

PROPERTY RISK (one location, one value, one occupancy) | +---------------------------+---------------------------+ | | | v v v VERISK CAT MODEL NON-CAT SEVERITY VIEW MEGA PROJECT ASSET INTEL hurricane / EQ / flood large individual losses what is actually at this event accumulation layer penetration GPS point, on which grid AAL / EP / PML expected layer loss node, next to which fab | | | | | +------+------+ | | | v v | | | CEDENT'S OUR OWN | | | SEVERITY CLAIMS + | | | PACKAGE MFL | | | | | | | +-------------+------+------+-----+----------------------+ | v PRICING VIEW + PORTFOLIO VIEW (rate, line, terms) (marginal capital, envelope)

Diagram: keep the roles distinct. The catastrophe model, the non-catastrophe severity view (fed by the cedent's transparent severity package and by our own claims and engineering, not by a licensed curve) and Mega Project Asset Intelligence answer three different questions and feed the same pricing and portfolio view. None of the three replaces another.

What ISO Rapid Valuator is, and why it is not licensed either

PSOLD is not the whole of Verisk's non-catastrophe property toolkit. ISO Rapid Valuator is the ground-up loss-cost tool: Verisk's 2021 excess-and-reinsurance overview describes it as automating detailed ground-up property loss costs from individual, banded or complex layered exposures, with customisable class and COPE selections (construction, occupancy, protection, exposure) for standard and non-standard risks, loss costs for 230 occupancies built from 52 million policies and $235 billion of losses, and results that aggregate for portfolio management, catastrophe-model integration, price monitoring and ceded-reinsurance decisions. In the same overview PSOLD holds first-loss scales for 38 occupancy groups, 60 amount-of-insurance bands and seven coverage and peril components (7 million curves from $38 trillion of insured value), and links to Rapid Valuator for ground-up and excess pricing [IRV-1]. Verisk's search summary of the current product page adds a database of more than 50 million policies and 5 million claims and expected losses by layer up to $1 billion; that page returned only its title to our fetch. The decision covers both products for the same reasons: the same calibration on ordinary commercial property, the same unclear delivery route, and the same absence of a decision the licence would change. In our architecture both are tools a cedent may have used; what we take from a cedent is the output and the assumptions behind it, and neither tool replaces the identity work of Mega Project Asset Intelligence.

ISO / VERISK PRIMARY PROPERTY DATA (class codes, loss costs, claims) | +----------> ISO RAPID VALUATOR : ground-up loss cost for one risk, | banded or layered, by class and COPE | +----------> PSOLD : size-of-loss curve, how much of that loss lands in an excess layer Neither licensed by Atlantic Re. Both calibrated on ordinary commercial property. Neither knows that the GPS point is a hyperscale campus.

Diagram: the two ISO tools sit on the same primary-property data; Rapid Valuator gives the ground-up cost, PSOLD distributes it into layers. A cedent that used them hands us the result with the assumptions; we do not run them ourselves.

What we do instead

The decision is not to price per-risk business without a severity view; it is to build that view from evidence we already hold or can demand, and to treat a cedent's curve output as one input to be challenged rather than as the answer. The table is the working rule, situation by situation.

SituationWhat we useWhy
A cedent supplies PSOLD output, or any severity analysis, with its submissionThe transparency package below, stored under lineage with the treatyThe number is accepted only with the assumptions that produced it; that is what makes it challengeable at every renewal.
A large single risk: a data center, a fab, or any risk whose insured value sits above the curves' calibrated bandThe engineer's maximum foreseeable loss (MFL: the largest loss a competent engineer judges credible if the protection systems fail), the scenario set in the scenarios section and the project's own BI/DSU studyAn industry curve was never fitted to this size, construction or re-qualification period; an engineer's scenario was written for it.
The frequency question: how often does the credible loss happen?Our internal claims, used as a challenge, not as a curveA small sample cannot replace a curve, but it can show when a cedent's expected loss is a fraction of what our own book has paid.
The identity question: what is at the GPS point?Mega Project Asset IntelligenceNo severity tool knows that an anonymous "high technology" row is a six-hall campus behind one substation.
The accumulation question: what else of ours is on the campus?The combined treaty and facultative view (the facultative example)The expected layer loss is one number; the campus total from one fire is the number the Board asks for afterwards.
A cedent will not provide transparent severity workPrice the opacity: a data-quality load on the technical price, a referral, or a decline; and count the caseOne opaque cedent is a pricing problem. A pattern of them on a material per-risk book is the revisit trigger, and the count is the evidence a gate would need.
Out of sample for the assets this document is about. PSOLD curves are calibrated on ordinary U.S. commercial property losses by occupancy and insured-value band: the published occupancy families run from offices and retail through light and heavy manufacturing to highly protected risks, across 60 amount-of-insurance bands whose top value should be confirmed with Verisk. A multi-billion-dollar hyperscale campus or a semiconductor fab is outside that sample. The objection is not that the curves ignore protection or business interruption (BI); PSOLD carries a highly-protected-risk occupancy family and a time-element component. It is that the bands were fitted on ordinary commercial claims and a campus of this value sits above the losses that shaped them, that its construction is unique, that six halls behind one substation are one risk in a way a per-location curve cannot see, and that a fab's re-qualification after a clean-room contamination can take months. Losses at such sites do not follow the curves, so a per-risk treaty exposure-rated on PSOLD understates the layer's expected loss precisely where our exposure is largest, and the price looks cheapest where it should be dearest. For mega projects use the engineer's MFL, the scenario set in the scenarios section and the project's own BI/DSU study (delay in start-up: the revenue lost if a project under construction opens late). Control: the platform flags every per-risk layer a cedent has priced on PSOLD where the risk's insured value sits above the curves' calibrated size band, and the flag is a data-quality exception that pricing must clear.

The transparency package to demand when a cedent supplies PSOLD or any severity analysis

Because Atlantic Re does not license PSOLD, the cedent's output is accepted only with the assumptions that produced it. The package is the price of not buying the tool, and it is cheaper than the tool. It is stored under lineage with the treaty so the same question can be asked at every renewal.

The calculation

  • PSOLD version and curve basis (vintage, data cut, any cedent recalibration), or the equivalent for whatever severity method the cedent used
  • Occupancy mapping: how each cedent class maps to a PSOLD occupancy group, especially how a data center or fab is mapped: to an office, heavy-commercial, manufacturing or highly-protected-risk group, since none of the occupancy families in Verisk's 2021 overview names a data center or a fab
  • Amount-of-insurance assumptions: what value the curve was run on, and whether business interruption is inside it
  • Coverage and peril assumptions (building, contents, time element; fire, all other perils)
  • Scaling factors applied for construction, protection and any manual adjustment

The outputs and the overrides

  • Expected excess claim count, limited (layer) severity and expected layer loss, per layer
  • Treatment of deductibles, attachment, limit, and any one-risk definition
  • Engineering MFL and PML per large risk, with the survey date
  • BI and DSU assumptions: indemnity period, extra expense, contingent extensions
  • Large-loss history: every loss above the attachment for ten years, as reported and as developed
  • Every material override to the curve output, with the reason and who signed it

The reinsurer then challenges the package with its own claims, engineering review, Mega Project Asset Intelligence and the combined treaty-plus-facultative accumulation view. A licence would have bought a second calculation; the challenge is what buys a better price.

Worked example: a large fire inside a hyperscale campus (illustrative)

ACME Financial Group's insurer cedes a per-risk XoL treaty to Atlantic Re: $50M excess of $25M any one risk. The location file carries one row for a site in western Nebraska: GPS coordinates, TIV $2,400M and the occupancy code "high technology". Nothing says what the site is.

ViewWhat it seesExpected loss to $50M xs $25MWhat it misses
Cedent PSOLD viewA $2,400M "high technology" property; the curve scales the ordinary commercial distribution to a very large insured value$0.5M a year (illustrative)That the row is a six-hall hyperscale campus with $960M of the $2,400M in business interruption, and that the curve was never calibrated at this size
Mega Project Asset IntelligenceThe GPS point resolves to Data Center A: six halls, 480 MW, one shared substation, a fab as its yard neighbour (the map)Not a number; an identityNothing on its own; it tells the other views what they are looking at
Engineering MFLOne hall lost to a fire that defeats the suppression system: $180M property damage plus nine months of that hall's BI, $120M, so MFL $300MLayer fully exposed by one credible scenarioFrequency; the engineer says what, not how often
Internal claimsTwo data-hall fires across about 40 data-center sites in the book in five years, one of which exceeded $30M as developedFrequency of a hall fire roughly 1 in 100 per site-year (illustrative)A small sample; used as a challenge, not a curve
Treaty plus fac accumulationData Center A already carries $70M across Cedents A, B and C (the facultative example); this treaty adds up to $50M more from the same fireCampus total $120M from one eventNothing; this is the number the Board asks for after the fire

The challenge. A 1-in-100 hall fire at MFL costs the layer its full $50M, and a 1-in-25 partial event of $40M costs it $15M: an expected layer loss near $1.1M a year (illustrative) against the cedent's $0.5M. Atlantic Re does not need a PSOLD licence to reach that conclusion, which is why it does not buy one; it needs to know the row is Data Center A, an engineer's MFL, its own claims and the campus total. Pricing moves from a rate on the PSOLD number to a rate on the scenario number, the one-risk definition is tightened so the six halls cannot be treated as six risks, and the campus total is written into the envelope that the facultative underwriter sees when the next submission arrives.

The governance story. If the fire happens, the account of it to the Board and to the BMA is not "the hurricane model missed it". The catastrophe model was never asked. The story is that the reinsurer understood the site, held a credible MFL and severity scenario, priced the non-catastrophe layer on it, and knew the total campus accumulation before it chose its line. That is the story the audit trail in the governance section is built to tell.

Property UWActuarialPortfolio MgmtEvery number above is illustrative; the structure is the point.

Why PSOLD does not solve the identity problem

PSOLD works from exposure characteristics, which is its virtue: it needs no insured name and no address, only a value and an occupancy. It is therefore blind to the one fact that changes the answer for a mega project. It cannot discover that an anonymous GPS point is a hyperscale campus, that the campus shares a substation with a fab, or that three cedents and one fac certificate already sit on the same yard. That is the job of Mega Project Asset Intelligence, and it is the reason the prototype's registry exists: 6,285 sites and 214 fabs, every fab hand-sourced with a URL per record from open sources after SEMI's World Fab Forecast was declined on price (US$11,100 a year per seat, recorded in the map's licence register; the seat is now an optional purchase decided at Gate G4 for the fab side of the mega-project module, the vendor table). A severity curve applied to a mis-identified risk is precise about the wrong building, whoever licenses the curve.

9.9 Casualty systemic accumulation: buying the correlation science

Natural catastrophe and cyber models do not cover liability. The non-natural accumulation subsection already names casualty clash as one of the four families the engine must group; this subsection says what to buy for it and where it sits in the roadmap.

Casualty accumulates differently from property. There is no footprint on a map. One product, chemical, legal theory or supply chain connects insureds that share nothing else, and the loss arrives across several lines and several policy years (the annual contract periods a claim is allocated to, often long after the policy was written). The non-natural accumulation subsection already gives the historical shape (asbestos, opioids, PFAS) and the engine's grouping key (industry, named insured group, product family); a defective battery chemistry, an AI system that gives harmful advice at scale, or a contaminated ingredient are the next ones. What the engine cannot do on its own is say which industries a new common cause will reach, through which trading relationships, and with what correlation.

COMMON CAUSE OF LOSS PFAS / defective battery / AI liability / product contamination | +--------------------+--------------------+ | | | v v v INSURED A INSURED B INSURED C (manufacturer) (distributor) (board and advisers) | | | CGL Products D&O / E&O policy year 1 policy year 2 policy year 3 | | | +--------------------+--------------------+ | v CASUALTY CLASH LOSS | v treaty recoveries + portfolio capital (BSCR reserve risk)

Diagram: one cause, three insureds, three coverages, three policy years. CGL is commercial general liability (bodily injury and property damage to third parties); products is product liability; D&O and E&O are directors' and officers' and errors-and-omissions cover for the people and advisers around the company. The loss reaches the reinsurer through every casualty treaty at once.

The specialist model

The Verisk Casualty Catastrophe Model (from the 2017 Arium acquisition) is built for exactly this. Verisk's brochure describes a framework to quantify correlation of exposures to systemic and emerging events across insureds, industries, lines of business and policy years, using an economic map of trading and commercial relationships between industries onto which a liability "footprint" (a contamination, a defective product) is imposed, so that the loss can be followed through supply and distribution chains and the legal duties between them. Its stated uses are an industry view of risk, exposure management against a catalogue of historical and stochastic liability scenarios, clash discovery across lines and years, capital and reserving, and risk charges for assuming or ceding liability portfolios [CAS-1]. Verisk completed the Arium purchase in January 2017 and placed it inside AIR Worldwide; the product page returned only its title to our fetch, so verify current scope, delivery platform and pricing with the vendor.

The alternative is Moody's CoMeta, the former Praedicat platform (Moody's acquired Praedicat in September 2024, three years after RMS). Moody's describes it as a casualty catastrophe modelling platform that links liability perils to named entities using Orbis data on more than 580 million companies and reports exposure at entity, portfolio and enterprise level, and runs horizon scanning over more than 300 emerging liability risks with litigation tracking [CAS-2]. The two differ in emphasis: Verisk starts from industries and trade flows, Moody's from named companies and the science and litigation behind each peril. A reinsurer with a treaty book (industry mix, few named insureds) leans towards the first; one with a large facultative or excess casualty book (named insureds) towards the second. Either way the named-entity side joins the same group graph the counterparty module already maintains.

What we keep and what we buy

Keep on our platform BUILD

Cross-line aggregation (the same insured group across CGL, products, D&O, E&O and umbrella treaties); the policy-year ledger; the capital impact through the BSCR reserve-risk and premium-risk charges (the BMA section); the decision logic: limits by industry and product family, referral triggers, and the envelope handed to the casualty underwriter. This is the same engine and the same graph as property; only the grouping key changes.

Buy from a specialist OPTIONAL

The event and correlation science: the catalogue of common causes, the industry economic map or the named-entity peril links, the probability that a cause reaches a given industry, and the scenario losses by line and year. This is hard to recreate, changes with every new mass tort, and is what the vendor's research team is for. Its output lands in the engine as one more scenario feed, keyed to our insured groups and industries, exactly as a Verisk footprint lands for property.

Phase placement

Phase 4 of the roadmap (mega-project and cyber accumulation) is where the third non-geographic feed belongs, and only if liability business is material: as an illustrative rule of thumb, if casualty reserves or casualty treaty premium exceed a fifth of the respective totals, or if a single named-insured group or product family already appears across more than one casualty treaty in the grouping the Phase 3 workbench produces. Below that threshold the engine's own grouping by industry and insured group, run against a short hand-built list of live mass torts, is the proportionate answer. The vendor decision is taken on the measured book, not on the brochure, and the model is bought as a feed, not as a platform.

Key takeaway: Three different sciences answer three different questions. The catastrophe model prices the event that hits many locations; the non-catastrophe severity view prices the single large loss and how much of it reaches a per-risk layer, built from the cedent's transparent severity work, engineering MFL and our own claims rather than from a licensed curve; the casualty model prices the common cause that reaches many insureds across lines and years. Atlantic Re buys the science it cannot recreate, declines the licence that would change no decision, and keeps the aggregation, the capital impact and the decision on its own platform. For hyperscale campuses and fabs, no curve, licensed or not, is a substitute for knowing what the GPS point is, an engineer's maximum foreseeable loss and the campus total.

9.10 Cedent intelligence: Schedule P, Schedule F and the history of changes

A submission tells us what the cedent wants us to know. Its statutory filings tell us what happened. Two of those filings, kept as a history of every change rather than as quarter-end snapshots, form a distinct intelligence branch of the platform: the cedent's own loss and reserve behaviour, and the way it transfers risk to others.

Not a generic "S&P data" box. The vendor section already lists SNL statutory data as a source. This subsection is about what the platform does with it: a change-event feed, a set of derived signals and a renewal workflow that belong to the CUO and Portfolio Mgmt, not to the data team. The CRO owns the same signals when the cedent is also a counterparty (see the counterparty section).

Two schedules, two questions

Schedule P: how the cedent's business and reserves develop

Schedule P is the actuarial part of the U.S. statutory annual statement. Plain English: for each line of business and each year in which claims arose, it shows what the insurer paid, what it still holds in reserve, and how those figures have moved since the year was first booked. Read year over year it gives loss development (how an old year's claims grow or shrink after they were first estimated), reserve revisions, line-by-line performance and, in the end, the quality of the cedent's underwriting. The NAIC quarterly instructions carry a Part 3 reserves schedule by loss year that shows how the prior year-end's loss and loss-expense reserves have developed through the quarter, with adjusting-expense payments and reserves allocated to loss year on the basis the insurer uses for its annual Schedule P [NAIC-QSI].

Schedule F: how the cedent transfers risk

Schedule F is the ceded-reinsurance schedule of the same statement. Plain English: a list of every reinsurer the cedent relies on, what each owes it, and what security stands behind that debt. The quarterly form lists only the reinsurers added in the year to date, grouped as affiliates, U.S. insurers, pools and associations, and all other insurers, each identified by an NAIC company code or a reinsurer identification number; the full panel with its recoverables and security is in the annual Schedule F [NAIC-QSI]. From it we read reinsurance recoverables (money the cedent expects back from its reinsurers on paid and unpaid claims), changes to its reinsurance panel, the collateral behind those recoverables, and the direction of its ceded strategy.

Both schedules are carried in S&P's SNL Insurance Regulatory Data, whose statutory reinsurance subset covers Schedule F/S relationships and whose Schedule P subset covers loss experience and reserves [SP-SNL]. The dataset page did not render for an automated check on 28 September 2026, so the current field list and delivery options should be verified with the vendor before contract.

Why a history of changes beats comparing snapshots

Most reinsurers compare one quarter-end filing with the next. That gives a net movement and hides everything in between. Where the licensed feed carries them, the platform should preserve each data change as an event: an operation (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE), the field that changed, the old value, the new value, a timestamp and a sequence number. A cedent files quarterly, so intra-quarter events come from amended filings, restatements and the vendor's own corrections rather than from monthly reporting; that is precisely what makes them informative. The difference is easiest to see on one number.

Worked example: one recoverable balance, two ways of looking at it (illustrative)

ACME Financial Group's U.S. carrier reports its recoverable from its reinsurance panel. Atlantic Re's treaty underwriter sees the same +$70M either as a single step or as a path.

ViewWhat the data showsWhat the underwriter learns
SnapshotJanuary recoverable $400M. April recoverable $470M. Net change +$70M.Ceded dependence rose 17.5%. Nothing about why, when or whether it is settling.
History of changesFebruary UPDATE +$55M (one reinsurer's balance restated). March INSERT +$30M (a new reinsurer appears on the panel). March DELETE minus $15M (a reinsurer leaves; its balance is commuted or reassigned). April UPDATE +$0M (balances confirmed).Net is still +$70M, but the path shows a restatement, a panel entrant, a panel exit and a reversal inside one quarter: timing, volatility and a change of strategy that a snapshot cannot show.

All figures illustrative. The path is what an underwriter would ask about at renewal; the net figure alone would pass unremarked.

The two data objects

Two event types are enough. Each row is one change to one field, never a whole restated schedule, so the platform can replay any point in time and can count reversals.

SchedulePChangeEvent company_id # the cedent's statutory entity (join to the group graph) statement_period # filing the change belongs to line_of_business # Schedule P line accident_year # year the claims arose (loss year) field_name # e.g. incurred_losses, ibnr_reserve, paid_losses old_value new_value operation # INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE change_timestamp sequence_no # order inside the same timestamp source_record_id # vendor row, for audit and re-pull ScheduleFChangeEvent company_id # the cedent reinsurer_counterparty_id # the reinsurer, mapped to our counterparty group statement_period field_name # e.g. recoverable_paid, recoverable_unpaid, loc_amount, funds_held, trust_amount old_value new_value operation # INSERT (new reinsurer) | UPDATE | DELETE (reinsurer removed) change_timestamp sequence_no source_record_id

The reinsurer_counterparty_id is the same identifier the group graph uses, so a reinsurer that is growing on a cedent's panel and shrinking on Atlantic Re's own retro panel is recognised as the same company. Field-level rows also let the data model keep the cedent's filed values separate from any value an analyst overrides.

Derived signals

Raw events are for the actuary. The underwriter and Portfolio Management see signals computed from them, each with a threshold the CUO sets and the CRO reviews.

SignalComputed fromWhat it flags
Reserve revision frequency and directionCount and sign of Schedule P UPDATEs to incurred or IBNR, by line and accident yearThree adverse revisions in a row is a pattern; one is noise
Largest adverse revisionMaximum single upward change to an accident year's incurred lossesA reserving surprise, and the line it came from
Cumulative adverse revision percentSum of adverse changes divided by the reserve first booked for that yearSystematic under-reserving rather than bad luck
Panel additions and removalsSchedule F INSERT and DELETE events on reinsurer_counterparty_idA changing ceded strategy, or reinsurers walking away
Recoverable change percentNet change in paid plus unpaid recoverables over the periodRising dependence on others to pay claims
Concentration changeLargest reinsurer's share of total recoverables, before and afterThe panel narrowing onto one name
Collateral changeShare of recoverables secured by letters of credit (a bank's promise to pay if the reinsurer does not), trust assets or funds heldSecurity thinning while balances grow; the same security a U.S. cedent needs to take statutory credit for its reinsurance, and the same test the collateral section applies to Atlantic Re's own retro panel [NAIC-1]
VolatilityNumber of reversals (an UPDATE undoing an earlier one) per periodFigures that are being managed rather than measured
MaterialityEach signal scaled to the cedent's surplus and to Atlantic Re's line on itWhich of the above actually matters to us

How it changes a renewal

The submission looks acceptable
ACME's U.S. carrier renews its property and casualty quota share. Loss ratios in the submission are in line with last year; the broker's presentation is clean.
Schedule P change signals
Three consecutive adverse revisions to general liability accident years 2022 to 2024, cumulative +11% on the reserves first booked (illustrative). Property years are stable.
Schedule F change signals
Recoverables up 17.5% between the January and April filings; two reinsurers removed from the panel; Reinsurer XYZ's share of recoverables up from 8% to 19%; the collateralised share down from 45% to 30% (illustrative).
The underwriter's questions
"What changed in the liability book?" "Which accident years and which claims drove the revisions?" "Why is ceded dependence rising, and why did two reinsurers leave?" "What security sits behind Reinsurer XYZ's balance?"
A better renewal conversation
Not an automatic surcharge or decline. The answers may justify a casualty sub-limit and a rate change, or they may show a deliberate, well-collateralised move to a stronger panel, in which case the same signals support a larger line.
The signals are a question generator, not a pricing penalty. Better information cuts both ways. A cedent whose reserve revisions have turned favourable, whose panel is broadening and whose collateral is rising is a cedent Atlantic Re can offer more capacity to, at a price the market's snapshot-readers will not match. That is the selection lever applied to cedents rather than to risks.

Licensing note. Historical-change delivery of SNL regulatory data is a licensed option that must be confirmed with S&P, including whether change events are delivered at field level and how far back the history runs; the standard subscription may deliver period snapshots only. The permitted uses of the feed (internal analytics, aggregation across cedents, display to a cedent or broker) go into the data-rights registry described under governance, and the cost sits in the licensing budget. Nothing in this subsection depends on the option: with snapshots only, the platform derives the same signals at quarterly resolution and loses the intra-quarter path.

9.11 Retrocession and true net exposure: the loss waterfall

Concentration cannot stop at gross exposure. The two-levels section states the gross-to-net chain and Scenario G works a retro purchase. What the platform needs in between is the waterfall itself: a transparent path from a gross loss to the loss Atlantic Re will actually bear after every reinsurer, bank and contract term has had its say.

1. Gross event or risk loss
The modelled or scenario loss to the ceded book: an event across a zone, or a single risk such as a campus fire.
2. Treaty and facultative response
What Atlantic Re owes its cedents under each treaty and facultative certificate, contract by contract.
3. Outward retrocession
The retro programme that responds: which contracts, which retrocessionaires, which shares.
4. Attachment, limit, occurrence and aggregate terms
The attachment point (the loss at which a layer starts to pay), the limit, and whether the contract counts losses per occurrence or in aggregate over the year.
5. Expected ceded recovery
What the contracts say the retrocessionaires owe. This is where most reporting stops.
6. Counterparty credit quality
Each retrocessionaire's rating, outlook and internal grade, from the counterparty section; a downgrade since placement lowers the recovery we can rely on.
7. Collateral, letters of credit and trust
What is secured, by which bank or custodian, and whether that bank is itself concentrated in the same event (collateral section).
8. Reinstatement cost
The reinstatement premium (the extra premium paid to restore a layer's limit after it is used) reduces the net benefit of the recovery.
9. Exhaustion and aggregate erosion
Earlier events this year have already used part of an aggregate limit; the layer may not respond in full, or at all.
10. Timing and collectibility stress
A haircut for recoveries that arrive late, are disputed, or fail, sized to the stress rather than to the base case.
11. True net retained loss
Gross loss less the recovery that survives steps 6 to 10.
12. Capital, liquidity and capacity remaining
The retained loss against available statutory capital and the BSCR, the cash needed before recoveries arrive, and the capacity envelope left for underwriting.
Worked example: the gross concentration is unchanged, but available capacity is not (illustrative)

Atlantic Re's peak-zone accumulation is the same on both dates. Between them, one retrocessionaire is downgraded and moves off the approved list for new attachments, an earlier storm has eroded an aggregate layer, and the bank behind a letter of credit is downgraded. Nothing changed in the gross treaty economics.

ViewBefore the retro changeAfter the retro change
Gross peak zone loss (the zone where the company's largest modelled event sits)$900M$900M
Expected retro recovery$350M$220M
Stressed collectibility haircut$20M$40M
Net retained loss$570M$720M
Available statutory capital after the loss (from $2,000M; tax and reinstatement premium ignored for clarity)$1,430M$1,280M
Against the $1,400M BSCR102%: above the BSCR, but below the 120% target capital level that triggers BMA engagement91%: below the BSCR itself
Underwriting implicationCapacity availableCapacity materially tighter

All figures illustrative and on the reference company. The capital rows are a stress view for the Board, not a regulatory calculation; the BMA's own treatment of a post-event position is covered in the BMA section.

The gross figure a peak-zone report would show is identical on both dates. The net marginal economics moved by $150M, and with them the answer to every underwriter asking for a line in that zone. This is why retrocession belongs inside the concentration and capacity engine rather than in a separate ceded-reinsurance report that Portfolio Management reads once a quarter: the engine has to recompute steps 6 to 12 whenever a retrocessionaire's rating, a bank's rating, an aggregate balance or an occurrence definition changes, and push the result into the capacity envelope the same day. Ceded Re owns steps 3 to 5, the Treasurer step 7, the CRO steps 6 and 10, and Portfolio Mgmt the whole chain.

Portfolio Management must also say where to write more

A concentration engine that only ever produces reasons to cut a line will be routed around. The same marginal-capital arithmetic that makes the peak-zone line expensive makes a diversifying line cheap, and the platform has to surface the second as loudly as the first.

Opportunity A

High stand-alone return. Overlaps the peak zone. Because every dollar of its loss lands where Atlantic Re already loses most, its marginal capital (defined under the profit levers) is almost its full stand-alone capital: marginal capital high.

Opportunity B

Lower stand-alone return. Diversifies by geography and peril. Its losses fall in years when the peak zone is quiet, so the portfolio needs far less extra capital to carry it: marginal capital low. B may create more value per unit of scarce capital.

Measure (illustrative)Opportunity AOpportunity B
Expected profit$16M$14M
Stand-alone capital and return$100M, 16%$100M, 14%
Marginal capital and return$100M, 16%$45M, 31%
Traditional account rankingA firstB second
Profit from $100M of scarce peak-season capital$16M (one A)$28M (two Bs, $90M)

The 12% hurdle used in the Data Center A example is the same hurdle here, and the arithmetic is the same as the portfolio-shape lever: return on marginal capital, not on stand-alone capital, is what the scarce resource earns. If Portfolio Management only appears when it wants underwriting to reduce a line, it becomes a brake, and underwriters will learn to bring it deals late. The winning model proactively finds underweight regions and perils, favourable attachment points where the market is over-paying for the layer, cedents whose Schedule P and F history supports more capacity (cedent intelligence), and places where a retro purchase or a capital raise would let the company compete harder than its peers. Each of those is a named number on an underwriter's screen, published before the renewal season rather than discovered after it.

Key takeaway: Two things the platform must make explicit: the cedent's own filings, kept as a history of changes, tell Atlantic Re what a renewal submission will not; and retrocession, credit, collateral and aggregate erosion belong inside the capacity engine, because the same gross exposure can leave the company with $570M or $720M of net loss (illustrative) depending on them. Both branches exist to find where to write more as much as where to write less.
10

What we should buy, integrate or build

Buy hard-to-recreate external data and models, integrate the internal systems of record, and build the cross-domain intelligence and decision logic ourselves.

DataCFO

The winning strategy is unchanged from v2: buy the external data and models that are hard to recreate, integrate the internal systems of record we already run, and build the cross-domain intelligence and decision logic ourselves. What has changed is the inventory. The prototype already owns an open mapping stack and a dozen licensed or public data sources, our catastrophe vendor is migrating its platform and now sells a data-center database of its own, and the free LEI parent-relationship file (a public 20-character legal-entity identifier whose registry also publishes who owns whom) turns out to be the cheapest backbone for the entity graph. This section lists every capability, says whether it is mandatory for the BMA filing or an optional profit lever, and names the challenger for each purchase so procurement can defend the choice.

Decision asked of you: approve the mandatory rows for immediate procurement or integration, approve the evaluation (not purchase) of the optional rows, and endorse the do-not-buy-twice list. The phase-gated budget split, with the gates that release each optional tranche, is in the profit section; the operating owners for each row are in the operating model.

Written for a general-business reinsurer [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E]. For a long-term (Class C / D / E) reinsurer the catastrophe rows become optional and the asset-side rows (investment book of record, issuer hierarchy) become the mandatory core, because its concentration filing is dominated by invested assets rather than modelled cat loss.

10.1 How to read the table

Every row carries one of seven action tags, or two where a source is partly in hand and partly still to buy or build. BUY / KEEP means we pay a vendor and should keep doing so. INTEGRATE means the data already exists inside the company and the work is a governed feed into Unity Catalog (the Databricks catalogue that records who may see which table, where it came from and when it changed). BUILD means our own intellectual property. HAVE means it already runs in the data-center prototype and costs nothing new; the row records its licence class so nobody re-buys it or republishes it by accident. OPTIONAL means buy only if a measured gap justifies it. EVALUATE means run a comparison at a named moment and decide then. NOT BUYING records a decision taken against a purchase, with the reasons and the trigger that would re-open it, so the question is not re-argued from the next brochure.

The column Mandatory for compliance? answers one question: would the BMA concentration and capital filing be defensible without it? Yes means the filing needs this data or an equivalent. Equivalent required means some source of this type is needed but the named vendor is a choice. No means it is a profit lever, phase-gated in the profit section. Licence classes: ODbL share-alike (open, but any merged database we publish must be offered back under the same licence), CC-BY (open, attribution required), commercial internal-use-only (paid, may not be redistributed), public record (government works, attribution where the publisher asks), BSD-3 / Apache 2.0 (permissive open-source software). The class matters because merging ODbL rows with paid Regrid parcels into one published database is the one licensing question the prototype has left open for counsel.

10.3 What drives cost

No cost bands are given here; procurement confirms them and the profit section carries the phase-gated budget. What the board should know is what each bill scales with, because that is what the design controls.

  • Regrid: per parcel record returned. Returned means billed, even if we discard the record; empty responses are free; a point search with a radius returns and bills every parcel in the circle. Self-serve plans include 2,000 records a month with $0.10 (Standard) or $0.15 (Premium) per additional record; above 10,000 records a month Regrid moves us to an enterprise licence. Calls are limited to about 200 a minute and 10 concurrent. Design rule: cache every resolved parcel, query with zero radius, de-duplicate cedent locations before calling. The prototype already does the first two: its per-parcel cache is invalidated only when a site's dot moves outside the cached lot, and its pipeline refuses a billed Regrid or Precisely run without an explicit confirmation (dcmap/lib/pipeline.mjs). The enterprise build keeps both rules and moves the cache into a Unity Catalog table. [REGRID-BILL] [REGRID-PLANS]
  • Esri: stored geocodes and sessions. Geocoding is 20,000 free a month then $0.50 per 1,000 if we do not store the result, and $4 per 1,000 if we do. Anything written to Unity Catalog is stored, so every cedent address we geocode with Esri costs the stored rate; the alternative is to geocode once through the prototype's existing pipeline and keep Esri for imagery. Basemap sessions and tiles bill only if we abandon self-hosted PMTiles. [ESRI-GEOCODE]
  • CyberCube: annual licence, sized by modules and portfolio. Portfolio Manager and SPoF Intelligence are licensed separately; this is typically the largest optional line and stops if the cyber phase is paused.
  • Databricks: consumption. Compute is metered per unit of work, so cost scales with how often pipelines run and how much they scan, not with user count. Daily concentration refreshes on a modest book are small; unbounded ad-hoc Genie queries (the natural-language question box over governed tables) are the item to budget and monitor.
  • D&B: tier. Priced by the number of entities monitored, the depth of linkage returned and the refresh frequency, API versus batch. Seeding with the free GLEIF file shrinks the tier we need.
  • Verisk: existing spend, re-tendered at migration. Synergy Studio pricing and the Data Center Exposure Database are new items in the same negotiation.
  • Verisk ISO PSOLD and Rapid Valuator: not bought. Both are separate ISO licences, and Touchstone would not distribute non-cat losses into excess layers unless PSOLD was licensed; the version 5 decision is to license neither, so the item leaves the Synergy Studio negotiation and its cost is nil until the revisit trigger in the table fires. The cost that remains is the analyst time to demand and challenge a cedent's transparency package, which is already in the pricing workflow. SEMI World Fab Forecast is priced per seat ($11,100 a year quoted to the prototype) and is an optional purchase decided at Gate G4; AM Best, IIR and an SNL change-history add-on are annual subscriptions to be priced with each vendor. [PSOLD-1]
Worked example: what one exposure file costs to resolve to parcels (illustrative)

A cedent submits a 40,000-location commercial property schedule. De-duplication by address leaves 12,000 distinct sites; 9,000 are already cached from earlier submissions, so 3,000 new lookups are needed. Unit prices are Regrid's published self-serve rates; the volumes are invented.

ApproachRecords returnedBill at $0.10 per recordComment
Zero-radius point lookup, cached3,000$300 at the list rate; $100 if the month's 2,000 included records are unusedOne parcel per site; cache hit avoids 9,000 calls
500-metre radius, no cache12,000 sites × about 30 parcels = 360,000$36,000, and the enterprise tier is triggeredEvery parcel in the circle is billed whether or not we use it
Free county layer first, Regrid only for gapsAbout 600 (one in five sites lacks a usable county layer)$60 at the list rate; nothing if inside the monthly allowanceThe prototype's actual order of preference

The point is not the dollar amount, which is small at this volume; it is that a radius parameter and a missing cache change the bill by two orders of magnitude, and that the same rule applies to Esri stored geocodes.

10.4 What we should deliberately NOT buy twice

The do-not-buy list
  • Do not build a cat model. Keep Verisk as primary. Decide explicitly whether a second model (Moody's RMS) or a blended and adjusted own view of risk is required for model-risk governance, cedent-data conversion and the rating-agency dialogue; store model versions, blend weights and adjustment factors as governed data in Unity Catalog. Plain English: regulators and rating agencies do not want us to trust one vendor's hurricane model blindly; they want to see how we challenge it. That does not mean rebuilding it, but it usually means a second opinion and a documented set of adjustments that become part of our capital numbers.
  • A second cat model is a pricing and capital decision, not a concentration decision. Evaluate Moody's RMS against Synergy Studio on model view, cedent-data conversion and total cost at the migration, not because this project needs it. Whatever is chosen, its outputs land as one more governed table; the concentration engine must not depend on which vendor produced them.
  • Do not license PSOLD, and do not let a cedent's PSOLD output price a mega project. PSOLD (Verisk's Property Size-of-Loss Database) is a set of industry loss-severity curves built from ordinary US commercial property claims reported to ISO, giving the distribution of loss size by occupancy, building size, coverage and peril; Verisk publishes it for pricing ground-up and excess commercial property layers. [VER-5a] The version 5 decision not to license it, or Rapid Valuator, is recorded in the table above with its revisit trigger. Verisk's 2021 product sheet lists highly protected risk classes and a business-interruption component among the curves, so the objection is not that those categories are missing; it is that the curves are calibrated on ordinary commercial claims. A hyperscale campus or a semiconductor fab sits above their amount-of-insurance bands, carries a value dominated by business interruption and delay in start-up, and has construction and re-qualification periods of months that no industry curve was fitted to. For mega-projects use engineering-based MFL (maximum foreseeable loss, the engineer's estimate of the worst credible single event with protections failed), scenario analysis and the project's own BI/DSU study (business interruption and delay in start-up, the income lost while the site cannot operate or open). Flag every per-risk treaty layer where a cedent's PSOLD-derived pricing covers exposures above the curves' calibrated size band. Plain English: industry loss curves tell us how badly a normal warehouse or office burns; they tell us nothing reliable about a $5bn chip plant, so a treaty priced on those curves may be cheap precisely where our exposure is largest, and paying Verisk for our own copy of the curves would not change that.
  • Do not replace the investment book of record or the treasury system with Databricks. Databricks ingests and governs those feeds; the accounting platform stays the system of record.
  • Do not let any broker's specialty programme become our cross-broker system of record. Broker platforms see one broker's placements; the entity graph must see all of them.
  • Do not buy two corporate-hierarchy products without a demonstrated data-quality reason. GLEIF is free and comes first; D&B is the primary paid source; BECRS or the Bloomberg / ICE feed is a challenger only where a measured gap (private cedents, securities) justifies it.
  • Do not buy a second data-center database before measuring the first. Verisk's US database and S&P 451 overlap with each other and with the open sources already in hand. License Verisk's as the second reference feed at the Synergy Studio negotiation; evaluate 451 against the prototype's inventory and pay only for the rows it adds.
  • Do not buy a bulk parcel licence before the per-record bill says so. The county layers are free, Regrid and Precisely are already licensed per site, and a nationwide Precisely load is a response to measured volume.
  • Do not buy a hosted tile service. The basemap is a self-hosted PMTiles file; the 2-million-tile allowance debate is moot. Esri spend, if any, is for imagery and feature services in a shared deployment.
Licensing rule for the whole table. Three sources were refused on licence grounds in the prototype. Two stay refused: HIFLD transmission lines via Esri (Master License Agreement forbids redistribution; corridors were built from OpenStreetMap instead) and any Google Maps or DataCenterMap extraction (terms forbid bulk use). The third, the SEMI World Fab Forecast (per-seat licence at $11,100 a year; fabs are sourced independently), stays refused today and becomes an optional purchase decided at Gate G4, as its row records. Two products are recorded as not bought by decision rather than by licence, ISO PSOLD and ISO Rapid Valuator, each with the trigger that would re-open the question. Every new vendor row above must enter the same register before its data enters Unity Catalog, and the open question of ODbL share-alike on a merged, published database goes to counsel before any paid or public release. The operating model assigns the owner.
Key takeaway: Of everything in the table, only four external things are mandatory for the filing: a corporate-linkage source (free GLEIF first, D&B for the rest), an issuer hierarchy for the asset side, a rating source for the reinsurers on Schedule XVIII (AM Best or an equivalent), and the cat vendor we already pay. The rest of the mandatory core is internal: five feeds we already run (positions, recoverables, letters of credit and collateral, cash and bank balances, investments) and the two things we build ourselves, the entity graph and the schedule-producing core of the concentration engine. Everything else is a profit lever that is either already in hand at no new cost, or optional and released only when a measured gap at a gate justifies it. The two purchases to time carefully are both Verisk: re-tender at the Synergy Studio migration, and fold the new US data-center database into that same negotiation.
11

How Databricks can help

The lakehouse holds the history, the entity mapping, the lineage and the regulatory logic; the web app presents it. That split is what makes a filed number reproducible.

Data

Databricks Unity Catalog is the governance layer built into Databricks: it decides who can see which table, column or row, records every access for audit, tracks lineage from source file to dashboard, and monitors data quality. Databricks AI/BI dashboards and Genie (the natural-language interface) sit on top of it, so an executive asking "what is our largest bank counterparty today?" gets an answer computed only from data they are entitled to see. [DBX-UC] [DBX-2] [DBX-GENIE]

This is not a greenfield platform decision. The data-center map (its subsection) already has a Databricks deployment designed and built to its first phase, and the concentration layer in the counterparty and asset concentration sections should land in the same workspace, the same catalog conventions and the same governance rules. One platform, one set of access controls, one lineage graph from a cedent's exposure file or a treasury balance to the number the Board sees.

Diagram: sources flow through the lakehouse into governed Delta tables; Unity Catalog sits under every consumer; the internal Portfolio Management app and the BMA reporting package read the same Gold tables.

11.1 Where the Databricks work stands today

Honest status, as of 2026-09-27. Map step 0 of the map's own migration plan (numbered separately from the enterprise phases in the roadmap) was built on 2026-09-23 and verified locally on 2026-09-26. It runs the prototype unmodified behind a proxy on Databricks Apps: workspace single sign-on in front of every route, data staged at start-up from two Unity Catalog Volumes (dcmap.app.data and dcmap.app.epoch), the 1.6 GB PMTiles basemap (a single file of map tiles read by byte-range, no tile server) range-proxied through the Files API, and every write route answered with 403 (DCMAP_READONLY=1). It is read-only and it is not yet deployed to a workspace: nothing past map step 0 is built, the hand-edit ledger is still files on a laptop, and the 60-script pipeline has not been moved. Source: databricksapps/README.html header badges and docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md section 11.

11.2 Four storage tiers, each doing one job

The repo's target architecture does not put everything in one kind of store. It uses four, and the split follows from what each is good at. The concentration tables (cedent exposure, treaty and fac, counterparty) join this design as new schemas beside the registry, not as a separate platform.

Data engineering

Ingest heterogeneous feeds, preserve raw history in Bronze, standardise identifiers (LEI, D-U-N-S, internal ids) in Silver, and compute enterprise aggregates in Gold. The registry's 60 Python pipeline scripts become Lakeflow Jobs with scheduling, retries and a run log; the paid-source guard (refuse a billed Regrid or Precisely run without explicit confirmation) is kept as a job parameter, not dropped.

Governance

Unity Catalog governs who sees treaty, fac, collateral, investment and counterparty information, and it is also how the vendor licences become enforceable instead of documented (see below). [DBX-GOV]

Executive analytics

AI/BI dashboards and Genie give executives natural-language access to governed metrics while respecting Unity Catalog permissions. Accuracy comes from the semantic layer underneath (column comments, certified example queries, metric views with synonyms, trusted SQL functions), not from the model. [DBX-AIBI]

11.3 How licences are enforced on the platform

The prototype's licence register (dcmap/lib/licences.mjs, rendered at /licences) records that Regrid and Precisely parcel attributes are licensed per record and must not be redistributed, that Esri World Imagery may not be redistributed, and that most of the registry is ODbL-derived (the OpenStreetMap share-alike licence: internal use is safe, a public or paid release is an open legal question). On a laptop those are notes. In a workspace they become mechanisms:

  • Row filters and column masks on the licensed columns, with grants that match each licence ("row filters restrict which rows a user can see in a table; column masks control what values a user sees for specific columns"). [DBX-9]
  • On-behalf-of-user tokens. Databricks Apps forwards the viewer's own access token on every request (X-Forwarded-Access-Token), so Genie and SQL run as the person looking at the screen, not as the app's service principal that can see everything. [DBX-AUTH] The viewer's e-mail, which Databricks Apps forwards in a separate X-Forwarded-Email header, is written into an edited_by column, so the ledger stops being anonymous. [DBX-12]
  • No embedded-credential dashboards on licensed columns. A dashboard published with the "shared data permission" option runs every viewer's query with the publisher's credentials and silently defeats the row filters; only "individual data permissions" runs them as the viewer. [DBX-10] Publish without embedded credentials, or build on a view that excludes the licensed fields.
Decision, not detail. Head of Data/IT General Counsel Moving the map from one laptop to a shared workspace is a change in licensing posture and must be made deliberately: the repo's open-questions table (docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md section 12, row 5) leaves Regrid and Precisely redistribution unassigned to any phase. This blueprint assigns it to Phase 1 (the ODbL share-alike position and the imagery licence are Phase 0 prerequisites in the roadmap), before the app is opened to anyone outside the build team. The rest of the data-rights posture is in the operating model.

11.4 The Genie rule

Genie answers questions; it does not move the camera. It always shows its SQL and its row count. Genie is text-to-SQL over curated Unity Catalog tables. It does not call functions, does not geocode and does not see the map. "Take me to London" is routed deterministically to a gazetteer in about a millisecond; "how many megawatts are in London" goes to Genie and takes seconds; any answer whose rows carry coordinates or a site id becomes a map action. Three trusted SQL functions (sites_near, place_bbox, top_locations), called by the app rather than by Genie, are the bridge between a verified Genie answer and the map. A number without its SQL would be the one dishonest surface in a system whose site pages cite every source row.
Example pipeline: from raw balances to the BMA schedules and the app (implementation detail)
BRONZE raw history, never edited (dcmap.raw.* ; conc.raw.*) cash_balances_raw · investment_positions_raw · receivables_raw reinsurance_recoverables_raw · collateral_instruments_raw (LOC, trust, funds withheld) gleif_lei_raw · dnb_hierarchy_raw · cedent_exposure_files_raw · treaty_fac_bordereaux_raw dcmap.raw.* : EIA-860, GEM, OSM, NYISO/PJM/ERCOT queues, Epoch AI, IM3, parcels ↓ validation, normalisation, identifier standardisation SILVER one row per real thing, effective-dated (conc.curated.* ; dcmap.curated.*) entity · entity_relationship (parent, guarantor, affiliate) program · layer · participation · collateral (SECURES obligation_id) cash_position · security_position · receivable_position · recoverable_position cedent_exposure · position · risk_measure · model_result dcmap.curated.sites · footprints · power_plants · substations · power_deps · parcels_* ↓ resolve global ultimate, apply netting and collateral rules, effective date GOLD decision-ready, one definition each (conc.serving.* ; dcmap.serving.*) enterprise_counterparty_exposure_daily · top_counterparty_concentration collateral_provider_concentration · affiliated_reinsurance_flow · portfolio_limit_breach bma_sched_xxi_top10_asset_counterparties bma_sched_xviii_ceded_reinsurance bma_sched_xixa_cash_and_cash_equivalents (Schedule XIX in the long-term handbook) bma_sched_v_c_top10_unaffiliated bma_sched_v_c_intragroup_transactions bma_quarterly_return_pack dcmap.serving.map_sites · site_h3_r{4,6,8} · gazetteer · exposure (metric view) ↓ Statement Execution API · AI/BI dashboards · Genie INTERNAL PORTFOLIO MANAGEMENT APP + BMA REPORTING PACKAGE

Table names are a proposal. The BMA Gold outputs are the schedules the concentration return actually needs (the BMA section); each is reconciled to Form 1EBS (Form 4EBS for a Class C / D / E reinsurer, whose handbook also still numbers the cash schedule XIX rather than XIXA) and statutory capital and surplus before it is filed. The registry tables under dcmap.* follow the naming already in docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md section 4.1.

Plumbing note: there is no official Databricks SDK for Node.js, so the app talks REST over fetch (Statement Execution, Files, Jobs, Genie) with either the app's own token or the viewer's forwarded one; the Python SDK matters in the pipeline, not the app. Use a serverless SQL warehouse: on DBR 17.0+ the H3 cell functions (the hexagonal grid the map already bins into) are not supported on classic warehouses. [DBX-5]

11.5 The scale limit the prototype already hit

One measured engineering fact shapes the enterprise map more than any vendor choice. MapLibre (the open-source GPU map renderer the prototype uses) fails silently when one GeoJSON source holds roughly 189,000 vertices: no error, the layer never appears. The prototype reproduced it with 19,367 building footprints (308,000 vertices), and footprints are now served per viewport from /api/footprints for that reason. A single cedent location file can carry hundreds of thousands of risks, so the design is zoom-banded from the start: H3 aggregates above metro zoom, viewport-clipped queries below it, pre-baked PMTiles for stable context layers. The number of features the browser holds is bounded by the viewport, not by the dataset. This is also why the H3 grid in Mega Project Asset Intelligence is the executive view of accumulation rather than a nice-to-have. [MAPLIBRE] [PMTILES]

Why Databricks rather than putting all logic in the web app?

The web app should be a presentation and workflow layer. The calculation history, entity mapping, source lineage, regulatory logic, model outputs and enterprise data should live in a governed data platform. That makes the answer reproducible, auditable and reusable by Finance, Risk, Underwriting and Portfolio Management, and it is what lets the BMA schedules and the daily management view be computed from the same rows. The one thing that stays in the app is the in-memory map model: 403 MB and a 427 ms rebuild is a good deal, and a query per pan would be worse.

Key takeaway: The platform is not hypothetical: the map's step 0 (the read-only lift) is built and verified locally, not yet deployed, and its four-tier design (Volume, Delta, Lakebase, app memory) is the one the concentration layer joins. Unity Catalog is where the BMA schedules, the management view and the vendor licences become one enforceable set of rules; Genie reads only those tables, always shows its SQL, and never moves the camera.

How a custom web app changes the operating model

The app is how the architecture becomes a daily business system instead of a warehouse people visit quarterly.

Portfolio MgmtCUOData

The web app is how the architecture becomes a daily business system instead of a data warehouse people visit quarterly. Part of it already exists: the data-center map is a working internal app with the provenance discipline this section asks for, and the enterprise pages are added beside it rather than built from nothing.

12.1 What the prototype UI already does

Exists today, in the repo (dcmap/), as of 2026-09-27. Every item below is running code, not a design.
  • HAVE Per-site shareable pages (/maps/site/<id>) that list every source row behind the site with outbound links; plant, fab and substation pages on the same pattern; operator pages.
  • HAVE Directory pages: /power (dependencies), /fabs, /footprints, /licences (the licence register, rendered so attribution travels with the product) and /data (pipeline freshness and change log).
  • HAVE Search palette over sites, operators, utilities, countries and grid zones, an un-geocoded site is still findable and links to its page instead of flying the map.
  • HAVE Timeline (Q1 2019 to Q1 2030) with build-out and largest-AI-campus charts.
  • HAVE Earthquake exposure panel: USGS ShakeMap MMI bands (Modified Mercalli Intensity, how hard the ground shook at a place on a I to XII scale) drawn per event, shaken sites, plants and fabs listed worst-first, each event with its own page.
  • HAVE Layer panel (facilities, footprints, parcels, plants, substations, transmission, water service areas, dependency lines, hexagon heatmap, earthquakes) and a 3D globe that bins into identical H3 cells (the hexagonal grid used for accumulation).
  • HAVE Edit pens writing append-only ledgers: site_overrides.csv (455 fields applied, each with a "how I know" note), footprint_overrides.geojsonl, name reviews, dropped points, simulated events. Corrections are never applied in place; the history is the record.
  • HAVE Wayback imagery viewer on the dot pages, so a site can be checked against dated satellite frames.
  • HAVE Underwriting export (src/export_underwriting.py): assets.csv, dependencies.csv, asset_dependency_links.csv shaped for the separate Reinsurance Underwriting Platform loader. This is the first join point between the registry and the treaty and fac book: an exact-located site or fab becomes an asset id a submission can be matched to. The export honestly ships estimated_tiv_m = 0.0, meaning "not established", because the registry does not estimate valuations; TIV (total insured value, what a building and its contents are insured for) comes from the cedent or the model, never from the map.
What it does not yet do is in the data-center map subsection: no cedent exposure join, no treaty or fac overlay, no TIV, no modelled loss, no authentication beyond the laptop (map step 0 in the Databricks migration phases puts workspace sign-on in front, once deployed). Those are the enterprise additions below.

Internal executive / Portfolio Management app

  • NEW Enterprise concentration dashboard
  • NEW Top 10 counterparty exposures and threshold alerts
  • NEW Drill from global ultimate (the top of a corporate family tree) to legal entity to instrument to source transaction
  • NEW Collateral and wrong-way risk view (the bank that secures our recoverable, the money a reinsurer owes us, fails in the same event as the reinsurer)
  • NEW Affiliated reinsurance flow graph
  • HAVE Mega Risk Map on MapLibre + self-hosted PMTiles + h3-js, with the hexagon accumulation of the registry's own measures (count, MW, capex)
  • NEW Insurance measures on the same hexagons: TIV, treaty and fac line, AAL, PML, marginal capital (the extra capital one more contract requires)
  • NEW Treaty + facultative overlap

Optional cedent / broker portal PHASE 5

  • Secure exposure-file upload
  • Data-quality exceptions, and a data-quality score per submission (geocoding resolution, completeness of construction and occupancy modifiers, BI values, currency of valuations) fed back to the cedent with its pricing consequence
  • "Please validate these 12 locations" workflow
  • Engineering-report exchange
  • Campus / asset match confirmation
  • Cedent severity-analysis upload where permitted: the cedent's PSOLD output (the industry severity curves for property losses, which we do not license ourselves) with the transparency package behind it

Data-use caveat. The portal must be designed so licensed layers (Regrid, Precisely, Esri imagery) and ODbL-derived layers can be withheld from external users, and so one cedent never sees another's data or a named-insured resolution of its own anonymised records. Cedents give us exposure data to price their treaty, not necessarily so we can identify their clients and compare them with a competitor's book. Most wordings allow portfolio accumulation; fewer allow re-identification. The data-use register in the operating model records which is which, per feed, before the map makes it easy.

12.2 Executive drill-down should be almost infinitely explainable
