12.4 A tile worth adding: collateral efficiency

Worked example: the collateral-efficiency tile on the Collateral & LOC page (illustrative)

Two numbers, side by side, per counterparty and in total:

  • Recognised collateral / total collateral. Collateral the regulator lets us count (eligible instrument, capped at the net exposure it secures, after haircut) divided by everything we actually hold. A ratio well below 100% means we are paying for security that earns no capital relief.
  • Annual fee on unrecognised collateral. The letter of credit (a bank's promise to pay if the reinsurer does not) and trust fees we pay, or the funds-withheld interest we forgo, on the part of the collateral that is not recognised.
CounterpartyTotal collateralRecognisedRatioFee on unrecognised (illustrative)
Reinsurer A (LOC, Bank X)$150M$95M63%$55M × 0.60% = $0.33M / yr
Reinsurer B (trust)$80M$80M100%$0
Reinsurer C (LOC, Bank X)$40M$12M30%$28M × 0.60% = $0.17M / yr

Illustrative amounts and fee rate. The point of the tile: over-collateralisation on one contract does not offset under-collateralisation on another, so the ratio is computed per obligation and then summed (the counterparty worked examples walk the calculation). Two LOCs from Bank X also make Bank X a concentration in its own right, which the same page shows.

Decision it drives: Treasurer Head of Ceded Reinsurance renegotiate, resize or restructure the instruments with the lowest ratio at the next renewal; that is one of the profit levers.

Key takeaway: Half the app exists: the registry map, its dependency graph, its earthquake panel and its append-only ledgers are running code with the explainability standard the whole system must inherit, and the underwriting export is the first join to the treaty and fac book. The new pages are the concentration, collateral, investment and capacity views, plus the seven added in this version (non-cat severity challenge, cedent intelligence, the true-net waterfall, counterparty credit, casualty systemic, the evidence review queue and data-rights controls); the BMA Concentration page is mandatory, and its question is whether four schedules reconcile to each other and to Form 1EBS (Form 4EBS for a long-term reinsurer).
13

Canonical data model: the part that makes everything reusable

Six canonical objects, with relationships stored as first-class data, are what turn every regulatory record into reusable decision data.

Data

Executives do not need to see every table, but the architecture succeeds or fails on a small set of canonical objects. The system will be asked "what is our net loss from this event on 1 January, after renewals". Answering that needs the treaty terms, who wrote it, which model version produced the loss, and which deals are bound but not yet started. v2's six objects could not hold any of those four things; this version can.

Entity

Bank, insurer, reinsurer, broker, issuer, corporate parent, cedent, affiliate, trustee. Keyed by LEI (the free global legal-entity identifier) where one exists, D-U-N-S (the D&B number) for private companies, and an internal id always. Carries risk_carrying_entity: which legal entity actually bears the risk when a deal is fronted (one insurer issues the contract in its own name and passes the risk to another).

Asset

Security, parcel, structure, campus, power plant, substation, investment fund. The registry's 6,295 sites, 33,632 footprints, 28,161 plants and 127 substations are Assets today, as files on the prototype; they become the dcmap.curated.* Delta tables at map step 2 of the registry sub-track (the registry's migration phases). Collateral instruments are not Assets; see Contract.

Contract

Treaty, fac certificate, retrocession (reinsurance we buy), affiliated reinsurance agreement, and every collateral arrangement. Structured as Programme → Layer → Participation with the financial terms, effective-dated, with a position_status (quoted, bound, in-force, expired).

Exposure

What could be lost, as a stock: cash and investment balances, receivables, recoverables, insured TIV (total insured value), limits. No model outputs live here.

Position

Our share after contract terms: the Exposure passed through attachment, limit, share and inuring covers (other reinsurance that pays first and reduces what reaches this contract). This is the number that changes at renewal without the underlying Exposure changing.

RiskMeasure

Derived numbers: AAL (average annual loss), OEP and AEP points (loss from the largest single event, or from all events, in a year at a given probability), PML, allocated capital. Each carries its basis, return period and a ModelResult reference.

ModelResult

A versioned run: model id and version, event set, own-view adjustment set, run date, and the ELT / YLT reference (event loss table, year loss table: the model's list of what each event or each simulated year costs). The model-governance requirement in the operating model is satisfied by this object or not at all.

Relationship

Parent/subsidiary, guarantees, SECURES (collateral to obligation), reinsures, fronts-for, supplies power, supplies water, belongs-to-campus. Every edge carries its basis: source, confidence, approver, effective dates. Already implemented for power in the prototype (below).

Scenario

Hurricane, earthquake (ShakeMap footprints exist in the prototype), cyber event, bank default, collateral impairment, cedent default under funds withheld, mega-project fire, substation loss.

Why three objects where v2 had one. A building's value, our share of it, and what a hurricane model says we would lose are three different kinds of number. Storing them separately (Exposure, Position, RiskMeasure) keeps every chart honest about which one it shows and stops anyone summing an AAL with a TIV.

13.1 Contract: programme, layer, participation

A reinsurance programme is a cedent's whole purchase for a class of business in a year; it is split into layers (bands of loss), and we hold a participation (our share) on each layer we write. The terms below are what turn an Exposure into a Position, so they must be data, not PDF.

Contract fields (implementation detail)
Program program_id · cedent_entity_id · broker_entity_id · class_of_business · underwriting_year currency · inception · expiry · attachment_basis (risk-attaching | losses-occurring) occurrence_definition · hours_clause (e.g. 72h wind, 168h flood) · inuring_covers[] Layer layer_id · program_id · attachment (retention) · limit · aggregate_deductible aggregate_limit · reinstatements (count, premium %) · peril_scope · territory_scope Participation (our line; effective-dated) participation_id · layer_id · share_pct · signed_line · written_line risk_carrying_entity_id (which of our legal entities bears it; fronting flag) position_status (quoted | bound | in-force | expired) valid_from · valid_to · superseded_by time_basis for reporting: written | bound-not-incepted | in-force | projected Collateral (a Contract sub-type, never an Asset) collateral_id · sub_type (LOC | TRUST_SINGLE_BENEFICIARY | TRUST_MULTI_BENEFICIARY | FUNDS_WITHHELD | GUARANTEE) direction (we post | we receive) · beneficiary_entity_id · provider_entity_id trustee_or_custodian_entity_id · asset_risk_bearer (us | cedent | reinsurer) eligible_asset_rules · funding_ratio · top_up_triggers · release_conditions look_through_reportable (bool) · expiry · evergreen_flag SECURES → obligation_id (the recoverable or reserve it stands behind) CounterpartyExposure (Silver, one row per counterparty x obligation x date) obligation_id · gross_amount · payable_amount · setoff_right_flag collateral_eligibility (regulatory) · internal_haircut (economic) cap_at_net_exposure (bool) · rating_basis (reinsurer | LOC issuer | affiliate override) future_balance_projection · effective_date

Field lists are a proposal. The regulatory netting and haircut rules that the CounterpartyExposure fields exist to reproduce are worked in the counterparty worked examples; the factors are in the BMA capital-charge subsection. Where the class of registration changes a rule, the field carries the value for [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E] as configured, not hard-coded.

13.2 Collateral is a relationship, not a balance

v2 listed "collateral instrument" under Asset and "LOC" under Contract, which contradicts its own collateral subsection. Here every collateral arrangement is a Contract with a SECURES edge to the obligation it stands behind, and its sub-type says who is exposed to whom:

  • Funds withheld means the cedent keeps our premium as security instead of paying it to us. That protects the cedent, but a large cedent that goes bust owes us a lot: the credit risk points at the cedent. The BMA even splits the treatment by who bears the asset risk (segregated assets we bear the market risk of are reported by look-through; otherwise the balance is treated like a reinsurance recoverable from the cedent). The asset_risk_bearer and look_through_reportable fields carry that distinction; the counterparty worked examples work one.
  • Trusts and letters of credit are the reverse: assets sit with a bank or trustee for the beneficiary's benefit. A multi-beneficiary trust needs the funding ratio and the rules for who is paid first.
  • Guarantees from a parent are a Relationship edge (GUARANTEES) with the guarantor as a counterparty in its own right.

Each structure moves risk to a different party, so each must be recorded as its own kind of relationship. The regulator also lets us net what a retrocessionaire owes us against what we owe them only if the contract says we can, and lets us count collateral only up to the debt it secures after a small haircut. If our system nets and offsets more freely than the rules do, the regulatory number and the management number will disagree, and both will be distrusted. That is why setoff_right_flag and cap_at_net_exposure are fields on the exposure row rather than assumptions in a spreadsheet.

13.3 Relationship, as already built: the power-dependency ledger

The "supplies power" edge is not a concept in this repo. The prototype's dependency ledger (dcmap/data/power_dependencies.json, with hand corrections in dependency_overrides.csv) holds 212 edges: 170 of them link loads to 127 substations and each cites the PJM TEAC or NYISO interconnection filing it came from (20 are queue positions since withdrawn, kept and flagged rather than deleted); the other 42 link sites to co-located power plants and cite a press report or a regulatory docket. Vouched resilience facts (backup power, substation aliases, load links) are carried on the edge. The map draws them as dependency lines, substation dots and supply lines; each US site also carries its water-utility dependency (EPA service areas) and the generation within 25 km. This is the Relationship object, in production, for one dependency type.

Worked example: the Kintigh cluster (from the prototype ledger, read 2026-09-27)

Kintigh is a 345 kV NYSEG substation in western New York (registry id sub-kintigh, placed from the OpenStreetMap way it aliases). Five ledger edges hang off it, every one citing an NYISO load-interconnection queue position; one of them (0359) is a position the queue has since withdrawn, which the ledger keeps and flags rather than deletes:

Load (queue #)Queued MWEdgeBackup powerBasis
Somerset Load (849), Lake Mariner Data II (1670), Wulf Compute Data Center II (1732): three positions, one registry campus250 eachprimary feedyes (battery, not diesel)vouched 2026-09-07 from a skeptic-upheld review
WNY STAMP (0580)300primary feedyesvouched
Verizon, Project Oasis (0359), since withdrawn from the queue75secondary feedunknownfiling only; kept and flagged as history, not counted as live

What the graph answers that a balance sheet cannot: four live queue positions (a fifth is withdrawn and kept for history), two registry campuses and one not-yet-matched load share one 345 kV feed, so a Kintigh outage is one event for all of them, and "backup power: yes" on the ledger says how long that event lasts before it is a loss. Queued MW is what the filing asks for, not what is built; the timeline layer carries the build-out. When the treaty and fac lines are joined (the data-center map subsection), the same edges give the shared-dependency contingent-BI accumulation in the asset worked examples. Scenario C ("diversified locations share one power dependency") is this pattern.

The standard every new edge inherits. The prototype's ledger records, on each row, the source, the filing reference, a "how I know" note, whether a skeptic upheld it, and the date. Every counterparty-group mapping (this bank is a subsidiary of that group), every SECURES edge and every economic-interdependence override in the enterprise system carries the same basis columns: source, confidence, approver, valid_from, valid_to. A mapping without a basis is not loaded.
Why relationships matter as much as balances

A traditional risk warehouse stores balances. This system also stores relationships. "$120M LOC" is just a balance until we know which bank issued it, which recoverable it secures, which parent owns that bank, the expiry, and what happens if the bank and the reinsurer are impaired in the same event. "250 MW campus" is just a row until we know which substation feeds it, which other campuses share that substation, and whether it has batteries. The relationship graph is what converts reporting data into decision intelligence, and it is the part of the model the prototype has already proven for one dependency type.

Key takeaway: Nine objects instead of six: Contract now holds programme, layer, participation and every collateral structure with a SECURES edge; Exposure, Position and RiskMeasure are separated so a value, our share and a modelled loss are never confused; ModelResult gives every risk number a version. The Relationship object is not theory: 212 evidenced power edges already run in the prototype, and their basis columns are the standard every counterparty and collateral mapping must meet.

13.4 Two more canonical objects: Evidence and Data rights

The Relationship object above says every edge carries its basis. Two things are still missing from the model as written: a way to say how sure we are of an edge, in a form a rule can act on, and a way to say what we are allowed to do with the data the edge was built from. Confidence, evidence and human review are mandatory; so is a record of rights. This subsection adds both as canonical objects, and reconciles them with what the prototype and the governance section already do.

Evidence: an algorithm's match is a claim, not a fact

A GPS match, a campus match or a power-dependency inference never becomes an unqualified fact because an algorithm produced it. A location in a cedent's schedule that falls inside a parcel is very probably that parcel; the parcel is probably part of the campus the registry names; the campus is possibly fed by the substation an interconnection filing mentions; the substation is perhaps supplied by the plant next door. Each step is a separate claim with its own evidence and its own error rate, and the errors multiply along the chain. If the platform aggregates every inferred edge as if it were true, the accumulation number is confidently wrong; if it aggregates none, it is honestly useless. The answer is to score each edge, band the score, and let the band decide what the edge may be used for.

Every relationship therefore carries a confidence band (CONFIRMED, HIGH, PROBABLE or POSSIBLE: a plain-language label over the numeric score, set by policy rather than by the algorithm that produced the score), the evidence behind it, when the evidence was seen, the dates the relationship held, who reviewed it, and whether a person overrode the machine and why:

AssetRelationship # one row per edge; supersedes, never overwrites - relationship_id - from_asset_id # location, parcel, campus, substation, plant - to_asset_id - relationship_type # LOCATED_IN / PART_OF_CAMPUS / FED_BY_SUBSTATION / # SUPPLIED_BY_PLANT / SHARES_WATER_UTILITY - confidence_score # 0.00 .. 1.00 from the matcher or the reviewer - confidence_band # CONFIRMED / HIGH / PROBABLE / POSSIBLE - evidence_source # CEDENT_SCHEDULE / PARCEL_LAYER / NYISO_QUEUE / # PJM_TEAC / PRESS / SITE_VISIT / MANUAL - evidence_url_or_doc # the filing, page or file, as the ledger cites it - evidence_date # when the evidence was true, not when we read it - effective_from - effective_to # a withdrawn queue position keeps its history - reviewer # a person, from the app's identity header - review_status # UNREVIEWED / UPHELD / REJECTED / STALE - manual_override # true when a person set the band by hand - override_reason # the prototype's "how I know" note - created_by_run_id # the pipeline run or the edit that wrote it

The band, not the score, is what the rest of the system reads. The policy that assigns bands is a governance decision taken once and versioned, so a change in the matcher's calibration does not silently move edges between bands. The ladder below shows a typical chain from a treaty location to a power plant:

Worked example: one location, four edges, two of them fit for automatic aggregation (illustrative)
EdgeScoreBandEvidenceMay be aggregated automatically?
Treaty location (GPS in Cedent A's schedule) is inside parcel 41-11899%CONFIRMEDPoint-in-polygon on a county parcel layer; the schedule also carries the street addressYes
Parcel 41-118 is part of the registry's AI campus96%HIGHParcel owner matches the operator; the drawn campus footprint contains it; a skeptic upheld the name reviewYes
The campus is fed by substation S-1278%PROBABLEAn interconnection queue position names the substation and a load of the right size; the campus has not confirmed itNo: counted in the shared-dependency stress with a flag, and queued for review
Substation S-12 is supplied by power plant P-754%POSSIBLEA press report and proximity; no filingNo: shown on the map as a dashed line, excluded from any number, held for a person to validate

Only the first two edges are suitable for automatic aggregation. The third is used, but only inside a stress view that says so, and the fourth is a lead for an analyst, not an input to a limit. The multiplication is the point: 0.99 times 0.96 times 0.78 times 0.54 is about 40%, so a report that treated the whole chain as fact would be more likely wrong than right about the plant, while being almost certainly right about the campus. The bands make that distinction visible on every screen. Data Portfolio Mgmt

The prototype already does most of this. Every hand correction in the data-center map is appended to a ledger with a "how I know" note, the research sweeps are adversarially reviewed and the verdicts kept, and the power-dependency ledger keeps a withdrawn queue position as flagged history rather than deleting it (#dcmap-position, #governance). The AssetRelationship object is that practice made into a schema: the "how I know" note becomes override_reason, the skeptic's verdict becomes review_status, and the basis columns the Relationship object already requires (source, confidence, approver, valid_from, valid_to) are kept and given a band. What is new is the band policy and the rule that only CONFIRMED and HIGH edges enter an automatic total. The review queue that this implies, "which low-confidence or material matches need approval before they affect a limit or a filing", is an application page in #webapp. HAVE BUILD

Data rights: the register, as an object the platform can enforce

The platform combines data with very different contractual rights: open share-alike map data, per-record parcel licences, rating feeds with display terms, cedent schedules that were sent to price one treaty, and our own claims. The operating model already keeps a data-use register for this (#op-licensing, and the cedent-feed register in #governance), and its rule is that a licence term becomes a Unity Catalog grant. The Data rights registry is what that register becomes inside the data model: one row per source, dataset and field, stating what may be done with it, so that a query, a model-training job or a portal page can be checked against it by a rule rather than by a person's memory.

DataRights # one row per source x dataset x field or object - data_rights_id - source_provider # REGRID / PRECISELY / SP / DNB / AMB / VERISK / # CYBERCUBE / OSM_ODBL / EPOCH / CEDENT_A / INTERNAL - dataset # e.g. parcels, SNL ratings, cat treaty schedule - field_or_object # * for the whole dataset, or one column - permitted_internal_use # ALL / ANALYTICS_ONLY / PLACEMENT_ONLY / NONE - permitted_model_training # true / false; Genie and ML feature tables read this - permitted_cross_cedent_aggregation # NONE / H3_CELL_TOTALS / CAMPUS_TOTALS / NAMED_ROWS - permitted_external_display # NONE / OWN_DATA_ONLY / AGGREGATES / WITH_CREDIT_LINE - retention_period # e.g. treaty term plus run-off; 7 years; 2 years - licence_expiry # contract end; null for open licences - jurisdiction_restriction # e.g. no export of parcel geometry outside the US entity - confidentiality_classification # PUBLIC / INTERNAL / CONFIDENTIAL / CEDENT_RESTRICTED - licence_class # SHARE_ALIKE / LICENSED_NO_REDISTRIBUTION / # DISPLAY_ONLY / ATTRIBUTION / REFUSED_ON_PRICE - enforced_as # the UC grant, row filter or column mask id - owner # the data steward accountable for the row - valid_from / valid_to

How it reconciles with the registers already in the document. The vendor table in #op-licensing has columns for internal use, portal use and "enforced as"; those are permitted_internal_use, permitted_external_display and enforced_as. The cedent-feed register in the governance section has permitted purposes, re-identification, retention, cross-cedent analytics and default role; those are permitted_internal_use, confidentiality_classification (CEDENT_RESTRICTED means re-identification is held behind a separate role), retention_period and permitted_cross_cedent_aggregation. Three fields are new, and each has already cost the prototype a decision: permitted_model_training, because a Genie room or a matching model trained on a cedent's schedule is a use the wording may not allow; licence_expiry, because a per-seat feed that lapses must stop appearing in a filing on the day it lapses; and licence_class REFUSED_ON_PRICE, because the prototype's register records that SEMI World Fab Forecast was declined at $11,100 a year per seat and that its 214 fabs came from open sources instead, and a future reader of a fab row must be able to see that provenance without opening the repository; the seat is now an optional purchase decided at Gate G4, and if it is bought the row's class changes on that date while the openly sourced fab rows keep theirs. Every row is enforced in Unity Catalog as a grant, row filter or column mask [DBX-9], and the open share-alike question on the OpenStreetMap-derived layers stays recorded as open, with counsel's decision as its valid_from [ODBL].

Information barriers: what Portfolio Management sees, and what the facultative underwriter sees

The sharpest use of the registry is inside the company, not at its edge. An information barrier is a rule that lets one function use a piece of data while another function, which would gain an unfair or unlicensed advantage from it, sees only the conclusion. Facultative detail is the case that matters here: a named facultative submission on a campus can identify the anonymous treaty locations that other cedents placed there, which is exactly what Cedent A's wording forbids. Portfolio Management may use the combined picture, because the data-use register permits accumulation; the facultative underwriter, who is about to negotiate with a broker, sees only what the decision needs.

Worked example: Campus C, two views of one number (illustrative)

Campus C is a hyperscale campus, larger than Data Center A in #fac-dc-a. Three contracts already touch it. The exposure column is what the cedents insure on the campus that flows into our contracts; the position column is our share after the treaty and facultative terms, the Position object's number. The single-campus appetite is the $150M the limit framework sets.

Portfolio Management sees

Cedent A treaty: $450M of campus exposure in the schedule, our position $45M.
Cedent B treaty: $300M, our position $30M.
Existing facultative (Cedent C, via Broker X): $75M, our line $20M.
Campus total: $825M of cedent exposure; our position $95M; headroom to the $150M campus appetite $55M; shared substation S-12 with one other registry campus.

The facultative underwriter sees

"Material existing campus concentration."
Supportable line: $25M to $40M.
Primary driver: existing campus accumulation.
Secondary driver: shared substation, contingent-BI wording to be tightened.
No cedent names, no broker names, no treaty identifiers, no exposure amounts by cedent.

The underwriter's answer is the same as it would be with the full picture: a $40M line takes our position to $135M, inside appetite with $15M kept back for the substation share; a $60M line would not be. What differs is that nobody on the facultative desk now knows which cedents are on Campus C, so the broker cannot learn it from us either. In #fac-dc-a the underwriter reads the campus page with the cedent rows visible; that is the view the registry allows only where every feed on the campus permits named cross-cedent display to the facultative role (Cedent B's facultative submissions in the governance register do; Cedent A's treaty schedule does not). Where any feed on the campus withholds it, the page collapses to the right-hand card, and the ladder of line, campus total, marginal capital and return is still computed on the full data behind the barrier. Fac UW Portfolio Mgmt CRO

RoleSeesDoes not seeEnforced by
Portfolio Management, CRO, Concentration CommitteeEvery contract on the campus by cedent, exposure and position, the substation edges with their bands, the marginal capitalNothing withheld; the data-use register permits accumulation for every feedGrant to the portfolio role on the Gold campus tables
Facultative underwriterThe decision output: concentration level, supportable line range, primary and secondary driver, the marginal-capital ladderCedent and broker names, treaty ids and per-cedent amounts, unless every feed on the campus permits itA column mask on the identity fields and a row filter on permitted_cross_cedent_aggregation, applied to the campus table itself (Unity Catalog applies filters and masks to tables, not to views), which the facultative page reads

Every figure in this subsection is illustrative. The roles and the enforcement mechanisms are those already set out in #op-licensing and the governance section; the on-behalf-of identity that makes a per-viewer filter possible in the Databricks App is described in #dcmap-position.

Key takeaway: add Evidence and Data rights to the canonical objects. Every inferred edge carries a score, a band, its evidence, its dates, a reviewer and any human override, and only CONFIRMED and HIGH edges enter an automatic total; the prototype's "how I know" ledger is that object in miniature. Every source, dataset and field carries a rights row that says what may be aggregated, trained on, retained and shown, enforced as a grant rather than remembered by a person, so that Portfolio Management can see three cedents on one campus while the facultative underwriter sees a supportable line and nothing that would let a broker learn who else is there.

Executive scenarios: what this lets us answer that we cannot answer cleanly today

Twelve situations the enterprise view answers cleanly, each ending in a decision and the people who take it.

CEOCROCUO

Five situations the company meets every year, each answered twice: once by the systems we have, once by one governed concentration view. Every scenario ends with the decision it enables and who takes it. All figures are illustrative unless they carry a citation or are marked "from the prototype". Scenarios F to L and the scenario matrix follow in Scenarios F to L.

The illustrative capital base is the one used in How the compliance budget becomes profit: $2,000M of available statutory capital and a $1,400M BSCR (the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, the regulator's formula for how much capital we must hold). One basis point (bp) of BSCR is therefore $140,000; 100 bps is $14M.

14.1 Scenario A: a financial group appears in four systems

Treasury banks with ACME Bank NA. Investments holds bonds issued by ACME Funding LLC. Ceded Reinsurance holds a letter of credit (a bank's promise to pay us if a reinsurer does not) issued by ACME Bank London, securing a recoverable (money a reinsurer owes us for claims we have paid or reserved) from Reinsurer XYZ. Finance carries a receivable from ACME Securities. Four systems, four names, no link between them.

What the four systems see

Bank account ACME Bank NA $70M Bond issuer ACME Funding LLC $65M LOC issuer ACME Bank London $120M Receivable ACME Securities $20M

Four unrelated names in four ledgers. Nobody adds them up, and nobody should add them up this way either.

What the enterprise graph sees

ACME FINANCIAL GROUP (global ultimate) Direct credit exposure $155M cash $70M + bonds $65M + receivable $20M (money ACME owes us or holds for us) Protection dependency $120M LOC securing $120M of Reinsurer XYZ's $180M recoverable (a safety net for someone else's debt)

The split matters. A bank guarantee is not a deposit. If ACME fails we do not lose $120M; we lose the safety net under $120M of Reinsurer XYZ's debt, and only suffer if XYZ then fails too. That is a wrong-way risk question (could the reinsurer and the bank that guarantees it be hurt by the same event?), not a size question. Version 2 of this document summed the four rows into one "gross linked amount" of $275M; that number is still the right one for one regulatory list, but it is the wrong one for the capital and the downgrade questions. So the right question about ACME is not "how big is the number" but "how many of our safety nets depend on this one bank, and what happens the day it is downgraded".

Six questions, and which system can answer them

QuestionAnswer the enterprise view givesMinimum solutionWinning system
1. What does each BMA schedule see? Three different numbers from one graph, for a general-business reinsurer [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E]:
Schedule XXI (concentration risk, assets only): $135M, the cash and the bonds, reported as one grouped counterparty and charged at ACME's rating. The LOC and the receivable do not belong here.
Schedule XVIII (ceded reinsurance): the LOC does not appear as our exposure. It appears as collateral against Reinsurer XYZ's recoverable, and it moves the collateralised part of that recoverable to ACME Bank's rating where that is higher than XYZ's.
Schedule V(c) and the quarterly return (ten largest unaffiliated counterparties across every type): $275M across four transaction types, with location and type, tested against 10% of statutory capital and surplus (the regulatory capital figure on the statutory balance sheet). [BMA-GB]		 Yes, if the grouping is done by hand each quarterYes, from one graph, reconciled
2. What share of which capital? Two yardsticks, not one. Against statutory capital and surplus the Schedule V(c) test is 10%: on a $2,000M base, $275M is 13.75% and must be listed as a linked exposure above the threshold; the direct credit part alone is 7.75%. Against the BSCR, what matters is the charge that moves (Question 6), measured in ECR dollars (the Enhanced Capital Requirement, the capital we must actually hold). Yes, one ratioYes, both, with the charge
3. What is the trend? Quarter by quarter, because the quarterly return repeats the Schedule V(c) items and the graph keeps every resolution dated (see the group graph). ACME grew from $190M to $275M in three quarters because Treasury moved a deposit and Ceded Re renewed the LOC facility at a larger size, each without seeing the other. Partly, by re-running the spreadsheetYes
4. 5. What reinsurance protection depends on ACME LOCs? Every LOC from any ACME entity, across every reinsurer it secures, as one number: here $120M on Reinsurer XYZ, but the same query finds the two smaller ACME LOCs behind Reinsurers P and Q that Ceded Re booked under the branch names.
