The minimum solution answers Questions 1 and 2. The winning system answers all six, and the last two are where the money is.

Worked example: the ACME downgrade, Question 4 (illustrative)

Set-up. Reinsurer XYZ is rated BBB (BSCR rating 4). ACME Bank is rated A (BSCR rating 3). XYZ owes us a $180M recoverable, of which $120M is secured by ACME's LOC and $60M is unsecured. No payables with a right of set-off (the canonical telling in the BMA section nets a $10M set-off first, giving $170M net, $52.4M net qualifying exposure and a charge of about $3.6M; the step-by-step in collateral concentration adds a $20M trust as well; the arithmetic here is kept shorter).

Today. The handbook recognises collateral at 98% (a 2% haircut), capped at the net exposure, and applies the higher of the reinsurer's and the LOC issuer's rating to the part the LOC covers, splitting the balance where the LOC covers only part [BMA-GB]. Qualifying collateral is $120M x 98% = $117.6M. The $2.4M residue of the secured part is charged at ACME's A factor (3.5%) = $0.08M. The $60M unsecured part is charged at XYZ's BBB factor (7.0%) = $4.2M. Reinsurance credit charge before the diversification credit: about $4.3M, roughly 31 bps of BSCR.

Case 1: ACME is downgraded to BBB, level with XYZ. The rating step-up disappears, but the LOC still counts as collateral. The charge moves from $0.08M to $0.17M on the residue: a rounding error. The capital number barely moves. What has changed is the wrong-way risk: reinsurer and guarantor are now both BBB, and the CRO's joint stress (both impaired in one credit event) is the number that matters.

Case 2: ACME falls below the rating our collateral agreement or the handbook's eligibility conditions require, or ACME declines to renew. The $120M of collateral stops qualifying. The whole $180M is charged at XYZ's 7.0%: $12.6M. Added charge about $8.3M, roughly 59 bps of BSCR, on this one recoverable. Verify against the current instructions handbook what the eligibility conditions for an LOC issuer are before relying on Case 1 or Case 2.

The replacement clock. Collateral agreements typically give the reinsurer a notice period (30 to 60 days is common; check ours) to replace a downgraded bank. Within that window Ceded Re must obtain a replacement LOC from an eligible bank or move XYZ to a trust or a funds withheld arrangement (we keep the premium instead of paying it over). Any US-domiciled cedent (the insurer that buys reinsurance from us) in the group has its own credit-for-reinsurance rules for which banks and trusts count: verify per state. The graph lists which reinsurers, which amounts and which dates, in one screen, on the day of the downgrade.

Worked example: the concentration charge if ACME is grouped correctly, Question 6 (illustrative)

The BSCR levies a separate concentration-risk charge on every dollar of exposure to our ten largest grouped counterparties, on top of the ordinary market and credit charges, at factors by asset class and rating (bonds 0.4% AAA, 0.8% AA, 1.5% A, 3.0% BBB; cash 0.3% for an A-rated bank, from 0% (rating 0) to 9% (rating 8); letters of credit 20%) [BMA-GB] [BMA-C4-24]. The mechanics and the full factor table are in the BMA section, where the capital moves.

  • Not grouped. ACME Bank NA at $70M and ACME Funding LLC at $65M each fall outside our ten largest asset counterparties. Concentration charge on ACME: zero. This is not a saving; it is an under-statement the supervisor can see, because Schedule V(c) lists the same names.
  • Grouped. ACME Financial Group at $135M is our sixth-largest asset counterparty. Bonds: $65M x 1.5% = $0.98M, about 7 bps of BSCR. Cash: $70M x 0.3%, the Rules 2024 Table 5A factor for cash at BSCR rating 3 (A-rated), = $0.21M, about 1.5 bps [BMA-C4-24]. Total added concentration charge: about $1.2M, roughly 8.5 bps of BSCR, most of it from the bonds.
  • The LOC. The LOC is not our asset and does not enter Schedule XXI. The factor table nevertheless lists a letters-of-credit class at 20%. That class is for letters of credit and guarantees the company carries as its own statutory asset on Form 1EBS line 14(d) (typically capital-support instruments approved by the BMA), not for an LOC held as collateral behind a recoverable: confirm with the auditor that none of ours is booked at line 14(d). If it did, $120M x 20% = $24M, about 170 bps, would be the largest single item in this whole example, which is exactly why the classification must be settled once, in the graph, not per quarter, in a spreadsheet.

Grouping correctly can raise the charge (the honest number) or lower it (where a family was double-counted across ledgers). Either way the CFO learns which ACME line is cheapest to shrink: moving $30M of the bonds to another issuer removes $0.45M of concentration charge; moving $30M of the deposit to a second bank removes $0.09M. At these factors the bond line, not the deposit, is the cheaper one to shrink, and the graph is what shows that before Treasury moves the wrong balance.

Where a long-term reinsurer (Class C, D or E) differs: the same-named schedules exist under the Long-Term rules with their own section numbering and factor tables (the Long-Term handbook carries both a Schedule XIX and a Schedule XIXA for cash counterparties, and Schedule XVIII's domestic-affiliate rule sits at C15.2); verify which applies against the Long-Term handbook [BMA-LT].

Decision this enables: whether to renew the ACME LOC facility at $120M, replace part of it with a trust before a downgrade forces the issue, and what single-bank limit to put on collateral providers in the risk-appetite statement (see operating model). CFO CRO Treasurer Head of Ceded Re

14.2 Scenario B: a facultative risk looks attractive until the treaty book is joined

A broker offers a facultative share (one risk, underwritten on its own; a treaty covers a whole slice of a cedent's book automatically) on AI Campus X, a $500M data center programme. The underwriter likes the risk: new build, sprinklered, good engineering report, strong rate. The question is not whether the risk is good. It is how much of it we already have.

Whose interest is insured decides what the $500M is. A colocation landlord insures the shell, plant and power train; a hyperscale tenant insures the IT equipment and its own business interruption; during construction a contractor's all-risks policy insures the works with a delay-in-start-up extension for the lender. Three insureds, three values, three periods on the same campus. The canonical campus record carries an insured interest field so a fac quote is matched to the right one (see Mega Project Asset Intelligence).

Proposed fac share, AI Campus X ($500M programme) | v Mega Project Asset Intelligence: campus id, parcel, substation, tenant, insured interest | v AI CAMPUS X already on our books Treaty A (Cedent 1, property pro rata) $40M Treaty B (Cedent 2, per-risk XoL) $30M Existing fac (tenant IT fit-out) $20M Shared substation with Campus Y (Scenario C) Combined line before the new fac $90M | v Portfolio Management: marginal capital, RORAC, retro maximum any one risk, line ladder

Diagram: the fac quote is joined to the treaty and fac positions already on the same campus before a line is offered.

The line ladder, with the metric that produces it

Marginal capital is how much more capital the whole portfolio needs if we add this deal: small when the deal diversifies us, large when it stacks on an existing peak. RORAC (return on risk-adjusted capital) is the deal's expected profit divided by that marginal capital. The hurdle rate is the RORAC below which a deal destroys value; 12% here. Expected profit here is premium less expected loss, expenses and the retro cost on the protected part: about $1.8M on a $25M line, $2.9M at $50M, $3.9M at $75M and $4.4M at $100M, rising more slowly than the line because the part above the retro carries no retro recovery. Capital rises much faster, and that is what drives the RORAC down.

Line offeredCombined line on Campus XExpected profitMarginal capitalRORACVerdict at a 12% hurdle
$25M$115M$1.8M$8M22%Attractive
$50M$140M$2.9M$18M16%Supportable
$75M$165M$3.9M$35M11%Below hurdle
$100M$190M$4.4M$55M8%Requires better economics

Illustrative. Retro per-risk programme maximum any one risk: $150M.

Why marginal capital is convex. Each $25M step costs more capital than the last because the campus already carries Treaty A, Treaty B and a fac share and shares a substation with Campus Y, so every new dollar lands on an existing peak instead of diversifying it, and capital is measured in the tail (TVaR, the average of the worst outcomes beyond the 99th percentile), where stacked exposure counts at nearly full value.

The constraint that usually bites first: "one risk". Our per-risk retrocession (the reinsurance a reinsurer buys) defines what counts as one risk: a fire division, a building, or every building within a stated distance. If the retro treats Campus X as one risk, its maximum any one risk of $150M is the most the retro will ever pay for the campus. Combined line at $50M: $140M, inside the retro. At $75M: $165M, so $15M is unprotected retained exposure. At $100M: $40M unprotected. That step change, not the rate, is what drops the RORAC from 16% to 11%.

Two questions the join must answer before the line is offered. First, does the cedent's own fac inure to Treaty A (that is, does Treaty A only see the cedent's exposure net of the fac it bought), in which case our $40M Treaty A share on the campus is smaller than the gross suggests? Second, does our retro treat Campus X and the neighbouring Campus Y, on the same substation, as one risk under its distance clause? Both answers come from wordings, not from the exposure file.

Whether the fourth $25M step is a good deal therefore depends on whether it pushes our total on that campus past the point where our own retrocession stops paying, and on how much extra capital it consumes. Both numbers come from joining the fac quote to the treaty book and the retro wording, which is exactly what the campus identifier makes possible.

Where the prototype stops today. The data center map already resolves a campus to one identifier with its parcel, substation and operator (see the data center map inventory). It carries no cedent exposure, no treaty or fac positions and no insured values: its underwriting export writes estimated_tiv_m = 0.0 and says in its own docstring that inventing one "would launder a guess into a pricing input" (src/export_underwriting.py). The ladder above becomes computable once the treaty and fac books are joined to the campus identifier, which is Phase 4 work on top of the registry, after the cedent-exposure join that begins in Phase 2 (see Mega Project Asset Intelligence and the roadmap). Until then the campus match is the deliverable, and it alone tells the underwriter that Treaty A, Treaty B and an existing fac are on the same site.

Decision this enables: sign $50M at quoted terms; offer $75M only if the retro maximum any one risk is raised or the rate improves enough to clear 12%; decline $100M. CUO Head of Portfolio Management Head of Ceded Re

14.3 Scenario C: "diversified" locations share one power dependency

Two data center campuses and a third large load, written through different cedents, sit tens of kilometres apart and never share an H3 cell (a hexagon in the geospatial grid the platform uses to bucket locations), a flood plain or a fire brigade. Ordinary catastrophe geocoding calls them diversified. They all take power from one substation, the pattern Example 5 in the worked examples measures at Bluff Creek and Scenario J in the further scenarios prices. The question is what that dependency is worth in dollars, and the honest answer is: two different numbers, and neither is the sum of the campuses' values.

From the prototype. The data center map's dependency ledger (dcmap/data/power_dependencies.json, 212 edges over 127 substations; 170 edges cite the NYISO interconnection-queue or PJM TEAC filing they come from and the other 42 cite a regulatory docket or press report by URL [NYISO]) already contains real clusters of this shape. One of the better-documented clusters in the ledger is the Kintigh 345 kV substation (NYSEG, Genesee and Niagara counties, New York), whose edges carry resilience facts vouched against a developer's SEQR filing, a 10-K and verbatim-checked press reports; it is drawn below from the ledger as it stands.
KINTIGH 345 kV substation (NYSEG) from the prototype | +-- Lake Mariner campus, Somerset 750 MW | NYISO queue #849, #1670, #1732 | dual 345 kV circuits, both into Kintigh | backup: battery UPS, no diesel on site, | duration not established | +-- WNY STAMP data center, Alabama NY 300 MW | NYISO queue #0580, single named POI | backup: 12 emergency diesel generators | +-- Verizon Project Oasis (secondary) 75 MW withdrawn NYISO queue #0359, withdrawn; kept as history Five filings, 1,125 MW queued (1,050 MW after the withdrawn filing), one substation.

Diagram: the Kintigh cluster as recorded in the prototype's dependency ledger and its vouched resilience facts (dcmap/data/dependency_overrides.csv). The ledger holds load, feeds and backup power; it holds no insured values, policies or sublimits.

Two things in that ledger change the underwriting answer and would never appear in a location file. "Dual 345 kV feeds from separate grids" sounds like redundancy; the ledger records that both circuits terminate at the same named substation, so the redundancy is in the wires, not in the dependency. And backup power differs by campus: one has diesel generators (which run as long as the fuel contract does), one has batteries of unestablished duration, which for a multi-day outage is the difference between a claim and no claim.

Two numbers, not one

1. Physical-damage accumulation

The full insured values of every campus on the substation, counted only if the dependency is itself a common physical cause: an ice storm or tornado track on the shared transmission corridor, a shared flood plain, a wildfire corridor, a shared battery-storage fire. A fault inside the substation does not damage the buildings it feeds. If no common physical cause exists, this number is zero for the dependency and the sites stay diversified for property damage.

2. Dependency accumulation

What the policies actually pay when the power stops. Standard property wordings cover loss of off-premises power only under a utility service interruption or contingent business interruption (CBI) extension (business-interruption cover triggered by damage at a supplier rather than at the insured), with a sublimit, a waiting period (often 24 to 72 hours before cover starts) and, frequently, an exclusion for overhead transmission lines. For a campus under construction, the exposure is delay in start-up (DSU, the lender's and owner's lost income if the project opens late). This number is the sum of sublimits and DSU indemnity, not the sum of values.

Worked example: the Kintigh cluster priced two ways (illustrative; the policies and values are invented, the cluster is not)
Site and insured interestOur share of PD limitUtility-service / CBI sublimitWaiting periodDSU or ALoP
Lake Mariner, landlord shell and power train (Treaty A)$60M$5M48 hnone (operating)
Lake Mariner, tenant IT equipment (fac)$45M$10M24 hnone
WNY STAMP, contractor's all-risks during construction (Treaty C)$80M$2M72 h$40M, 24-month indemnity

Physical-damage accumulation: $185M of PD limit sits on one substation, but it counts as one accumulation only under a common physical cause. The prototype already runs one event-footprint join (USGS ShakeMap footprints against the registry, worst-shaken sites first); a winter-storm or tornado footprint over the Kintigh corridor would use the same pattern. Without such a cause, PD stays diversified.

Dependency accumulation from a substation outage: at most $5M + $10M + $2M = $17M of service-interruption sublimits, and only for an outage longer than each waiting period, so a 12-hour fault costs nothing and a five-day outage costs up to $17M. Backup power reduces it further: the diesel-backed site may not claim at all if fuel lasts; the battery-backed site claims once the batteries drain. Add the construction risk: if the outage or a substation transformer failure delays STAMP's energisation, DSU pays lost income for up to 24 months. With transformer lead times of two to three years, a single burnt transformer can stall a multi-billion-dollar project for longer than the indemnity period, so the $40M DSU is the largest number in the cluster and it comes from a policy that is not a data center policy at all.

The comparison the map cannot make on its own: $185M (PD, conditional on a common cause) against $57M (dependency: $17M of sublimits plus $40M of DSU). Version 2 implied the first; the second is the everyday exposure.

If the substation fails, the buildings are not damaged; the tenants lose revenue, and most policies only pay a limited amount for that after a waiting period. So the shared-power problem is real but measured in sublimits, not in the full value of the campuses. During construction the bigger exposure is delay: a burnt transformer can stall a $5bn project for two years. AI campuses today are largely under construction, which is why DSU on the contractor's policy, not property damage on the operator's, is where the shared-substation accumulation usually lands.

Geographic diversification can coexist with dependency concentration. Mega Project Asset Intelligence adds a class of accumulation that ordinary catastrophe geocoding does not reveal, and the dependency ledger is the working implementation of the "supplies power" relationship in the canonical data model. What it needs from the rest of the platform is the join to cedent exposure and wordings: the insured interest, the sublimits, the waiting periods, the indemnity periods (Phases 2 to 4, see Mega Project Asset Intelligence).

Decision this enables: set a dependency-cluster appetite per substation (a cap on the sum of service-interruption sublimits and DSU we carry on any one feed), and require the cedent's utility-service wording and the campus's backup-power facts before binding any campus already on a mapped substation. Head of Portfolio Management Property underwriting CRO

14.4 Scenario D: internal reinsurance makes one entity look safer but the group is not

US Insurance Co (A below), the US insurer in the group, cedes $500M of reserves to its affiliated Bermuda reinsurer, Atlantic Re (B below), under a 50% quota share (we take a fixed percentage of every policy, and the same share of its losses). A's balance sheet improves, its rating-agency capital improves, its US regulator sees a well-protected company. Nothing has left the group. The $500M has moved from one drawer to another, and the group is only safer if B does something with it that A could not.

What the legal-entity view showsWhat the group view must trace
A's net reserves fall by $500M; A's recoverable from B rises by $500MGroup net reserves are unchanged; the recoverable and the liability cancel on consolidation
A holds statutory credit for the reinsuranceOnly if B posts the collateral A's regulator requires (trust, LOC or funds withheld), which encumbers B's assets and creates B's own collateral concentration (Scenario A)
B's premium and reserves grow; B looks like an ordinary reinsurer with one large cedentWhether B buys external retrocession, and at what attachment; whether B holds capital against the assumed risk at the group's appetite; whether B cedes onward to another affiliate, and whether the exposure now concentrates in one line, one peril or one asset class at B
Within Bermuda, a cession from one Bermuda entity to another domestic affiliate is rated 0 in Schedule XVIII and carries no reinsurance credit charge at entity level [BMA-GB]That is exactly why the group view must look through the chain: entity-level capital does not see risk that stays inside the family

The BMA already asks this question. For the BMA the US entity's cession is a reportable intra-group reinsurance arrangement every quarter, and at group level it nets to zero; the regulator's group return therefore already asks the question this scenario poses. The fields are counterparties and location, aggregated exposure limits gross and net by counterparty rating (read as outstanding reserves at the reporting date), premium flows gross and net, and the share of our reinsurance that is internal, filed in Schedule V(c) and every quarterly return at entity and group level [BMA-GB] [BMA-GR]. An intra-group transaction is material to the group at 5% of the group's available capital and surplus for a single transaction or 10% for a linked series, and at entity level above 10% of statutory capital and surplus; a $500M cession on a $2,000M base is 25%, material on every test, so its purpose, terms, duration and performance triggers are also filed. See the affiliated-reinsurance dashboard for the full table and the compliance calendar for the quarterly dates.

The collateral condition. For A to take credit for the reinsurance, B must generally post collateral for the ceded liabilities unless it qualifies for reduced collateral under the cedent state's credit-for-reinsurance rules (Bermuda reinsurers may qualify as certified or reciprocal-jurisdiction reinsurers; verify B's status with A's regulator). If B posts a $500M trust, the assets in it are encumbered: they cannot be sold to pay B's other claims, and if they are the same ACME bonds as in Scenario A, the group's counterparty concentration has just been re-labelled as collateral. The group view links the cession, the collateral instrument, the assets inside it and their issuers, which is the chain the legal-entity view cannot see.

Worked example: three ways the $500M ends up (illustrative)
  1. B buys external retro. B cedes 40% of the assumed book to unaffiliated reinsurers with an aggregate stop-loss above the group's 1-in-100 net loss. Group risk falls by the retro; the cost is the retro premium and the reinsurance credit charge on the new recoverables. This is the case where the internal cession did what it claimed.
  2. B holds capital. B retains the book and holds capital against it at the group's appetite. Group risk is unchanged; capital is now held in Bermuda rather than in the US, which may be cheaper (BSCR factors, tax) or not. The decision is a capital-efficiency one and the group return shows it plainly.
  3. B concentrates it elsewhere. B invests the $500M trust in a single asset class or cedes onward to another affiliate rated 0 at entity level. Group risk is unchanged or higher, and nothing in A's or B's entity return says so. Only the look-through (tracing each holding to its ultimate obligor) finds it.

Decision this enables: whether the intra-group treaty earns its collateral cost, where B's external retro must attach to keep group net loss inside appetite, and what to write in the group Schedule V(c) narrative before the supervisor asks. CFO CRO Group Risk Treasurer

14.5 Scenario E: cyber single point of failure

Hundreds of insureds across six cedents look unrelated by industry and geography. They run on the same cloud region, the same identity service or the same payments processor. When that provider fails for three days, the losses arrive together, and they arrive in more than one line of business.

The terms that decide the answer

Affirmative vs silent cyber

Affirmative cyber is cover that names cyber events and prices them: a cyber policy or a cyber endorsement. Silent cyber (non-affirmative cyber) is cyber loss that falls into policies that never mention it: a property policy's business-interruption extension, a marine or energy policy, a casualty treaty. Silent cyber is the accumulation regulators worry about most, because nobody priced it and nobody limited it.

How cyber reinsurance is structured

Cyber reinsurance is overwhelmingly quota share (we take a fixed percentage of every policy and every loss) and aggregate excess of loss (we pay once the cedent's total cyber losses in a year exceed an attachment point). Accumulation is therefore measured on ceded aggregates and on event definitions, not on per-risk lines: an hours clause (all losses within, say, 72 hours of one cause count as one event) and a waiting period decide whether a three-day cloud outage is one loss to one treaty or many small losses to many.

Exclusions and attribution

War and state-actor exclusions decide whether a systemic event is covered at all. If the outage is attributed to a state-backed attack, an exclusion may remove the loss from the affirmative book while leaving it in the silent book, or the reverse, depending on each wording. The accumulation engine needs the exclusion wording per treaty, not just the limit.

CISSA, because the formula has no cyber charge

The BSCR standard formula's man-made catastrophe module lists terrorism, credit and surety, marine and aviation; it has no cyber charge. Cyber accumulation must therefore be quantified in the CISSA (the Commercial Insurer's Solvency Self-Assessment, Schedule IX: the insurer's own assessment of the capital it needs) [BMA-GB]. The Bermuda formula has no standard cyber charge, so we must show the regulator our own estimate.

Worked example: Cloud Region X goes dark for three days (illustrative)

Set-up. Six cedents' cyber books, 1,200 insureds in total. A SPoF (single point of failure) mapping, of the kind CyberCube's SPoF Intelligence data product provides alongside its Portfolio Manager model [CYB-SPOF], finds 340 of them running production workloads in Cloud Region X. Scenario: a 72-hour regional outage, no state-actor attribution.

Where the loss landsTriggerOur ceded aggregate at riskEvent testNet to us
Affirmative cyber, four quota sharesDependent business interruption after an 8 to 12 h waiting period$180MOne event under a 72 h hours clause$60M after cedents' own retentions and our cyber aggregate XoL
Affirmative cyber, two aggregate XoLsCedent's annual cyber losses breach attachment$50M limitAttaches only if the year's losses already ate the retention$0 to $50M, depending on the year
Silent: property treatiesNon-damage BI and CBI extensions$40M of sublimitsExcluded in 60% of wordings, sublimited in the rest$16M
Silent: technology E&O on a casualty treatyClaims against the insureds' own customers$25MOccurrence wording, no hours clause$10M, developing over two years

Result. A net loss of about $86M if neither aggregate excess-of-loss attaches, and up to $136M if both do; $26M of it arrives from treaties that never mention cyber. The property and casualty numbers are the ones today's cyber portfolio tool cannot see, because they live in other systems; our enterprise engine connects the CyberCube output to those treaties, to the retro and to the capital model, and the same figure becomes the CISSA cyber scenario.

The campus is the single point of failure. A hyperscale campus is simultaneously a property risk and a cloud-region dependency. The AI campus in Scenario B and the Kintigh cluster in Scenario C are physical buildings with a TIV and a substation; they are also the data halls behind Cloud Region X. The same canonical asset in the mega-project registry should carry the property values, the power dependency and the cyber dependent-BI exposure, so that a substation outage (Scenario C), a fire (Scenario B) and a cloud-region failure (this scenario) are recognised as three views of one node. That link is a genuinely differentiating one, and today no vendor tool holds all three sides of it.

Cyber losses do not respect the line of business they were written in. A cloud-region outage can trigger cyber policies, property business-interruption extensions and technology E&O at the same time. The same campus we map for fire is the one whose outage we should model for cyber.

Decision this enables: cap the ceded cyber aggregate dependent on any one cloud region, decide whether to buy an aggregate XoL or catastrophe layer for it, ask the property and casualty desks to close or sublimit the silent cover, and file the CISSA cyber scenario with a number the board has seen. Cyber portfolio manager CRO Head of Ceded Re CUO

Key takeaway: each scenario is the same move: resolve the thing that appears under different names in different systems (a bank, a campus, a substation, an affiliate, a cloud region) to one node, join every position to it, and read off two numbers, the regulatory one and the economic one. The regulatory number is what the compliance budget must produce anyway. The economic number is the decision: renew or replace the LOC, sign $50M not $100M, cap the substation, price the internal treaty, buy the cyber layer. Scenarios F to L continue in the next block.

14.6 Scenarios F to L: seven more decisions, each ending in a number and a name

Scenarios A to E above show what the enterprise view can see. The seven below show what it lets us decide, who decides it, and which regulatory obligation the same evidence discharges on the way. Every figure is illustrative unless it carries a citation.

How to read them: each scenario starts from a real moment in the business calendar (a June Florida renewal, a retro placement, a regulator's letter, an investment committee, a large facultative offer, a cyber outage, a rating review). It then shows the question the enterprise concentration engine answers, the arithmetic behind the answer, and the single decision that follows. Terms of art are explained the first time they appear; hover any dotted term for its glossary entry.

Scenario F: a Florida renewal where Portfolio Management hands the underwriter an envelope and the underwriter trades line for price

Every 1 June the Florida property catastrophe market renews. A cedent (the insurer that buys reinsurance from us) asks for a share of a treaty layer: an automatic cover for a whole slice of its book rather than a single risk. The question is not only "do we like this cedent" but "how much of our remaining Florida wind capacity should this deal consume, and at what price".

Today the underwriter is given a flat line limit. In the winning system, Portfolio Management hands over a capacity envelope: the line sizes and prices at which the deal still clears our return hurdle, computed against the live portfolio the night before. The underwriter then negotiates inside that envelope without going back for approval.

Worked example: Sunshine P&C, Florida wind layer $150M excess of $250M, 1 June renewal (illustrative)

The layer pays the cedent's losses above $250M up to a further $150M. The cedent asks for a 20% line (a $30M limit) at a 14% rate on line, which means the annual premium is 14% of the limit we put up: $4.2M. Our catastrophe model puts the layer's expected annual loss at 6.5% of limit. Brokerage and expenses run at 10% of premium. The Florida wind appetite is a net 1-in-100 AEP (aggregate exceedance probability) loss of $500M (25% of the $2,000M capital base, the Board limit in the limit framework, on the same book that Example 4 in the asset section measures) (the annual-aggregate view: all storms in a season, the same annual-aggregate basis the BMA uses, although the BMA's own figure is the 99% TVaR (tail value at risk: the average loss across the worst 1% of modelled seasons), which sits above the 1-in-100 point, and it includes reinstatement premiums [BMA-GB]); the book already sits at $448M, so $52M of headroom remains. The occurrence view (OEP (occurrence exceedance probability), the single worst storm) is what the layer itself responds to; both are shown, never one in place of the other.

The envelope prices each line step on its marginal capital: how much more capital the whole company needs the day this line is added, on the capital measure that binds for Florida wind (here the rating-agency model, not the BSCR, the BMA's standard capital formula). Marginal capital rises faster than the line because every extra dollar stacks on our existing Florida peak.

LineLimitPremium at 14% RoLExpected loss (6.5%)Expenses (10%)Margin
10%$15.0M$2.10M$0.98M$0.21M$0.92M
20%$30.0M$4.20M$1.95M$0.42M$1.83M
25%$37.5M$5.25M$2.44M$0.53M$2.29M
30%$45.0M$6.30M$2.93M$0.63M$2.74M

The second table sets each line's margin against the capital it consumes.

LineMarginMarginal capitalRORACvs 12% hurdle
10%$0.92M$5.0M18.3%write
20%$1.83M$12.5M14.6%write
25%$2.29M$19.0M12.0%at hurdle
30%$2.74M$28.0M9.8%below

RORAC is return on risk-adjusted capital: margin divided by marginal capital. The 30% line fails at 14% rate on line. It passes at 16%: premium $7.2M, margin $3.55M, RORAC 12.7%. So the envelope reads: up to 20% at 14%; up to 25% at 15% or better; up to 30% only at 16% or better; nothing above 30% because a 35% line ($52.5M) would exceed the $52M of AEP headroom, on the conservative assumption that the whole limit is lost at the 1-in-100 point and the retro does not respond, and that headroom has to last the rest of the renewal season. The underwriter can now trade line for price in the room. The broker counters with 25% at 15%: premium $5.6M, margin $2.62M, RORAC 13.8%. Signed.

What was joined to produce the table: the treaty terms (attachment, limit, reinstatements), the cedent's exposure file mapped to H3 cells, our existing Florida positions, the retro programme's attachment, and the binding capital model run against the live book. None of that is new data; it is the join that is new.

What is different from a limit. A flat limit says "no more than $30M". An envelope says "$30M at 14%, $37.5M at 15%, $45M at 16%, and here is why". The first produces arguments after the renewal; the second produces a signed line during it.

Decision this enables: the underwriter signs 25% at 15% rate on line inside a pre-approved envelope, with the capital consequence already known and recorded. Portfolio Mgmt CUO CRO

Scenario G: a retro purchase where the panel's collateral sits in the same two banks that hold our cash

Retrocession is the reinsurance a reinsurer buys. When we cede part of our catastrophe risk to a panel of retrocessionaires, each of them becomes a debtor to us the day a big storm hits. Some are rated companies; some are collateralised vehicles whose only promise is the cash in a trust or a bank's letter of credit (an LOC: a bank's promise to pay if the retrocessionaire does not). The collateral protects us against the retrocessionaire. Nothing protects us against the bank.

Worked example: renewing the $350M excess of $150M occurrence retro programme that Example 4 in the asset section works (illustrative)
RETRO PANEL ($350M limit, 14 retrocessionaires) ├─ 6 rated traditional retrocessionaires ........ $150M (unsecured, A- to AA-) └─ 8 collateralised vehicles ..................... $200M (unrated; credit = collateral) ├─ LOCs issued by BANK P ................... $120M ├─ LOCs issued by BANK Q ................... $80M └─ trust accounts, custodian = BANK P ...... no separate limit; $110M of assets posted above the LOCs as additional security OUR OPERATING CASH ($420M) ├─ BANK P .......... $150M (36%) ├─ BANK Q .......... $110M (26%) └─ 5 other banks ... $160M BANK P GROUP, ONE COUNTERPARTY, THREE ROLES cash depositary + LOC issuer + trustee/custodian

Ceded Re sees a well-spread panel: no retrocessionaire above 12% of the limit. Treasury sees a cash book within its own bank limits. Only the enterprise view puts the two together: Bank P group is at once our largest cash counterparty, the issuer of 60% of the LOCs securing our retro, and the custodian of the trust assets. That is wrong-way risk: the protection is most likely to fail in exactly the systemic stress in which we most need it.

Three regulatory mechanics make this a capital number, not only a prudence point. First, on Schedule XVIII (the ceded-reinsurance schedule of the capital return) an LOC counts as qualifying collateral at 98% of face, never more than the net exposure, so a fully collateralised recoverable carries almost no net qualifying exposure; whatever residual remains is rated at the higher of the retrocessionaire's and the LOC issuer's rating (C25.2(f) to (i)) [BMA-GB]. The BMA sets no rating floor for the bank; the retro wording, the trust agreement and the cedent-side collateral rules do. If Bank P falls below the rating those documents accept, the LOCs must be replaced inside the notice period, and if they cease to qualify as collateral the $120M is charged at the vehicle's own unrated factor of 35%, about $42M of capital before the diversification adjustment. Second, the credit charge on catastrophe recoveries is 10% of gross minus net PML (probable maximum loss) minus funded arrangements, with collateral counted at 98%, so collateral that stops qualifying raises that charge directly (the catastrophe return's instructions following D10.5, items g to i). Third, the cash charge carries a diversification adjustment of 40% multiplied by one minus the largest single bank's share of total cash: at 36% the adjustment is 25.6%; if the largest bank were held to 20% it would be 32% (Fixed Income instructions (d) to (e)).

StressWhat failsRecoverable left unsecuredCash at riskExtra BSCR credit charge (order of magnitude)
Storm onlynothing$0$0none
Storm + Bank P downgraded below the rating the retro wording acceptsBank P LOCs stop being acceptable collateral$120M secured only by a bank we no longer accept, until replaced$0up to 35% x $120M, about $42M, if the LOCs cease to qualify (before the diversification adjustment), plus a replacement-collateral scramble inside the notice period
Storm + Bank P and Q impaired$200M of LOCs, trust access delayedup to $200Mup to $260M of deposits frozen or haircutthe retro programme is worth $150M, not $350M, on the day we collect
Cap LOC issuance by bank group
No single bank group to issue more than 25% of the collateral securing the panel; new vehicles to post trust assets with a custodian that is not a top-three cash bank.
Move cash before the storm, not after
Bring the largest bank below 20% of operating cash; the diversification adjustment rises and the wrong-way pair is broken.
Re-cut the panel on capital, not tradition
Rank each retrocessionaire by capital released per dollar of ceded premium after its credit charge; the 40% diversification credit on reinsurance balances grows as the largest retrocessionaire's share of net exposure falls (D9.9).

Decision this enables: renew the programme with a per-bank-group collateral cap, a trust-first rule for new collateralised capacity, and a treasury transfer that takes Bank P below 20% of cash, all approved in one meeting because the three exposures appear on one screen. Ceded Re Treasurer CRO CFO

Scenario H: the BMA questions a filed concentration figure and gets a lineage-backed answer within the hour

Schedule XXI lists our ten largest asset counterparties, grouped where entities are related or connected, valued on the Economic Balance Sheet and on an unconsolidated basis, with fund holdings measured on a look-through basis, meaning by the assets inside the fund rather than the fund itself [BMA-GB] (grouping test C31.2; EBS valuation and unconsolidated basis C31.2g; the look-through rule for funds is the general one in B6). The return is signed by two directors (one may be the CEO) and either the CRO or the CFO [BMA-FIL-4], and the return and its supporting documentation must be kept at the principal office for five years from filing and produced on request (Rules paragraph 6, applied to PML workings at handbook C16.2f [BMA-GB]; Group Rules paragraph 6(5) [BMA-GR]; verify the entity-level retention rule against the current Rules and instructions handbook). When the regulator asks a question, the people who signed want the answer to be the same one the system gave in December.

Worked example: the letter about counterparty number three (illustrative)

Northwind Financial Group is a different family from ACME; the figures below are the platform's own, not Scenario A's. The BMA writes: "Row 3 of Schedule XXI shows $212M to Northwind Financial Group against $150M the prior year. Please explain the movement, confirm whether fund holdings were included on a look-through basis, and confirm whether Northwind Asset Management is included in the group." The old answer to that letter was a two-week reconstruction by three teams. The new answer is a drill:

FILED Schedule XXI row 3 ....................... $212.0M snapshot 2027YE-v3, locked 28 Mar 2028 └─ gold.top_counterparty_concentration ....... $212.0M run 2028-03-27 22:10, model set CR-2027.4 ├─ Northwind Bank NA cash $70.0M Schedule XIXA line 4 src: TMS feed 31 Dec ├─ Northwind Funding LLC bonds $88.0M Schedule II src: custodian 31 Dec ├─ Northwind Capital Trust look-through $54.0M B6 full look-through src: fund holdings file └─ Northwind Asset Mgmt no exposure $0.0M entity in group, nothing held grouping evidence: D&B global ultimate 4 Nov 2027; 1 economic-interdependence override, approved Concentration Committee 14 Nov 2027, evidence attached movement vs 2026YE: +$40M bond purchase (Feb 2027); +$22M look-through newly applied to Fund Delta after holdings file received; no reclassification

The reply, with the lineage pack attached, goes out the same afternoon. It carries the locked snapshot identifier, the source-record identifiers, the grouping evidence and the approver of the one manual override. The regulator's second question, "would the figure differ on a consolidated basis", is answered from the same tables because every position carries its risk-carrying entity.

Key takeaway: a filed number that can be reproduced from source in an hour is a number the signatories can defend. A filed number that needs three teams and two weeks is a finding waiting to happen. The same lineage answers the auditor, the rating agency and the Board's audit committee.

Decision this enables: the CFO replies to the BMA on the day, without a restatement risk, and the Board's audit committee is shown the drill rather than told about it. CFO Data CRO

Scenario I: an investment committee finds one private-credit sponsor inside three funds and sets a limit it never had

Private credit is lending to companies through funds rather than public bonds. The fund is the legal counterparty; the borrowers inside it are the economic risk. A sponsor is the private-equity firm whose portfolio companies those borrowers are. Three funds from three managers can hold loans to the same sponsor's companies, and a sponsor in trouble tends to be in trouble across its whole portfolio at once.

For the BMA, a fund is charged by what we can prove about its contents: full look-through by default; failing that, by the fund's target allocation; failing that, by assuming it fills its riskiest permitted bucket first; failing all three, as an equity holding of type 'Other', the highest rung of the charge ladder [BMA-GB] (B6.7 to B6.9). Missing holdings data is therefore a capital cost as well as a blind spot.

Worked example: three funds, one sponsor, no limit (illustrative)
HoldingOur valueHoldings data receivedOf which Falcon Capital portfolio companiesLook-through rung
Fund Alpha (Manager 1)$150Myes, quarterly$38Mfull look-through
Fund Beta (Manager 2)$120Myes, quarterly$31Mfull look-through
Fund Gamma (Manager 3)$90Mno, target allocation only$26M (estimated from sponsor disclosures)target allocation (B6.7)
Direct co-investment loan$25Mn/a$25Mheld directly
Falcon Capital, all routes$120M6.0% of statutory capital and surplus of $2,000M

Each fund is inside its own manager limit. No sponsor limit exists because until the asset graph resolved the borrowers to their sponsor, the number could not be produced. The $120M is also 60% software companies, so it is a sector concentration wearing a sponsor's name. Because the sponsor is a corporate group, the same resolution feeds the Schedule XXI grouping test and, if it ever reached the top ten, the concentration charge (D6).

The committee does three things. It sets a sponsor limit of 5% of statutory capital and surplus ($100M) and a 3% sub-limit for any one sector within a sponsor. It re-prices: the $20M above limit stays only if the next capital call is trimmed and the new commitments carry a spread at least 75 basis points wider than the portfolio average, otherwise it is sold down at the next liquidity window. And it makes holdings-level data a condition of every future commitment, because Fund Gamma's missing file is costing capital on the ladder and hiding the very concentration the committee just found.

The positive side. The same look-through that found Falcon shows $410M of private-credit exposure with no sponsor above 2% of capital and full holdings data. That portion can grow. Measured limits are what let the CIO take more yield, not less, inside evidence the BMA and the rating agencies will accept.

Decision this enables: a Board-level sponsor limit, a re-priced over-limit position with a dated exit, and a data condition on new fund commitments, all minuted with the numbers that justify them. CIO CRO CFO

Scenario J: a large facultative data-center offer during the AI build-out, and what the map shows about the substation

A facultative risk (fac) is one specific risk reinsured on its own terms. In an AI build-out the offers arrive fast and large: a campus worth billions, mostly under construction, with the builder's-risk cover and a delay in start-up (DSU) cover that pays lost revenue if completion slips. The insured interest changes over the project's life: the contractor and owner during construction, the landlord's shell and plant afterwards, the tenant's IT equipment separately. A fac submission has to say which of these it is.

The map answers a question the submission cannot: what else of ours is downstream of the same power. This is the dcmap prototype's job (the Mega Project Asset Intelligence part of the insurance-risk accumulation section): campus and substation resolved to canonical assets, each power-dependency edge citing its PJM or NYISO filing, and, once the join is built, our treaty and fac positions attached to each. The prototype does not yet carry cedent exposure, treaty or fac lines, and on-site generation is recorded for few sites; the example below assumes that join exists.

Worked example: $100M line requested on the Orion campus, fourth tenant of the Bluff Creek substation (illustrative)

Example 5 in the asset section measured this yard: three existing positions with a dependency accumulation of $195M against the $200M named-dependency limit Portfolio Management set on it. This scenario is the offer that lands on it.

BLUFF CREEK 345 kV substation (single transformer bank; replacement lead time 24-36 months) │ ├─ ORION campus (offered fac) ......... $2.4B at completion, 24-month build, builder's risk + DSU ├─ DC-1 colocation campus ............ Treaty A, 12% share; our TIV share $900M; │ utility-service sublimit $25M, 72h waiting period ├─ DC-2 hyperscale campus ............ Facultative, $60M line; our TIV share $1,400M; CBI sublimit $50M, 48h └─ Fab, phase 2 under construction ... Treaty C, 8% share; our TIV share $4,000M; DSU $120M, 30-day waiting period

Two accumulation numbers must be kept apart. The physical-damage accumulation is the full value of every site only if they share a physical cause (the same flood plain, the same wildfire corridor, a shared battery-storage fire). They do not; a transformer fire at Bluff Creek damages nothing at the four sites. The dependency accumulation is what we would actually pay if Bluff Creek went down for months: the sublimited contingent business interruption and utility-service extensions at the two operating sites (loss of income from a supplier's or utility's failure, paid only above a waiting period and up to a sublimit), plus the DSU exposure on the fab and on Orion, where a lost transformer can stall completion for two years.

SiteOur physical-damage shareOur dependency share if Bluff Creek loses its transformer bank
Orion (requested $100M line)$100M$40M of the line is DSU; a transformer loss during commissioning is inside the indemnity period: up to $40M
DC-1 (Treaty A)$900Mutility-service sublimit, our share $25M
DC-2 (Facultative)$1,400MCBI sublimit, our share $50M
Fab, phase 2 (Treaty C)$4,000MDSU, our share up to $120M
One substation eventnot additive (no common physical cause)up to $235M, of which $195M was already measured in Example 5 and $40M is new, against the $200M limit on this yard; and with no retro protection: our per-risk retro treats each site as its own risk, and the cat retro responds only if the substation fire meets its loss-occurrence definition and the wording admits non-damage and contingent BI losses, which most do not; treat it as unprotected until Ceded Re confirms otherwise

So the $100M offer is not a $100M question; it is the $40M of DSU that takes a named dependency past its $200M limit, a question that did not exist before the map joined three cedents' positions and a broker's submission to one substation. Two other checks come from the same join: the combined line on Orion across the fac and any treaty exposure on the campus against the retro programme's maximum any one risk, and the marginal capital of the line against the hurdle, as in Scenario F.

The underwriter has two honest offers. Offer 1: a $60M line, with utility-service interruption and DSU arising from off-site power sublimited to $5M with a 72-hour waiting period; the yard sits at $200M, exactly at its limit. Offer 2: the full $100M line, DSU from off-site power sublimited to $20M, at a rate 35% higher than the cedent's indication, which is roughly what the marginal capital of the additional dependency exposure costs at the hurdle; the yard then sits at $215M and needs a Concentration Committee exception with an expiry, or the fab's DSU share trimmed at its renewal as Example 5 already proposed. Either is defensible. Silence about the substation is not.

Why this is a profit lever and not only a warning. Competitors pricing off the submission alone will either take the $100M at the indicated rate and carry an invisible clash on a substation that already carries $195M of our dependency exposure, or decline a good campus out of caution. We can do neither: we can take the physical-damage risk we like, price the dependency we can see, and say why in one sentence to the broker.

Decision this enables: a smaller line with a contingent-BI and off-site-power sublimit, or the full line at a price that covers the dependency, chosen with the substation's other three tenants on the screen. CUO Property UW Portfolio Mgmt CRO

Scenario K: a cloud identity provider fails and the SPoF graph gives a loss estimate by treaty inside a day

A single point of failure (SPoF) is one technology that many otherwise unrelated insureds depend on: a cloud region, a payments processor, an identity provider that signs every employee in. When it fails, hundreds of our cedents' clients lose access at once. The cyber accumulation graph (the cyber part of the insurance-risk accumulation section, fed by CyberCube SPoF Intelligence, the dependency-mapping add-on to Portfolio Manager [CYB-SPOF]) already knows who depends on what; the enterprise engine knows which of our treaties each of those insureds sits under and on what terms.

Three features of cyber reinsurance shape the estimate. Most cyber treaties are quota share (we take a fixed percentage of every policy) or aggregate excess of loss (we pay once the cedent's total losses from an event pass an attachment). Nearly all dependent-business-interruption cover has a waiting period, commonly 8 to 12 hours, before it pays. And some exposure is silent: business-interruption extensions inside property or technology E&O treaties that were never priced as cyber. The BMA standard formula has no cyber catastrophe scenario (its man-made module covers terrorism, credit and surety, marine and aviation only; cyber premium and reserves are charged like any other line), so the number we produce here is also the number that belongs in our own solvency self-assessment, the CISSA (our own annual solvency self-assessment, filed with the capital return) [BMA-GB] (C18).

Worked example: a 30-hour outage at identity provider IdP-1, the event-day version of Example 6 (illustrative)

Example 6 in the asset section is the pre-event scenario on this dependency: the same nine cedents, the same 640 insureds (210 of them in two cedents' books, counted once), a 72-hour outage, $92M against the $100M cyber-event limit. The real outage lasts 30 hours.

The number is a fifth of the pre-event scenario because the outage is short enough that the aggregate covers do not attach and treaty D's 72-hour waiting period is never reached; those two features were worth $18M of silent cover and most of the $74M of affirmative cover in the 72-hour case. The range is wide because attribution is not yet known: if the outage is later attributed to a state actor, war exclusions in some of the underlying policies would bite and the number falls; if data was exfiltrated as well as access lost, notification and liability costs push it up. Both branches are on the screen with their assumptions, on day one. The previous comparable event took three weeks to reach a first number, by which time the rating agency had already asked.

Decision this enables: a reserve, a retro notice and an external message set on the first day with a stated range, instead of three weeks of silence followed by a surprise. CRO Cyber Portfolio Mgmt Claims CFO

Scenario L: a rating-agency review where the concentration evidence carries the capital model narrative

A Bermuda reinsurer holds capital to satisfy three referees at once: the BMA's BSCR, the rating agencies' models (S&P's capital adequacy criteria, AM Best BCAR), and its own internal model. For a property-catastrophe book the rating-agency measure often binds, because the agencies give less diversification credit and stress the cat tail harder than the BSCR; which one binds must be measured on our own book, not assumed. Agencies also score enterprise risk management: whether the company can show, not assert, that it knows its concentrations, measures them against a stated appetite, and acts. That score feeds the rating, and the rating feeds the price of capital and the share of the market that will trade with us.

Worked example: the annual review pack, produced from the platform in a week rather than assembled in a quarter (illustrative)
Analyst questionEvidence producedWhere it came from
Who are your largest counterparties, and do the internal numbers agree with what you filed?Top ten groups reconciled to Schedules XXI, XVIII and V(c), with the grouping evidence and every override's approverScenario H lineage
How much of your recoverable book is secured, and by whom?100% of recoverables with a linked collateral status; over-collateralisation removed; no bank group above 25% of collateralScenario G restructuring
How dependent are you on your largest retrocessionaire?Largest retrocessionaire 18% of net reinsurance exposure; the BMA diversification adjustment on the credit charge is therefore 40% x (1 - 0.18) = 32.8%Schedule XVIII data, D9.9

Is capital linked to strategy?CISSA sections cross-referenced to the appetite statement and to the limit register the underwriters actually useSection operating model

The narrative the CFO tells is short: we hold capital against risks we can name, measure and drill to source; our concentrations are chosen, not discovered. The illustrative consequence is that the agency's ERM commentary moves from "adequate" to "strong", and the capital plan for the year is accepted without an additional buffer. Whether that is worth a notch, a basis-point spread on the next debt issue or a broker's decision to lead with us, it is money that arrives because the evidence existed.

The same pack answers the BMA's own tests: the concentration schedules, the Cat Return's (Schedule X, the catastrophe risk return) questions on vendor-model reliance and liquidity (C19.1 and C19.2) and the CISSA's use test, which asks whether the self-assessment is integrated into decision-making (C18.3) [BMA-GB]. Group-level filers show the intra-group reinsurance flows from the same tables [BMA-GR].

Decision this enables: the Board approves the capital plan and the growth budget for the peak zones on the strength of evidence the agencies have already accepted, rather than holding a precautionary buffer against questions nobody could answer. CFO CRO CEO Board

Scenario matrix: which graph, which profit lever, which regulatory obligation

Each scenario uses at least one of the three graphs in the target architecture section, pulls at least one of the profit levers in "How the compliance budget becomes profit", and produces evidence the BMA asks for anyway. The point of the matrix is the last column: every decision above starts from data the regulator already makes us assemble; four of them add one join the return does not ask for (F: the binding capital model's marginal capital; I: borrower-to-sponsor resolution; J: the substation dependency ledger; K: technology-dependency data), and those four are exactly the optional build.

Key takeaway: the compliance data and the profit data are the same data. Scenarios H and L are evidence assembled from what the other scenarios produce and cost little beyond the mandatory build; F, G, I and J are the decisions that pay for the optional build; K is the one that stops a bad week becoming a bad year. Which capital measure binds, and what "too much" means, are set in the operating model; the scenarios only work once those two things are written down.

14.7 Scenarios M and N: where to write more, and one stress instead of five

Two more decisions, added in this version. Scenario M is the one Portfolio Management is rarely asked for: not "reduce the line" but "write this one instead". Scenario N is the stress test a Board actually needs: one hurricane run through underwriting, retrocession, counterparties, collateral, investments and liquidity at once. Every figure is illustrative and uses Atlantic Re's numbers ($2,000M available statutory capital, $1,400M BSCR, $5,500M invested assets).

Scenario M: Portfolio Management says "write more", and the enterprise capital view ranks two treaties the other way round

A control function that only appears when it wants a line cut is ignored by the people who write the business. The winning model uses the same accumulation engine to find where the next dollar of capital earns the most: underweight regions, diversifying perils, favourable attachment points, and the moments when retro or capital availability lets us compete harder. The mechanism is marginal capital (the extra capital the whole portfolio needs if we add this one deal), already the basis of the capacity envelopes in Scenario F.

Worked example: two treaties at the 1 January renewal, one budget of capital (illustrative)

Two offers reach the treaty desk in December. Treaty A is a Florida-heavy US property catastrophe layer; Treaty B is a European windstorm and Japanese earthquake quota share from a cedent we have not written before. The desk's traditional ranking uses each contract's stand-alone expected return: the profit it is expected to earn divided by the capital it would need on its own.

ViewTreaty A (US wind, peak zone)Treaty B (Europe wind, Japan EQ)
Expected annual profit$17.6M$11.2M
Stand-alone capital, and stand-alone expected return$110M, 16%$80M, 14%
Peak-zone overlapHigh: it stacks on Atlantic Re's largest net position (Florida wind, net 1-in-100 of $448M against a $500M appetite in Scenario F)Low: perils and regions the book is underweight in
Marginal capital (the enterprise view)$100M, almost all of its stand-alone capital, because nothing in the portfolio offsets it$45M, because diversification absorbs the rest
Return on marginal capital (RORAC: expected profit divided by marginal capital)17.6%24.9%
RankingTraditional: first. Enterprise: secondTraditional: second. Enterprise: first

Treaty A is the better contract on its own and the worse use of Atlantic Re's scarce capital: every dollar of marginal capital it consumes is a dollar of Florida headroom that Scenario F's envelopes are already rationing. Treaty B earns less per contract and more per dollar of capital, and it moves the book toward the diversification that the rating-agency models and the BSCR aggregation both reward. The right answer is often both, at the right size: B in full, A at a reduced line inside the envelope, which is the negotiation Scenario F describes.

The ranking is only as good as the net numbers behind it. Marginal capital is measured after retrocession, so a change in the retro programme, or a retro partner's stressed collectibility, changes the answer without any change in the gross treaty economics; the true-net waterfall is what keeps the marginal capital honest. And the figures are illustrative twice over: the capital model that produces marginal capital must be validated before any RORAC reaches an underwriter (governance).

Decision this enables: Portfolio Management publishes, before each renewal season, a short list of where the book wants to grow (region, peril, attachment, cedent type) with the marginal-capital price of each, and the treaty desk is measured on return on marginal capital rather than on stand-alone return or premium volume; that is profit lever 3 pointed at growth instead of restraint. Portfolio Management CUO Treaty UW CRO

Scenario N: one hurricane, six balance-sheet lines, one enterprise stress instead of five silo stresses

Today a Board sees five stress tests from five owners: the cat team's net loss, ceded re's recoverable, treasury's bank exposure, the CIO's market shock and the treasurer's liquidity ladder. Each passes. None is run on the same event as the others, so nobody sees that a single Gulf hurricane hits all five at once, and in the same direction. The enterprise graph lets one event be pushed through underwriting, retrocession, counterparties, collateral, investments and liquidity together, and reports capital, liquidity and remaining capacity as one result.

Worked example: a 1-in-100 Florida hurricane run as one stress across Atlantic Re's balance sheet (illustrative)
StepWhat the event doesCapital effectLiquidity effect, first six months
1. Property lossesGross treaty and fac loss $700M; the retro programme is expected to recover $250M; net $450M-$450M-$250M of claims paid before retro cash arrives
2. Retro recoverable risesThe $250M recoverable becomes the largest single asset we are owed; Reinsurer XYZ, our largest retrocessionaire, carries $120M of it and is downgraded one notch after the same event-$25M stressed collectibility haircut (10% of the recovery)Timing: retro cash lags claims by 60 to 120 days
3. Collateral bank weakensACME Financial Group, issuer of the letter of credit that secures XYZ's share, is placed on negative watch; the LOC falls below the eligibility clause and $80M of recoverable is uncollateralised until it is replaced-$8M higher reinsurance credit charge and replacement cost-$40M of collateral top-ups demanded by our own cedents under their trusts
4. Market sell-offEquities (10% of the $5,500M) fall 20%; credit spreads widen 100 basis points on the $2,000M corporate bond book (about two years of spread duration)-$110M equities and -$40M bonds, both marked to market on the economic balance sheet-$15M of margin and variation calls on hedges
5. Liquidity demandClaims, top-ups and margin fall due before retro cash, in a market where selling bonds realises the marksRealised losses if forced to sellTotal call $305M against $260M of unencumbered liquid assets available inside 30 days
StressCapital after stressCoverage of the $1,400M BSCRPasses the Board's 110% floor?
Underwriting silo (step 1 only)$1,550M111%Yes, barely
Counterparty and collateral silo (steps 2 and 3)$1,967M140%Yes
Investment silo (step 4)$1,850M132%Yes
Liquidity silo (step 5 in normal markets)n/an/aYes: the $305M call is met from $260M liquid plus orderly bond sales
One enterprise stress (steps 1 to 5)$1,367M98%No; and the $45M liquidity gap is met either by selling bonds at the bottom or by drawing a facility from the same bank that is on watch

Nothing in the enterprise run is exotic; every line is a stress one owner already runs. What changes is the joint: the retrocessionaire, its bank, the bond book and the liquidity ladder are all correlated to the hurricane, and the silo tests assume they are not. The Board's floor is illustrative, and so is every amount; the shape is the point. It is also the shape the regulator asks about: the Cat Return's liquidity questions and the CISSA's own stress and scenario testing are answered from the same run [BMA-GB].

The pieces already exist in this blueprint. The liquidity view of the limit framework supplies the ladder that step 5 is measured against; the collateral calculator is what prices step 3, because an LOC that falls below its eligibility clause is exactly the haircut-and-cap arithmetic it runs; the counterparty graph supplies the XYZ-to-ACME link that makes step 3 wrong-way risk (the bank that secures our recoverable weakens in the same event as the reinsurer) rather than coincidence. Scenario N is not a new model; it is the same tables run in one order on one event.

Decision this enables: the CRO replaces the five silo stresses in the Board pack with a scenario library run on the enterprise graph (hurricane, earthquake, cyber event, bank default, collateral impairment, mega-project fire, large non-cat loss), each reported as capital, liquidity and remaining capacity together; the Board sets its floor on the combined result; and the treasurer pre-arranges a committed liquidity facility with a bank that is not also our largest letter-of-credit issuer. CRO CFO Treasurer CIO Board

Key takeaway: the same engine that says "too much" must also say "more here": ranked on marginal capital, the diversifying treaty beats the peak-zone one even though it earns less per contract, and the ranking is only trustworthy when the true-net waterfall sits underneath it. And a stress test that is run in five silos passes five times and fails once when run as one event; the Board should see the one.
15

Governance and auditability: every answer must be explainable

Every filed number and every capacity decision must be traceable from the board metric to the source transaction, the mapping, the model version and the approver.

CROData

A winning system cannot be a black box. An executive must be able to drill from a board-level metric all the way to the source transaction and understand every mapping and adjustment. The people who sign the return will insist on it, and so will the people who license us the data.

Four kinds of lineage answer four different questions. The prototype already keeps all four for the mega-project registry; the enterprise system keeps them for every counterparty, collateral instrument, position and treaty.

Source lineage

Which internal or vendor feed produced the record, at what time, under which licence?

Mapping lineage

Why was an entity assigned to this parent, group or campus? On what evidence, approved by whom, effective from when?

Model lineage

Which Verisk, CyberCube or capital-model version and which assumptions produced this loss or capital number?

Decision lineage

Who approved the override, the limit, the exception or the capacity decision, and what did they see when they did?

15.1 Regulatory lineage: the people who sign, and what the signature obliges

The audit trail is not a data-team preference. It is what the signatories of the return need in order to sign. The Capital and Solvency Return (CSR: the annual capital filing that carries the BSCR, the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement, and its schedules) carries a declaration, and the Financial Condition Report (FCR: the narrative report on solvency and risk management that is published on our website) is signed by the CEO. Every concentration figure on Schedules V(c), XVIII, XIX and XXI is therefore a number a named executive attests to, and the workings behind it are producible on demand for years afterwards.

DocumentWho signs, Class 4 and 3BWho signs, Class 3A and long-term Class C, D and EWhat it obliges us to keep
CSR declarationTwo directors (one may be the CEO) plus the CRO or the CFO [BMA-FIL-4]Two directors plus the insurer's principal representative; the Class 3A and Class C requirements use the same wording [BMA-FIL-3A] [BMA-FIL-C] [BMA-FIL-DE]Work papers and documents used to prepare the BSCR submission, "retained and kept available for examination and discussion with the BMA" (handbook A1.12); the documentation behind the gross probable maximum loss for at least five years after filing, at the registered office (handbook C16.2f) [BMA-GB]
Financial Condition ReportThe CEO plus a senior executive responsible for actuarial, risk management, internal audit or compliance; published on the insurer's website within 14 days of filing [BMA-FIL-4] [BMA-FIL-DE]A public narrative that must agree with the schedules; any later restatement is visible to brokers and rating agencies
Group CSR (where we are the designated insurer)Furnished by the designated insurer; a copy kept at the principal office for five years from the filing date and produced to the BMA on direction (Group Rules para 6(5)) [BMA-GR]Five years of reproducible group concentration and intra-group figures
Any returnKnowingly or recklessly making a false or misleading statement or return is an offence; under the Group Rules the fine on summary conviction is up to $50,000 (para 9) [BMA-GR]A defensible basis for every grouping judgement, because "we sorted the spreadsheet by name" is not one
What this means in practice. The rules fix five years for the group CSR copy (Group Rules para 6(5)) and for the PML documentation (handbook C16.2f), and set no end date at all for BSCR work papers (handbook A1.12), so five years is the shortest horizon we should plan for. That turns "reproducible" from a nice property into a requirement: the platform must be able to regenerate the 2027 Schedule XXI in 2032 from the snapshot, the mapping rules and the vendor hierarchy as they stood on the filing date, not from today's data. That is why the regulatory snapshot is a locked, versioned set of tables (see the security model) and why every mapping is dated rather than edited in place. For a Class 3A or a long-term [Class C / D / E] entity the same rule applies, with the principal representative in place of the CRO or CFO on the declaration; only Class 4 and 3B put the CRO or CFO on it.

15.2 The "basis" column: the standard the prototype already sets

The data-center map was built with the discipline this section asks for, so the enterprise system inherits a working standard rather than inventing one. In the repository today:

  • Every site, plant, fab and operator page lists the source rows it was built from, each with an outbound link to the original record (dcmap/server.mjs per-site pages; see the map inventory).
  • Every hand correction is appended to a ledger, never written over the original, and carries a "how I know" note: the site ledger dcmap/data/site_overrides.csv is 473 lines long with 455 fields applied, and separate ledgers hold drawn footprints, name reviews, dropped points and simulated events.
  • Research sweeps are adversarially reviewed: one agent proposes, a skeptic re-argues every rejection, and the verdicts are kept as files in dcmap/data/review/ (campus parcels, campus places, load identities, backup-power findings, the Epoch H100 cross-check). The skeptic re-probed every public parcel layer before it was registered and rejected five candidates; 32 name-conflict pairs were researched and each given a verdict a skeptic tried to break.
  • The licence register renders as a page (/licences) so attribution travels with the product, and the /data page shows which pipeline step is stale.
  • The Databricks design insists that a Genie answer (Databricks' natural-language query assistant) always shows its SQL and its row count, so a number is never an oracle.

The enterprise rule is the same one, written down: every counterparty grouping, collateral link and asset mapping carries a basis: the source, the evidence, a confidence, the approver, and effective-from and effective-to dates. The CounterpartyRelationship object in the canonical data model already has these fields; the governance rule is that a row without them is not allowed into the regulatory snapshot.

Worked example: one correction in the prototype, and its enterprise counterpart (illustrative field values, real field shape)

A site in the registry was placed by a geocoder on the lot next to the actual campus (this happened in the prototype; the identifiers below are fictional). The correction went into the ledger as a row, not as an edit to the source file:

site_id = site-example-tx-001 field = lat,lon old = 33.6412,-96.9231 (geocoder, town-level) new = 33.6388,-96.9204 (parcel centroid) how_i_know = "Example County parcel 2024-118-004, owner matches the operator's filing; Wayback imagery 2025-03 shows the halls on this lot" edited_by = <steward> (X-Forwarded-Email once on Databricks) effective_from = 2026-09-12

The same shape on the counterparty side, for the grouping decision that moves a number on Schedule XXI:

entity_id = ent-00417 (Northbank Trust Co.) group_id = grp-0031 (Northbank Financial Group) relationship = control (wholly owned subsidiary) basis_source = D&B linkage, global ultimate DUNS 12-345-6789, pulled 2026-11-03 evidence = "Annual report 2025 p.112 lists NTC as 100% subsidiary" confidence = high approver = Head of Ceded Re; Finance review 2026-12-15 effective_from = 2026-11-03 effective_to = (open)

When the BMA asks in 2028 why Northbank Trust was grouped with the letter-of-credit (LOC) bank of the same name, the answer is the row, not a memory.

Unity Catalog (Databricks' governance layer: one catalog of tables with permissions, lineage and audit attached) contributes access control, table- and column-level lineage, an audit log of who read and changed what, discovery and data-quality monitoring to this design [DBX-GOVa]. Access and change events land in the platform's system audit tables [DBX-AUDIT] and are joined to the application's own approval ledger. The four lineages above are therefore mostly configuration, not code; the part we must build is the basis column and the approval workflow around it.

15.3 Data rights: what we own, what we rent, what we may show

The prototype's licence register (dcmap/lib/licences.mjs, rendered at /licences) is the single source of truth for what each source obliges, and it records its unresolved questions as unresolved: "the costly error in a licence register is the permissive one". The enterprise platform inherits the register and adds the commercial feeds with tighter terms (D&B, S&P, Verisk, CyberCube), whose contract scope is set out vendor by vendor in the operating model. This subsection is the executive summary of the classes and of the rule that makes them enforceable.

How Unity Catalog makes a licence term enforceable rather than documented

On a laptop, "do not redistribute" is a comment in a file. On the platform it becomes four mechanisms, all taken from the repository's Databricks design. The general security model, including the same on-behalf-of identity and audit logging, is in the operating model; this list is the licence-specific part.

  1. Row filters and column masks on the licensed parcel tables and on vendor identifier columns, so that a user outside the licensed role never receives the rows or the values, whichever tool asks [DBX-9].
  2. Queries run as the viewer. Databricks Apps forwards the signed-in user's token (X-Forwarded-Access-Token), so Genie and SQL run on behalf of the person, and the filters apply per viewer rather than to the app's service principal [DBX-AUTH].
  3. The ledger stops being anonymous. X-Forwarded-Email is written into an edited_by column beside the "how I know" note.
  4. No dashboards with embedded credentials on licensed columns. A dashboard published with embedded credentials runs as the publisher for every viewer and silently defeats the row filters. Publish without them, or build on a view that excludes licensed columns. This is a release check, not a guideline.
Two decisions before anyone outside the build team opens the app. The imagery licence, and who will see it. The repository's own words: moving to a shared workspace "is a change in licensing posture you should make deliberately". The register assigns no phase to the Regrid and Precisely redistribution question; this blueprint assigns it to Phase 1 (see the roadmap), and the ODbL share-alike position to counsel as a Phase 0 prerequisite.

15.4 The data-use register for cedent and broker feeds

Vendor licences are one constraint; the other is what our cedents and brokers allowed when they sent us their exposure. Cedents give us their exposure data to price their treaty, not necessarily so we can identify their clients and compare them with a competitor's book. Most wordings allow portfolio accumulation; fewer allow re-identification of insureds; some restrict retention. We should know which is which before the map makes re-identification easy, because resolving an anonymised location schedule to a named parcel, owner and campus is exactly what the mega-project module does.

The rule: one register row per feed, recording the permitted purposes, the retention period, and whether re-identifying insureds is allowed; the default is accumulation-only, with named-insured resolution held behind a separate access role. The row filter on cedent_id means a cedent using a future portal sees its own data and its own quality feedback, never another cedent's.

Cedent B, large-property facultative submissionsPricing; accumulation; matching to the canonical campusYes: the submission names the insured and the siteSeven years (our records policy)Campus-level overlap with other lines is allowed; the other cedent's premium is not shownRe-identification role for the fac desk
Cedent C, cyber portfolio bordereauPricing; accumulation; CyberCube dependency analysisOnly at aggregate (technology dependency counts)Two years after expiryDependency-cluster totals onlyAccumulation-only

Each row is a Unity Catalog grant, so an analyst querying named insureds across cedents from outside the re-identification role gets no rows and leaves an audit entry, which is the early-warning signal in the risk register.
