16

Operating model, governance and risk appetite

Risk appetite and limits, decision rights, the team, data licensing, security, model governance and adoption: the parts that decide whether the system is actually used.

CROCFOData

The sections from target architecture to governance describe a system. This section describes the company around it: the limits it measures against, the people who may say yes and no, the team that runs it, the rules for data we own and data we rent, and how underwriters and investors are moved from "interesting dashboard" to "this is how we decide". A board judges delivery risk here, not in the architecture.

Key takeaway: the engine tells us where the concentrations are; the appetite says which are acceptable; decision rights say who acts; licensing says who may see what. Without all four, every red cell on the map is an argument rather than a decision.

16.1 The risk appetite and limit framework this system serves

A risk appetite is the Board's written statement of how much of each kind of loss the company is prepared to carry, expressed as limits on measurable things. The BMA expects one: the Insurance Code of Conduct asks for "detailed policies on concentration and allocation limits, including counterparty, assets and sectors" and "detailed exposure limits" around individual counterparties, intra-group transactions, sectors, off-balance-sheet items such as guarantees and letters of credit, and "zones or territories" [BMA-COC] (paragraphs 49(b) and 50(b), August 2022 revision). The Capital and Solvency Return then asks Class 4 and 3B insurers to describe "the process for setting and embedding risk limits" and "the process undertaken to monitor material risk concentration" in Schedule V [BMA-GB] (section C16.2o, 2024 year-end edition; verify against the current instructions handbook for our class).

The table below is the limit set the platform must be able to measure on day one. Every threshold is illustrative: the real numbers are a Board decision taken in Phase 0 (see roadmap), and the point of the table is the columns, not the values. "Capital" means the denominator named in the appetite statement; for the BMA's 10% materiality test on Schedule V(c) and the quarterly return that is statutory capital and surplus (at group level, 5% and 10% of available capital and surplus for intra-group materiality), while the ECR ratio uses available statutory capital and surplus on the economic balance sheet, and every limit record must say which denominator it uses (see the BMA section).

Limit typeIllustrative threshold (Board to set)OwnerReviewEscalationHow the platform monitors it

Worked example: what a limit record has to contain (illustrative)

A limit that lives in a policy document cannot be monitored. A limit that lives in a table can. Each row of the limit register carries: limit_id, measure (which curve, return period, gross or net, which denominator), threshold_amber, threshold_red, hard_limit, owner, approver, review_cadence, effective_from, effective_to, approved_by_board_on. When the Board changes the peak-zone limit from 25% to 22% of capital on 1 October, the old row is closed and a new one opened, so a breach report dated 15 September still shows the limit that applied that day.

The first time the register is loaded it will expose that some limits in the current appetite statement cannot be measured with the data we have (a look-through limit with no look-through data, a campus limit with no campus id). That is a finding, not a failure: the roadmap gate G1 requires every Board limit to be either measurable on the platform or explicitly re-worded.

Decision: the Board re-words or withdraws any limit that cannot be measured on the platform by gate G1. It does not keep an unmeasurable limit on paper, because a limit nobody can test is a limit nobody can breach.

Two rules that keep the framework honest. First, a limit is measured on resolved entities, not on legal names; a breach produced by an unresolved name is shown as "unresolved exposure" so the data problem is fixed rather than argued about. Second, "capital" in a limit always names its denominator. A 10% single-counterparty limit against BMA statutory capital and a 10% limit against rating-agency capital are two different limits and the register holds both.

16.2 Decision rights: who may say yes

Four decisions recur every week once the platform is live. Each needs one accountable person, a small set of people who must be consulted, and an audit row. The workflow fields already exist in the counterparty model (manual_override_flag, approval_id, effective_from, effective_to in the group graph); what is missing is the names.

1. Override an entity mapping

Example: D&B says a Cayman vehicle is a stand-alone company; Ceded Re knows its only business is fronting for Reinsurer XYZ. The data steward proposes the override with evidence (a treaty schedule, a rating report, a filing). The domain owner for the exposure type approves; the CRO approves if the change moves any group across an amber threshold. Effective-dated, reversible, never overwritten.

2. Approve an economic-interdependence group

The BMA's connected-counterparty test is wider than ownership: two counterparties are one if financial difficulties at one "directly or indirectly affect the ability" of the others "to perform their financial obligations" [BMA-GB] (C31.2b). That is a judgement, so it is a committee decision: the Concentration Committee approves each economic interdependence group with written reasoning, and Finance reviews the list before the year-end filing.

3. Sign a capacity envelope

A capacity envelope is the headroom an underwriter may use in a zone, class or campus without asking. The CUO signs envelopes quarterly from the appetite headroom the platform computes; the Head of Portfolio Management proposes them; the CRO confirms they sit inside the Board limits. A deal outside the envelope is not forbidden; it is a referral with a recorded reason.

4. Accept a limit breach

Some breaches are worth accepting for a defined period (a renewal that will lapse in 60 days, a bank downgrade that will be cured by a replacement LOC). The limit owner proposes acceptance with an expiry date; the CRO approves up to the hard limit; anything above the hard limit is a Board decision. Accepted breaches appear on every report until they expire; they do not disappear because they were approved.

RACI for the recurring decisions

RACI names who is Responsible for doing the work, who is Accountable for the outcome (exactly one person), who must be Consulted before the decision and who is Informed after it.

The Concentration Committee. A monthly meeting chaired by the CRO with the CFO, CUO, Head of Portfolio Management, Treasurer, Head of Ceded Re, CIO and Head of Data. Standing agenda: new and expiring breaches, economic-interdependence groups proposed since last month, collateral provider changes, capacity envelopes for next quarter, data-quality scorecard, model version changes. Its minutes are the "decision lineage" that governance promises; the platform writes the approval ids, the minutes explain them.

16.4 Data governance: stewardship, sources of truth, quality, time and audit

Stewardship of entities

One counterparty entity exists once, with one id, and every domain refers to it. The steward owns the id; the domain owns the exposure. A bank appears in treasury as a deposit holder, in investments as an issuer, in ceded re as an LOC issuer and in the mega-project registry as a campus lender: four rows, one entity, one global ultimate. When the steward merges two entities, the merge is a dated event with a reason and the exposures follow automatically; when a merge is wrong, the split is another dated event. Nothing is edited in place.

Two of these rows are also KPIs in the profit levers (the profit section): recoverables with linked collateral and fund assets under look-through are the data conditions for the capital-release lever, so the scorecard is where the Board sees the money being unlocked month by month.

Decision this month: the Committee gives Ceded Re until the next meeting to lift linked recoverables from 88% to 95%, and keeps the collateral efficiency figure out of the CFO's Board pack until then, because a saving computed on 88% linkage would overstate the fee released.

Effective dating

Effective dating means every fact carries the period it was true for, and nothing is overwritten. An ownership change on 1 March creates a new parent edge from 1 March and closes the old one on 28 February; the year-end schedule re-run in April still groups the December exposures the way they were grouped in December. This is what allows a filed number to be reproduced (see model governance below) and what allows a before-and-after of a capital charge to be shown honestly.

Audit trail

Three trails, all queryable: the source trail (which feed, which file, which row, when), the mapping trail (who merged, split, overrode, with what evidence and approval id), and the decision trail (who signed the envelope, accepted the breach, promoted the model version). The prototype already holds the first two for its domain: every site page lists its source rows with links, and every hand correction sits in an append-only ledger with a "how I know" note. The enterprise system inherits that standard and adds the third trail through the approval workflow.

16.6 Security and access

Treaty, facultative, collateral and investment data are among the most sensitive records the company holds. The design principle is that the platform never has more rights than the person looking at it.

On-behalf-of identity

The application runs queries as the viewer, not as a service account. When user authorization is enabled for the app with data scopes (Databricks documentation still labelled it a public preview when this was written; confirm status with the workspace administrator), Databricks Apps pass the user's token on each request (the x-forwarded-access-token header) so that Unity Catalog permissions apply to the person [DBX-AUTH]. The same identity is written into edited_by on every override and approval, so the ledger is never anonymous.

Row-level filters and column masks

Unity Catalog row filters and column masks "restrict the rows and column values a user can see at query time" [DBX-9]. Treaty and fac rows are filtered by underwriting team and class; collateral and LOC facility rows by Treasury and Ceded Re roles; investment positions by the CIO's team; vendor-licensed columns by licence role. An executive sees aggregates across everything; a line underwriter sees the campus, the treaty lines on it and the headroom, not the other cedents' premium.

Audit logging

Access and change events are kept in the platform's audit tables (system.access.audit) [DBX-AUDIT] and joined to the application's own approval ledger, so "who read the collateral tables in the week before the renegotiation, and what did they run" is a query (the audit table records access at table level; the SQL text sits in system.query.history, so a row-level "who looked at Reinsurer XYZ" is answered from the query text, not from a per-row log). Retention follows the record-keeping policy for regulatory filings.

Production reporting kept apart from analytics

The regulatory snapshot is a locked, versioned set of tables that only the pipeline writes and only Finance releases. Analysts and Genie work on the curated and serving schemas, never on the snapshot. A number in a filing can therefore be traced to a snapshot version, and no exploratory query can change it.

One warning from the prototype's own design notes. AI/BI dashboards can be published with embedded credentials, which runs every query as the publisher for every viewer and silently defeats the row filters. Any dashboard that touches treaty, collateral, investment or licensed parcel columns is published without embedded credentials, or built on a view that excludes them. This is a standing rule, checked at every release.

16.7 Model governance: versioning and the reproducibility of a filed number

The platform will hold outputs from external models (Verisk, CyberCube), an internal capital model, and its own mapping logic. All three change over time and all three feed capital numbers, so all three are governed the same way.

  1. Every model output is a versioned object. ModelResult (proposed in the data model) records the model, its version, the event set, the adjustment set (our own view of risk applied on top of the vendor view), the run date and a reference to the event-loss table. A hex cell's PML without a model version cannot be compared with anything, so the platform does not display one.
  2. Promotion is a decision. A new Verisk or CyberCube release, or a recalibrated internal model, runs in parallel for one cycle; the actuarial analyst documents the change in modelled loss by zone and treaty; the CRO approves promotion; the Concentration Committee is informed; envelopes are re-signed if headroom moved. The BMA's catastrophe return (verify the schedule name and items against the current instructions handbook) exists partly to see how we challenge vendor models, so this record is regulatory evidence, not overhead.
  3. Mapping logic is versioned too. The entity-resolution rules, the override set and the economic-interdependence groups have a version id that is stamped on every regulatory snapshot. Re-running the year-end schedule with the December mapping version must reproduce the December number to the dollar.
  4. Reproducibility test at every gate. Pick one filed number (the largest counterparty group, the peak-zone net PML, the recognised collateral total). Re-run it from the snapshot with the recorded versions. If it does not match, the gate is not passed.
  5. Marginal-capital numbers carry model risk of their own. A marginal capital figure shown to an underwriter is a function of the live portfolio and the capital model version; the workbench shows both on the quote record, and the pricing use of the number (the RORAC hurdle) is reviewed by the CRO annually as part of the internal model validation cycle. The CISSA "use test" asks exactly this: that the risk assessment "be integrated into the insurer's decision-making process" [BMA-GB] (C18.3).
Worked example: reproducing a filed number six months later (illustrative)

In April 2028 the auditor asks how the 2027 year-end counterparty exposure to "ACME Group, $155M direct" on the concentration schedules was produced. The steward opens snapshot ye-2027, which records mapping version m-2027-12-31-03, source loads tms-20271231, ia-20271231, cr-20271231, and the limit register version. The query re-runs and returns $155.0M: $70M cash at two ACME legal entities, $65M ACME bonds held in three funds under full look-through, $20M premium receivable from an ACME-owned cedent. Of that, $135M (the cash and the bonds) is the Schedule XXI line, because Schedule XXI carries balance-sheet assets only; the $20M receivable joins it on the Schedule V(c) ten-largest-unaffiliated list, where all four items ($275M, including the LOCs) are tested against 10% of statutory capital and surplus. Separately, $120M of LOCs issued by ACME appear under "protection dependency", not in the direct total. The override that put the Cayman vehicle into the ACME group is shown with its evidence, approver and 14 November effective date. The answer takes twenty minutes and no one rebuilds a spreadsheet. The auditor closes the query with no restatement. Had the re-run returned a different figure, rule 4 above would have failed the snapshot, and the difference itself, not a rebuilt spreadsheet, would have been the finding.

16.8 Change management and adoption: the first ten decisions

A capacity workbench that underwriters do not open is a cost. Adoption is designed, not hoped for, and it starts with the people who lose something: an underwriter loses the freedom to write to a flat limit; a treasurer loses the habit of over-collateralising to be safe; a portfolio manager gains a queue of referrals. Three mechanisms make the change stick.

Envelopes replace flat limits in the authority framework

The underwriting authority document is amended so that authority is expressed as headroom inside a capacity envelope, and the envelope is only available in the workbench. Writing to the old flat limit stops being an option rather than being discouraged. The same amendment moves the CIO's limit register onto the platform: a limit that is not on the platform is not a limit.

Training by doing, on live deals

Two half-days per team, taught by the product owner and one underwriter who used the workbench in the pilot, on that team's own renewals. No generic demo. Each underwriter leaves having run a marginal-capital comparison on a deal they know. Treasury and Ceded Re get the same treatment on the collateral efficiency tile.

Incentives that point the same way

Underwriting scorecards add "share of premium written above hurdle RORAC" and "post-bind accumulation surprises" (target zero) beside premium volume. Treasury's objectives add "fee on unrecognised collateral". Portfolio Management's add "referrals answered within one business day". Nobody is asked to use a tool; everybody is measured on things only the tool can show.

The first ten decisions

Adoption is proven by decisions, not logins. The plan names the first ten decisions that must be taken on the platform, each with the person who takes it and the evidence it leaves behind. The list is illustrative in its specifics; the discipline of naming ten is the point.

How this section maps to the BMA's expectations, and what to verify
  • The Insurance Code of Conduct (August 2022 revision) asks for concentration and allocation limits by counterparty, asset and sector (paragraph 49(b)) and exposure limits by counterparty, intra-group, sector, off-balance-sheet guarantees and letters of credit, and zones or territories (paragraph 50(b)) [BMA-COC]. The limit table above is built to those categories.
  • Schedule V of the Capital and Solvency Return (section C16.2o for Class 4 and 3B) asks for a description of the risk appetite "including the process for setting and embedding risk limits" and "the process undertaken to monitor material risk concentration" [BMA-GB]. The limit register, the scorecard and the Concentration Committee minutes are that description.
  • Schedule V also asks Class 4 and 3B insurers for a risk register listing material risks, their owners, impact and probability, and the mitigation in place (C16.2p) [BMA-GB]. The programme risk register above uses those columns so it can be lifted into the filing.
  • Schedule XXI groups counterparties by control and by economic interdependence (C31.2b, criteria (a) and (b)). The decision rights above put that judgement in a committee with written reasoning.
  • The CISSA "use test" (C18.3) expects the risk assessment to be integrated into decision-making. The first-ten-decisions plan is the evidence.
  • Verify: section numbering and wording against the current year's handbook for our class, and against the Group instructions if we file as a group. The 2024 year-end General Business edition was used here; the BMA published the 2025 edition on 18 December 2025 and re-issues the handbook every December, so section numbers must be re-checked against the current edition before each filing.

Bermuda hooks. Two Bermuda requirements apply to the platform as a material system and should be named in the security policy (verify current wording with Compliance): the BMA's Insurance Sector Operational Cyber Risk Management Code of Conduct, which requires a cyber-risk programme proportionate to the insurer, a named senior owner, and notification to the BMA of a material cyber reporting event within 72 hours; and the Personal Information Protection Act, in full force since 1 January 2025, which governs any personal information in cedent exposure files (named insureds who are individuals, contact details in broker submissions) and the viewer identities the ledger records. The data-use register in licensing therefore carries a personal-data column, re-identification of individuals sits behind the same separate role as named-insured resolution, and the platform is listed in the company's cyber-incident response plan with the Head of Data as the named owner.

17

Implementation roadmap

Start with the data the BMA return needs, because it creates immediate compliance value; design every table and identifier so the advanced use cases need no re-platforming.

CEOCFOData

The roadmap has two tracks and five gates, G0 to G4. Track A is mandatory, funded now by the compliance budget and dated to the BMA filing calendar. Track B is optional, approved in principle and released phase by phase on measured evidence from the gate before. Nothing in Track B may borrow people or weeks from Track A.

Dashboards without limits are wallpaper. Before any screen is built we should agree what "too much" means (the risk appetite and limit set), time the underwriting tools to the renewal seasons where the money is made, and use the regulator's own self-assessment, the CISSA (Commercial Insurer's Solvency Self-Assessment, Schedule IX of the same return), to earn credit for the better analytics rather than only filing the schedules. The handbook says the CISSA "should be integrated into the insurer's decision-making process", which it calls the use test [BMA-GB]: a capacity workbench that underwriters actually use is CISSA evidence.

17.1 Phase 0 prerequisites: decisions that are cheaper now than at the first gate

1. Confirm the class and the rulebook
[Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E], group status and designated-insurer role; this fixes which schedules, factors and dates apply (see the class decides the rulebook).
2. Board-approved risk appetite and limit set
Peril-zone OEP and AEP, single risk, cedent, counterparty, collateral provider, sector and issuer, each with an owner and a denominator (see the limit framework). Without it a "breach" table has nothing to compare against.
3. ODbL and imagery decisions with counsel
The share-alike position on a public or paid release, and the imagery provider for a shared deployment, decided before the app is opened to anyone outside the build team (see data rights).
4. One accountable sponsor and a product owner
CFO or CRO as sponsor; a product owner from Portfolio Management (see team). The sponsor signs every scope change to Track A.
5. Capital model access and a baseline
The current BSCR run, the rating-agency capital run, and the last filed Schedules V(c), XVIII, XIX and XXI as the before picture that Gate G1 measures against. Alongside Phase 1, and outside the compliance budget, a thin capital track: the existing capital model run once to give allocated and marginal capital for the largest 50 treaties before the next 1/1 renewal, so that Phase 3 starts from a measured baseline rather than a blank page.

17.3 Anchored to two calendars: the filing calendar and the renewal calendar

Track A is dated to the regulator's calendar; Track B is dated to the underwriter's. For a 31 December year-end the quarterly financial returns are due by 31 May, 31 August and 30 November (for insurers not in a BMA-supervised group), and the annual Statutory Financial Return and CSR by 30 April, extendable on application but never beyond 31 July; the group return by 31 May, never beyond 31 August; the FCR on our website within 14 days of filing [BMA-FIL-4] [BMA-GS]. The full calendar with signatories is in the compliance calendar. The renewal seasons that matter for a general-business reinsurer are 1 January (most of the treaty book), 1 April (Japan) and 1 June to 1 July (Florida and US wind); a capacity tool that lands in February misses a year of decisions.

The safe path to G1. Producing the first year-end from a new platform and filing it in the same month is how programmes create restatements. Track A therefore runs the 2026 year-end in parallel: the platform produces every concentration schedule beside the existing process, Finance reconciles the two and signs whichever figures it trusts for the 30 April 2027 CSR, with the platform's schedules and the reconciliation in the working papers. The differences become the G0 evidence, the first live filing is the 31 May 2027 quarterly return, and G1 is measured at the 2027 year-end. Track A never puts a filing date at risk.

Each phase changes what the BMA, the auditors and the rating agencies receive, not only what we see. The CSR for a general-business insurer includes the BSCR schedules, the CISSA (Schedule IX), the Catastrophe Risk Return (Schedule X) and the FCR [BMA-FIL-4]; the 2025 model also scores our submission's data validation on a dashboard the supervisor sees.

17.5 Sub-track: the registry onto the lakehouse

The data-center map already has a written migration plan with its own estimates (docs/databricks-apps-architecture.md, section 11). Its design keeps four storage tiers: a Unity Catalog Volume for the tile archive, imagery and snapshots; Unity Catalog Delta tables as the registry; Lakebase for the hand-edit ledger; and app memory for the derived payloads (403 MB, rebuilt in 427 ms locally). They assume one person who knows the codebase, they are the repository's own words, and they nest inside the blueprint phases as follows. Lakebase is Databricks' managed Postgres for the hand-edit ledger; PMTiles is the single-file tile archive the MapLibre map reads by HTTP range request; Unity Catalog Delta tables become the registry itself.

The repository's own summary: "Phases 0 and 1 are the migration. Phases 2 to 4 are the platform." (map steps 0 to 4 in the numbering used here). The cost model for the platform (serverless warehouse, app compute, Lakebase, sync pipelines) is one of the open questions carried in governance and must be modelled before Phase 2 is funded.

Sequencing rule: start with the data required for defensible BMA reporting because it creates immediate compliance value. Design every table and identifier so the same foundation can support the advanced portfolio use cases without re-platforming. In this version the rule has teeth: Track A is ring-fenced and dated; Track B is released only on evidence at the prior gate; and the registry sub-track keeps the map's identifiers (site, substation, campus) as the join keys the insurance-side tables will use, so nothing built in Phase 0 is thrown away in Phase 4.
Key takeaway: Track A delivers the year-end schedules from the platform in parallel first (the 2026 year-end) and live second (the 31 May 2027 quarterly return, then the 2027 year-end), so no filing date is ever at risk and G1 is measured rather than asserted. Track B is approved in principle and released gate by gate: asset look-through after G1, the capacity workbench timed to a named renewal season after G2, mega-project and cyber accumulation after G3, and a portal only after counsel's licence decision. The registry's own migration plan, with its two-week, four-to-six-week, one-week and two-to-three-week estimates, nests inside those phases unchanged.

Track A charter: the fence around the mandatory deliverable.

  • Definition of done. Schedules XXI, XVIII, XIXA and V(c) and the quarterly ten-largest list produced from Gold tables; reconciled line by line to Form 1EBS and statutory capital and surplus; every grouped counterparty carrying evidence, approver and effective dates; every recoverable carrying a linked collateral status; the concentration and credit charges computed before and after correct grouping; a reproducibility test passed on one filed number; Finance signs. Nothing else is Track A.
  • Scope boundary. Track A refuses, by name: the capacity workbench, marginal-capital runs, the H3 join of cedent exposure, look-through beyond what Schedule XXI requires, any portal, any dashboard for underwriters. Requests for these are logged as Track B candidates and answered after G1.
  • People boundary. Track A has named people; Track B may not borrow them, and the sponsor signs any exception in writing with its effect on the filing date stated.
  • Calendar boundary. No Track B change is deployed to shared tables in the eight weeks before a filing lock or filing date; the regulatory snapshot is written only by the pipeline and released only by Finance (see security).
  • Change control. Any change to a Track A table, rule or factor set after the year-end lock is a versioned change with a reason, an approver and a re-run of the reproducibility test; the Concentration Committee sees the list monthly.
  • Reporting. Track A burn-down is reported to the sponsor fortnightly against the dated plan; a two-week slip is escalated to the Board Risk Committee, not absorbed.

The map deliverables in the data center map section sit in Track B except deliverable 1 (registry onto the lakehouse with identity), which is a security and licensing prerequisite and is funded as infrastructure, not as an optional lever.

18

The investment case executives should remember

Not another compliance system: a governed intelligence layer that first makes reporting complete, faster and auditable, then uses the same facts to improve underwriting, investment, retrocession, collateral and capital decisions.

BoardCEOCFO

We are not proposing another compliance system. We are proposing a governed enterprise intelligence layer that first makes concentration reporting complete, faster and auditable, and then uses the same entities, relationships and exposures to improve underwriting, investment, retrocession (the reinsurance a reinsurer buys for itself), collateral and capital decisions. This page puts the case in the form a budget approval needs: what is sunk, what is optional, what each part returns, when, with what confidence, and what the Board is asked to decide today.

Every range on this page is illustrative and is taken from the eight profit levers and the Atlantic Re illustration; none is a forecast. Gate G1 replaces the ranges with measured numbers from our own year-end before any optional spend is released.

Permanent: D&B or linkage, Databricks core, Regrid cache refresh, supportVendor renewals, Databricks consumption, model and version refresh, supportAllReviewed at every gate: "what is the run cost now, and which of it stops if we pause here"

Illustrative: the bands are those used in the budget table for a mid-size reinsurer and exist to show the structure. Procurement replaces them with quotes before the Track A budget is finalised; team ranges are in the operating model.

18.2 Benefit by lever: timing and confidence

Three families. Measurement levers arrive first and need no one to change behaviour: they are what the compliance budget already buys. Decision levers need a Treasurer or a CIO to act on a number they can now trust. Behaviour levers need underwriters to use a tool through a renewal cycle. Confidence falls in that order, and so should the Board's willingness to count the money before it is measured.

18.3 Payback as a range, with the two sensitivities that matter

The optional increment in the illustration is $9M of build across Phases 2 to 4 plus $3.5M a year of run cost once everything is live. Three cases, all illustrative, show why the gates exist:

CaseLevers countedAnnual value (illustrative)Against the optional incrementWhat it tells the Board
Measurement only7 at mid-range and 1 at 200 bps (below its mid-point)$4.4MCovers the run cost of the mandatory platform; does not justify the $9M optional buildThe compliance budget pays for itself and no more. This is the floor, and it is why Track B waits for G1 evidence rather than being funded on the thesis

Sensitivity 1: how much capital is actually released

Lever 1 at the bottom of its range (100 bps, $14M released) is worth $1.7M a year in the illustration; at the top (400 bps, $56M) it is $6.8M. Until G1 measures the real delta from grouping counterparties correctly and linking collateral, the honest number is a range, and the Board should treat the case as unproven.

Sensitivity 2: what released capital can earn

The value of lever 1 is proportional to the hurdle: at a 10% hurdle the mid-range release is worth $2.8M a year, at 12% $3.4M, at 15% $4.2M. The lever matters most in a hard market, which is also when capacity envelopes (lever 3) are worth most. Neither sensitivity changes lever 7, which is why it is the floor.

The rule the Board is asked to hold management to. Gate G1 replaces every illustrative range above with measured numbers from our own year-end: the charge delta reconciled by Finance, the collateral over-recognition in dollars, the entity-resolution error rate on a hand-checked sample, and the days saved on the schedules. No optional tranche is released before that. Progress after G1 is reported against the 6, 12 and 24-month KPI scorecard every quarter, and the questions in what the board should ask at each gate are the agenda.

18.4 What each path delivers

If we stop at compliance

  • Top-counterparty, recoverables and collateral schedules produced from the platform, reconciled to the general ledger, signed by Finance.
  • Days from year-end to reconciled schedules down by a third at 12 months and by half at 24 (illustrative targets from the scorecard); auditor and BMA data follow-ups on those schedules at zero.
  • Roughly $4.4M a year in the illustration: 30 to 50% of the manual effort on those schedules, plus whatever capital the corrected charges release.
  • Collateral that earns no regulatory credit identified in dollars, even if nobody then renegotiates it.
  • But the information goes dormant after filing: the same graph that could price a $500M fac line or reshape the retro programme is used four times a year by Finance.

If we build the full architecture

  • Every BMA record becomes reusable decision data: one entity graph serves the return, the Treasurer, the CIO and the underwriting floor.
  • Counterparty, investment and underwriting risks seen together; wrong-way risk pairs (collateral whose issuer is related to the obligor) and shared-dependency clusters found before the loss (lever 6: in the illustration one $75M cluster at 2% annual probability, $1.5M a year of expected loss avoided).
  • Portfolio Management measures the marginal capital of the next transaction; underwriters receive capacity envelopes instead of generic limits (levers 3 and 5: $8.7M a year at mid-range in the illustration).
  • Treasury and the CIO act on trusted numbers (levers 2 and 4: $12.8M a year at mid-range).
  • About $27.4M a year at mid-range against $3.5M of run cost, with the two measurement levers alone covering the mandatory platform. Illustrative, netted at G2, proven at G3.

18.5 Decision requested

The resolution the Board is asked to pass is set out in full in the case on one page; in summary:

1. Approve Track A now. Phases 0 and 1 funded from the compliance budget within the $4 to 8M band (to be confirmed by procurement), ring-fenced and dated to the dated plan: the 2026 year-end schedules produced in parallel with the existing process, the first quarterly return filed from the platform on 31 May 2027, Gate G1 at the 2027 year-end. Name the executive sponsor (CFO or CRO) and the product owner from Portfolio Management.

2. Approve Track B in principle, released at gates. Phases 2 to 4 within the $5 to 11M cumulative build band plus vendor data and run cost as scoped, each tranche released only on measured evidence at the prior gate (G1 for Phase 2, G2 for Phase 3, G3 for Phase 4) with the Board free to continue, pause or re-scope; Phase 5 subject to counsel's licence decision.

3. Commission the Phase 0 prerequisites. The Board-approved risk appetite and limit set (see the limit framework); the ODbL share-alike and imagery licence decisions with counsel (see data rights); confirmation of our BMA class [Class 4 / 3B / 3A, or C / D / E] and group status.

4. Adopt the reporting cadence. The quarterly KPI scorecard and the gate questions as standing items; the programme risk register in the operating model reviewed at each gate.

The money spent satisfying the BMA is not a throwaway compliance cost. It buys the plumbing every other decision in this document runs through, and the tables above are how we will know, gate by gate, whether the taps are open.

Key takeaway: the compliance budget is sunk and pays for itself through reporting cost and the capital the corrected charges release; that floor is measured at G1. The optional increment is small next to the levers it unlocks, but the levers are decisions and behaviour, not arithmetic, so the Board approves Track B in principle and releases it only as each gate reports measured evidence.

18.6 What peers already do, and where this would put us

None of the pieces of this programme is novel; the combination on one governed graph, at a mid-size reinsurer, is less common. Each claim below about a named company or regime should be checked against its own public filings before it appears in a Board pack.

  • Large reinsurers run proprietary portfolio systems. RenaissanceRe has for years described in its annual report a proprietary integrated system for underwriting, exposure management and capital allocation (REMS), and attributes its portfolio construction to it (verify the current 10-K wording). Reinsurers with Solvency II or BMA-approved internal models (the largest European and Bermudian groups) allocate marginal capital per deal as routine and express underwriting authority in those terms. Capacity envelopes and RORAC hurdles are therefore standard practice at the top of the market and the exception below it.
  • Banks solved connected-counterparty grouping a decade ago. The Basel large-exposures framework (in force from 1 January 2019) requires banks to group connected clients by control and economic interdependence and to investigate interdependence above 5% of Tier 1 capital, which is the wording the BMA borrowed (see the grouping rule). Every bank we hold cash with runs a bank-grade corporate-family graph against us; few reinsurers run one against their banks.
  • Lloyd's forces multi-line clash and cyber scenarios. Lloyd's realistic disaster scenarios require syndicates to report against prescribed multi-line and cyber scenarios each year (verify the current RDS list), which has pushed London-market carriers to join property, casualty and cyber exposure on one basis. A Bermuda reinsurer with London-market cedents is asked those questions second-hand.
  • Data center accumulation is nobody's solved problem. Brokers and carriers have published market commentary since 2024 on the difficulty of insuring multi-billion-dollar campuses and the DSU exposure during construction (verify against current broker reports); no vendor sells a substation-dependency dataset for insurance use, which is why the prototype built one from public filings. Here the company would be early, with the risks and the pricing advantage that implies (see Scenario J).
  • Rating agencies score the process, not the tool. S&P's ERM assessment and AM Best's ERM building block reward demonstrated risk controls and risk-adjusted decision-making; the peers whose ERM is scored 'strong' can show the evidence chain that Scenario L describes.
Key takeaway: on counterparty grouping and marginal-capital pricing this programme is catch-up to the top of the market and to the banks; on mega-project dependency accumulation it is early. The Board should expect the first to be judged against peers and the second to be judged against its own gate evidence.
19

Questions executives will ask

Direct answers to the questions a board, a rating agency and an underwriting floor will ask before and after approval.

BoardAll

19.1 Questions executives will ask

Twenty-nine questions, each with a short answer. Where a number is not sourced it is illustrative and says so. Links point to the detail elsewhere in this document.

Scope and strategy

Why not just buy a vendor concentration tool and be done?

Because no vendor tool holds our data. The BMA return needs our cash, bonds, reinsurance recoverables (money other reinsurers owe us), each letter of credit (LOC: a bank's promise to pay us if that reinsurer does not) and intra-group treaties joined to one governed set of counterparties (see BMA minimum reporting). A packaged tool still needs that join built, and it then owns the answer we sign for. We do buy the parts that are commodity: corporate family trees (D&B, and the free GLEIF Legal Entity Identifier register, which records who owns whom), cat science (Verisk), cyber dependency data (CyberCube), parcel data (Regrid). We build only the entity graph and the join to our own books, because that is the part that is ours and the part that makes the capital numbers move. See buy, integrate or build.

Is this an IT project or a business project?

A business project with an IT delivery track. The signatories of the Capital and Solvency Return (two directors plus the CRO or CFO for a Class 4/3B insurer) attest to the concentration figures, and issuing a false or misleading document under the Insurance Act 1978 is an offence unless the signer proves they had no knowledge of the falsity and took every reasonable precaution (s.50); the group rules add a fine of up to $50,000 for a knowingly or recklessly false return (Group Rules para 9) [BMA-FIL-4]. The business owns the definitions (what is one counterparty, what collateral qualifies, what limit applies); IT owns the plumbing. Sponsor: CFO or CRO. Product owner: Portfolio Management. Data owners: Treasury, Investments, Ceded Re, Underwriting, Finance. See governance and decision rights.

How much of the budget is mandatory, and how much is our choice?

Mandatory: the counterparty graph, the collateral link to each recoverable, the affiliated-reinsurance register and the four BMA views (Schedules XXI, XVIII, XIXA and V(c), plus the quarterly return). That is Track A in the roadmap; under the dated plan it runs the 2026 schedules in parallel, files the first quarterly return from the platform on 31 May 2027 and the 2027 year-end from it. Optional, released only on evidence at each gate: asset look-through (seeing the bonds and loans inside a fund we hold, not just the fund) and limits, the capacity workbench, mega-project and cyber accumulation, the portal. Illustrative split for planning: roughly 40 to 50 percent of the total is mandatory; the rest is where the profit levers live and can be paused phase by phase.

What are we buying versus building?

One rule decides it: buy anything a vendor can sell to our competitors on the same terms, build anything that only makes sense joined to our own books. The full line-by-line list is in buy, integrate or build. What we build is short: the entity graph with its override workflow, the join from every book to that graph, the collateral-to-obligation link, the H3 cell accumulation over our positions (H3 divides the map into hexagons of a chosen size so exposure can be added up per hexagon, independent of ZIP codes or county lines), and the BMA output tables. The Mega Project Asset Intelligence registry is already prototyped in the data-center map; the build there is the join to treaty and facultative (fac, single-risk) lines, not the map. See Mega Project Asset Intelligence.

What would make you stop the programme?

Four signals, each checked at a gate. (1) Gate G1 missed: the year-end schedules cannot be produced from the platform and reconciled to the general ledger. (2) Entity resolution accuracy below target: more than a handful of false merges or splits found by Finance in the top-50 counterparties. (3) No measured capital delta after G1, meaning the data corrections did not move the BSCR (Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement: the regulator's formula for how much capital we must hold), so the optional levers are unproven. (4) Adoption failure: underwriters or the CIO still run decisions outside the tool one renewal after G3. Any of these pauses the next optional tranche; only the mandatory track continues.

Regulator and rating agencies

What does the BMA actually get from us, and when?

For a 31 December year-end: quarterly returns by 31 May, 31 August and 30 November (ten largest unaffiliated exposures, intra-group transactions and reinsurance); the annual Statutory Financial Return and Capital and Solvency Return by 30 April (extendable on application, never beyond 31 July) including Schedules V, XVIII, XIXA and XXI, the CISSA (the insurer's own written assessment of the capital it needs) and the Financial Condition Report; group returns by 31 May (five months, from the Group Supervision Rules rather than [BMA-3]). If we are a member of a group the BMA supervises, the quarterly return is filed at group level rather than by the entity. The FCR goes on our website within 14 days of filing. Filing is through the SubmIT portal from the 2025 year-end [BMA-FIL-4]. Verify dates against the current filing requirements for our class.

What if the BMA rules change?

They will: the BMA re-issues handbooks, filing requirements and BSCR models each year-end (the 2025 set on 18 and 19 December 2025, with the BSCR models republished on 17 February 2026), the group solvency rules were amended in 2022 (twice) and 2024 [CONYERS], and group supervision was widened again from 7 January 2026 [CONYERSa]. The design absorbs this because the graph stores facts (who owns whom, which collateral secures which balance, which entity wrote the risk) and the schedules are views on those facts. A rule change is a change to a Gold table (the final, decision-ready layer of the data platform, see the Databricks section) and a factor set, versioned and dated, not a rebuild. The same is true if we change class or group status.

How does this help with S&P and AM Best?

Both agencies run their own capital models and an ERM assessment. AM Best's BCAR (its capital adequacy ratio) charges reinsurance recoverables by the reinsurer's Best's rating (from about 2 percent for A++ to over 50 percent for weak reinsurers), gives full credit for funds held, and recognises trust funds and letters of credit as offsets worth at most 90 percent of the charge they secure; S&P's 2023 capital criteria give explicit diversification credit through correlation matrices across asset and insurance risks. The same resolved counterparty and collateral data that lowers our BSCR charge therefore lowers rating-agency capital, and a demonstrated concentration-control process is what the ERM review scores. Practical effect: fewer data follow-ups, a defensible answer to "what is your largest single exposure", and evidence for the ERM narrative. The blueprint should name which capital measure binds per deal (see the pricing question below).

What does "wrong-way risk" mean for us in one sentence?

Wrong-way risk is when the thing protecting us fails for the same reason we need the protection: a letter of credit from a bank in the same group as the reinsurer whose debt it secures, or collateral made of bonds issued by the reinsurer's own group. Example (illustrative): a $120M LOC from ACME Bank secures Reinsurer XYZ's recoverable; as ACME is downgraded the uplift shrinks, because the BSCR uses the higher of the reinsurer's and the LOC issuer's rating (GB handbook C25.2(i)); if ACME also ceases to qualify as an acceptable issuer under our cedents' collateral rules, the LOC has to be replaced. The charge and the cash call therefore arrive exactly when ACME's own troubles are hurting our bond holdings in ACME. Decision: the limit register caps any one LOC bank, and an LOC from a bank in the same group as the reinsurer it secures, or from a bank we already hold bonds in above the cap, is not counted as eligible collateral without a Concentration Committee exception. See collateral concentration.

What does a limit breach look like operationally?

A breach is a row, not a red light. The limit register holds the limit (single counterparty amber at 7.5 percent of capital, red at 10 percent, as in the limit framework), the measure, the owner and the escalation path. When the nightly refresh crosses it, the platform writes a breach record with the exposure, the contributing positions, the date and the owner, and opens a task. The owner must either bring the exposure down, obtain an approved exception with evidence and an expiry, or escalate to the Concentration Committee. Every state change is logged. Without a Board-approved appetite there is nothing to breach, which is why appetite is a Phase 0 deliverable. See the limit framework.

Data and platform

Why Databricks rather than our existing warehouse?

Three things the warehouse does not give us in one place: row-level governance with audit and lineage (Unity Catalog, the Databricks permissions and audit layer, decides who sees which cedent's rows, a cedent being the insurer that passes risk to us, and records every access), native geospatial and H3 functions for accumulation at scale, and a supported way to run natural-language questions and the map app inside the same permission model. The data-center prototype is packaged as a read-only Databricks App (workspace SSO is supplied by the platform once deployed); it was verified locally on 26 September 2026 and has not yet been deployed to a workspace. If the existing warehouse can meet those three tests, keep it; the graph design is platform-neutral. See the Databricks section.

How is the data-center map related to all this?

It is the working prototype of one component: the asset registry for AI data centers, semiconductor fabs and the power they depend on. Today it holds about 6,300 live sites (6,285 on 27 September 2026), 28,161 power plants, 214 fabs and 212 substation-dependency edges, each citing the PJM or NYISO filing it comes from. What it does not yet have is our money: no join to cedent exposure, no treaty or fac lines, no insured values (the export deliberately writes TIV (total insured value) as zero rather than guess). It becomes a profit lever the day a facultative submission is matched to a campus and the treaty lines already on that campus appear beside it. See Mega Project Asset Intelligence and what already exists.

Who owns the entity graph?

One named data steward owns it day to day, reporting to the Head of Data, with a product owner from Portfolio Management and the Concentration Committee as the approver for any override (for example, grouping two legally separate entities as one counterparty under the economic-interdependence test). Every node and edge carries source, confidence, approver and effective dates. Finance reviews the groupings used in the return before filing. Vendors supply evidence; they never own the answer. The prototype already works this way: about 455 hand-corrected fields (473 ledger rows) in an append-only ledger, each with a note on how the correction is known.

How do we stop it becoming another dead spreadsheet?

By making it the only path to something people must do. The BMA schedules are produced from it and nowhere else, so Finance keeps it correct. Underwriting authority for large lines is expressed as headroom in it, so underwriters keep it current. The CIO's limit register lives in it. Data-quality scores are visible per source owner. If a number can be produced outside the platform for a regulatory or authority decision, the platform dies; the operating model removes that option.

How do we know the numbers are right?

Four controls. Reconciliation: every schedule ties to Form 1EBS (the economic balance sheet inside the Capital and Solvency Return) and statutory capital and surplus, and cash and positions tie to the custodian and the investment book of record. Lineage: every figure drills to its source rows; the BMA can call for supporting information on request, the handbook requires the workings behind the catastrophe PML and AAL to be kept for five years after the return is filed (C16.2f-h), and a designated insurer must keep the group CSR for five years (Group Rules para 6(5)). Challenge: entity groupings are cross-checked between D&B and the free GLEIF parent file, and disagreements are queued for review. Validation: the 2025 BSCR model scores our data on its DV Dashboard tab (the BMA says the score is informative only and does not block filing, so we treat it as a floor, not a control) [BMA-FIL-4]. The KPI is auditor and BMA follow-up queries on these schedules: target zero.

What if D&B's hierarchy is wrong?

It sometimes is, and the design assumes it. D&B is one evidence source among three: GLEIF Level 2 parent data (free, self-reported by the entity) [GLEIF], the issuer hierarchy from Bloomberg or ICE on the asset side, and our own overrides. Where sources disagree the steward records a verdict with evidence, and that verdict, not the vendor, is what the return uses. Two thresholds are set in advance: any counterparty above 5 percent of capital (illustrative) is checked by hand every quarter, and any change to a top-ten grouping needs a second approver.

Can Genie or natural language be trusted for regulatory numbers?

No, and it should not be asked to. Regulatory numbers come from governed Gold tables with locked versions at quarter-end. Genie, the Databricks tool that turns an English question into a database query, is for exploration: an executive asks "which bank holds most of our cash today" and gets an answer computed from tables they are entitled to see, always with the SQL and the row count shown, so anyone can check it. The prototype's design routes exact questions deterministically and reserves Genie for analytical ones, and runs every query as the viewer, not as the app. Anything that reaches a filing or an authority decision is a governed report, never a chat answer.

How do we handle vendor licence limits and ODbL?

Licences become enforceable rather than documented. Regrid and Precisely parcel data are internal-use only, so their columns carry Unity Catalog row filters and masks, and publishing a dashboard with embedded credentials on those columns is prohibited by policy, because such a dashboard runs as its publisher and would silently bypass the filters. Regrid bills per parcel record returned [REGRID-BILL], so every resolved parcel is cached once. Most of the registry is ODbL share-alike (OpenStreetMap-derived): internal use is covered by the licence's use-within-an-organisation relief (ODbL 4.5(c)) on our register's reading, but any external release that merges it with licensed parcels needs counsel before Phase 5. That decision is a Phase 0 item, not an afterthought.

What about cedent data confidentiality in a portal?

Cedents give us exposure data to price their treaty, not necessarily to let us identify their clients or compare them with a competitor's book. The platform keeps a data-use register per feed: permitted purposes, retention, and whether re-identification is allowed. The default is accumulation-only use, with named-insured resolution behind a separate access control. In the portal a cedent sees only its own rows, enforced by row filters, and any cross-cedent view is aggregated to H3 cells above a minimum count. General Counsel signs off the register before any external user is admitted.

What if a cedent will not give us GPS coordinates?

We price the uncertainty rather than pretend it away. Location data arrives in three tiers: address or GPS (geocoded and cached), zone or CRESTA aggregates (CRESTA zones are the insurance industry's standard geographic areas for reporting catastrophe exposure; these are disaggregated into hexagons with a stated method), or the cedent's own model output (a badge on the cedent, not a dot on the map). Each tier carries a data-quality score that becomes a pricing load or capital buffer, and the portal shows the cedent what their missing data costs them. Illustrative: a submission at zone level only might carry a 5 to 10 percent load on the technical price. That feedback is the fastest way to get better data next year.

Money and operations

How long until underwriters actually use it?

Underwriters use it when it answers a question they already ask, in the meeting where they ask it. The first such question is "what else do we have on this campus, cedent or dependency", which the capacity workbench answers in Phase 3 (Gate G3 is use in one live renewal). Timing under the dated plan: the mandatory track produces its first live filing on 31 May 2027 and its first year-end at the 2027 year-end; the workbench is built after G2 and lands before the 1 June 2029 renewal at the earliest, otherwise 1 January 2030. Adoption is enforced by expressing large-line authority as headroom in the tool, so the alternative is not available.

What is the run cost once it is built?

Illustrative rule of thumb: 20 to 30 percent of cumulative build per year, plus vendor licences. Permanent items: an entity-linkage feed (D&B or equivalent), Databricks core consumption, parcel cache refresh, Verisk (assumed to be existing spend; confirm). Pausable items tied to optional phases: CyberCube (likely the largest optional licence; procurement to confirm), S&P 451, Esri premium basemaps and stored geocoding (Esri charges $4 per 1,000 stored geocodes with no free tier for stored results; one-off lookups that are not stored have a free monthly allowance [ESRI-PRICE]). The map itself runs on MapLibre and self-hosted tiles with no per-tile bill. Procurement confirms bands before the Board sees a number.

How does this affect our reinsurance buying?

Retrocession (the reinsurance a reinsurer buys) becomes a capital decision with visible arithmetic. Two BMA mechanics reward it directly: recoverables are charged by the reinsurer's BSCR rating net of qualifying collateral, and a diversification credit of up to 40 percent grows as our largest retrocessionaire becomes a smaller share of the total (the factor values and the size of the credit: verify against the current instructions handbook). Worked example (illustrative, the same one worked step by step in where the capital actually moves): Reinsurer XYZ, rated BBB (BSCR rating 4), owes us $180M, less a $10M payable with a right of set-off, so $170M of net exposure at a 7.0 percent factor is a charge of $11.9M. A $120M LOC from ACME Bank, rated A, counts at 98 percent ($117.6M) and takes the net qualifying exposure to $52.4M; the charge falls to about $3.6M, releasing about $8.3M of ECR on one reinsurer. That figure is before the diversification adjustment and before the BSCR covariance step, so the capital actually freed is somewhat less; our Schedule XVIII preparer confirms the reading we file. So spreading retro across more rated or collateralised counterparties, and buying where marginal capital is highest, is where the budget pays back. Decision for the Head of Ceded Reinsurance: the retro panel is chosen on capital released per dollar of premium, not on price alone. See collateral concentration.

Which capital measure decides whether a deal is worth writing?

The strictest one on that deal. We satisfy three referees at once: the BMA (BSCR, with the ECR being the higher of BSCR and the minimum margin, and a target of 120 percent of ECR, the BMA's target capital level (verify against the current instructions handbook)), the rating agencies (S&P capital model, AM Best BCAR) and our own internal model. They treat cat, credit and diversification differently, so the binding constraint changes deal by deal. Price must cover the marginal capital of the binding constraint: expected margin divided by that capital, the RORAC (return on risk-adjusted capital), must clear the hurdle. Illustrative: a $50M line with $4M margin and $20M marginal capital earns 20 percent against a 12 percent hurdle; in a peak hexagon the same line might need $45M and earn 9 percent. Decision: write the first; decline or reprice the second unless retro bought against that hexagon brings its marginal capital down to where the hurdle clears.

What is the first thing an executive will see on screen?

One page, five tiles, one map. Tiles: ECR ratio and headroom to the 120 percent target; largest single counterparty as a percent of statutory capital and surplus, with the grouped family named; recoverables with linked qualifying collateral as a percent of total; number of open limit breaches with owners; days to the next BMA filing and the data-validation score. Below them the H3 map of net exposure by hexagon, coloured against appetite, with mega-project campuses and their power dependencies as a toggle. Every tile drills to the rows behind it. Nothing on that page is typed in by hand.

What happens on day one of a catastrophe event?

By the end of day one the CRO has four numbers, each with its basis stated. Footprint exposure: the event footprint (the US Geological Survey's ShakeMap of ground-shaking intensity today, Verisk footprints when linked) intersected with the registry and the geocoded book, worst hexagons first, the pattern the map already runs for earthquakes. Estimated net loss by contract after terms, from pre-computed event loss tables (the cat model's estimated loss per contract for each simulated event, produced before any event happens), gross and net of retro. Cash calls: claims by month, collateral top-ups cedents can demand, reinstatement premiums we owe on retro (the premium paid to restore cover after a loss uses it up), against liquid unencumbered assets by currency. Counterparty watch: which retrocessionaires and LOC banks now carry the recoverable, and which are in the same footprint. No model re-run is needed for any of them.

If every gate says pause, what have we spent and what do we keep?

The floor is Option B in the case on one page. If G1 says pause, we have spent Track A only: $4 to 8M of build (illustrative, procurement to confirm) and $1 to 2M a year to run it. We keep a counterparty, collateral and affiliated-reinsurance graph reconciled to the general ledger, the four schedules and the quarterly return produced from it, a measured before-and-after of the concentration and reinsurance-credit charges, and the two measurement levers, worth about $4.4M a year in the Atlantic Re illustration, which is why the mandatory platform pays for itself and no more. If G2 says pause, add $2 to 4M of Phase 2 build and $0.5 to 1M a year of data: we keep fund look-through, the limit register with phantom-breach detection and the CIO's yield lever. If G3 says pause, add $2 to 4M for the workbench: we keep marginal capital and RORAC per deal and one renewal season of evidence. Nothing bought at an earlier phase is thrown away at a later pause, because every phase writes to the same tables; what stops is the next tranche and the run cost tied to it (CyberCube, S&P 451, imagery), which the ROI frame lists as pausable.

Why is a data center map in a paper about BMA compliance?

Because it is the only part of the winning system that already exists, and it proves the working method the mandatory track will use: resolve a thing that appears under different names in different files to one governed record, attach evidence and an approver to every correction, and keep a ledger that says how each fact is known. The map does that for 6,285 sites and 212 power-dependency edges; the counterparty graph must do it for banks, issuers and reinsurers. It is not funded by the compliance budget: its lakehouse migration is infrastructure (a security and licensing prerequisite, the registry sub-track), and joining it to our treaty and facultative lines is Phase 4, released at G3 and worth lever 6 only if a cluster is found. If the Board wants the paper without the map, Track A is unchanged; what is lost is Scenario J and the early position in an accumulation class no vendor yet sells (see what peers already do).

Why are we not licensing PSOLD?

Four reasons, recorded in version 5. Verisk's own Touchstone 2021 (9.0) database reference withdrew non-catastrophe detailed loss analysis and the AIRPSOLD database, so the delivery route is unclear. The curves are calibrated on ordinary commercial property and out of sample for hyperscale campuses and fabs. Our per-risk book is priced from cedent transparency, engineering maximum foreseeable loss, our own claims and the map. And the licence would be cost without a decision it changes: cedents already run PSOLD, so we demand the package behind their number instead (see what we do instead). The decision is re-opened at a gate only if per-risk XoL on ordinary commercial property becomes a material line and cedents will not provide transparent severity work.

Key takeaway: every answer above comes back to the same three assets: one governed counterparty graph, one join from every book to it, and a Board-approved appetite to measure against. The regulator pays for the first; the second and third are where the profit is.

What changed in versions 3 to 5

Corrections to version 2, what version 3 added, what was folded in from version 4, the version 5 decisions, and what remains unverified.

All

Version 2 argued by architecture. Version 3 was produced by auditing version 2 from six angles (BMA regulation, vendor claims, reinsurance domain, the profit thesis, the user interface, and alignment with the data-center map that already exists), then rewriting every section against those findings, adding the missing sections, and having every new passage reviewed by a fact refuter and an editor before it was accepted. What follows is the honest list: what was wrong, what was added, and what could not be verified.

22.1 Corrections to version 2

Where (version 2 section)Version 2 saidVersion 3 saysWhy it matters
Section 4, referencesCited the 2025 Long-Term Instructions Handbook as the source for concentration reporting.The Long-Term handbook applies to Class C, D and E life reinsurers. A property-casualty reinsurer (Class 4, 3B, 3A) files under the General Business handbook. The company's class is now stated as a placeholder and every schedule is given for both.Wrong rulebook, same schedule numbers: an easy mistake that is expensive to find late.
Section 4Treated Schedule XXI as the home of all counterparty concentration, including recoverables, receivables and letters of credit.Schedule XXI (Concentration Risk) is asset-side only and feeds the BSCR concentration charge. Reinsurance recoverables and their collateral sit in Schedule XVIII; the ten largest unaffiliated exposures across every type, and intra-group transactions, sit in Schedule V(c) and the quarterly return.Reporting the wrong amount on the wrong schedule is a regulatory finding either way.
Section 4Described concentration as a disclosure and governance requirement.It is also a capital charge: a distinct concentration-risk charge on the ten largest asset counterparties and a reinsurance credit charge by BSCR rating, net of qualifying collateral, with a diversification credit of up to 40 percent.This is the mechanism that turns compliance data into capital, which is the whole thesis.
Section 2"Gross → ceded → collateral → counterparty → retro → net".For a reinsurer, ceded and retro are the same transaction. The chain is now gross assumed, net of retrocession, retro recoverable, collateral and set-off, residual credit exposure by group, net retained loss plus credit-risk capital.Double-counted a step and omitted the one that creates credit exposure.
Section 5, Scenario AAdded a $120M letter of credit to cash, bonds and a receivable to reach a "$275M gross linked amount".A bank guarantee is not a deposit. ACME is now shown as $155M of direct credit exposure and $120M of protection dependency, and the downgrade question is asked properly.Summing them overstates exposure and hides what actually happens when the bank is downgraded.
Section 5.2Collateral described only as protection we receive.A Bermuda reinsurer mostly posts collateral (Regulation 114 trusts, multi-beneficiary trusts, letter-of-credit facilities, funds withheld). Encumbered assets, liquidity, fees and top-up triggers are now part of the picture.The cost of collateral is one of the largest levers available and was missing.
Section 7AAL, EP and PML used without definition; "marginal capital by hex".Definitions box added; occurrence and aggregate curves distinguished; the BMA yardstick named (net 99 percent TVaR, annual aggregate, including reinstatement premiums). Allocated capital goes on the map; marginal capital is computed per deal in the workbench because it is not additive.Two "1-in-100" numbers can differ by a third depending on the curve.
Section 7, Scenario CA shared substation accumulated the full insured value of every site on it.Loss of off-premises power is usually a sublimited utility-service or contingent business-interruption extension with a waiting period. Two numbers are now shown: physical-damage accumulation and dependency accumulation, plus delay-in-start-up during construction.The dependency risk is real but is measured in sublimits, not total values.
Section 7.1, 8, 9, 10ArcGIS positioned as the map; Regrid caching, H3 aggregation and the lakehouse described as future work.The prototype already runs on MapLibre GL JS, self-hosted PMTiles and h3-js, already caches parcels with a placement-aware rule, already renders an H3 hexagon heatmap, and already runs read-only on Databricks Apps (built 2026-09-23, verified locally 2026-09-26, not yet deployed to a workspace). Esri is optional.The board should not fund building what exists; it should fund joining it to the book.
Section 7.1Verisk Touchstone treated as a stable platform to keep.Touchstone 2025 (13.0) is the last full release; Verisk Synergy Studio has been available since 15 June 2026, and Verisk launched a U.S. Data Center Exposure Database on 3 September 2026. Integrations target Synergy Studio; the Verisk data-center database becomes a second reference feed.A multi-year integration must target the successor platform.
Section 8, references"S&P Company-Level Linking"; a D&B white paper; Esri's 2 million tiles.The S&P product is the Business Entity Cross Reference Service (BECRS); the D&B white paper link is dead and was removed; Esri's 2 million figure is a basemap-tile allowance and stored geocodes have no free tier. GLEIF LEI Level 2 added as the free parent-relationship backbone.Procurement and budget accuracy.
Section 8"Do not buy a second natural-cat platform"; PSOLD mentioned without explanation.Do not build a cat model, but decide explicitly on a second model or a blended own view, because the BMA cat return and rating agencies expect model challenge. PSOLD is calibrated on ordinary commercial property and is out of sample for hyperscale campuses and fabs.Model-risk governance and mega-project pricing.
Section 14, 15Overlapping phase durations, no gates, no mandatory-versus-optional split, no numbers.A gated two-track plan anchored to the filing calendar, and a one-page return-on-investment frame with illustrative ranges that Gate G1 replaces with measured figures.A board cannot fund a gesture.

22.2 Added in version 3

  • Executive summary with the resolution, four options, an assumptions register, what is out of scope, a dated plan with one calendar (parallel run of the 2026 schedules, first quarterly return from the platform 31 May 2027, G1 at the 2027 year-end), reading paths by persona, and a how-to-read guide. All worked examples and scenarios now run on one reference company, Atlantic Re ($2,000M capital, $1,400M BSCR, $5,500M invested assets), one family of invented names, and the limits in the operating model.
  • How the compliance budget becomes profit: eight levers with mechanism, data, KPI, owner and illustrative range; illustrative economics; the mandatory-versus-optional budget split; the KPI scorecard at 6, 12 and 24 months; what the board should ask at each gate; how this fails.
  • The BMA section rewritten around the entity's class, the four places the BMA asks for concentration, the capital-charge mechanics with verified factors, the filing calendar, a ledger-to-schedule worked example, and what auditors and the BMA will ask.
  • Worked examples end to end for counterparty resolution, economic-interdependence overrides, collateral recognition and joint stress, funds withheld versus trust versus letter of credit, affiliated chains, wrong-way risk, issuer look-through, structural limits, hexagon accumulation, peak-zone capacity envelopes, shared dependencies and cyber single points of failure.
  • Three interactive calculators (illustrative): one group in four ledgers, collateral under a wrong-way stress, and the price of a line.
  • The data-center map: what already exists, with measured numbers and the files that state them, what it cannot yet do, its licensing constraints, and the Databricks path already designed.
  • Operating model, governance and risk appetite: limits, decision rights, team, data governance, licensing and legal, security, model governance, adoption, programme risks.
  • Scenarios F to L and a scenario matrix; questions executives will ask; a glossary with hover definitions on every dotted term.
  • Interface: reading paths, search that dims rather than hides, boardroom and skim modes, light and dark themes, printable with sources, copy-link on headings, keyboard shortcuts, phone layout.

22.3 Folded in from the separate version 4 draft

A version 4 draft written on the version 2 base (28 September 2026) carried material that version 3 lacked. It was compared block by block against both; what version 3 already covered was left as it was, and the rest was rewritten in version 3's style, checked against vendor pages and the audits, and placed where it belongs:

  • Non-catastrophe property severity: Verisk ISO PSOLD and ISO Rapid Valuator kept distinct from the catastrophe model, a when-to-buy decision table (replaced in version 5 by the decision not to license), the transparency package to demand from a cedent's PSOLD, the hyperscale-fire example, and the audit's warning that PSOLD is out of sample for mega projects (insurance section).
  • Casualty systemic accumulation: the common-cause clash diagram and the specialist correlation model as a Phase 4 buy if liability is material (insurance section).
  • Cedent intelligence: Schedule P and Schedule F as a distinct branch, change events instead of snapshots, derived early-warning signals, and how they change a renewal conversation (insurance section, roadmap Phase 2).
  • Retrocession and true net exposure: the gross-to-true-net loss waterfall, the before-and-after retro table, and the rule that Portfolio Management must also say where to write more (insurance section, Scenario M).
  • Credit quality beside concentration: ratings, outlook, watch status and limit utilisation on every counterparty group, AM Best as the insurance-counterparty source, and derivatives, repo, securities lending, FX and liquidity relationships in the same graph (counterparty section).
  • Evidence and data rights as canonical objects: confidence bands with the rule that only confirmed and high-confidence links aggregate automatically, the data-rights registry, and the information barrier between what Portfolio Management sees and what a facultative underwriter sees (data model section).
  • Cross-domain stress orchestration as Scenario N; new vendor rows (AM Best, Rapid Valuator, casualty model, SEMI, Industrial Info Resources, SNL history) and application pages.

22.4 Version 5 decisions

Two decisions by the executive sponsor, applied across the document on 28 September 2026. Neither is re-argued in the text; each is recorded with its reasons and, where one exists, the trigger that would re-open it.

DecisionWhat changed in the documentWhy
No PSOLD. The company will not license Verisk ISO PSOLD, and not ISO Rapid Valuator either.The severity subsection is retitled what we do instead of licensing PSOLD and its when-to-buy table becomes a what-we-use-instead table; both vendor rows read NOT BUYING with the reasons and the revisit trigger; the Phase 3 vendor list, the application-page row, the cost list, the do-not-buy list, the glossary entries, the out-of-scope list and the FAQ all say the same thing. The transparency package, the hyperscale-fire example and the out-of-sample warning stay, because none of them depends on buying the tool.Verisk's own Touchstone 2021 (9.0) database reference withdrew non-catastrophe detailed loss analysis and the AIRPSOLD database, so the delivery route is unclear; the curves are calibrated on ordinary commercial property and out of sample for hyperscale campuses and fabs; the per-risk book is priced from cedent transparency, engineering MFL, our own claims and the map; the licence would be cost without a decision it changes. Revisit trigger: if per-risk XoL on ordinary commercial property becomes a material line and cedents will not provide transparent severity work, the decision is re-opened at a gate.
SEMI World Fab Forecast is an option, decided at Gate G4.The vendor row reads OPTIONAL BUY AT G4 with the price (US$11,100 a year per seat); the Phase 4 row of the roadmap, the map's fab row and refusals list, the governance data-rights table and the data-rights object all keep the prototype's refusal and add the G4 option. It is no longer "evaluate".The prototype declined the seat and sourced its 214 fabs openly with a URL per record; what the open sources do weakly is forward-looking fab construction, capacity and technology detail, which is needed only if the fab side of the mega-project module (Phase 4) asks for it. G4 is where that is known.

22.5 What remains unverified or assumed

Read before relying on any regulatory figure.
  • The company's BMA class and group status are placeholders. Every schedule and factor quoted is from the 2024 and 2025 year-end General Business handbooks and the Class 4/3B and Group rules as amended in 2024; long-term (Class C/D/E) reinsurance credit factors were not independently checked and must be confirmed from that rulebook.
  • The direct URL of the 2025 year-end General Business handbook could not be located; the 2024 edition is cited and the BMA's Q4-2025 update confirms the 2025 edition was published on 18 December 2025.
  • Several vendor pages (S&P 451, Precisely, D&B Direct+) block automated retrieval; their claims rest on search listings and public summaries and should be confirmed with the vendor.
  • All money figures in worked examples, calculators, lever ranges and the hero are illustrative orders of magnitude, not company data. Gate G1 replaces them.
